Tuesday, 3rd February, 1942.
VOLUME XXV.
The Fifth Session of the Fifth Parliament of Northern Ireland appointed to
meet on 3rd February, 1942, in the Sixth
year of the Reign of King George VI, was
opened by the Governor (His Grace the
Duke of Abercorn, K.G., K.P.) in
person.
The House met at Ten Minutes before
Twelve of the Clock, Mr. SPEAKER
(Right Hon. H. G. H. Mullholland) in
the Chair.

H.
G. Young,

His Grace the Governor of Northern
Ireland commands this Honourable
House to attend immediately in the

SESSIONAL ORDERS.
ELECTIONS.
Ordered, That all Members, who are
returned for two or more places in any
part of Northern Ireland do make their
Election for which of the places they will
serve, within one week after it shall
appear that there is no question upon the
Return for that place; and if anything
shall come in question touching the
Return of Election of any Member, he is
to withdraw during the time the matter
is in debate; and that all Members returned upon double Returns do withdraw
till the Returns are determined.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath been elected or returned
a Member of this House or endeavoured
so to be, by bribery, or any other corrupt
practices, this House will proceed with
the utmost severity against all such persons as shall have been wilfully concerned
in such bribery or other corrupt
practices.

Sessional Orders
HOUSE OF COMMONS
WITNESSES.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any persons hath been tampering with
any Witness in respect of his evidence to
be given to this House, or any Committee
thereof, or directly or indirectly hath
endeavoured to deter or hinder any person from appearing or giving evidence,
the same is declared to be a high crime
or misdemeanour; and this House will
proceed with the utmost severity against
such offender.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath given false evidence in
any case before this House or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed
with the utmost severity against such
offender.
ROYAL ULSTER CONSTABULARY.
Ordered: That the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary do take
care that, during the Session of Parliament the passages through the streets
leading to this House be kept free and
open, and that no obstruction be permitted to hinder the passage of Members
to and from this House, and that no
disorder be allowed in the precincts of or
in the passages leading to this House,
during the Sitting of Parliament, and
that there be
annoyance therein,
or thereabouts, and that the Serjeant-at-
Arms attending this House do communicate this Order to the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary aforesaid.

KING'S SPEECH.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to report that
the House has this day attended in the
Senate to hear His Grace's Speech on
behalf of His Majesty to both Houses of
Parliament, of which I have for greater
accuracy obtained a copy. The Speech is
as follows:
OUTLAWRIES BILL,
"for the more effectual preventing Clandestine Outlawries,'
was read
the First time.
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
The war has entered upon its third
year, and the people of Northern
Ireland, in common with their fellow
citizens in Great Britain and the
Empire, face the tasks and ordeals of
the future with resolution, confidence
and courage.
On the recent arrival of American
troops in Northern Ireland my Government extended a cordial welcome to all
ranks. I see in this historic event a
new demonstration of unity of purpose
between the British Empire and the
United States of America, and I am
confident that the result will be a
further strengthening of those ties of
kinship and those common ideals which
mean so much for the future of the
world.
I have learned with deep satisfaction
of
the
close co-operation existing
between the Civil Government and all
branches of His Majesty's Forces.
This cordial and harmonious relationship, invaluable in time of peace, is
indispensable in dealing with the special
problems created by a state of war.
Splendid and self-sacrificing help was
given to the authorities and the civil
population during and after the savage
air attacks on part of our area last
spring. This noble service, rendered so
ardently and in such abundant measure,
won unstinted admiration and praise.
The behaviour of the Civil Defence
Services under most arduous war conditions was exemplary, and the moral
of the people, unbroken by trial and
suffering, illuminated a dark and tragic
period in our history. I am glad to
know that further measures have been
developed for the defence and protection of our citizens.
Whilst thousands of our men and
women have volunteered for service in
His Majesty's Forces, it is my fervent
.

hope that the demand for more recruits
for all branches of the fighting services
will be met in ever increasing numbers,
and that those whose duties are indispensable to war production will join
either the Ulster Home Guard or the
Civil Defence organisations, which are
vitally necessary for the maintenance of
a strong Home Front.
The Ulster Home Guard and Special
Constabulary continue to perfect their
organisation and training under military direction, and I am confident that
all ranks will be ready to meet any
emergency which may
arise.
Our farmers have made a striking
contribution to the demand for increased food production, and approximately five hundred and thirty
thousand acres of old grassland have
been ploughed up since the commencement of hostilities, involving the
payment to farmers of over one million
pounds. I am glad to note the continued success of the scheme for the
imp
nprovement of agricultural holdings
and to learn that during the past year
more than thirteen thousand applications for financial assistance were
approved and over one hundred and six
thousand pounds were paid by way of
grants. A gratifying response has also
been made to the appeal for an increase
in the acreage under flax, and I trust
that the agricultural community,
realising the extent to which the
fighting services are dependent upon
flax for essential parts of their equipment, will redouble their efforts as a
public duty and make a still greater
contribution in the present year.
My Ministers have given unremitting
attention to the problem of the
mechanisation of farming. Since the
outbreak of war over two thousand
eight hundred agricultural tractors and
flax pullers have been made available,
and, through the machinery of the
Government Hire Purchase Scheme,
equipment to the value of two hundred
and fifty thousand pounds has been
distributed to farmers and tillage contractors. Over one million pounds
worth of machinery has been purchased
for use on our farms in Northern Ireland since the war began.
of workers will be available to assist our
farmers in harvesting the crops during
the coming year.

as far as possible, an adequate number

I am gratified by the extent to which
the industrial capacity of Northern
Ireland is being increasingly utilised on
war work, and also by the reduction in
the number of unemployed persons
during the year ended December last
from sixty-nine thousand six hundred
and forty-three to twenty-eight
thousand one hundred and sixty-four.
My Government will continue to investigate fully every means by which
the energy and skill of our people can
be put to still greater use in the
national effort.
All practicable steps will continue to
be taken, in co-operation with the local
authorities, for the health and wellbeing of our people. Arrangements are
being made for the maintenance of
hospital and medical services under
emergency conditions, and I am pleased
to learn that it has been found possible,
through a revision of the derating
grants in rural areas, to give increased
financial assistance to local authorities,
which will enable them to provide
essential services on an improved
standard, particularly in relation to
public health matters.
The question of juvenile delinquency
under war-time conditions is receiving
attention, and I trust that the steps
which it is proposed to take to deal with
this problem will have beneficial results.
The War Savings Campaign, promoted and inspired by 80 many
enthusiastic voluntary workers, continues to receive a large and growing
measure of support. More than thirtyfour million pounds have been invested
and lent to the Imperial Government
since November, 1939.
Among the measures which will be
laid before you will be Bills providing
for the extinction of the outstanding
debt of the Unemployment Fund
amounting to over two million pounds,
and also for a substantial reduction,

My Government continues to give
close attention to the welfare of our
workpeople employed in industry, particularly in undertakings engaged upon
war work. It is gratifying to know
that an increasing number of firms are
establishing canteens for the provision
of hot meals at reasonable charges.

Our schools continue to discharge

I beg to move :

"Your Grace,

in

to offer

our
In moving this Address, I would like
to acknowledge the honour which has
been done to my constituency by my being
permitted to undertake this task. This
is the second time in four years that
Queen's University, which I am proud to
say returns four Unionist Members to
this House, has been so signally recognised.
The Gracious Speech refers to the close
co-operation existing between the civil
Government and all members of His
Majesty's Forces. We have no doubt
that this relationship will continue and
be extended to the gallant troops who
have now reached Northern Ireland from
America. If any further proof of
Ulster's loyalty were required, the allocation by Great Britain of this Province as
the camping ground for these troops
should cause carping criticism to cease.
You may remember when in 1917 the
Americans arrived John Masefield wrote:
"They had said goodbye to home that
they might offer their lives in
in the
cause we stand for." The same reason
exists to-day; we welcome them to our
homes.
Since the last session of Parliament
opened this Province has suffered from
Debate on the Address

Debate on the Address
3 FEBRUARY 1942
indiscriminate attacks from the air,
causing much material damage and loss
of life. The reaction of the civil population to these experiences was wonderful
and inspiring; it had the effect of bringing all classes into closer communion,
actuated by the determination to stand
up to these attacks, as had their brethren
across the Channel.
The experience of those of us, who
were brought into intimate contact with
the heroic rescue workers, and later with
those maimed pieces of humanity, will be
a remembrance of suffering stoically
borne and the birth of a determination
that such things must not happen again.
Since then further measures have been
developed for the defence and protection
of our citizens by a very large increase
in improved shelter accommodation and
the provision of billets and communal
hutments outside the most vulnerable
areas. It is to be hoped that all will
combine to render effective the steps
taken by the Government for the security
of the people.
What of the Civil Defence Services,
the auxiliary fire service, the wardens
and members of A.R.P.; the V.A.D.s
and the staffs of first-aid posts? During
those shattering hours they worked unceasingly, selflessly, without regard to
danger. We cannot express sufficiently
our gratitude to them for past services
and continued preparedness for
future.
The Ulster Home Guard deserves our
admiration, and every means should be
taken to see that its members lack
nothing in clothing, equipment or
comforts. It is the least we can do for
a body of men which voluntarily devotes
its leisure and holidays to perfect itself
for the ordeal which may come.
I trust
that the appeal for further enlistment
will find a ready response, so that all may
feel they form a part, however small, in
the machine which is working to preserve
our National Freedom.
ing co-operation we have been afforded.

which exists between the Government's

of the people, whether infants or those of

The arrangements made for the maintenance of hospital and medical services
under emergency conditions have been
well conceived and I would like to express

profession for the provision made, facilities granted and the valuable and will-
My hon. and learned Friend, the
Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry
of Agriculture, who moved a a similar
Motion two years ago, finished up his
speech by a reference to the measures
being taken for the safety of children.
Perhaps I could not do better than finish
my remarks by a reference to their
education.
Northern Ireland, I make bold to say,
possesses the finest educational system to
be found anywhere. Primary education
is carried out in cheerful and healthy surroundings; ample opportunity is afforded
those who wish to proceed to higher
standards or university qualifications. To
this satisfactory achievement, the service
given to the Ministry of Education by the
hon. and may I say in place of gallant,
genial Lady who represents that Ministry
in this House has been outstanding.
It is a source of gratification to all to
record the response of school and university students to the call to service in the
Air Training Corps; I have been a witness.
of their youthful enthusiasm and desire
for knowledge. It is safe to say that the
training they are receiving will be of the
utmost benefit to the nation in the future.
There is no mention in the Gracious
Speech of any contentious legislation, so
is it too much to hope that all will join,
irrespective of creed, class or political
faith, to ensure through service and
sacrifice the early success of His Majesty's
Arms. I beg to move.
Mr. JOHN BAILEY (in morning
dress): I rise to second the Address in
reply to the Gracious Speech which has
been so ably proposed by the hon. Member
for the University. I would like to
acknowledge at once the honour that has
been done to my constituency by my being
permitted to undertake the task-a constituency which is one of the most loyal
Debate on the Address

Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. John Bailey]
in the Six Counties, if not in the Empire,
and one which I am very proud to represent.
I wish to take an early opportunity of
saying how welcome the American troops
are in Northern Ireland. Not alone for
the amount of extra protection they will
give to the Empire, but for themselves
alone, we welcome them. I know they
will be taken into the homes of the people
and treated very kindly for, after all,
the majority of them are our own kith
and kin, who in years gone by emigrated
to that great country which we all admire
so much. I remember reading a book
when only ten years old about a great
American, entitled "From tan-yard to
White House," the life story of General
Grant. This book gave me inspirations.
which I will never forget.
With regard to the Civil Defence
services I wish to say a word of praise. I
had the privilege of driving a first-aid.
party to Belfast on Wednesday morning
in Easter week last year, and had the
opportunity of seeing that and other
parties working under circumstances
which it would be impossible to describe.
I can only say that no praise is too great
for the work that was done. Indeed
hundreds of acts of heroism were performed that morning.
The next subject which I am going to
refer to is agriculture. Farming is the
greatest among the arts for it is first in
supplying our necessities. I wish now to
allude to another great American,
President George Washington, who once
said that "Farming was the most healthy,
the most useful and the most noble
employment of man." Be that as it may,
I know that our farmers deserve hearty
congratulations for the work they have
done during the past year in very adverse
circumstances. Thousands of acres of
land have been tilled which had been

That is a sentiment with which I profoundly disagree, as I disagree with many
other sentiments not only put forward

The first thing I should like to consider
in regard to the Speech is that it deals.
with the third year of war.
It speaks
about the close association of all sections

does not serve the present day. We are

living in a new age, with a new kind of

I deplore the use of the word "Empire"
in the opening paragraph of the Speech.
It is time we departed from things which
are anachronisms. The old conception
is as dead as the dodo; as peculiar as the
monster washed up from the sea the other
day. The word "Empire" rests upon a
basis of subjugation. It is dead so far as
Great Britain is concerned, and so far as
the democratic countries of the world are
concerned. It is the Commonwealth we
ought to talk about. Northern Ireland
in its relation to the Commonwealth can
play a distinctive part and has a part to
play. The Commonwealth implies just
what it means. We are held together on
the basis of a common weal, on the basis
of equality, and particularly on the basis
of equality of service and equality of
responsibility. I prefer that term to be
used. I trust that before many years
other sections not as yet fully in the
Commonwealth will be entitled to full
Commonwealth status, and that the resultant benefit that will accrue will go ahead
by leaps and bounds in consequence of
the Commonwealth idea, which is the
soundest idea.

be part of a national housing policy.
Such a policy would not only envisage
all these elements, but it would envisage
the question of rent. When we put up a
proposition to the Prime Minister, or any
Cabinet Minister, about houses being built
of a type that will give the people decent
accommodation and enable them to live
good and healthy lives and develop their
manhood and womanhood to the fullest
extent, they ask: "Where is the money
to come from and how are the rents to be
paid?"
Has it ever struck the Government that
it is possible, in the development of a
national housing scheme, to fix rents in
relation to the income? The fairest way
to house the people is to fix rents in proportion to their earning power. Let it
be 5, 10, 12 or '15 per cent. of the
income. These are things missing from
the King's Speech. Instead we have the
weary recital that we have had for years
about some things that are as dead as
the dodo. Some of them will never
in the way the Government
expect. Education, housing, unemployment, widows' pensions, old age.
pensions, the question of disallowing
people of 70-one of the greatest scandals
of the war-all these things have been
consistently neglected by the Government.
I notice that as a sort of sop to the
Government's supporters the King's
Speech says that the Government is looking into the question of grants to local
authorities. In page 3 of the Speech it
says that they are going to give grants
to the local authorities. I would like to
ask what they are going to do about
Belfast, which has suffered more than any
other part of this country. It suffered
very much worse than many of the
boosted centres across the water. I have
been in almost every one of them
and I can speak the truth. Belfast's
income has been diminished. What
do the Government propose to do in
regard to that? They have given no
indication whatever. Representations
have been made to the local authorities
by the Lord Mayor, the City Treasurer,
the Town Solicitor and the Town Clerk.
These representations have been based on
the assumption that as a result of the loss
of rateable property through blitzes and
other elements coincident thereto the
rates in Belfast may go up to the extent
of 3s in the £. Representations have been
made to devise some national scheme to
assist Belfast in the hour of crisis.
I ask the Government to declare what
they are going to do. I ask them not to
be satisfied with trying to palm off vague
suggestions to the body politic that they
are going to have an expert who will tell
us what is to be done in the sweet by
and by-when we are not here. We want
something tangible. We want a declaration from the Government that they
are not satisfied with the existing condition of things from the point of view of
organisation. We want something carried
out through organisation and co-ordinated
effort. Until the Government put
private profits and interests second we will
not get the best results.
What I say
with regard to that applies to other
sections of the community. I am not
applying it to one section. I want all
sections to have the privileges, institutions
and the cherished things for which our
forefathers died. These are the things
which we ought to be proud to defend. I

daily by the Germans, and equipment,
especially in the air, was insufficient. The
Labour Government must accept its responsibility and the Labour Party in
Great Britain must accept their responsibility, because the equipment was short
when the war broke out.

As regards the industrial position, I
feel, as the hon. Member for Willowfield
has raised the matter, I ought to state the

number of unemployed has fallen by
41,479. It is true that during the same

and fly for safety. They were not placed
in a happy position as regards the place
of abode where they could spend a few
nights. Would members of the Government like to spend a night in the union,
as many residents of Belfast had to do?
The working classes in Armagh flung open
their homes to those people, but the privileged classes failed to do their duty in
that respect.
Those who had ample

accommodation and beautiful homes failed

the matter, but I believe, if a similar

system would operate. Can we be

will be different? Can we be assured that

We are told of the magnificent help.
given by the Home Guard and "B"

Guard. We are not desirous of being

my constituency in South Armagh-I

are entitled. I am afraid that many of
our suggestions as to the smaller farming

farmers. We are told that the Ulster
Farmers' Union is the voice of the farming community. That is not so. Until
the small farmers take responsibility
themselves they will never get any benefit
from the Government.
We have also been told of the industrial
capacity of Northern Ireland. I am cona
versant with the industrial situation in
this area, and had experience in the
industrial field in Scotland for ten years.
I wonder how it is that the Northern
Government can blandly suggest they have
done something for industry. If members
of the Government made tour of
Lurgan, Portadown, Armagh, Annvale
and Bessbrook, they would find, despite
all the propaganda about flax production,
that the linen industry is practically in a
state of utter ruin. We have often
appealed to the Government. We have
tried to influence them. Ministers take
trips across to London to see what is going
on there, but we find that they have never
yet made an attempt to get down to
business to see for themselves the state of
industry in this area. We have appealed,
long before and during the war, for the
appointment of a special commissioner to
look into conditions. Despite all the
boasting as far as the war is concerned,
industrial ruin still exists.
The problem of unemployment gets
little show in the King's Speech. It
would have been better if the speech had
been wholly confined to unemployment
and the building up of industry. That
would have been something worth talking about and would have been appreciated. It is said that the numbers of
unemployed have been reduced extensively.
We know how they have been reduced.
The Government and the Assistance Board
have thrown off benefit women who
served 40 or 50 years in industry as not
being normally insurable. These people
should be spared from the horrors of
poverty. The Prime Minister and some
of his colleagues have often told us
Ulster is a paradise. It is a paradise
for the chosen few-for the political
friends of the Government.
You can never solve unemployment or
bring prosperity to Northern Ireland by
shipping and conscripting our workers.
I would like to know what the Government's reconstruction plan is going to be
in so far as the well-being of the worker
is concerned. Thousands and thousands
of workers have been shipped across the
Channel. When the war finishes and
these people return home where are they
going to find any employment? This
shipping of men across the water is a
most peculiar way of bringing prosperity
to the country. Mention is made of the
local authorities in the King's Speech.
As a member of a local authority I find it
very difficult sometimes to understand the
attitude of the county councils in relation
to the blind. An Act of Parliament was
passed here and was amended in 1938.
It gave county councils authority to deal
with the blind. I am sorry to say that
the Act is not carried out in its entirety.
It is known that the maximum amount
given to a blind person in Co. Armagh
is 5s. I would like to ask the Prime
Minister is it fair that those who are
afflicted by blindness should also be
afflicted by poverty?
We are also told that much will be
done in regard to hospitals to bring about
redress. In the city of Belfast, the city
of Armagh, and elsewhere, we have in-

Mr. BROWN: Now that flax has
reached the dizzy eminence of being
mentioned in the King's Speech I make
no apology for returning to the subject,
because throughout the four long and
weary years between now and my entry
into this House I have pleaded both during the war and before the war started,
with voice and pen, and in every way I
could, for the growing of more flax and
the growing of more food. I make no
apology whatever for returning to the
question. As some doubt was cast on my
statement in this House last night that
some of the 1940 flax crop had not yet
been processed, and as after I left this
House last night I was told that if some
of the 1940 flax crop had not yet been
processed the Government cannot be
blamed for the act of some unenterprising farmer I am here back in this House
again to-day to tell you it was neither
fault nor failure on the part of the
farmer. The farmers have never let you
down. They have not let you down now,
and they will not let you down in future.
The farmers are blameless in this matter.
There has been no failure of any kind
whatever on the farming front, none
whatever, and there will be none till
victory is won.

ments have broken down it is not due to

I feel that in our own trade there is

something to think about. Here is a

I am glad that our Government is

will meet us all at the end of the war. I

war. I know that unless we win the war
there will be no after-war problems for

Building and Reconstruction to take

being put into execution at the end of the
war.
I am glad to notice by the Gracious
Speech that our Government is moving in

appointed an expert in this matter to

I am
glad he has been appointed, even though

Great problems remain; great problems

willing to pay an income tax of 10s in

for a number of years after the war we

be re-established, our industries reorganised, and so that our soldiers may

numbers. I hope we will get these things,
and I for one will work to the best of my
ability to bring them about.
But there is one thing that will have
to be done. Our broken-down cities will
have to be rebuilt, and I hope they will
be rebuilt on a plan far exceeding the

good for the men who are fighting for us

I hope they will find a country ready to
receive them, and worthy of evrything
they have done.

to provide work in the distressed areasthis cannot be disputed-I asked in this
House to be allowed to go to Great Britain
to induce the British authorities to declare Northern Ireland a distressed area.
I had one volunteer from the Government

and anxious to go to the responsible

in the building of factories, which are

This Government refused to move one
step with the object of having Ulster
declared a distressed area, so that a share
of the grants then being made could be
obtained. The result is that we have had
to stand on the quay side and watch the
fathers, the sons and the daughters of the
working classes being driven to Great
Britain to fill the factories that part of
our money went to erect. That cannot
be denied. The Government are solely
responsible for the state of affairs that
exists in our midst to-day. The Government are solely responsible for the waste.
of labour that is taking place in Northern
Ireland, because the people cannot find
useful work to perform in the interests of
the nation. We have not the factories;
we have the men, we have the women, and
we could build up many units of industry
suitable to the national cause.
The last thing I want to say is this.
The Prime Minister may think that he
will get quietly to the end of his day and
generation. I have known him for many
years as Minister of Labour, then as
Minister of Finance, and now as Prime
Minister. I do not think I have once
used a harsh word to him since he became
Leader of the Government, because the
personal contact that I had with him as
Minister of Labour gave me the impression that he was like the curate's egggood in parts.
The PRIME MINISTER: Thank you
for the compliment.
Mr. BEATTIE: But I do not want
him to be like the curate's egg while he
is Prime Minister. I want him to be
fresh, like the one egg a week we are
supposed to get. I want him to have
new ideas and new inspirations, and not
to ask the Members of the dull, drab,
backward Opposition to make suggestions
to him in order to prop up the organisation of which he is the head. It would
take all the props that it would be
possible to put below the foundation of
the Ulster Tory Party to keep it erect.
We of the Opposition are here to criticise,
and I hope we will criticise fairly, justly
and helpfully. I want to ask the Prime
Minister when was the opportunity ever
given to any Member of the Opposition
to bring forward their ideas of what
should be put into operation.
The PRIME MINISTER: Do it now.
Now is your time.
Mr. BEATTIE: The Prime Minister
suggests that I should do it now. When
you are making a political speech
presume you give certain time and
attention to thoughts of a more important
kind. One would require long and due

I believe a good effort could be made in

Members of this House.

If I may very shortly just run over
the story of the work of my Ministry,

executive functions in this country whatsoever. They could not order any man
to do any work. In fact, the ridiculous
position arose that my right hon. Friend,

Labour man came over by aeroplane and

I make no apology whatsoever for the
war effort in Northern Ireland. I will

chief industry, are now doing work of
another type and doing it magnificently.
Therefore there is no apology needed for
our effort.

I do want to say this. It will require
co-operation and interworking between all
employers and employees, because I regret
to say that there are many people still in
this country who imagine they can fight
the war by continuing to sit in an armchair listening to the nine o'clock news.
They cannot. We have all got to make
up our minds that whatever our job is,
whether it is the hardest job in the world,
flying or in the Army or Navy, whatever
it is, the only way we can win the war
is going all out, forgetting all those
comforts we enjoyed in the past. Those
comforts have got to be put aside at present. There are a lot of employers and a
lot of trade union representatives who are
out to give all they can in the war effort.
There are some, on the other hand, who
may be looking to the future. I say this,
that if the future interferes with the war
effort then forget the future. I hope with
a real understanding of the effort required
men and women will co-operate to get the
maximum they can get out of the war
effort, and that by so doing we shall play
no small part in the victory that lies
ahead.

cannot understand why when there is a
scheme in existence there should be that
flooding. The reason is because one or
two men on the river are so "cussed" that

their portion to be cleaned out. In war
time we really cannot allow things like
that to stop us, and we are bringing in
an order to say that where the vast
majority of the farmers-say two-thirds.
-on the little streams have agreed to take
on the cleaning of those streams we will
bring in compulsory powers to make the
other farmers do their share. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) We will thereby
be able to get right on with this work at
once.
The third question is very important,
because it deals with labour, which we
always treat with respect. It is the question of agricultural labourers. As you
know, we had a committee sitting upon
this question. It is a matter of great
importance owing to the fact that our
agriculture has increased with such
enormous strides and that we had and
will have a great shortage of labour for
the harvest. We have decided that where
a farm labourer is a recognised farm
labourer he will always remain so, and
when he is unemployed he will have to
put in his card as a farm labourer. He
still remains a farm labourer and can be
I called off when the necessities of the
country demand that he should be
called off.
But there is a difficulty because there
may be a lag between the time the man
is paid off his job and the time he gets
another job. We are going to meet that
by paying him while he is on the dole.
his full wages as an agricultural labourer.
By that means no injustice will be done
to the man. I do not think at a time
like this any of us would desire that a
man should be unjustly treated. Furthermore, either the man himself or the
farmer if he feels an injustice has been
committed has a right of appeal, and
that appeal will be dealt with promptly.
I think this will be of great assistance to
our farming next summer, and it ought
to give our farmers confidence when they
put in their flax and other crops that we
will be in a position to assist them with
the labour to get those crops saved. I
have said I am speaking by the courtesy
of my friend the Member for Shankill,
and I will not stand any longer between
him and the House. Therefore, having
answered the questions, I will sit down,
and once again thank the hon. Member.

The Prime Minister invited constructive criticism, and asked hon. Members
to put forward any ideas they had in their

It arose on a Motion put down by the

What does that committee consist of?
The Prime Minister himself and two
Parliamentary Secretaries. Quite candidly, I disagree entirely with the composition of that committee. It is not the
function of two or three Members of this
House only to deal with such a vital
problem. The Prime Minister is far too
busy a man to have time to devote to the
details of post-war reconstruction; his
work as Prime Minister requires his full
attention. Of the two Parliamentary
Secretaries one is a lawyer, and a very
good lawyer indeed, I am told; but
neither has any experience whatever of
town planning; neither has any experience
of local government-they are not members of local governing bodies.
I am going to put forward a suggestion
which, if adopted, in my opinion will have
far better results than placing the solution
of this enormous and vital problem in the
hands of two men, nobody knowing what
they are doing. Whether the Belfast
Corporation knew anything or not, I do
not know. The Royal Society of Ulster
Architects knew nothing whatever about
what was going on. I am going to
suggest a surer foundation on which to
build up post-war reconstruction than the
efforts of two Members without any knowledge of that particular subject. The
Government should set up a commission
on a broad basis to deal with this problem
and thus remove it entirely from the
realm of party politics, and place it outside the business of this House altogether.
The business of this House is to get on
with war production. The Minister of
Commerce said to-day there could be no
future until the war is won; while the
war is on it is all nonsense talking about
the future.

obtained, so as to cover all the ground
as far as possible. Men who are experts
in their own spheres could bring forth
their ideas. Obviously you have the
Society of Ulster Architects, the
Chambers of Commerce and Chambers of
Trade; people interested in social reform
could deal with social problems. Industry
must, of course, be represented, and there
would be members of county councils and
corporations. These people would form
a broad basis from which to go into all
the problems involved. That would take
the task away from the few people who
are now trying to deal with it, and who,
I say, are not competent to deal with
this enormous problem.
If this central Commission were set
up, and sub-committees were appointed
on the lines I have suggested, the subject
would be taken outside the realms of
party politics. The Commission could
obtain advice from experts from the
other side of the water or from their own
country; the experts could come in and
give evidence. An effort should be made
to get the best brains available to bear
upon this matter, and to induce the
youth of this country to have a say in
what the country should be like when the
war is won. The Government have
asked for constructive criticism. I have
tried to meet that request. I hope that
what I have said will bear fruit, and that
something better will be done than to
leave this matter in the hands of two
Parliamentary Secretaries who are not
qualified to deal with it.
and gallant Friend. The sub-committee
of the Cabinet intends only to make a
preliminary survey of the situation—
that is all-and to get certain advice in
connection with the problem. When they
come to consider what it is best to do in
reference to this matter, the Government
will take into consideration the suggestion which the hon. and gallant Member
has thrown out.
The PRIME MINISTER: With the
permission of the House I should just like
to say a word or two to remove a misunderstanding from the mind of my hon.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: May I thank
the Prime Minister for the information
he has given? Members have not been
told what is going on. If, as I have
already said, the Government would tell
the House what is going on they would
get far less criticism. I am very glad
to hear that it is only a preliminary
survey in which the Parliamentary
Secretaries were engaged. I hope something will be done on the lines I have
mentioned. I thank the Prime Minister
for his explanation, and I hope this
thing will be treated on
a very much
broader basis.
Question put, and agreed to.
Resolved, That an humble Address be
presented to His Grace the Governor of
Northern Ireland, as follows:
Your Grace,
We, His Majesty's most dutiful and
loyal subjects, the Commons of Northern
Ireland, in Parliament assembled, beg
leave to offer our humble thanks to
Your Grace for the Speech which Your
Grace has addressed to both Houses of
Parliament.
Ordered, That the said Address be
presented to His Grace by such Members
of this House as are members of His
Majesty's Privy Council in Northern
Ireland.
Adjournment.
Resolved, "That this House do now
adjourn." (Lord Glentoran.)
Adjourned accordingly at Five
o'clock until Tuesday next,
pursuant to the Resolution
of the House of this day.

FLAX SEED PRICES.
3. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state if prices
have yet been fixed for flax seed for 1942,
and if so, what they are.
Mr. MAGINESS: I have been asked to

for flax seed in 1942 were fixed by an
Order made by the Ministry of Supply

Those
prices are 56s per cwt. for Class I and

Northern Ireland, and Class II all other
varieties.

6. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister

present being imported into Northern

view of the fact that the distance from
Welsh ports to Belfast is (approximately)
350 miles or 700 miles for the double
journey, as compared with (approximately) half the distance from North-West
English ports and South-East Scottish
ports; and whether the loss through slack
and rubbish necessitates additional
journeys thereby adding further to
traders' costs and consumers' burdens;
and what steps the Minister proposes taking to adequately safeguard the interests
of traders and consumers in Northern
Ireland.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Sir
Basil Brooke): I am aware that there
exists a prejudice against Welsh coal for
domestic use in Northern Ireland and that
the proportion of slack is higher than in
the high grade English coal which
importers here are accustomed to handle.
I have been assured by the responsible
Ministers in London that it is imperative
that Northern Ireland in common with
certain English districts, should take its
share of Welsh coal. During my recent
visit to London, this matter was further
discussed, and I am glad to be able to say
that arrangements are now being made
to make available for Northern Ireland
increased quantities of domestic coal from
certain districts in the north of England.
The hon. Member will appreciate that,
while every effort is being, and will be
made to provide suitable coal in adequate

ULSTER LINEN INDUSTRY.
7. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Commerce whether the linen industry of
Northern Ireland has been scheduled as a
war industry as has been done in the case
of the cotton industry in Great Britain,
and whether it is enjoying all privileges
and concessions extended to the cotton
industry.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I understand
that the cotton industry has been
scheduled as an
essential industry in
order to retain sufficient labour in that
industry to meet essential requirements.
There is not at present sufficient essential
work to absorb the labour available in
the linen industry and the question of
scheduling this industry as essential does
not therefore arise.
In regard to the second part of the
question, I am not aware of any special
privileges or concessions having been
granted to the cotton industry. The
treatment of the linen industry, like that
of all other industries, is obviously conditioned by the availability of raw
material and the extent to which output
is essential to the national effort.
Mr. BROWN: Is it a fact that there
would be adequate raw material to keep
our linen mills and factories going if it
were not sent to Scotland to keep the
mills and factories going there?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: No, sir.

8. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister

Oral Answers
Oral Answers
10 FEBRUARY 1942
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): Under the present arrangements the minimum wage of a male
temporary clerk remains at 67s 6d per
week, including war bonus of 10s during
the first three years of his employment
and then, subject to satisfactory service,
proceeds by annual increments of 2s 6d
per week to a maximum of 80s per week,
including the 10s war bonus. I do not
propose at the present time to revise this
scale of remuneration.
em-
As regards the second part of the hon.
Member's question, I think that he will
agree that our Government has always
been anxious to give ex-servicemen the
most favourable opportunities for
ployment in our Government Service, and
I am sure that the British Legion will
support the accuracy of this statement.
In respect of vacancies on the establishment I should explain that the present
practice in our Service is to allocate
certain number of appointments
periodically to the best of the temporary
clerks, who have served in one or other
of the Departments for at least two years
in the
case of candidates for the
established grade of clerk, or at least five
years in the case of candidates for the
established grade of male clerical assistant.
It is intended to continue this practice
so long as there are candidates of the
requisite standard in the temporary
grade. I am satisfied that by this means
we are likely to ensure a better standard
of proficiency in the permanent ranks of
the Service than if we were to confer
established status on
every temporary
clerk who has completed a prescribed
period of service. I understand that in
the British Civil Service the present
arrangements confine the right
establishment to those temporary clerks
who had been in Government employment
prior to 1st April, 1937; the system which
operates in our Service does, on the other
hand, permit of consideration being
given to the merits of men who entered
the Service even after that date-an
arrangement which has obvious advantages
from the point of view of maintaining a
fair standard of efficiency in the permanent ranks.

BANBRIDGE AND DRAINAGE
RATE.
10. Mr. JOHN BAILEY asked the
Minister of Finance whether he has seen
a resolution from the Banbridge Urban
District Council protesting against inclusion in the Bann Catchment Area, which
imposes a liability of approximately
£2,000 on the urban district; whether he
is aware that the low-lying areas of Banbridge are still liable to flooding, and
whether, in view of this fact, he is prepared to take steps to relieve the town
from the said monetary liability until
these urban areas are protected from such
severe flooding.
Mr. BARBOUR: Yes, sir. I have seen
the resolution referred to. I cannot accept
the view that flooding in the Banbridge
urban district has not been alleviated by
the Bann Drainage Works. As the hon.
Member is aware, these works were not
intended to relieve flooding completely in
any area, and it is to be expected that the
greater rapidity with which flood water
leaves Lough Neagh owing to the
drainage works will have its effect in
diminishing the duration of flooding in the
Banbridge neighbourhood. Accordingly I
am not prepared to relieve the Banbridge
urban district from its liability under the
Drainage Act, 1929.

Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): In the absence of the
Prime Minister, I have been asked to
reply.
The answer to the first part of the hon.
Member's question is in the negative. The
restrictions on travel between Great
Britain and Northern Ireland were necessarily imposed by the Imperial Government on grounds of national security and
lack of adequate transport facilities. It is
obvious, therefore, that I have no control
over the issue of the necessary permits in
Great Britain.
The Ministry of Home Affairs acts as
the agent of the Imperial Government in
the administration of the regulations in
Northern Ireland, and so far as exit permits are concerned the system, in my
judgment, has worked in a satisfactory
manner.
Mr. THOMAS BAILIE: Is the right
hon. Gentleman not aware that there is
a surplus of accommodation from England
and Scotland to this country, and does he
not consider that Northern Ireland citizens should be treated as Northern Ireland
citizens, and not as aliens?

WAGES OF LABOURERS IN
ARMAGH COUNTY.
18. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is aware of
the deplorable condition of poverty prevailing amongst labourers employed by the
Armagh County Council at a weekly wage
of 34s 10d, that the men pay not less than
3s 6d per week rent and rates, and 7s 6d
for coal, that families as large as twelve
children, or fourteen, including husband
and wife, have to be maintained on these
inadequate rates of wages; and whether
the Minister will consider the advisability
of exerting pressure upon County Councils
to pay a living wage or, alternatively, introducing legislation to enforce reasonable
wages standards, as has been done in the
case of agricultural workers.
Sir DAWSON BATES: When the hon.
Member gave notice of his intention to ask
this question the rate of wages paid to
labourers employed by the Armagh
County Council was as stated by him.
The question of the revision of the rate
of wages had, however, been considered at
a recent meeting of the Finance Committee
of the Council, when, on the motion of
Mr. P. Agnew, M.P., seconded by Mr.
D. C. Malcolmson, it was decided to postpone taking a decision until further information was obtained. This matter was
again considered at a meeting of the
Finance Committee which was held on
the 3rd instant, when it was decided to
fix the rate of wages paid to surfacemen to
40s 4d per week, and the labourers are
now being paid at that rate.

COMPENSATION FOR CROPS LOST.
27. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he has considered
the question of paying compensation to
farmers in respect of crops lost through
the failure of the Government to provide
sufficient tractors and implements to
handle the requirements of their Tillage
Order; whether the Minister has considered the advisability of the formation
of a tractor corps for Northern Ireland;
whether it is a fact that the Ministry is
charging full prices for implements and
tractors brought into the country under
the Lease Lend Act, and to which
account are the payments credited, and
what provision is being made for an
adequate supply of labour for harvesting.
Mr. MAGINESS: I have been asked
to reply. I cannot agree to entertain
any proposal that compensation should be
paid to farmers in respect of crops lost
during the last harvest, nor can I admit
that the loss was occasioned by the
failure of the Government to provide
sufficient tractors and implements. Hon.
Members will realise that weather conditions were particularly unfavourable
during the last harvesting season, and
that even had supplies of machinery and
implements been very much greater a
certain proportion of the crop would have
been lost. At least a substantial part of
the loss was due to the fact that farmers
postponed their ploughing till too late in
the season and the crops were consequently late sown. It is perhaps not
generally known that until very recently
the Ministry's efforts to obtain supplies
of agricultural machinery and implements
have been supplementary to those of the
trade. The Ministry has, however, constantly devoted the greatest attention to
the question of ensuring that so far as
possible sufficient supplies of machinery.
and implements would be available and
has consistently taken the risk of ordering supplies in excess of those thought.
necessary by farmers and the trade.

Sir DAWSON BATES: I have seen
the various statements in the Press

Member. The reasons why my Department refused to approve of the appointment of Mr. Allen have been set out in
two letters, dated the 15th day of

Sir DAWSON BATES: A number of
convicted prisoners in Belfast Prison were
recently punished, in accordance with the
regulations for disobedience of orders and
for disorderly conduct in their cells.

WORK IN LINEN MILLS.
Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he can state if it is
not possible to keep the linen mills of
Northern Ireland employed to a greater
extent than about a third of normal production in the midst of a total war,
especially when
when cotton operatives in
Lancashire are working overtime; whether
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE :
The present degree of unemployment in
the linen industry is due to shortage of
raw material. It is misleading to draw
a comparison between activity in the
linen and cotton industries since a proportion of the capacity in the latter industry-which in any case depends on a
different raw material-has been eliminated by the process of concentration.
It would also be erroneous to attribute
the lack of activity in the linen industry
to the shipment of flax from Northern
Ireland, since all raw material produced
in the United Kingdom must be utilised,
not for the purpose of providing employment in
any particular district or
section of industry, but in accordance
with the vital war requirements of the
country.
It is, however, true that the raw
material position has deteriorated and.
this deterioration has adversely affected
the Northern Ireland industry. After
consultation with representatives of the
industry, I have put forward to the
appropriate Imperial Ministers proposals
designed to increase activity in the industry, both by the use of alternative
raw materials and by the production of
essential articles not normally produced
in Northern Ireland. Some measure of
assistance along these lines has already
been given, but I am not yet in a position
to say to what further extent these proposals will be accepted.

Referring to housing conditions in
various parts of Belfast that gentleman.
states that in and around Edward Street,
in courts and passages off the Newtownards and Ravenhill Roads, between North
Queen Street and York Street, and in
the neighbourhood of Cromac Street, common defects are damp, mouldering walls,
rickety stairs, broken floors and crumbling

These conditions are prevailing in the

grave reflection on our housing administration and the Government. The learned
investigator proceeds to report and I
take it he is a man of strict impartiality
and integrity and a man who would not
put his pen to any document unless satisfied it was true in substance and in fact.
He says that of a total of 104,157 families
4,440 were living in densities of more
than two persons per room.
This represented 8.5 per cent. of the population, as
compared with 14.4 per cent. in 1926.
There were 2,697 houses, or 2.7 per cent.
occupied by two or more families. The
percentage varied from 0.8 per cent. in
Ormeau ward to 10.9 per cent. in Smithfield. Although the position in 1937 was
considerably better than that in 1926 in
respect of overcrowding the proportion of
houses occupied by more than one family
and the number of families occupying
one- to three-roomed houses, it cannot be
regarded as satisfactory.
These conditions exhibit the unchecked
evils of control and unimaginative development and parsimony in the use of
building land. That is the conclusion to
which that gentleman, Dr. Carnwath, has
been driven. He states: :-
"That the object of the builders was
to construct as many houses as possible

on the same plot of ground without

These conditions were rampant in the

"Considering the
accommodation,
the rents seemed high. In a group of

to be a converted scullery."
Then he calls attention to defects and

houses in Belfast, generally large houses

There is power, I understand, to prevent

wonder has the power been exercised. I
wonder has the Ministry taken steps at
any time to see that power rigidly applied

It is a remarkable fact, bearing on our
housing accommodation, that Belfast has
only one acre of public open spaces for
920 of the population, as against Manchester with one acre for 493, Liverpool
with one acre for 532, Birmingham one
acre for 645, and Glasgow about the same
ratio. I have reason to believe that one
acre for about 200 of the population
would be the right ratio. It is a lamentable fact that no other city in the United
Kingdom is so badly in need of parks
and public spaces as the city of Belfast.
Power is vested in the Corporation, and

Corporation in this respect to control

do say that that power being vested in
the Corporation, and being subject to the

be ruthlessly exercised to check any recurrence of the evil of jerrybuilding for

unenviable notoriety.
Referring to the danger of splitting up

might have been exercised in regard to

speculators as a matter of pure speculation. I do not intend to weary the House
any longer. But I do say that only a
trifling sum would be needed to scour
this city of Belfast from the slime and
shame of the slums-only a small sum,
only a microscopic drop in the ocean of
public expenditure that is going on all

day by day.
But I feel one looks in vain to the
Government to take any step of that kind.
We have waited for twenty years for some
step of that kind to be taken. We have
waited in vain. I daresay we may wait
for another twenty years before any proper
step is taken to remedy the evil. The
Government have not a particle of sympathy with the class affected by this
Resolution, the very poorest class in the
community. I say the Government have
not a particle of sympathy with that
class, who have very few to speak for them,

evil which this problem presents.

151 Housing Conditions in Belfast HOUSE OF COMMONS
Housing Conditions in Belfast 152
[Mr. Byrne]
would suit the working classes. I will ask
the House to listen for a few minutes to a
statement which I am going to make with
regard to the position of housing in
Belfast Corporation.
Since the clearance of the Hamill Street
area the Corporation has not undertaken
any clearance and rehousing schemes,
principally on account of the lack of
financial provsions in the Planning and
Housing Act (N.I.), 1931, and the paucity
of the financial assistance provided by the
Government in the Housing Act (N.I.),
1939. In England and Wales, under the
English Housing Act, 1930, the State contribution is a grant, payable for forty
years, of £2 5s per person displaced for
whom new rehousing accommodation is
rendered available. In certain circumstances this grant is increased to £3 10s
per person. The contribution from the
rate by the local authority is fixed at £3
15s per house per annum for forty years.
The State aid provided by this Act enabled authorities in England and Wales
to embark upon many clearance and
rehousing schemes.
The Government of Northern Ireland
in 1931 introduced a Planning and
Housing Act practically on the same lines.
as the English 1930 Housing Act, save in
one respect-it failed to make any provision for financial assistance and left the
entire cost of any scheme to be borne by
the local authority. The Corporation protested strongly and asked that provision
for financial assistance on the lines of the
English Act should be introduced, and
undertook to formulate schemes provided
reasonable assistance was forthcoming
from the Government. The financial aid
was not forthcoming.
Again in 1938 a further Housing Bill,
to enable local authorities to provide
houses for the purpose of rehousing
persons of the working classes dispossessed
as a result of the clearance or improvement of unhealthy areas, was introduced
by the Government. Under this Bill the
Government proposed to contribute onethird of the cost of each new house up to
a figure of £150. The "cost of the
house" did not include the cost of the
site. Rents of any houses built were to
be subject to the Ministry's approval and
were not to exceed 3s 6d per week free of
rates. I agree they were generous. The
rent was to be very low, but they were
not giving the necessary assistance in
order that houses might be built at a
reasonable price. A careful calculation
of the Corporation's position having
regard to the outgoings in respect of
ground rent, interest and sinking fund,
rates, fire insurance, repairs, vacancies
and management was made, and it was
estimated that a weekly instalment of
12s 10d would be required to meet these
outgoings, thus leaving a deficit after
crediting the permitted rent of 3s 6d free
of rates of not less than 9s 4d per house
per week to be borne by the Corporation.
The Government was putting the responsibility on the Corporation in not giving
sufficient grants in order to encourage
that body to erect houses. As they did
not give the necessary financial assistance
it was impossible for the Corporation to
go on with a building scheme. In view of
the Report of the medical superintendent
officer of health, which stated that at that
time approximately 2,000 houses were
required the ratepayers would have been
faced with an annual sum of approximately £49,000 over a long period of
years.
The Government made slight modifications in the Bill in respect of rent, which
was raised to 4s per week except in certain
cases where with the Minstry's approval
the rent could be raised to a figure not
.exceeding 6s per week. After further
consideration the Corporation decided
that the terms of the Act imposed too
heavy a burden on the ratepayers and
again asked that assistance on the lines
given in England and Wales should be.
applied to Northern Ireland. Up to the
present time the position is unchanged,
and accordingly in view of the heavy
burden likely to be imposed on the ratepayers the promotion of any schemes has
been deferred.

Mr. MIDGLEY: In conformity with
the notice I gave earlier this afternoon
I now beg to raise the question of coal,
owing to the unsatisfactory nature of the
reply given to my question by the
Minister of Commerce. I should like,
for the benefit of the House-and I am
sure it will be to its benefit-to present
a few points from a memorandum which
I prepared some time ago on this question. I should like first of all to point
out that this Welsh coal now being imported into Northern Ireland is only a
steam coal, not a house coal, and contains
upwards of 50 per cent. slack on discharge
for which there is no outlet except for
industrial purposes, which can only
absorb about 25 per cent. Slack cannot
be allowed to accumulate on the quay,
else in time it would occupy all the space
available, and therefore imports of coal
would be restricted or cease altogether
for want of ground on which to discharge.
Domestic consumers are complaining
bitterly of this Welsh coal. They cannot get it to light, give hot water or burn
satisfactorily, not to mention the dirt
left behind in grates. Merchants are
finding extreme difficulty in handling this

coal, shipowners being reluctant to send

complications and slowing down delivery

English collieries state they are in a

ROBINSON CHRIST CHURCH
CHARITY.
1. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Finance whether he can state
what is the reason for the delay in preparing a scheme for the Robinson Christ
Church Charity, Kilmore, Co. Down, as
directed by the Court of Chancery nearly
three years ago.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): The delay in the case referred
to by the hon. and gallant Member is due
partly to its inherent difficulties which
make a satisfactory scheme anything but
easy to formulate; and partly to the
. pressure of other work in connection with
urgent matters arising out of the war
which were engaging the attention of the
Attorney-General then in office.
I understand, however, that a draft
scheme has now been prepared which will
shortly be placed before the interested
parties with a view to having the whole
matter brought again before the court at
an early date.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Arising out
of that reply as to what the delay is due
to, is it not a fact that no steps were taken
during the three years to deal with this
matter?

employed in the Northern Ireland linen
industry is capable of dealing with both.
retted and unretted fibres. This, of

7. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of

understand that there may be small lots
of dam-retted flax from the 1940 crop

other purposes.

textile contracts.

"B" SPECIAL CONSTABULARY.
10. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister

been drawn to the grave discontent which
prevails amongst the "B" Special Constabulary, who are performing full-time
duty of national importance, because of
the persistent policy of ignoring their
applications for wages adjustments and
the provision of adequate clothing, which
would place them in a comparable position
in every respect with the R.U.C., with
whom they perform identical service; and
whether he will take steps to provide this
force with machinery for the submission
of applications and the ventilation of
grievances similar to that operating for
the R.U.C.
Sir DAWSON BATES: No representations have been made by the "B"
Special Constabulary who are performing
full-time duty. These men have received
war bonus and war duty allowance in
addition to their ordinary pay. They
receive special issues of uniform when
mobilised.
I do not think it is necessary or desirable to set up representative bodies for
this force.

CLASSIFICATIONS OF PEOPLE
UNEMPLOYED.
12. Mr. THOMPSON asked the
Minister of Labour whether he can give
the House details as to the classifications
of the men and women at present unemployed; and whether he can assure the
House that no men are being brought
into Northern Ireland to fill jobs that
could be filled by men at present unemployed in Northern Ireland.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): As regards the first part of the
hon. Member's question, I must inform
him that it has been agreed with Great
Britain that it would not be in the
national interest to give details of the
classifications of the men and women unemployed.
As regards the second part of the question, the House is aware that my Ministry has been instrumental in bringing
into Northern Ireland, from time to
time, skilled workers whose services were
urgently needed. I can assure the House
that such transfers are not made unless
we are satisfied that we have not men
available locally who would be able to
fill the jobs and that no unskilled
labour whatever has been brought into
this country under the auspices of my
Ministry.

Under the procedure which has been
adopted, groups of shelters, not exceeding four in number, are allocated to contractors in the various districts, and
contractors are not allowed to proceed
to the demolition of further shelters until
at least three of the four demolished have
been replaced by new shelters.
The answer to the second part of the
question is in the negative. A working
week of 60 hours is, I understand,
normally observed both on demolition and
construction; though it is possible that
conditions for example, heavy frostmay interfere with construction without
necessarily holding up demolition.
I have impressed upon the City Surveyor
the necessity of ensuring that an adequate
amount of public shelter accommodation
is preserved during the replacing programme.

farmers who have no contract and have
green flax straw in stacks, and who will
have to sell such straw after 16th
January, 1942, will not be entitled to the
extra £2 per acre to be paid to farmers
in respect of unretted flax straw to cover
increased harvesting costs in 1941;
whether the delay in disposing of it is
due to processors having at present more
flax than they can handle, and not to any
fault of the farmers; and whether he proposes to take any steps to remedy this
state of affairs.
Mr. MAGINESS: I have been asked
to reply. The answer to the first part of
the question is in the affirmative. The
hon. Member will appreciate that farmers
who sell after the date mentioned know
that the factory price has been increased
sufficiently to permit of the payment of
£2 per acre more than if the sale had been
effected from July to October last.
The apparent delay in disposing of the
straw is due to the fact that, with such a
large acreage to handle, the factories will
be fully employed during the year, and
obviously some crops must be processed
later in the year.
The Ministry has already taken steps to
ensure that all green flax crops have
either been purchased or that the growers
will receive from the Ministry an advance
payment of £10 per acre. In the latter
event these growers are no worse off than
those who had sold their crops under
contract early in 1941.
The Ministry has always kept in view
the desirability of ensuring the sale of
these crops at the earliest possible opportunity.
Mr. MAGINESS: There will be an
advance payment of £10 an acre.

any steps, or do they propose to take

grow flax will get the appropriate increase?

Increase of Pensions.
Mr. HENDERSON: I have great
pleasure in moving the following Motion:
"That, in the opinion of this House, all
old age pensions, insurance pensions,
widows' pensions and blind persons' pensions, should be increased to 30s a week, and
in the case of orphans, that the allowance
for the first child should be 7s 6d a week,
and for each additional child 5s a week.
I do not think I will have much trouble
in converting the Prime Minister to my
way of thinking, that is, if he has any
Christian ideas about him at all. The
cost of living has gone up high, and yet
the widows and orphans in this country
are in exactly the same position as when
the Act of Parliament was passed a long
time ago.
Not one solitary increase has
been granted to the widows and orphans
of this country. At the present time a
widow is receiving 10s a week, with 58
for the first child and 3s for each additional child. If you send a dog or a cat
to any of the homes you have to pay up
to 15s a week to have them kept in these
homes. If it takes 15s or 16s to keep a
dog in the Dogs' Home, surely to goodness
it is not too much to ask that this House
should give a child 7s 6d. I am not
asking an exorbitant figure.
Is there one Member in this House who
has any children could keep one of them
on 7s 6d a week? If you have a boy of
11 years of age and you go to buy a pair
of boots that would have cost 7s 6d you
will pay 19s or 20s, and if you buy a
suit of clothes it is about 100 per cent.
up too.
I have not been extravagant in
asking 7s 6d for the first child. If you
take a widow with two children, she has
18s to live on, and if she has three
children she has 21s. She has to pay anything from 5s 6d to 10s 6d or 11s a week
for a home in a fairly respectable neighbourhood. Of course,
as far as the
workers are concerned the difficulty is to
get a decent home, because all the neighbourhoods are respectable. But as far as
the conditions of the home are concerned
they are terrible. There is great trouble
with the bad boys of Belfast, the delinquents. What is the cause of these boys
getting into trouble? It is because the
Parliament of this country will not give the
widowed mothers, in a good many cases,
sufficient money to keep them at home.
The breadwinner dies and the mother has
to go out to work for them, with the result
that there is no one to control the three
or four children. I know the Minister of
Labour will get up in this House and say
"We cannot have that, for we are following step by step with Great Britain."
This is one of the times we want you to
get out of step with Great Britain. I am
not satisfied if these gentlemen, who call
themselves Members of Parliament, want
to starve the widows and orphans in Great
Britain. I am not going to stand for that
here. The pensions being paid in Great
Britain are nothing but pure and unadulterated starvation, and it is because of
that I want the increase. The question
will arise, how is it going to be done.
Australia increased the pensions to 30s a
week years ago.
I do not expect much sympathy from
the right hon. Gentleman, because the
Government have always been opposed to
pensions. When old-age pensions were
brought into the British House of
Commons the political friends of the
right hon. Gentleman opposed them.
When it was suggested they should receive
5s a week we were told that the country
would go into bankrupcy. They got the
5s, and Britain became stronger. When
they asked for an increase to 10s we were
told the country would be bankrupt, but
they are still paying the 10s. I want the
Prime Minister to pay attention to this.
I would ask the Prime Minister would he
like to be in the position that my wife
would be in if I were to die to-morrow.
Unfortunately I have never attempted to
save money. I put it into politics, so
that I should be in this House to look
after the interests of the people. I
sacrificed something and the sacrifice I
made means that if I were to die tomorrow my wife would have to live on
10s a week and my little boy of 11 or 12

a week. She would have to depend on
her family to keep her.
I want the widows and orphans to be
living decently and comfortably just as
if the bread-winner was alive. Would

by the Bangor surveyor who refused to
accept responsibility for the use of this
sand. The shelters are being erected by
the Ministry of Public Security, and the
local surveyor is giving his assistance in
his capacity as surveyor for certain
works connected with the erection of the
shelters. The surveyor, quite properly,
seeing this sand at once judged it to be
his duty to write to the Ministry dissociating himself from any responsibility
in connection with it. That was on a
date in January, and it was not, if I
read this report correctly, until after the
protest was made-that was on 13th
February, only a few days ago that an
analysis was made and a report given.
The report of the Ministry's Inspector
Reference was made here to the colour
of the sand and to an organic
test. It has been subjected to that test
in Bangor, and it has been found to fail.
despite this report I have before me. I
venture to suggest also that the test of
the concrete that has been made in actual
construction has been made as the result
of passing it through a number of sieves.
At any rate, as the sand is there deposited
I understand it is the intention to use it in
its raw state and without any treatment
at all. I do not want to deprive the
responsible Minister of the opportunity of
giving a word or two in reply. I should
have liked to deal with the matter at
greater length, but I am unable to do so.
in the time available, and I will content
myself by supporting the Bangor surveyor
in his refusal to use this sand.
I say it is criminal-and I am not using
that term inadvisedly-in the extreme to
use for the purpose of air-raid shelters
sand which has been condemned by the
local surveyor, by some of the Ministry's
technical officers, and by practically every
builder within the town of Bangor. I
want to know where this sand has been
supplied to as well as to Bangor. I think
it is of vital importance that proper
materials which commend themselves to
practical men should be used.
Mr. HENDERSON: I want to associate myself with the hon. Member for
North Down. I have seen this sand,
which is full of loam. It is for air-raid
shelters that are being constructed in
Belfast. It is nothing more or less than
sabotage to use that dirty sand, with
loam, to make concrete. I cannot understand why the Ministry of Public Security
is neglecting its duty. I have asked one.
of the heads of departments to go to the
air-raid shelters in McTier Street to see
the state of affairs that exists. In Germany, people who built shelters like that
would be shot, the workers who built them
would be shot, the contractor would be
shot, and the clerk of works would be

Sand for Air Raid Shelters

Adjournment
[Mr. Henderson]
shot. The like of those shelters could not
exist in any other part of the world. Part
of that sand went into these shelters.
The construction of those shelters is a
disgrace. No wonder they are trying to
pull them down; but pulling them down.
and reconstructing them is not the right
thing to do. People who are guilty of
playing tricks with the construction of

The lives of the people are at stake, the

POLICE FEDERATION FOR
NORTHERN IRELAND.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is prepared
to issue instructions to members of the
R.U.C. and "B" Specials that permission.
has been granted to members of these
bodies to form a Police Federation for
Northern Ireland, so as to keep in step
with the force in Great Britain and carry
out the recommendation of the British
Home Secretary to every policeman and
special to join an organisation.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not prepared to issue instructions as suggested
to members of the constabulary forces in
Northern Ireland, because to do so would
be illegal and misleading.
The existing law in regard to the Police
Federation in Great Britain will be found
in the Police Act, 1919, whilst the statutory authority for the constitution of representative police bodies for the Royal
Ulster Constabulary is laid down in the
Constabulary and Police (Ireland) Act,
1919, as applied by the Constabulary Act
(Northern Ireland), 1922.
Last week I informed the House in
reply to a question by the hon. Member
for Willowfield that I did not think it
was necessary or desirable to set up representative bodies for the Special Constabulary, and I see no reason for departing
from that view.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask the
right hon. Gentleman whether he is going
to insist upon that answer being carried
into effect; whether he is aware that there
is an organisation known as the Police
Federation alive to-day in the body politic
of the R.U.C., and whether he desires
that work to be carried on in secret or in
public, and will he state which is in the
best interests of the force?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have already
stated that under the Police Act there is
a representative body formed which is a
statutory body, and I have no right to
approve of any other body.
THE PRESS OFFICER.
3. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Prime
Minister whether it is a fact that the
best services of the Press officer are not
being made use of by the respective
Ministries; and whether he will issue instructions to each Minister that all Press
information must be given to the respective newspapers through the medium of
the paid officer of the Government.
The PRIME MINISTER: It is the
normal practice for official Departmental
communications to the Press to be made
through the Government Press Office, and
an increasing volume of material continues to be issued by that office daily.
There are, however, occasions on which
the Press make inquiries direct to individual Ministries with a view to obtaining
information on special points of interest,
and I consider that the present arrangements are working quite satisfactorily.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask is
it a fact that the Minister of Commerce
and the Minister of Home Affairs do not
avail of the full services of this officer,
and whether they go direct to the Press.
It is only one section of the Press they
go to; and in view of that fact will the
Prime Minister inform these two right
hon. Gentlemen that they must issue their
reports through the medium of the Press
officer to whom we pay a salary for the
betterment of our whole new service. ?

I
The PRIME MINISTER: Yes, sir,
have considered the suggestion made by
the hon. Member that the flag of the
United States of America should be flown
on this building. The arrangements for
the flying of flags on State Buildings in
Northern Ireland are subject to approval
by the Crown. I have been in touch with
the authorities and am authorised to state
that they sympathise fully with the desire
to show all honour to the American forces,
but it has been pointed out that, in the
case of this building, which is the seat of
the civil Government in Northern Ireland,
the flying of flags has a special significance, namely, to show that either the
Governor is present in person within the
building or that the Senate or the House
of Commons are sitting.
It has, therefore, been decided that
only His Grace's Standard and the Union
Jacks should be flown on this building in
accordance with previous practice.
It will be realised, however, that some
special occasion might arise in the future
when it would be appropriate that the
American flag should be flown in accordance with a special direction from the
Crown.

Position and Outlook of Linen Industry.

That this House views with concern

Ireland and calls upon the Government

war effort.

to expand their efforts.

That is the effort the Ministry of Agriculture is making to correct that state of

The farmer, his chum, will comply, and

before and it will go on worse now.
If
that is the Government way of winning
the war and the way of other governments for winning the war across the

the linen trade at the present moment

They had forgotten all about it. Vested

women and child labour, and yet the
Government tell us they have done their
duty towards this industry.
I do not know what the Government's

Naturally, the Government will tell us
