ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Housing (Temporary Accommodation)
Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): This is a short Bill
necessitated by the exigencies of the war.
Following upon the air attacks in Northern Ireland, a number of local authori-
Housing Bill-
Second Reading
25 FEBRUARY 1942
ties were approached by persons whose
houses were destroyed for permission to
erect temporary buildings for human
habitation, in many cases on the sites of
the former houses. My Ministry was
consulted in regard to the matter, and it
was agreed that in view of the extreme
emergency existing local authorities would
be justified in permitting temporary
buildings to be erected, on condition that
these should be removable by the local
authority as and when circumstances
justified such a course.
As the law stands at present, however,
Section 43 (1) of the Planning and
Housing Act (N.I.), 1931, has imposed
on local authorities the duty of making
and enforcing building by-laws, and as
these by-laws do not provide for the
erection of temporary buildings of the
character indicated it is necessary to
legalise any action already taken or to be
taken in the future to enable approval
to the erection of these buildings to be
given. The Bill, therefore, empowers a
local authority, subject to such directions
as may from time to time be given by
the Ministry of Home Affairs, to consent
to the erection and use for human habitation of buildings, the method of construction of which does not comply with the
building by-laws in force in their area.
In giving their consent, however, a local
authority may, if they think fit, attach
conditions with regard to the situation,
sanitary arrangements and protection.
against fire of any building. The local
authority may also fix, and from time to
time extend, the period during which a
building shall be allowed to stand.
The Bill also provides penalities for
the breaking of any condition attached
to the consent and for failure to remove
any building within the time allowed.
There is also a retrospective clause in the
Bill whereby buildings that have been
erected in contravention of building bylaws since the 1st April, 1941, and before
the passing of this Bill are covered, and
also a provision enabling a local authority
to attach to such buildings the same conditions as if the buildings had been
erected after the passing of this Bill.

The drawing up of a code of by-laws

Mr. BEATTIE: I do not know who is
acting as spokesman for the Ministry of
Public Security, but one thing I want to
do is to ask what the Government are
doing in regard to the air-raid shelters
in the various divisions of the city of
Belfast. I understand there has been
what you would call a terrible amount of
malpractice operating within the ambit
of the Ministry of Public Security. We
have passed through a terrible time, and
little did we think what we were depending upon to protect us. To-day it is an
eye-opener to everyone, both inside and
outside this House, and the public want
to know what the Government is going
to do with the people who were responsible for endangering the lives of the
whole community at that particular time
by setting it down that the work they
did was carried out in accordance with
the specifications of the Ministry of
Public Security.
Little did I think on the terrible nights
the people had to pass through the danger
they were running, not from the fellow
above, but from the shelters they were
depending upon to protect them. In my
own division I was surprised to see the
number that had been blown to
smithereens. I saw one which an Austin
Seven knocked down. I inspected several
others which have since been taken down,
and I say here and now that the persons
responsible for their erection should be
brought before a court of justice and
made pay in accordance with the crime
they have committed. The people have
found out about these things, and no
matter what I or the A.R.P. authorities
may say they will be chary of taking the
protection recommended.
I can see a new orientation in the protective measures being adopted at the
moment, and I certainly approve of them.
They are something with which to be
satisfied, and I say this having watched
them being erected. In regard to the
ones which have gone and those that are
now being removed something should be
done in reference to the builders. I was
informed on reliable authority this morning that there are certain persons in this
city trying to cloak some of the people.
responsible. I was greatly surprised when
given the names of the people concerned.
I held up my hands in holy horror when
I thought of the standing of those who
would try to protect the criminals who
endangered the lives of the public. I am
asking the Ministry of Public Security
not to take this as a wild statement from
me, or what is rumoured throughout the
city; I am asking them to take this matter
up and see that no influence of any kind
will allow any individual to escape the
penalty which, if found guilty, he is
entitled to receive.
I remember one case where a man ran
about with a revolver looking for the
builder of a shelter. The right hon.
Gentleman knows that happened in my
own division. I said it was wrong, a
mistaken idea, but the man said he knew,
because he had lost his wife and three
of a family, and he added, "If I get him
he will be no more." That was early on
and I did not believe it, but by heaven I
believe it now after having seen what
happened. I ask the Ministry of Public
Security to give the matter the serious
attention which, I believe, the public are
demanding it should receive. I ask them
to see that no one will try to protect the
culprits, but that they will bring them
before the bar of justice.

is not correct to state that there has been
a terrible amount of malpractice, and it
is not correct to state that there are large
'numbers of shelters which have been
badly built. I think the problem should
be put in its proper perspective. Most of
the shelters erected are perfectly good and
sound, and have been so proved by examination. There are a few which, on examination, were found not to be up to the
mark. In such cases the Civil Defence

I
There has been and there will be a
number of public shelters, especially in
the centre of the town, taken down.
should not like the impression to go out
that these were bad shelters; they were
not. They were built in 1940 and were
quite good at that time, but knowledge
has increased during the period since then
-knowledge gained not only by the experience in Belfast, but from air raids in
Great Britain. It must be remembered
that the power of the bomb had become
much greater than we had any reason to
anticipate in 1940. At that time we were
looking forward, if I may use the expression, to daylight raids of nothing like the
intensity which took place in the winter
and spring of 1940 and 1941. That being
so the shelters now being built are of a
much stronger and improved type.
Having finished, or almost finished, the
communal shelter programme in Belfast
we thought, and the Civil Defence
Authority also thought, that it was time
these old 1940 shelters, which, let me
again remind hon. Members, were good,
should be replaced by a stronger type
which we could erect from the knowledge
gained in the last year. Great care has
been taken to see that the shelters which
are being taken down will be replaced by
a new and improved type. They are not
all being taken down at once, and then
improved shelters will be erected in their
place; they are being taken down gradually, and no contractor will take down
more than four without replacing them
with the improved models. Therefore, I
think it would be unwarrantable for
Members to exaggerate, either here or
amongst the public, the condition of the
shelters. By far the greater number of
the shelters built are sound and good,
giving as much protection as that particular type can possibly give. They will
not give protection against a direct hit by
a heavy bomb. No shelter we can erect
will do that.
Except in a very few cases-it must be
remembered that a large number were
erected an examination has shown that
the shelters which were erected were properly built. I would say-I am not for
the moment blaming any hon. Memberthat any tendency on the part of anyone
to disturb public confidence in these
shelters might have very serious consequences. I should like hon. Members to
realise that the public shelters being
pulled down in the centre of the town are
not being pulled down because they are
bad; they are being demolished because
we are able, with the knowledge recently
gained, to build better ones, and because
we think that only the best we can erect
are good enough for the people of Belfast.
Another matter was mentioned by the
hon. Member. He suggested that the
persons responsible for building bad
shelters would, in some way, be cloaked
from any punishment by people who
carried great weight or authority. Speaking for myself and for the Ministry of
Public Security, I can say that there is
110 one who has sufficient weight or
authority in Belfast, or in the United
Kingdom, to prevent this Ministry from
doing its duty to the public. No one has
tried to prevent the Ministry from doing
its duty to the public. We have had no
suggestion from any quarter to the effect
put forward by the hon. Member. I may
say that if any suggeston were made to
the Ministry of Public Security to prevent it from doing its duty, or to cloak
men who had failed in their duty in
regarding to the building of these shelters,
the person making such suggestion would
run into serious danger from the legal
course which the Ministry would adopt.
It is an offence to make any such suggestion, and any person who makes it will
be amenable to the common law. The
Ministry of Public Security gives no
countenance to the suggestion made by
the hon. Member that it is amenable to
influence from any quarter.

accept it as correct. When I invited the
Prime Minister he came, and the Parliamentary Secretary who made that statement came with him actually to see them.
They were amazed. I am not going to
read to-day all that the Parliamentary
Secretary said, because it will probably
come in better on another occasion. At
all events there is no use in labouring
the thing twice if it is to come up again,
except from the point of view that it is
a matter of extreme urgency.
These shelters that are being pulled
down were built since the raids. The
particular one I was interested in, on one
side of the Shankill Road, is opposite the
site of a shelter in which 27 people were
killed. The shelters were reinforced, but the
inside of them, between the walls!
The Prime Minister said he would not
defend such work. I know he would not.
The Prime Minister came promptly when
he was invited to come; he had no hesitation in coming. I am not talking so much
about the builder. What about the experts and inspectors? What about the
experts? Why, the experts, or the
so-called experts, are the curse of the
British Empire. You will read of
millions being spent. I know the money
is spent, I know the contractor gets it,
but what does he do for it? Experts!
to see the man who would go up there and
tell the people differently; he would not be
there two minutes. That is not the only
scandal in connection with A.R.P. As
far as I am concerned, I am satisfied to
leave it there for the present.
This is the way some of them look at
the building. I know it is, it must be,
or it could not happen. I did not tell the
Prime Minister what was in my mind
when I 'phoned him up. I had not to do
it, because he immediately complied with
my request; but if he had not done it
there would have been a meeting called
forthwith at a point where I have
addressed 20,000 people. I should like
I have said before I have confidence in
the Financial Secretary of the Ministry
of Finance, because any complaint that
I ever brought to him was immediately
attended to, and was not bolstered up.
Although he made the statement that I
do not accept, I know he was not responsible for that himself, because he could
not be he was not long enough in the
position. I was told he is the only one I
ever said a good word about. I think the
House will hardly agree with that if they
have been listening to me from time to
time. I do not think there are very
many about whom I say a bad word, but,
at all events, if anybody thinks that, it
is up to me to live up to my reputation
as far as it is given to me. I can do that,
too. I have plenty of material at my
disposal-no scarcity.
Now, I want to pass to another subject.
This is the case of an old-age pensioner
named William J. Heron. His wife was
a patient in the infirmary, and she was
evacuated to Dungannon. He did not
know she was evacuted. I am not blaming anyone for evacuating her, though
there might be blame attached to someone
for not communicating with the old man.
At the same time we, who have had experience, all know how difficult it was to
make communications at the time. I
make no point about that. The patient
was in the infirmary, and the danger was
there. The authorities had to do something; they evacuated her, and they evacuated others. The woman died in the
place to which she was evacuated in
Dungannon. No blame attaches to anyone for her death. The pair had no
family.
This old-age pensioner brought his wife's
remains back to Belfast. He had insurance of £18 12s 2d, and the cost of
bringing back the remains worked out at
a little bit less than that, £18 10s 11d.
That was the total of the account for the
funeral expenses; it covered everything.
The account would have been four guineas
less if the woman had died in Belfast.
The whole thing hinges round that four
guineas, that is, the undertaker's fee for
bringing the remains from Dungannon to

Belfast. He thought he might have got
that four guineas. The Guardians said
they could not pay it; the Ministry said
they could not pay it. I thought he

listening to me will think he might have
got it. The authorities took the old
woman from Belfast to Dungannon.
She died there. The cost of bringing
back the remains to Belfast was four
guineas. I think every reasonable person
will think he should have got that
amount. He would not look for it at all,
but for the fact that he needs it. It is
not greed at all; it is want.
We know that money is being thrown

It was the second case I had brought

were able to satisfy him, and I thanked

concerned. In this case he was not able to

1. Mr. AGNEW asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether she will compel
education committees to adopt the scheme
for providing meals and milk for
children attending schools in Northern
Ireland; whether any education committee has the right to refuse to operate
the scheme, and whether in the case of
The
PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mrs. Parker): The
Ministry has already written to all
education authorities advocating
setting up of schemes for the provision
of meals and milk to children in
attendance at elementary schools and is
at present awaiting replies. The Ministry's proposals
proposals have aroused great
interest and are being examined very
carefully by the authorities concerned.
It will be appreciated that co-operation
is the essence of the 1923 Act and that
the Ministry and the education authorities have worked and are working
together harmoniously in the interests of
the school children and their education.
I am very reluctant to believe that the
question of compulsion could arise in
connection with meals, and therefore I
have not found it necessary to look into
the legal aspects of the case. In view of
the generous grants that are being made
available I do not anticipate that the
Ministry will be obliged to consider any
such drastic action as suggested in the
hon. Member's question.

NUMBER OF CIVIL SERVANTS.
5. Mr. HENDERSON asked the Prime.
Minister whether he can state the
number of civil servants, permanent and
temporary, employed by Northern Ireland in 1941, and the number employed
in 1942.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): I have been asked by my right
hon. Friend to reply.
At the first of April, 1941, the
beginning of the current financial year,
there were 2,299 permanent officers in
the Civil Service of Northern Ireland.
The number at the 28th February, 1942,
was 2,319.
The number of temporary employees at
the same dates were 3,174 and 3,963
respectively. These figures include prison
officers and industrial staff.

Ireland and their children.

premature to say whether such a course
as is suggested will be followed.

Sir DAWSON BATES: I understand
that the facts are as stated by the hon.
Member except that neither the order
nor the minute was posted in the barrack.
Complaints were received at the

Lighting Restrictions Order, a matter of

deprecate the manner in which the matter
has been dealt with and steps have been

PRICES OF COAL.
8. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Commerce whether there is a fixed price
for the various grades of coal, and, if so,
what is the price per ton of No. 1 and
No. 2 grades respectively of Welsh coal,
C.I.F., Belfast; also the price charged to
the consumer.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Sir
Basil Brooke): There is a fixed price for
each grade of coal sold in Belfast.
Welsh coal for domestic purposes is
classified in Grade No. 2, the price of
which has been approved by my Ministry,
after investigation, at 70s 6d per ton net.
The f.o.b. price of Welsh coal at Bristol
Channel ports approximates 34s 6d per
ton, and the sea freight charge has been
adjusted by means of a subsidy from
public funds to a level of 8s per ton. The
insurance charges, including war risks,
amount to 8d per ton, which gives a c.i.f.
price of 43s 2d per ton at Belfast. In
fixing the net selling price of this coal,
regard has been had to the large proportion of slack included in each cargo and
to the fact that the importer has to meet
the cost of discharge, handling and
bagging, loading and transport, and his
general overhead expenses.

From the day I entered this House
until the present I have never known the
Government to be generous to the widows,
the orphans, or the aged. They are not
generous to-day. The one period of my
life I always remember was in 1927 when

Government robbed the old-age pensioners of £366,000. They did not always

either for workers or employers so long
as work is continued.
I must add, however, that in the present case, if there is substance in the hon.
Member's fears that a general stoppage of
work is to be apprehended, it would seem
that there are some who would not scruple
to use strike action as a means of coercing
the Government. This is a serious
matter at any time, but particularly now
when the nation is engaged in a life and
death struggle, and I should make it
plain that the Government will not yield
to pressure of this kind.

Mr. MIDGLEY: I am very sorry that

Mr. GORDON: I have made way for

427 Threatened Strike of Workers HOUSE OF COMMONS
Threatened Strike of Workers 428
[Mr. Gordon]
I have left him as much time as I took
myself.
Mr. MIDGLEY: The difficulty is there
is another hon. Gentleman who wants to
come after me on a particular question.
I do not expect to be able to say anything very helpful or constructive in the
time at my disposal. I do not know as
much about this as the Minister of
Labour, but I wish to make some general
observations which I hope will be helpful.
I say this for what it is worth to everybody concerned in Belfast. I am not at
any time going to take part in anything
in a partisan spirit while the country is
at war and the destiny of our heritage
is in danger. I am not going to be inveigled into any situation involving
partisanship so far as the war is concerned. I will not be jockeyed into that
position.
I am going to tell the Prime Minister
and the Minister of Labour it is time
some effort was made in this community
towards allaying feelings of suspicion that
prevail at the present time. There must
be some misguided people in our community, not only on the employers side,
but sometimes on the workers side as well.
The advice they get is not always good.
They cannot claim a monopoly of wisdom,
but there is this about the workers which
has been said to me. I have been on
several occasions at two of the leading
firms in regard to the Savings Campaign,
and it has been put up to me that there
is a feeling abroad that the law, as
operated by the Law Officers, is operated
against the workers and that there is no
disposition at any time to make the
employers amenable to the law. Whether
that is so or not you know better than I
do, but at any rate it is a suspicion that
is abroad and is being quoted very
extensively.
I should like to appeal to the Prime
Minister, to the Minister of Labour, and
to the Minister of Commerce-the three
in one and one in three; that is not intended as blasphemy, though I should not
have liked to say it to the deputation
yesterday-to take steps to get some kind
of conference called which will be
thoroughly representative, at which the
full position can be explored, and in
which the principles of law and order that
govern industry and the maintenance of
production can be laid down clearly and
in such a way that people will know how
they will have to walk in the future. I
believe that will be all for the general
good.
The reason I repeat that appeal now is
this and I hate to say it-I know, and
other people on the Government Front
Bench know, that the situation here is not
as happy as it ought to be. Our production is not what it ought to be. Moral is
not what it ought to be. Esprit de corps
is not at the present time what it ought
to be. These are things of paramount
importance. When I think of the fact
that all we have and are is in the balance
at the present time, that we have lost vast
sections of our influence at the present
time, and may be threatened with the
loss of more, and that our rights and
privileges may be destroyed for centuries,
I feel that no situation should be allowed
to develop which would hinder the war
effort.
I should like the Prime Minister, down
to his humblest colleagues, to join
unitedly in making an appeal which will
reassure the workers that they will get
justice and fair treatment, and that the
employers will be treated on a basis of
equality so far as the law is concerned,
and, above all, to try to inculcate into
the minds and souls and consciences of
our people at the present time a supreme
determination to put forward a united
effort so that in this dark hour, the
darkest hour in all humanity's history,
we may emerge with some vestige of our
liberty and freedom still unimpaired.

there is no foundation for that rumour.

endeavour, as best I can, to give every

and I do not intend for one moment to

In the case to which the hon. Member

my duty, if the law was to be enforced.
I have not anything to say as to the rights
or wrongs of trade disputes, but everyone
will realise that there is no kind of dispute
so capable of giving rise to honest and
determined differences of opinion. It is
for that reason that the Order provided
that there should be no strike until the
machinery of negotiation could be brought
into operation. For that reason it was
provided that in the case of a trade
dispute there should be a period of 21
days after the reporting of the dispute in
which the employees could not strike, or
in which, in the case of employers, there
could not be a lock-out.
In this particular case the offence had
nothing to do with the merits of the
dispute, but with the fact that before
the 21 days had run out-well before it
-those concerned had taken the matter
into their own hands and gone on strike.
My recollection of the

POSITION OF VOLUNTARY
AMBULANCE OFFICERS.
2. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Public Security whether he can state if
workmen who qualified for and obtained
the St. John Ambulance Certificate and
are attached to the division, in their firm,
of voluntary ambulance or casualty
officers, are fully insured in the case of
death or injury by enemy action while
in the execution of their duty; and
whether such men, after their ambulance
training and service, are liable to be
conscripted or compelled to perform fire
watching.
Major SINCLAIR: Members enrolled
in the Civil Defence detachments in their
places of employment, including ambulance and other casualty services,
whether qualified under the Order of St.
John or otherwise, are covered under the
Personal Injuries (Civilians) Scheme
made by the Ministry of Pensions in the
same way as other civil defence volunteers.
This extends to injuries arising out of
and in the performance of their civil
defence duties in addition to those referred to by the hon. Member.
All male persons working at premises
to which the Fire Prevention (Business
Premises) (Northern Ireland) (No. 2)
Order, 1941, applies are liable for the
performance of fire-prevention duties for
periods not exceeding 48 hours every four
weeks at the premises at which they
work, unless they are exempted under
that Order. Exemption of civil defence
volunteers as such, whether they are
members of the firm's or of the local
authority's organisation, is confined to
those of whom it can be certified that
prior to 1st October, 1941, they had
undertaken and were performing civil
defence duties for periods amounting in
the aggregate to not less than 48 hours
in each month and who continue to perform civil defence duties for such periods.

and to make it clear, if an employee goes

treated in the matter of fire-watching the

I remember the genesis of these
supplementary pensions, and it might be
as well to refresh the memories of hon.
Members as to how they came about.
Just prior to the beginning of the present
war a Motion was moved in the British
House of Commons for the doubling of
old-age pensions, making them £1 per
week. Certain esteemed Members who
are now killing Hitler with their mouths
and who were then appeasing him said
we could not afford to do this; that it
would cost so much per year. I forget
what the cost was, but it was infinitesimal
compared with the vast sums we have had
to spend on the war since 3rd September,
1939. But that campaign resulted in
bringing about the supplementary pension
scheme. Public opinion forced that backward weary Government to do something,
and so they introduced supplementary
pensions.
original pension should be doubled, within
the limits of the supplementary scheme.
I have not seen this carried into effect.
Since the Government was reconstituted
under Mr. Churchill the changes to which
the Minister has referred came about and
it is those changes that have made it
imperative for him to ask for this supplementary sum. I remember Mr. Ernest
Bevin making the statement that there
could be an income of £6 a week going
into a household, and yet the pensioners
would be entitled to a supplementary
pension of a substantial nature. I have
had some hundreds of these supplementary pension cases pass through my hands
and I have not come across such a case.
I, therefore, feel that the whole question
should be approached from the broadest
and most human point of view, because
when the changes were announced under
the Churchill administration it was
clearly the spirit and intention of the
House to implement as far as it was possible the demand that the amount of the
I know the Minister and his esteemed

case after case of households where a very

a great many cases the means that have

I think an explanatory statement ought
to be issued at the earliest possible date
by the Ministry giving the basis of award

only a general knowledge of what amount
a man is entitled to receive. There is a
general assumption on the part of the

of a pension can be considered. But
between that figure and lower meanswhether it is in Savings Banks or in the
form of a disability or wounds pensionthere are various grades of cases in respect

for a supplementary pension will know

In ninety cases out of a hundred people
make an application and it is turned

Appeal Tribunal. After they do that, or
even if they do not appeal, they go to
their local M.P. If he happens to be a

inundated with applications for other
Divisions which should not come to us at
all. I therefore ask the Minister to keep
all these things in mind and follow the

tion of supplementary pensions paid to
old-age pensioners in charitable homes:
these are also paid on the same conditions
as in Great Britain. The reason these
people do not get supplementary pensions
is that they are not in need; the supplementary pension is based entirely on the
question of need. People in charitable
homes are provided for; they get their
pensions just the same as people in workhouses. They are provided for, and at
the same time they have their old-age
pensions, which they can spend in any
way they like, and can use to procure
extras.
There are some cases in which supplementary pensions may be payable, such
as old-age pensioners in hospitals in which
a certain contribution has to be made
towards their upkeep. In those cases
supplementary pensions, I understand,
are payable. I do think that where an
old-age pensioner is living in a home and
is provided for, there is no hardship
inflicted because he or she is denied a
supplementary pension.
I am rather sorry that the hon. Member
for South Armagh used the word "inquisition" in dealing with this question of
supplementary pensions. Since I became
associated with the Ministry of Labour I
have been round most of the employment
exchanges in Northern Ireland, and I have
also visited the offices of the Assistance
Board. I have gone very carefully into.
the administration of these supplementary
pensions, and I have found on all occasions that the officials of the Ministry
deal most sympathetically with all applications both for old-age pensions and
supplementary pensions. I do think that
the officials dealing with these pensions
are entitled to some gratitude for the care
and earnestness and sympathy with which
they meet every individual case that comes
before them. There is no such thing as
an inquisition held.
So far as anonymous letters are concerned since I became associated with the
Ministry of Labour I have never received
an anonymous letter, but I have received
many letters from old-age pensioners and
others, and in some cases I am glad to
say that little difficulties that kept them
from getting pensions have been removed.
In many cases the question of giving
supplementary pensions could not be
entertained because the statutory conditions did not entitle the applicants to
those pensions. I should like to assure
the hon. Member for South Armagh that
the Ministry do not give out pensions or
supplementary pensions on anonymous
letters. The Ministry's officials go carefully into every application, and the
pensions are given not because of anonymous letters are sent in, but because they
believe the applicants are in need.
When an application is made for a
supplementary pension, which can only
be granted when need is established, I
think the Ministry and the officials would
be failing in their duty if they did not
make the necessary inquiries to see that
the conditions prescribed are complied
with, but there is no inquisition whatever.
Inquiries are made, and the question of
need is paramount, and is the deciding
factor in all cases.

The hon. Member knows there must be

forward. As the hon. Member knows,

but there is more than the solicitor

there must be at least three persons before
the case is heard. When there are three
persons present the decision would probably be two to one; it is not the decision
of the chairman.

The hon. Member could not defend, and
I could not defend, the holding of a
court in every townland where there
happens to be an old-age pensioner. The
Ministry decided that it would not be an
economic proposition to have a court, with
all its attendant expenses set up unless
there are several cases to go before it.
The Ministry selects what it considers
the most convenient centre for the
number of people who have to be heard,
and it so happens that for Darkley people
Portadown is the nearest centre. While
it may
be somewhat inconvenient for the
applicants to travel to Portadown, the
Ministry makes it as easy as possible by
providing the old-age pensioners with

energy on their part and on the part of
some of their friends to go a certain
distance to get the supplementary pension. I think the Ministry should not
be blamed for trying to economise, and
for refusing to set up courts all over the
country in places where there are only
one or two cases to be heard. I think

AIR-RAID PROTECTION.
1. Mr. HENDERSON asked the Prime
Minister whether he is satisfied with the
arrangements made for the protection of
the civil population, and buildings, in the
event of another air raid on Northern
Ireland.
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY
(Major Sinclair): I have been asked to
reply. In view of the fact that this
question is asked in this House I must
assume that the hon. Member refers to
those measures for the protection of people
and property which are the function of
the Ministry of Public Security. The
answer is, accordingly, in the negative, as
that Ministry will never be satisfied, but
will continue to alter and improve its
arrangements in the light of changing
conditions in the war situation and of the
methods of attack adopted by the enemy.
Mr. HENDERSON: Arising out of the
hon. Gentleman's statement is he satisfied
with the air-raid shelters that are being
constructed and are endangering the lives
of nearly all the population of the
working-class districts?
will be satisfied until things have been
put right.
Major SINCLAIR: I have stated that
the Ministry is not satisfied and never
Mr. NIXON: If the Minister is not
satisfied what is he going to do or what
is the Ministry going to do with the people
responsible for what has happened?

Mr. JOHN BAILEY asked
Minister of Commerce whether he can
state if it is a fact that a very large proportion of the workers in the textile trade
will shortly be unemployed owing to
shortage of raw material, and that at the
same time the available, raw material is
being imported to Great Britain; and

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Sir Basil Brooke): As I have already
informed the House, the shortage of raw
material is likely to cause further unemployment in the linen industry, The
available material is being allocated to
meet Government requirements. Some
of these fabrics cannot be manufactured
in Northern Ireland, but, in so far as

Ireland, I am bending my energies
towards this desirable end.

Major SINCLAIR: Hon. Members
will observe that an additional £124,660
is required in connection with this Vote.
This is a very
big increase over the
original Estimate which, I regret to say,
has been necessitated largely by circumstances which arose as a consequence of
the destructive enemy air raids on our
Province in April and May of last year.
Commencing, therefore, with the subhead dealing with new works, alterations,
and purchases, where there is an increase
of £105,075, I would point out that as
a consequence of these raids it became
necessary to take further measures to ensure the safety of Government buildings
I will confine myself to saying that included in these measures was the setting
up of premises where centralised control
operations could be carried out in the
event of future enemy activity over our
territory and the provision of dumps of
emergency building materials outside
Belfast which could be drawn on for repair work in the event of serious damage
being caused to stocks of this material in
vulnerable areas. It will be seen that an
item of £51,000 has been included to
cover the cost of the materials which will
be held in reserve in these depots.
Hon. Members will appreciate that in
certain Government Departments located
in Belfast documents and records are
being dealt with, the destruction of which
would cause considerable confusion and
interfere seriously with the conduct of
official business. A policy of decentralisation was therefore decided on and accordingly the staffs of those Government
Departments dealing with these irreplaceable records were dispersed to
districts where it is hoped they will be
less liable to attack. A sum of £26,550
is required to meet the cost of this work.
In connection with the sum of £4,600
for additional staff accommodation at the
Law Courts, I would point out that there
is serious congestion in that building, and
that the steps necessary to overcome this
by providing for the housing of overflow
staff in huts adjacent to the building have
been taken with due regard to economy
and with an eye to the minimum disturbance of administration.
The remaining items do not call for
much comment on my part, and I will,
therefore, refer to them as briefly as
possible.
The £460 for alterations at Stormont
Castle was the amount required to provide additional accommodation for Government staffs in that building. This was a
very necessary step to relieve congestion
in the main building at Stormont.
Hon. Members will learn with pleasure,
I think, that the Belfast Corporation has
by agreement with the Government undertaken to extend the trolley-bus service
from Stormont gates, Massey Avenue
entrance, to and from Stormont building.

Rev. ROBERT MOORE: I have rather
different kinds of feelings as to whether I
should intervene in this debate at all. The
Motion proposed by the hon. Member for
South Down has certainly been astutely
drawn up. He had on the Order Paper for a
length of time another Motion covering part
of the ground covered by this Motion. He
has withdrawn apparently part of the
previous Motion dealing with compensation
for farmers who had lost part of their harvest.
I am not briefed in any way, nor have I
any intention of putting up a case for the
Ministry of Agriculture except in the very
briefest way, but I think it is well for this
House to face the facts. The fact is that
most, if not all, the loss-and there are
different views as to the amount of the lossthat did take place was due not to the
Ministry of Agriculture but to Providence.
It was due, in other words, to the weather.
It turned out that we had to face one of the
worst and trickiest harvests almost in
memory. I think we ought to recognise that
neither the Ministry of Agriculture nor any
other Ministry can make anticipatory
arrangements for a harvest except on the
law of averages. On that law of averages a
certain amount of labour, including military
labour, was available.
If the weather had been ordinarily decent
the chances are that all the crop would have
been saved, and saved with comparative
ease, but as it turned out the harvest was a
most unenviable one and the whole process of
harvesting was lengthened and prolonged to
a very great extent. Not only was it
lengthened, but in the meantime the
crop was so tangled and twisted that
the machinery that had been provided
was in many instances quite useless. In
regard to flax that was perhaps truest of all.

Any Member bringing forward a Motion
such as this should ask himself: does this
Motion help? If it does, it should be
brought forward; if it does not, it should be
left unspoken. Does it help either the
farmer who is producing the food or the
Ministry which is attempting, and attempting successfully, to direct that production?
Is it calculated to assist in the task in which
everybody should engage at the present
time? The answer is clear. Such a Motion
does not help. Such a Motion can only
have the effect of hindering.
The constant reference by the hon. Member
to heavy losses during last season, the
constant reference to the incompetence of
the Ministry, the constant reference to
machinery which was not brought over, and
to labour which was not provided, will leave
a sense of grievance in the minds of some
farmers, and that condition of mind is
bound to hinder the drive for food which
we are all making to-day. I would be
flattering the hon. Member if I thought
that his efforts would have a great effect,
but even the hon. Member's efforts are
bound to have some effect. They are
bound to stick in some farmers' minds, and,
even by so much, what he has said to-day,
and what he has said on other days, is
hindering food production which is very
necessary.

CLASS III. No. 7.
ROYAL ULSTER CONSTABULARY.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £70,495 be granted to His Majesty
for the service of the year ending 31st
March, 1942, to defray the salaries and
expenses of the Royal Ulster Constabulary including police women."
Sir DAWSON BATES: This Vote
deals, as the Chairman has stated, with
the Royal Ulster Constabulary, and while
the net sum required seems large, the
services being performed by the Force are
so numerous, by reason of war-time conditions, that an increase of less than 8
per cent. over the original Estimate is
not alarming.
The transfer of control of the R.U.C.
from the Ministry of Public Security to
the Ministry of Home Affairs was effected
during the financial year, and I am glad
to record that it was carried out with a
minimum of disturbance of the service.
The first item, sub-head "Pay," involves a sum of £4,000, and this is caused
by the employment of civilian staffs to
cope with additional work and to release
police clerks for ordinary duty. The
amount required under sub-head" Allowances" is over £60,000. This additional
sum is necessary mainly because of the
increases in war bonus payments to the
police following the grant of similar
increases to police forces in Great Britain,
and because of the payment of war duty
allowances to the R.U.C. Payment of
war duty allowances to the police in Great
Britain was made with effect from 1st
July, 1940, but as the conditions under
which it was paid in Great Britain did not
apply in Northern Ireland until last
spring, when the Province suffered severe
enemy attacks, payment of the allowance
was not authorised until the 1st May,
1940.
Mr. BEATTIE: 1941.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Yes, that is
quite right, 1941. Increases in the cycle
maintenance allowance and the boot
allowance payable to the police have
recently been authorised, and the additional sum required under these headings
is included. The extra sum of £2,800
required under sub-head "G1" is to
cover the cost of renting premises to
replace others destroyed by enemy action.
Supplementary Estimates-
Royal Ulster Constabulary
11 MARCH 1942
The additional sum of £2,500 under subhead "K" covers mainly the provision of
additional telephones and the alteration
to existing installations due entirely to
war conditions. Taking it all round the
increase is not unreasonable, having regard
to all the circumstances I have mentioned.
I beg to move.

I would say that during a period of war

Minister of Public Security.

Exchequer and Financial Provisions
[Money].
Considered in Committee under Standing Order No. 65.
[Sir ROBERT LYNN in the Chair.]
Motion made, and Question proposed,
Major SINCLAIR: The resolution which
is
at present before the House is of
considerable importance inasmuch as it
provides the means of extinguishing within
a relatively short space of time the Suspense
Debt of the Unemployment Fund which
under present arrangements made with the
Treasury would not be completely extinguished until the year 1995. It is perhaps
desirable to outline shortly the history of
this Suspense Debt. The 1926 agreement
with the British Government required that
the debts of the Northern Ireland and the
British funds should start from parity and
as there was an excess debt of some
£3,400,000 on the Northern Ireland Fund,
this was placed to Suspense. After certain
adjustments had been carried out, the
amount of the Excess Debt was reduced to
£3,000,000. The 1926 agreement made no
provision for the liquidation of the Suspense
Debt but the interest thereon remained
chargeable against the Northern Ireland
Unemployment Fund.
A subsequent agreement in 1929 provided
that £100,000 per annum should be transferred as a charge against the Northern
Ireland Exchequer, the Northern Ireland
607 Financial Provisions [Money]-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Committee
[Major Sinclair]
Fund being correspondingly released from
liability. The interest on the outstanding
balance from year to year continued to be
payable from the Northern Ireland Fund
but no provision was made for the extinction
either of the Suspense Debt remaining in
the Account or of the balance represented
by the payments of £100,000 per annum
taken over by the Exchequer. This arrangement operated for six years, the Fund
Excess Debt being then £2,400,000 and the
liability assumed by the Exchequer in relief
of the fund a total of £600,000.
When a new agreement in 1935 was
entered into, this provided that the
£2,400,000 should be extinguished at the
rate of £40,000 per annum, this amount
being charged to the Northern Ireland
Fund together with interest on the outstanding balance and this meant, in effect,
that provision was made through the
Reinsurance Agreement.
Repayments to date at this rate have
brought the Excess Debt down to a figure
of £2,120,000 as at 31st instant, but the
£600,000, which was taken over by the
Exchequer, remains in the form of a borrowing in our books by virtue of a disallowance
of the Joint Exchequer Board, who refused
to agree to the payments at the rate of
£100,000 per annum being charged against
Northern Ireland revenues. Accordingly
last year a provision was made whereby
the securities in the Capital Fund to the
requisite extent were deemed to represent
cover for this borrowing. This was a logical
arrangement seeing that the Capital Fund,
prior to 1936 when the last agreement was
igned, had received substantial sums for
accumulation against the Suspense Debt.
It was represented that these windfalls
provided an opportunity for dealing with the
Suspense Debt or a considerable portion of
it in one operation, thereby relieving the
Northern Ireland Exchequer and the British
Exchequer (under the Reinsurance Agreement) of future liabilities for principal and
interest. I am glad to say that the Treasury
have agreed to this in principle, provided
that the Ministry of Finance makes available.
for the same purpose certain moneys in our
Capital Fund which are free for the purpose
and which were formerly earmarked for it.
The Ministry of Finance has now represented to the Treasury that having done
much to increase employment during the
period in question by guaranteeing loans.
to shipowners and having paid out in the
process large sums in implementing the
guarantees which have been given, it is
only fair that, now that very substantial
amounts are being returned to the Northern
Ireland Exchequer by the shipping firms,
whose financial position has been bettered
by the recent change in conditions, the
Ministry of Finance should be allowed to
deal with these windfalls, firstly, in extinguishing the outstanding Suspense Debt
and secondly, in wiping out the uncovered
Exchequer £600,000 borrowing.
We have heard a lot lately about a postwar policy. Well, we can at least say that
we are to-day taking a definite step forward
in that we are wiping out a long outstanding
debt, and therefore clearing the way for the
tackling of post-war problems unhampered
by the dead weight of this Unemployment
Suspense Debt, the extinction of which
would otherwise have been a prior charge
on public funds for many years to come.
Nor will this arrangement in any way
impede the war effort as these moneys, as
and when they are received, will be lent
to the British Government by way of
investment in the various war-time securities.
I beg to move.

TEACHING OF IRISH.
1. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether she can state the
number of pupils receiving instruction in
Irish in the elementary and in the secondary schools, and whether the attitude of
the Ministry is still to treat Irish as a
foreign language.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mrs. Parker): The
number of pupils receiving instruction in
Irish at public elementary schools on
31st December, 1940, was 11,570, and the
subject was taught in 128 public elementary schools.
The Ministry has no definite figures as
to the number of pupils receiving instruction in Irish at preparatory and secondary schools, but the subject is taught
in 29 such schools, and it may be assumed
that the large majority of the 4,259
pupils enrolled therein are receiving instruction in the subject.
It is not the intention of the Ministry.
to change its policy in regard to the
teaching of Irish.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Does the Parliamentary Secretary disapprove of Irish
being treated as a foreign language?
Mr. CAMPBELL: Does the Parliamentary Secretary remember the statement of a Minister not so long ago that
Irish was a foreign language? Does it
follow from her reply that she does not
concur in that?
Mrs. PARKER: In actual fact according to the wording in our regulations
Irish is not referred to as
as a foreign.
language. In our regulations it comes
under the heading of languages other
than English, the same as Latin and
French.
Mrs. PARKER: I think I have given
a definite answer as to the ruling of my
Ministry on the subject.
NEEDS OF THE BLIND IN
ARMAGH.
3. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether his attention
has been drawn to the efforts of Armagh
County Council to help the blind and
whether the amount estimated for 1942-43
is sufficient to provide for the needs of
the blind of this county; and whether the
Minister will take this matter up with
the county council in order that the needs
of the blind may be provided for in
accordance with the 1938 Act.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): Frequent representations have been made to my Department with regard to the administration
of the Blind Persons Acts by the Armagh
County Council. The estimated expenditure under the Acts for the financial
year 1942-43 is £3,000, which is three
times as great as the Estimate for 1940-
41. As the hon. Member is aware, each
case is considered on its merits, and if
he can supply me with particulars of
any case which he considers is being
harshly dealt with, I will take the matter
up with the county council.
A special circular is being addressed to
all county councils asking them to give
sympathetic consideration to the needs of
the blind in their county, particularly in
view of the generous grants recently made
by the Government in relief of rates.
THE DEPUTY A.R.P. OFFICER.
4. Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Public Security whether he can state the
salary and allowance paid to the deputy
A.R.P. officer, Mr. R. W. McKibbin;
whether he can state the name of the
building firm in which this officer is, or
was, interested; whether this firm is building, or did build, air-raid shelters; and
whether this officer used an A.R.P. or
other public car to take his family to
Portrush.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
12 MARCH 1942
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY
(Major Sinclair): I have been asked to
reply. Mr. Robert W. McKibbin,
deputy A.R.P. officer for Belfast, is in
receipt of a salary of £500 per annum.
No allowance is paid to him; he is, however, entitled to refund of expenses necessarily incurred while travelling on public
duty, including the usual mileage rate
for the use of his own car.
Mr. McKibbin was formerly connected
with the building firm of J. McKibbin,
which ceased business in 1937. This firm
has not built any air-raid shelters.
I am informed that on one occasion, on
the 24th December last, when his own
car had broken down, Mr. McKibbin
received permission to use an A.R.P. car
for the purpose of visiting his family,
who were residing at Portrush, providing
his own petrol. This concession was
apparently given on account of the fact
that Mr. McKibbin's own car had broken
down while in use on the public service,
but it was quite irregular, and instructions have been given to prevent any
similar use of A.R.P. cars in future.

Major SINCLAIR: I have been asked
to reply. Senior officers of the civil
defence services in Belfast occasionally
visit, as part of their duty, social functions organised by the volunteers in connection with their units. Generally these
officers have private cars which they may
use for this purpose, but the use of
official cars has been permitted where
necessary to enable officers to attend.
Apart from this the use of official civil
defence transport for purposes of the kind
indicated is not allowed, and if the hon.
Member has knowledge of specific cases
of abuse of this privilege I hope he will
give me particulars in order that they
may be examined.
desirable for the promotion of the team

I propose to have the whole question.

EIRE WORKERS IN NORTHERN
IRELAND.
6. Mr. BAILIE asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state how many
skilled and how many unskilled operatives
from Eire have secured employment in
Northern Ireland since October, 1939;
how many of these are registered with
employment exchanges, and whether he
can state what steps it is proposed to
take to deal with this infiltration as soon
as Northern Ireland workers return to
Northern Ireland upon the cessation of
hostilities.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): I regret to have to inform the
hon. Member that the figures for which
he asks are not available.
As regards the second part of the
question, all persons insurably employed
in Northern Ireland must obtain contribution books or cards from the employment exchange, and my Ministry has a
number of inspectors continually engaged
in enforcing this provision and prosecuting employers where necessary for noncompliance with it.
My Ministry is unable to prevent employers from taking workers from Eire
if they so desire; but I should add that
the whole of this very difficult problem
is at present under serious consideration
by the Government.

Member, I may say that the number of
agricultural workers sent to Great Britain

45. These men were sent on a "loan"

AGRICULTURE (Mr. Maginess): I

The facilities granted in connection

MARKETING OF FRUIT.
11. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether, in September,
1941, Lord Woolton, Minister of Food,
made an Order regarding the marketing
of fruit, in which he placed it in two
classes that below two inches, which was
to be sold to manufacturers, and that
above two inches, which was to be sold
to the market or whatever way the grower
or merchants wished, at the price
specified; and whether this Order applied
to Northern Ireland without interference
or amendment by the Government of
Northern Ireland.
Mr. MAGINESS: I have been asked
to reply. The answer to the first part
of the question is that an Order entitled
the Home-grown Apples (Maximum
Prices) Order, 1941, was made last
September by the Minister of Food prescribing certain conditions, including
maximum prices, for the sale of apples
by growers, wholesalers and retailers.
This Order applies to Northern Ireland.
With regard to the second part of the
question, the Rules made under the
Marketing of Fruit Act (Northern Ireland), 1931, provided inter alia for the
grading of fruit intended for shipment
to Great Britain. Under these Rules
apples of less than 2 inches in diameter
and blemished apples of 21 inches or
over could not be shipped as graded fruit.
These Rules were relaxed during the past
season so as to permit the shipment of
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Mr. Maginess]
unblemished apples of two inches or over
as graded fruit, thus bringing the Rules
as regards size of apples into conformity
with the provisions of the Maximum
Prices Order. With regard to apples
which are unfit to be shipped as graded
fruit the Ministry grants permits in pursurance of Section 4 of the Marketing of
Fruit Act, 1931, to shippers to send such
apples to Great Britain for bottling,
canning or other manufacturing purposes.
Mr. NIXON: Does the Ministry of
Agriculture in any way supersede or
otherwise interfere with the Order made
by Lord Woolton's Department, the
Ministry of Food?
Mr. MAGINESS: No, sir. The
Ministry of Agriculture do not interfere,
but they can, of course, endorse and can
make their own regulations.
Mr. NIXON: But do the Ministry of
Agriculture not make their own regulations in such a way as to make it more
difficult for exporters here than Lord
Woolton would make it if his rules were
left untouched.
Mr. MAGINESS: We are in a different
position. We spent many years in
building up an apple trade in Great
Britain with the result that Northern
Ireland apples immediately prior to the
war were known as good apples, whereas
some 10 or 15 years ago they were known
as the worst apples on the British market.
We do not want to interfere with that
in any way. We believe that unless we
keep these regulations on we would be
destroying our apple trade in Great
Britain which we hope will go on after
the war as it went on previous to the
war.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of that
admission by the Parliamentary Secretary
how is it that one day the Government
plead that all food and foodstuffs are
subject to regulations made by the
Ministry of Food and the next day when
it suits them they come in with their own
regulations to supersede and interfere
with those resolutions?

to erection and use of buildings for

Debate resumed on Amendment (11th

to add the following new sub-section :-
--
"(5) The powers of a local authority
under this section shall not extend to
that part of any rural area within a

of any adjoining urban area, nor to

Question again proposed.
the first place, I desire to make it
perfectly clear that I have the fullest
sympathy with the object of the Bill. I
think that remark should apply to every
Member of the House, but nevertheless
the very nature of the Bill is such that
it demands a certain amount of assurance
that suitable safeguards will be provided
with regard to the public health, particularly in densely populated areas.
What I have in mind, and what the
Amendment is intended to give effect to,
is that densely populated areas will have
the not unreasonable right to be assured
that within a reasonable distance from
their boundary there will not arise conditions that will be a menace to the public
health.
Mr. THOMAS BAILIE: I would
like to add briefly to what I have already
said with regard to this Amendment. In
com-
I am aware of the conditions at the
present moment in the rural areas. I am
thinking of one rural area in particular
when I make that remark in which the
conditions are a disgrace to any
munity. There are conditions which
could not be tolerated and I feel free to
say this, and, in saying this, I am telling
the actual truth, that at the present time
human excreta is being deposited upon
the surface of the gardens of houses in
certain rural areas. So long as an urban
council is informed that conditions of
that kind exist, and are in danger of
continuing to exist, it is not only their
right but their duty to ensure that the
public health will be safeguarded and
maintained.
We are apprehensive that without a
qualification of this kind danger might
arise to the public health. This is a permissive Bill, and the Amendment I have
brought forward is a fair Amendment.
We are asking that our areas-I am
speaking now from the urban standpoint
-will be preserved for a distance of two
miles, but, on the other hand, we are
willing, so far as urban areas are concerned, to put in the same concession
with regard to one half-mile within our
boundary. While we seek our own preservation we acknowledge the rights of
other authorities. Therefore, the Amendment is reciprocal, and I see no reason
why, if it is accepted by the Government,
it should not have the whole-hearted
support of every Member of this Committee.
This does not represent landlord legislation. I submit that this Amendment,
and, in fact, the entire Bill, is designed

Mr. MAGINESS: The net Supplementary Vote required is £10,930. Of the
gross sum of £35,941, the principal increase is due to the employment of
additional staff whose salaries, wages and

The recruitment of this extra staff has
been due to (1) the rationing of animal
Provision is also made for the expenses

AGRICULTURAL SERVICES.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding
£9,040 be granted to His Majesty for the

641 Supplementary Estimates-

12 MARCH 1942
Ministry of Commerce
1942, to defray the expenses of the

Mr. MAGINESS: The net total required under this Vote is £9,040. There
are two principal items. The first is an
amount of £10,000 to provide financial
assistance towards the erection of new
limestone grinding plant in Northern
Ireland on the lines of a scheme in operation in Great Britain. Under the scheme
assistance will be afforded to producers of
ground limestone in those districts where.
there is a shortage of supplies, and where
the want can be supplied by the extension
of existing plant of established producers
or by the setting up of new plant by new
producers. Producers will only be
assisted where it can be shown that the
normal pre-war demand for lime is insufficient to justify an increase of plant, or
where the producer, though willing to
install plant, has not the necessary capital.
A condition of the scheme is that the
producer is bound to dispose of the lime
from the new plant for agricultural purposes only and will not be allowed to
diminish his sales of supplies for these
purposes from his existing plant. The
scheme, it will be seen, is complementary
to the Lime Subsidy Scheme, which is
financed by the Imperial Government.
When it is borne in mind that since the
beginning of hostilities over half a million
acres of old grassland have been brought
under cultivation, the need for such a
scheme will be at once manifest.
The second large item is £15,000 for
advance payments at the rate of £10 per
acre of harvested flax to growers who have
no means of dam-retting their crop, and
are temporarily unable to dispose of it in
the green state to processing factories.
As hon. Members will observe, the
advance will be repaid next financial year
by deduction from the prices untimately
payable by the processing factories for
the crops.
Every effort has been made to increase
the acreage under flax, a vital part of the
Northern Ireland war effort. A guarantee
was given that farmers who grew flax
during 1941 would find a market for the
crop in the form of harvested dried straw
if they had not facilities for having their
crops dam-retted. Those who succeeded in
placing contracts with processing factories
for the purchase of green flax crops received
interim payments of £3 per acre at
brairding time, and £7 an acre when the
crop was harvested. There were, however, approximately 1,500 acres of flax
grown by farmers who have no damretting facilities and who have been
unable to sell the crop in the green state
to one of the processing factories. The
Ministry will have to ask these concerns
to handle this surplus flax also, and
advance payments of £10 per acre will
be made to the growers. This outlay of
£10 per acre will not be recovered until
the green flax is scutched at the factory
and the scutched green fibre is sold to the
Ministry of Supply. The scutching in
many cases will continue until September,
1942, so that the financial outlay will not
be fully recovered until that month at
the earliest.
As will be seen, savings have been
effected to the extent of £28,250, the
principal item being £17,000 in respect of
the purchase of agricultural machinery.
Under the new conditions created by the
spread of the war to the Far East, the
supplies of imported tractors and
machinery for which we had hoped will
not, I am afraid be forthcoming during
the present financial year. I beg to
move.
Question put, and agreed to.

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-

COMMERCE (Sir Wilson Hungerford):
Hon. Members will observe that the
Supplementary Estimate, which asks for
an additional sum of £5,840 for the
current year, comprises two main items.
The first makes provision for the additional staff which has had to be assigned
to this Ministry since the main Estimates.
were before the House almost a year ago.
The second relates to expenditure incurred

schemes. I should like to point out to

The additional staff is engaged almost
entirely on work arising out of war-time
services. One of these services to which
I should draw attention is the Control of
Factory and Storage Accommodation. As
hon. Members will be aware, the use of
accommodation for factory and storage
purposes throughout the United Kingdom.
is now under Government control. It
seemed eminently desirable that so far as
Northern Ireland was concerned the
functions of the Board of Trade in this
respect should be entrusted to the Ministry of Commerce, which was in a specially
favourable position to decide claims which
might involve the displacement of existing concerns in order to procure accommodation essential to the national effort.
I am glad to be able to inform the House
that the Board of Trade concurred in this
view and appointed an officer of this
Ministry as Regional Controller of
Factory and Storage Accommodation in
Northern Ireland.
Hon. Members will appreciate that conditions in this area are not quite similar
to those obtaining in many other parts
of the United Kingdom. Here we still
have a substantial number of workers
who have not been absorbed in the war
effort. We have thought it well to make
clear to the authorities concerned that,
while at all times we are most anxious to
facilitate the various Controls and
Services in securing storage accommodation, our first concern is to secure employment for our unemployed workers,
and so enable them to play their part in
the war
war effort. While, therefore, we
gladly welcome any productive unit to
this area, we are naturally hesitant about
agreeing to any storage project which
might throw even a relatively small
number of workers out of employment.
take steps to make available the necessary labour and accommodation. I
should add that steady progress is being
made in securing essential storage in this
area, and in such development the closest
contact is maintained with representative
trade interests likely to be affected.

Other war-time services for which provision is required include the control and
allocation of building materials, coal

The additional functions which have

Provision in regard to the emergency

Fire Services (Emergency Provisions)
Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Major SINCLAIR: I am speaking
this afternoon on behalf of a most disappointed man. The Minister has been
very anxious to attend here this afternoon
to ask the House to give a Second Reading
to this measure which he believes will add
greatly to the efficiency of the country's
war effort so far as fire-fighting is concerned. Although I am glad to say he
is a great deal better, his medical advisers
feel that he should not, at present,
attempt to pilot a measure of major
importance through this House, and in
these circumstances it falls to me to ask
you to give favourable consideration, to
the Government's proposals.
The Bill is designed to make great
changes in the fire service of the Province
and the Government would not ask for
such wide powers were it not clear that
drastic action is needed to build up the
resources of the country in men, equipment and organisation to meet the most
dangerous form of attack which the enemy
has yet devised-that of the combined
fire and high explosive raid. Although
the Government's proposals have been
placed before and accepted by the Civil
Defence Advisory Commitee composed of
Members of both Houses, I think it is
only fair that before being asked to grant
these very wide powers the House should
have a full explanation of the reasons for
the Bill, and in order to fill in the background of the scheme I think it advisable
to make a short survey of the growth of
fire services in war-time as compared with
the more or less static peace-time position.
In peace-time every county borough and
urban district had a fire brigade, and
fire-fighting serviees of a more limited
scope were also maintained by a dozen or
more rural districts. The lay-out of these
brigades ranged from Belfast with its 80
Fire Services Bill-
Second Reading

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Major Sinclair]
full-time men and adequate modern
equipment to country places with obsolete
hand-operated pumps manned by enthusiasts who left their normal occupations
to tackle any fire which they could reach.
The tendency was to rely for fighting
serious fires upon the brigades which
maintained full-time staffs, and the
clumsy-looking red engines of the Belfast
Fire Brigade probably hold the speed
record for day or night runs from Belfast
to all the adjacent provincial towns.
Apart from the highly efficient fulltime brigades in Belfast and Londonderry
there are throughout the country
members of peace-time fire brigades who
give only part-time service. They are
known as "retained" men, and although
they have not had the concentrated training in fire-fighting that full-time regular
firemen have been given, they nevertheless
form most valuable additions to the
country's fire-fighting strength. Their
knowledge of fire risks in their own

I have given the House an account, I

The reason I am asking for these new
powers is, therefore, no reflection whatever on the past help which the Government has had, help which will, I hope,
continue, particularly during the early
teething troubles of the new fire service.
The sole reason for the change is this.
Fighting a fire in peace-time is a vastly
different matter from standing up to fires
arising from enemy action. In peacetime, fires are fortunately no more than
isolated breaks in the even tenor of a
fireman's life: the problem they present
is purely the technical one of pouring the
right amount of water into the place
where it will do most good, the water
supply is unlimited and the dangers are
those clearly visible in the fire itself. In
war a street, a block of streets, half a
town may be on fire at the same time.
The question may not be of putting out
all fires at the same time, but of deciding
priorities of the utmost urgency and
importance. Bombing may have broken
the mains and cut the water supplies to
trickle. It may
be necessary to
improvise arrangements to bring water
from a great distance, and all this difficult
and dangerous activity, far in excess of
the scale involved in any peace-time fire,
must be carried on while the bombs fall
and the streets are full of perils in
addition to those of the fires themselves.
a
This is not a technical problem for a
small corps of experts, it is a job with
all the
the features and importance of
military operation. Service such as that
required in an incendiary raid can best
be given by a force under unified command, unified control, and a unified
system of training. No local authority,
however proficient and however willing, can
give this centralised direction to the fire
service, and the only remedy is national
control applying equally to the entire
Province. For these reasons the Government proposes, if this measure becomes
law, to co-ordinate all the fire services of
Northern Ireland into a single national
fire service.
The House will appreciate that to make
any violent changes in the existing

organisation or to discard the valuable

In this there is work for women as well

utility. If I thought it would I would

regulations. It is called a Ministry of
Public Security. It has failed to give
the public of Belfast any sense of
security. It is really a misnomer. We
had the grim and gruesome experience
of two raids in April and May last, and
to those in Belfast who had to go through
that ordeal the experience was most deplorable. The fire-fighting services failed
utterly. Houses in Belfast were burned
to the ground which might have been
saved. There was an appalling lack of
water. There was water available in
some districts which the hoses could not
raise high enough to get to the fires that
broke out in the upper parts of the
houses. It was a very melancholy and
disappointing experience, and if we are
to judge by the results of those two

failure by the authorities to grapple with
the situation. I do hope the position
has changed now and that it has improved, but so far as efficiency is concerned I have no sense of security on
that point.

improved and increased.
Mr. BEATTIE: I feel that I am
rather in a difficulty in regard to this
centralised scheme for the fire-fighting
services. As one who has always stood
for national services, I do not see how I
can oppose this Bill. But while the
principle of national service is embodied
in this measure, there are a lot of things

in Belfast. Then there is the Derry Fire
Brigade. Outside those two cities you
have what are called auxiliary fire
brigades, which are made up of people in
the community who are registered as
willing to play their part in dealing with
a fire that may break out in the town or
village.
Mr. NIXON: Plenty of them are in
jobs already.
When this national fire service is recruited, how do you expect to find the
necessary man power to man the service
so as to give the necessary protection to
the Six Counties? In some respects our
man power has been depleted, and I do
not know how you are going to get a paid
personnel, because I expect this national
service will have a paid personnel. If the
job is worth doing, it is worth being paid
for. I should like to support the plea of
the Member for South Down that there
should be equality throughout the service
in regard to pay and conditions. If the
hon. Member continues to pursue that
policy he will land in the right place.
Whether they are working in Belfast or
Newry, the requirements of the firemen
are the same, and therefore, under this

the personnel should be the same. That
has not been so in the past. I feel that
this Bill might provide a way of escape
for a certain type of people in Northern
Ireland-those who wish to pretend that
they are doing work of national importance when they are challenged with the
question: "Why are you not in the
Army?"
Mr. BEATTIE: A large number of

service, and I know it is not because of
their love for it that they are there, but
in order to escape military service. I
hope this Bill is not a cover for those
jokers who are ready to rally to anything
but what is right. We were not very
far apart when the bombs were dropping.
You, I am sure, felt the tremor of the
earth where you were sitting. Assuming
the worst had happened on that occasion,
and we were depending for protection--
we expected to be protected by the
Ministry of Public Security-on the firefighting services, we would have been
depending on a broken stick. No such
thing existed in our area.
I have endeavoured to get appliances
put at the disposal of the fire fighters in
A.R.P. posts who are anxious and willing
to operate them when the necessity arises.
The only response I received was a suggestion that those attached to these posts.
should put their hands into their own
pockets, buy an Austin Seven chassis, and
build up a fire-fighting machine from that
foundation. That is not the way to carry
on business of a very serious kind. I hope
that is not the kind of machinery the
personnel which is to be recruited under
this Bill will be provided with. I hope
they will not be handicapped by lack of

On that Monday morning at 3-30 I was
on the highway in my own division along
with other Members of this House, and I
witnessed the glorious display given by
the Dublin Fire Brigade. I stood for
over an hour watching the work carried
out by the men who came a long way to
help to extinguish the fires in the city
of Belfast. They did not ask for thanks;
all they asked was to be allowed to come
and help us in our distress. There is not
an hon. Member in this House or anybody outside it who does not appreciate
the valuable work done by the brigades
which made a long journey in the middle
of the night. This House is entitled to
return its most grateful thanks to these
men. If the time ever arrives when they
require help in the same direction we
will do our best to aid them. Belfast

A Personal Explanation.
Mr. NIXON: With your permission and
the permission of the House I want to refer
to a matter on which I was speaking yesterday and which was inadvertently misrepresented in the report of "The Belfast
News-Letter" of this date, and as the
misrepresentation causes, in my opinion, a
libel on a respectable citizen, I want to
Mr. Nixon raised the question, pro
testing against the price charged to an
old age pensioner for the funeral of his
wife, an evacuee, whose body had been
brought from Dungannon for burial in
Belfast. A sum of £18 12s. 8d. had
been drawn on a policy of insurance,
and the undertaker's charge was
£18 10s. 11d., plus £4 4s. for bringing
the body from Dungannon.
That is a complete misrepresentation of
what I said. In the first instance I had no
authority from the old-age pensioner to
make any protest or attack on the firm of
undertakers, and none was made. The
second mistake in the report, and which is
even more serious, is that the charge was
£18 10s. 11d., plus £4 4s. Not at all. The
£4 4s. is included in the £18 10s. 11d.
Briefly, the facts as I put them are these.
The protest was against the action of the
Ministry in refusing to pay that £4 4s. to
the old-age pensioner. This old-age pensioner and his wife lived in Seventh Street.
She was taken ill and taken to the infirmary,
and while there she was evacuated to
Dungannon. The pensioner had no knowledge that she was evacuated. It was not
conveyed to him in any manner whatsoever.
Only when he went to see her he was told
she was in Dungannon. She died in Dungannon and he had to bring back the
remains, and he thought, and I thought,
that the Ministry should have done so. My
protest, and it was the only protest the
pensioner authorised me to make, was
against the action of the Ministry in not
paying that four guineas. That is all and
I am not going to argue the case again,
except, perhaps, I might be permitted to
add this. I do not know, but I think it is
about 45 miles to Dungannon, and you will
not get a taxi to take you to Dungannon
and back for four guineas.
Adjournment.

DELIVERY OF BALLYALLOLY
SAND.
1. Mr. THOMAS BAILIE asked the
Minister of Public Security whether he
can state to what districts, other than the
borough of Bangor, sand is being delivered from Ballyalloly pit for the purpose
of erecting air-raid shelters.
PARLIAMENTARY
The
SECRE-
TARY
THE MINISTRY OF
PUBLIC SECURITY (Mr. Maginess):
I have been asked to reply.
OF
At the present time, sand from Ballyalloly is being purchased by the City
Surveyor, Belfast, for use in the erection
of air-raid shelters. Recent tests have
confirmed that this sand is very suitable
for the purpose.
It may be that sand from the pit in
question will in the future be purchased
for use in other districts, but of course a
great deal will depend upon the adequacy
of other local supplies and the economic
use of transport facilities.

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): It is a standing rule
of my Department that the payments
made by local authorities to officers who

ULSTER UNION CLUB RAID.
13. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state if the Ulster Union Club was raided
by police last week; whether any person
on the premises was detained; whether

mainly Protestant, of standing in literary,
