and spirit,
spirit, and friendship between
Northern Ireland and Eire.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The club
referred to was raided last week by the
police, but no persons on the premises
were detained, nor were any seditious
documents found thereon.
The events leading to the raid were:
the discovery of arms and a large quantity
of seditious literature in the garage and
home of a person who admitted that he
was a member of the I.R.A., and also of
the Ulster Union Club. In a search of
another house, occupied by members of
the Ulster Union Club, the police found
duplicating machine, a typewriter,
parts of a printing machine, a subversive
document in course of production on the
duplicating machine and a number of
articles in manuscript, which obviously
emanated from I.R.A. sources, and were
intended for duplication. A large
quantity of paper and duplicating ink,
and a document relating to the Ulster
Union Club were also found. In the
house of another member of the club a
revolver and literature relating to the
Ulster Union Club were found, whilst in
the houses of other members of the club,
documents of a subversive nature were
discovered.
The cases against these persons are still
sub judice.

The Resolution asks that Parliament
should authorise the payments necessary
for putting into force the Fire Services
(Emergency Provisions) Bill. One of the
provisions of that Bill is to set up additional fire services. The main policy of
the measure is the co-ordination, for the
emergency, of all or any of the fire
services provided by local authorities or
for the unification, in whole or in part,
under the control of the Ministry, of all
or any of those services, and, in addition,
the provision of additional fire services.
Can the Financial Secretary say that
any case exists for these additional firefighting services? We are not told how
many men constitute the fire service, and

matters which affect the national interest

House. They are divulged and treated as
public matters across the Channel, and
why it should be thought contrary to the
public interest to divulge the facts in
regard to the number of persons engaged
and the number likely to be engaged
under this Bill I cannot follow. The
multiplication of men is not the real

question of efficiency at the head. It is
leadership which counts more than

I speak with more reason on this question, because on Saturday last at the

I am, however, directing my remarks

For example, on the 21st September,
1941, when 29 shelters had been condemned the Minister said:
I am satisfied that there is a great
improvement in the provision of shelters
in Belfast. In the last four months
the amount of shelter accommodation

which many of these shelters have been
disapproved and a new type of shelter
adopted in their stead. My line of criticism at this point is: (1) That a change
of policy in regard to the shelter programme has apparently been adopted
without the knowledge of this House, and
(2) that many of the shelters which have
been characterised as satisfactory had in
actual fact proved to be unsatisfactory
because of the unsatisfactory nature of
their design, and because of the inferiority
of their construction.
In September the number which had
been condemned was 29, but I understand

I have already alluded to the nature of
the shelters which have been erected in
Northern Ireland. Over twelve months
ago, and considerably prior to the
optimistic description given to them by
the Minister, shelters of the pitched roof
variety were hopelessly out of date, and
A.R.P. officers who visited England on an
A.R.P. course were laughed at and
derided when they stated that these were
being erected in Ulster. At that time
they were regarded as the relic of a
bygone age, though they were being proceeded with here in Northern Ireland.
That leads me to suggest very seriously
that there appears to be an absolute lack
of co-ordination between the Ministry on
this side and that in Great Britain. The
discovery of the uselessness of the old type
of shelter should have been made earlier
-not by air raid experience in Northern
Ireland-but as a result of earlier
experience in England. Had that been
done, much waste of expenditure of public
money would have been avoided. As it
is, many of these public shelters are being
allowed to remain, the only changes being
that lavatories of the reinforced type are
being added to the ends of these, and it
would appear that the only safe place in
these shelters as they exist to-day is in the
reinforced additions that have been made
to them in the way of lavatories.
Now I fully agree that the phases of
civil defence have changed so frequently
that a Ministry of more than ordinary
ability is required for this work.
I question very much whether such a Ministry is
in existence. I am quite satisfied to
express the opinion that the technical and
engineering side of the Ministry is hopelessly impeded by the administrative side.
The Ministry of Public Security is
generally recognised as a Ministry which
does not know its own mind. That fact
is recognised by every local authority in
Northern Ireland with which it has to do.
It is noted for its ability to reverse its
decisions. Its speed ratio is greatest in
the reverse gear.
No longer ago than yesterday I happened to call upon an A.R.P. officer, and
I beheld on the table of his office and
in front of that A.R.P. officer
a huge pile of memoranda with blank
forms which had been sent to be completed. Actually, most A.R.P. officers
are busy filling in returns to the Ministry
and most local authorities are inundated
with Civil Service communications which
lead nowhere in a limited sphere such as
Northern Ireland. It is all right for
these Civil Service methods to be carried
on in England where there is a vast area
of country to be covered. I suggest
that it is a needless waste of time
to adopt the same methods in Northern Ireland which is somewhere about
the same size as Yorkshire. I find from
Hansard that in connection with this
Ministry it was admitted that 194
private cars, consuming 85,000 gallons of
petrol per annum, were being used, and
perhaps to a large degree being wasted
in the work of the Ministry of Public
Security. Surely it is not unreasonable.

Mr. NIXON: That is an unusual thing

Lieut.-Colonel MITCHELL: The Committee saw that the question of defence was
a purely military one. We required someone
who could go to the General Officer Commanding in Belfast and to say: "Are you
satisfied that everything reasonable is being
done for the protection of the people of
Belfast in the event of the Germans coming
over?" That took place before there had
been an air raid. Sir James Cooke-Collis
was present. The first question asked at
that Committee was: "Have the people
not been asked to stay put?" The question
of shelters, which is being discussed here
to-day, is beside the issue. The people
have already been advised to stay put, and
not to go into the streets. They should go
to the safest place in their own homes. The
House would remember that during one of
the enemy raids a direct hit was obtained
on a shelter and over thirty people were
killed. If they had stayed in their own
homes, probably only three or four would
have been killed.
Sir James Cooke-Collis said that not one
of the shelters would stand a direct hit.
We know of streets with 10, 15 or 20 shelters,
and of streets with no shelters at all. If the
people in certain streets had a right to
shelters, surely the people in the other streets.
had a similar right? The Civil Defence
Committee recommended that someone
should be appointed to approach the General
Officer Commanding, with a view to seeing
that we had the same protection as was given
to any other place in the United Kingdom.
The result was that my right hon. Friend
(Mr. MacDermott) was appointed Minister
of Public Security. I hold that there is no
way of securing the defence of the people
but through the military. We have a
committee and if it is not a good one it can
be strengthened and made fit for anything
we want it to do. At the time the Committee was appointed things were in a very
dangerous way and none of us ever said a
word in this House in public, because we
did not want it spread abroad. It was
kept quiet, and the right hon. Member for
the University who was our Minister then,
and Defence Liaison Officer with the
Ministry across the water naturally advised
us to be very careful about what we said,
as we did not know where it would go. If
the present Committee were strengthened
there is no reason why we should be compelled to appoint another committee to
inquire into the administration.

and I hope to be able to prove it.
Then there is the question of deep

of discussing the possibility of deep

I do not necessarily mean deep downward. I mean deep inward as well. In

and perhaps other areas throughout
Northern Ireland.
present time. I wish to discuss defective

The next thing I want to raise, if I am

In my

It is under the aegis of this

been loaned by the Ministry to co-operate
between the Ministry and the local

Most of that work, if not indeed all, is

the cost-plus basis, and I say that is

a classical example. As I came down the
Antrim Road to-day I passed a block of
houses that I know were blitzed, because
I was there when they were blitzed on

originally that those houses should be removed and new houses, if any, erected in
their place, but eventually it was decided
to reconstruct those houses. They are still
reconstructing them after all this lapse of
time, and judged by the alacrity already
displayed, they are likely to be reconstructing them next Easter, that is twelve
months after the damage took place.
That is an aspect to which I also wish to
draw attention.
Another very important question to
which I wish to refer is the lack of effective
co-ordination in the welfare, evacuation,
rest centres, billets, etc., all kindred services associated with this Ministry. All
these last year were interwoven in the one
747 Ministry of Public Security

Adjournment
[Mr. Midgley]
administration. Now they have been
segregated, but the segregation does not,
in my opinion, necessarily lend itself to
greater efficiency, and so on Tuesday next,
when I am elaborating this point, I will
ask just exactly what the Government propose to do in the matter of co-ordination.
By co-ordination I mean this. As one
who took an active part in local affairs
last year when the blitzes occurred, and
went out to do what he could to assist in
the calamitous situation which developed
from the adverse circumstances which
confronted many thousands of citizens, I
realised there was a lack of co-ordination,
and the hearts of the people, in addition,
were broken by the experiences through
which they went, apart altogether from
the calamity which befel them. They
were sent from one place to another, and
from one part of the town to another.
The pivot at that time was supposed to
be the City Hall, but despite the best will
and determination on the part of those
who wished to ease the pains and stings
of the people at that particular time, the
organisation was not effective enough to
cope with the abnormal situation which
developed, with the result that people were
sent about from point to point, and place
to place, to such an extent that finally
their deep sorrow and their deep woe were
added to very considerably as a result of
these experiences.
Finally, I want to review, if I get the
time next Tuesday, in a comprehensive
way what I consider is a very clamant
need at the present time, the need for a
Ministry of Social Welfare. I believe
that a case has been made out for the
appointment of such a Ministry which
will be charged with responsibility for
the segregation of all the work on the
welfare side from the question of civil
defence and public security. In that
way they would be able to give closer
attention and a stricter regard to the requirements of the masses of the people in
the abnormal conditions prevailing at the
present time. I have outlined very
briefly and very imperfectly the points
with which I mean to deal next Tuesday.
Incidentally, I should like at this stage
to let the Government know that in all
I have said, and in all I am about to say,
no imputation and no reflection is meant
by me to be cast upon the right hon.
Gentleman who presides over this Department, and who, through ill-health, is
precluded from being here this afternoon.
I regret he is in that condition of illhealth. I wish him a speedy recovery,
and I hope that when he has that
complete recovery he will get a chance to
justify his selection and to vindicate hist
power to reorganise his Department.
Having said that I have cleared the deck
for the points I will deal with next Tuesday. After I have put these points and
been backed up by other speakers, I take
it that the Parliamentary Secretary, as
well as the Prime Minister, will outline
what the Government's policy is.

Mr. NIXON: I want to make a final
protest against this Bill, not against the
question of co-ordination, as was suggested

that the Bill has already been used to

and for the purpose of finding jobs for
them. I condemn that policy. It is that
principle which has reduced the British
Empire to its present unfortunate position-putting men in high positions not
because of what they know, but because
of whom they know. In Northern Ireland, as I suppose in Great Britain, a
number of people have taken advantage
of the war to make a bit for themselves
or to shove into safe, secure jobs someone
related to or belonging to themselves as
a cloak against going into the Army and
defending the country. That we all
know, and this is what I object to. I
doubly object to anyone who professes to
be a patriot taking up a position to get
round that corner.

Mr. ELLIOTT: By leave of the House.

interest.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): A considerable
number of loans have been made to persons
in Portstewart and other places under the
Small Dwellings (Acquisition) Acts (Northern Ireland),
Ireland), 1899-1923, for the
purpose of erecting or purchasing
dwelling-houses. The rates of interest in
respect of advances to borrowers vary, in
the case of Portstewart from 41 per cent.
to 5 per cent., according to the date on
which the advance was made.
These advances are met by the local
authorities by means of borrowings from

to interfere with the rate of interest
charged by banks, and so far as the rate
of interest charged by the Government
itself on
loans from the Government
Loans Fund is concerned, I would remind
the hon. Member that these rates of
interest are fixed having regard to the
rate of interest payable by the Government on their own borrowings for Government Loans Fund purposes. The answer
to the last part of the question is, therefore, in the negative.

BUILDING WITHOUT A PERMIT.
4. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he can state if Lord
Londonderry was prosecuted for spending a sum exceeding £100 on a building
without a permit from the Ministry of
Commerce; whether there is the same
law for the Belfast Corporation and
Lord Londonderry; and whether the
Belfast Corporation have exceeded the
£100 limit in respect to any private
houses they undertook to repair without
a permit.
Sir WILSON HUNGERFORD: I
have been asked to reply.
The answer to the first part of the
question is that Lord Londonderry was
prosecuted for carrying out work of reconstruction exceeding the amount permitted by Defence Regulation 56a at the
time when the work was undertaken.
With regard to the second part of the
question, under Defence Regulation 56a
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Wilson Hungerford]
there is a distinction between the work
which local authorities and private individuals can undertake on dwellinghouses without authority. Private individuals cannot undertake any building
work including repairs which costs more
than £100. Local authorities, on the
other hand, may carry out repair work
to dwelling-houses without special permission from my Ministry. The extent
to which local authorities may perform
this repair work is, of course, governed
by the Housing (Emergency Powers) Act
(Northern Ireland), 1939, as amended by
the Repair of War Damage Act (Northern Ireland), 1941.
With regard to the third part of the
question, the local authority would not
require to obtain authority from my
Ministry for work on private houses
costing more than £100, unless the work
involved rebuilding or reconstruction.

MISUSE OF MOTOR-CARS.
5. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Prime Minister whether, in view of the
misuse of motor-cars and consequent
waste of petrol, as disclosed in the House
of Commons, he will issue definite and
stringent orders to every Government
Department that no Government car or
Government hired cars will be used for
any private purpose whatsoever.
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY
(Major Sinclair): I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend to reply.
The Government has always been fully
alive to the necessity for preventing unnecessary use of official cars and strict
rules have been laid down. In view of
the present vital need for maximum
petrol economy the Government is considering what further steps can be
taken to ensure that these rules are
rigidly observed and that the fullest
possible use is made of other forms of
transport where available.
Mr. BROWN: May I ask the Deputy
Prime Minister whether he can tell us if
the same stringent rule will be applied
by the Government in regard to the waste
of paper that is going on?
Mr. SPEAKER: That question does
not arise, and the Deputy Prime Minister
is not in the House.

NEWRY POTATO PROCESSING
FACTORY.
7. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state the contract price for the erection of the new
potato processing factory in course of construction in Newry; and whether he can
state the price at which potatoes for this
and similar factories in Northern Ireland
are to be purchased, and the method to
be adopted in purchasing such potatoes.
The prices to be paid for potatoes for
processing in these factories will be the
ruling control prices for variety and district at the date of delivery of the
potatoes, provided they are of the requisite
standard. The method to be adopted for
purchasing the potatoes has not yet been
decided, but it is under discussion with the
Ministry of Food, for whom my Ministry
is acting as agent. In the meantime, all
potatoes bought by my Ministry on behalf
of the Ministry of Food are for immediate
consumption or for the end of season
reserve.
Mr. BROWN: May I ask the Minister
does he not agree that it is very unsatisfactory that these potatoes are going to be
paid for at the controlled price, in view
of the fact that his Ministry has previously
stated that would not be the case?
Lord GLENTORAN: No, my Ministry
never said anything of the sort. I should
have taken the strongest action if potatoes
for these factories had not been paid for
at the agreed price, which was approved
of by the Ministry and arranged and fixed
with the farmers of England and Scotland. What we made clear was this, that
in peace time the class of potatoes required
for these factories will not be paid at the
same rate and never has been paid at the
same rate where these factories exist as
the price for potatoes now.

In reference to grants to local authorities we know that at the present time

I come now to the Ministry of Labour.
Whilst we allocate large sums for the
relief of unemployment it is not the best
remedy. I feel that the Government,
despite its many years in office, has failed
to tackle the problem of unemployment in
a manner in keeping with the requirements of Northern Ireland. Week by
week and day by day we find that the only
solution left to the Government of
Northern Ireland, notwithstanding the
fact that it has had a great industrial
record in the past, is to compel our
workers to go elsewhere. What do we
intend to do when this terrible war is
finished? When all those engaged shall
return to their respective homes, what
will be found in Northern Ireland? I
would like to know what the Government

I was very glad to hear the hon. and

who wished to take up a position. It

were sent to any part of Northern Ireland
without due consideration or without information being given to them as to their
destination. I see advertisements in the
Press seeking young women for
N.A.A.F.I. canteens. When they apply
they may find that the jobs are in any
part of Northern Ireland. That is a
matter for the girl replying to the
advertisement.

The hon. Member for Pottinger took

Northern Ireland without intimating to

If Members of the House object to my

sending them to positions in their own

Mr. GORDON: I thought that would

Before I reiterate what I have already
said in this House on this matter might
The hon. Gentleman says I should not
send agricultural workers to Great
Britain. I do not. I think I explained
to him within the past few days that I
had sent from 50 to 70 agricultural
workers to England to carry out a specific
job, and that I had made arrangements
whereby, when the work was completed,
about the month of May they would return
home. The hon. Geentleman will remember that I issued an Order "freezing"
agricultural workers to their own occupation; but in the winter season and early
spring huge numbers of agricultural
workers become unemployed. When it is
impossible to find agricultural employment
for them, I have to offer them work of
some kind, and they are given to understand that, under the terms of the Order
I have issued, while they are permitted
to accept employment say in aerodromes,
in quarries, or in other occupations, they
come back to agriculture when
required to do so.
must

resuming agricultural work at once, we
are bound to pay him full agricultural

My hon. Friend raised once again the

that he takes in the people of his constituency who appear before the tribunal.
I am proud of the part he is playing in

I do not object to criticism from the hon.

I have a good deal of sympathy with
another point raised by the hon. Gentleman-that when men are interviewed by
young women they are not in a position

agree with him. There are also bound to

to a man objections that she could put up
to a woman. If a woman is interviewing
a man he cannot give his reasons for
refusing a job as freely as he would to a
I agree with that, and I will take
man.
Sometimes, of course, a difficulty arises.
As I explained to the House on the last
day I was asking for money in order to
meet the cost of the staff; we have
reduced our staff considerably, and as a
result we are not able to deal in the way
we should like with the many problems
that arise. But, so far as is possible, I
will arrange that men will be interviewed
by men and that women will be interviewed by women, so that neither sex will
be faced with any difficulty in that
respect, and neither will be able to claim
that he or she had a case of considerable
strength, but because of the interview
being conducted by a person of the
opposite sex he or she was unable to put
up the case.
As to the concluding remarks of the
hon. Gentleman, I have only to say that,
as Minister of Labour, I shall continue,
notwithstanding the criticism that has
been levelled at me, to send men and
women across the water to discharge their
duty in the interests of the nation, so
that, when the war is over, they will be
able to say they have played their part in
helping forward the British victory, and
in assisting in the hour of peril the
country of their birth.

Oral Answers to Questions.
RUBBER BOOTS WITHOUT
COUPONS.
1. Mr. BAILEY asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he is aware that
in England farmers and workers engaged
in farm and land drainage work can
obtain without coupons rubber boots,
oilskins and overalls on presentation of a
certificate from
county authority;
whether this applies to Northern Ireland,
and if so, whether he can state from what
authority certificates can be obtained for
this purpose.
a
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Lord Glentoran): In Northern Ireland
rubber boots, oilskins and overalls can be
purchased free of coupons on a certificate
issued by the county agricultural executive officer when that officer is satisfied
that the articles are required by a farmer
or farm worker for agricultural purposes.
This certificate is accepted by retailers
instead of coupons.
FLAX SEED SUPPLIES.
if
2. Mr. BAILEY asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state
adequate flax seed supplies will be available in time for sowing this year.
Lord GLENTORAN: At the moment
sufficient flax seed to sow 61,500 acres has
been issued to the trade. Supplies are
arriving daily from Great Britain, and in
addition, as the hon. Member is aware,
the processing factories in Northern Ireland are producing their quota. The
general position is much better than at
the same period last year when seed for
only 35,200 acres had been distributed.
I am glad to say there is a great demand
for seed this year, and also that I have
no doubt that I will be in a position to
meet it.

ELEMENTARY SCHOOLS PUPILS.
4. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether she can state the total
number of pupils enrolled in the public
elementary schools in the first year of the
Ministry and the total number enrolled
last year.
Mrs. PARKER: The total number of
pupils enrolled in public elementary
schools on the 31st December, 1922, in the
first year of the Ministry, was 198,385.
It is not possible at this stage to give the
number of pupils enrolled on the 31st
December, 1941, but the enrolment on the
31st December, 1940, was 186,333.

TUBERCULOSIS IN NORTHERN
IRELAND.
5. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state the number of persons diagnosed as
suffering from tuberculosis in Northern
Ireland.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): According to the
latest records, that is, for the year ended
December, 1940, the number of persons
diagnosed as suffering from tuberculosis in
Northern Ireland is 7,389.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Yes, sir.
Through the various clinics every step is
taken. I may add that through the
tuberculosis hospital in Belfast we have
improved matters to a very great extent.
Mr. HENDERSON: Is the Minister
aware that there are hundreds of children
attending public elementary schools every
day suffering from tuberculosis and
mixing among healthy children, and will
he state whether any action has been
taken to see that these children get proper
treatment?
JUVENILE DELINQUENCY.
7. Lieut.-Colonel MITCHELL asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether he
has yet come to any decision with regard
to the question of implementing the report of the Lynn Committee dealing with
juvenile delinquency.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have not
yet received the final report of the
Departmental Committee on Juvenile
Delinquency, but I understand it will
soon be ready.
With regard to the Interim Report, I
hope shortly to introduce legislation on
the subject of the constitution of
juvenile courts. A revised Order in
Council dealing with probation officers
is being prepared for submission to His
Grace the Governor, and search for
accommodation for a remand home for
girls is continuing.

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): I have been asked by my right
hon. Friend to reply.
The numbers, of course, vary from time
to time, but the latest available information indicates that the number of
separate premises owned by the Government of Northern Ireland is 273 and the
number of premises rented is 214. With
regard to the rented premises, I think I
should point out to the hon. Member
that a large number of these have been
rented since the outbreak of war in pursuance of the Government's dispersal
policy, and some of the premises owned
by the Government of Northern Ireland
have been let or lent, in whole or in part,
to Departments of the Imperial Government and other public bodies.

that, in view of the very costly method

DAMAGED TRAILER PUMPS.
9. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Public Security whether he can state the
number of trailer pumps injured or put
out of order during the two main raids
on Belfast; whether any qualified
engineer is employed or has been employed to instruct the firemen in the care,
maintenance, or use of these pumps; and
whether Mr. Andrews, the newlyappointed adviser on fire services in Northern Ireland, is a qualified engineer in
respect to any branch of engineering connected with fire fighting.
on
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC
SECURITY (Mr. Grant): I am informed that apart from the pumps
completely destroyed as a result of enemy
action during the two main raids
Belfast repairs to the actual appliances
or to their tyres were required in upwards
of 40 cases. Some of the damage was
due to falling debris, some to cuts from
glass, and the remainder resulted from
the heavy continuous work imposed upon
the pumps during these raids.
The personnel of the regular auxiliary
services includes skilled mechanics and
other members with wide experience in
motor engineering whose services are
availed of to give instruction in the care
and maintenance of pumps, and all personnel undergo a course of training in
the use of these appliances.
I am also informed that Mr. Andrews
is not a qualified engineer. His duties
are of an administrative type not requiring engineering knowledge or experience.
Mr. HENDERSON: Can the Minister
state who was responsible for giving Mr.
Andrews this very important appointment?
Mr. GRANT: I am responsible.
Mr. NIXON: And who was responsible
for giving you your appointment?
Mr. GRANT: The Prime Minister.

ISSUE OF INSURANCE CARDS TO
EIRE WORKERS.
15. Mr. JOHN BAILEY asked the
Minister of Labour whether he will make
an order to stop the issuing of insurance
cards to men and women coming from
Eire until all the unemployed in Northern
Ireland who want work are in jobs.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): I must inform the hon. Member
that under the Unemployment and Health
Insurance Acts contributions must be
paid whenever a person enters insurable
employment in Northern Ireland, and it
is the duty of my Ministry to provide
books or cards for the purpose. I have
no power under the Insurance Acts or the
Emergency Powers (Defence) Acts to
alter or remove this obligation.
I should point out that, even if the
action suggested could be taken, it would
merely give a preference to Eire workers.
I could not prosecute employers for noncompliance with the Insurance Acts in
respect of such workers if they were not
allowed to get the necessary books or cards
and they would thus have the services of
Eire workers cheaper than Northern
Ireland workers, because they would not
have to pay health and unemployment
contributions in respect of them.
Lieut.-Colonel HALL-THOMPSON :
May I ask the Minister if steps could be
taken, if they are not already taken, to
see that the names and addresses of such
persons as receive cards from him on their
first arrival from Eire are handed over to
the R.U.C. so that they can report if
necessary on the suitability of the persons
for employment in Northern Ireland from
the security standpoint?
Mr. GORDON: The whole matter
raised by the hon. and gallant Member
is under consideration at the present time.

Gentleman consider the trade unions
responsible for the interchangeability of
their members whether north, south, east
or west? The trade union principle is

of years.
I will see that those rights are
maintained.

Londonderry fully manned.
That is a very serious state of affairs.
It appears that the gentleman in charge
up there I need not mention his name;
I suppose it is well known to the Ministry-says: "If buildings do not burn we
will have no raid," which is the most
fantastic distortion of the facts I have

Belfast, and I happened to be there myself, was carried out when not one building was burning, and when the whole
district had been lighted up by the flares
that were dropped from enemy planes.
The man who reasons in this way does
not appear to have a full comprehension
of the potentialities arising from a raid;
but, even if that were true it would not

alter the moral position at the present

There is one statement in which I

the greatest amount of compulsion, from

spirit of compulsion should be employed
if people have not developed a civic conscience to make them realise the dangers

to shoulder as much responsibility as it

would I had the imagination of Mr.

It is from that angle I have spoken

I let my mind go away across the seas
to-day to where I have relatives. I have

enjoy. I therefore say it is the Government's duty to do all in its power to
remove discontent by being constructive,

we have done and hand over the heritage

I am not here to make any apology for
the Ministry of Public Security. That
Ministry needs no apology either from
me or from anyone else. It was set up
by Parliament almost two years ago to
perform certain work, and I challenge
anyone on the opposite side of the House
or outside the House to say that in the
performance of its work it has either been
remiss or negligent. Hon. Members remember the circumstances under which
the Ministry was called into being. There
had been an invasion of the Low
Countries. France had collapsed. There
was a threat of imminent danger. There
was a desire on the part not only of
Members but on the part of the general
public that a Ministry should be formed
to deal with nothing else but the question of public security, so that it could
concentrate, and the Ministry was formed.
During those two years the Ministry has
dealt with the subject, and I challenge
hon. Members to say that the work it has
done in those two years is anything but
work which calls for the highest praise
even from certain Members of the
Opposition.

What is the position with regard to
the shelters? I would ask hon. Members
to separate in their minds public shelters
from domestic or communal shelters.
Speaking broadly the public shelters are
those shelters in the streets which are
meant to give shelter to those using the
streets in the day time. They hold 50
people and they were built in the
summer of 1940. Not one of these
shelters was a bad shelter. When I say
not one I believe there was one which in
the course of erection was found to be
defective and it was built up so that no
one could use it. With that exception
not one was bad, nor was there any defective work attached to the shelters.

down to-day. They are being pulled

Before I go to the question of the sand,
I want to say one or two things concerning
my own attitude. I have been in public
life for more than thirty years, and I have
never been accused, up to the present, of
insincerity. Since I entered this House
almost a year ago-it will be in three days
-I do not think any Member will be able
fairly to say that I have endeavoured to
indulge in any criticism which was not, so
far as my knowledge goes, constructive.
I have never stood for destructive
criticism. The Parliamentary Secretary
is bound to admit that if there is any default on my part, or on the part of
Members on this side, it is due to one fact
and that is the inadequacy of the information imparted by his Ministry to this
side. I have no desire to cover any mistake prior to becoming a Member of this
House. It was stated by the late Minister
that 194 cars were in use by the Ministry.
I freely concede that would include the use
of police cars as well. That is a mistake
I attribute to the fact that I was not a
Member of the House. I concede that a
number of cars were put in use for the
Ministry of Public Security. If I made
a mistake in that matter, I should freely
acknowledge it.
The question of public shelters was one
which the Parliamentary Secretary dealt

question is really the most important

The Parliamentary Secretary said there is

there are a very large number of districts

the part of air-raid wardens exist. I would
be much happier if I were able cordially
to agree with the Parliamentary Secretary
and be able to say to him that it is a

complete unanimity and enthusiasm on the
part of A.R.P. workers throughout the
country. Nothing would give me greater
pleasure than to make that statement.
Can that statement be truthfully made
this afternoon? It has been stated openly
here that in Derry, an important city,
such dissatisfaction exists that almost the
whole personnel of the A.R.P. body have
threatened to resign. In face of a statement of that kind can the Parliamentary
Secretary seriously and truthfully say or
suggest that entire satisfaction prevails
throughout the area covered by his
Ministry? We are here to face facts, and
if anything I have said can be construed
as being wrong, or untruthful, or insincere I am, above all men, most willing
to acknowledge any mistake. I moved
this Motion with one object, and one
object alone, that was to ensure that
within the administration of the Ministry
of Public Security such a condition of
things will exist as will command the confidence and the support of the outside
public. Does such a spirit of confidence
exist? Has the attitude of the Ministry
been such as to ensure that such public
support will exist? I most emphatically
say, no, and I say that this Motion
justifies itself on that account.
The Parliamentary Secretary has

some
other members of the Bangor

autocracy on the part of the Ministry of

It is that spirit of autocracy and

It is only evading the real issue and the

The Bangor borough surveyor
demned the Ballyalloly sand on his own
initiative, and I knew nothing about that
until he took his stand. I know that
the borough surveyor is a man of utter
conscientiousness who cannot be bought.
He is a man of experience, and knows
good sand from bad sand. When the
sand from Ballyalloly pit was delivered
in Bangor he immediately complained to
the Ministry and declined any responsibility for its use. What was the result?
Officials came from the Ministry of
Public Security-whether in low- or highpowered cars does not matter, high-power
cars belong to another Ministry I could
mention-and immediately corroborated
the attitude of the Bangor borough surveyor and condemned six loads out of
seven; in other words, if the local officer
had not condemned those six loads out of
seven, in all probability from that hour to
the present moment shelters throughout
the Borough of Bangor would have been
built of defective Ballyalloly sand.
I say the Parliamentary Secretary
has not displayed an adequate conception of his duty as Parliamentary
Secretary to his Ministry. If he
really was actuated by what he says,
a desire to do the best he can in the in-

terests of the lives and safety of the people,

The story is a pathetic one. What did

there ensued a lengthy correspondence in

it must be recognised that the paramount

This is not a light matter, and I have

Whether the Parliamentary Secretary

The Parliamentary Secretary says if he
attends to pigs and poultry in the morning
and civil defence in the afternoon-affecting the safety of a million and a quarter
people he says that is all right so long
as he does the work well. It might be
all right but for the lost crops. It might
be all right if 102 shelters were not condemned in Belfast for improper construction, and it would be all right if people
could not come into the city of Belfast and
walk off with £4,800 of this Ministry's
money in broad daylight. It would be all
right, but for this Ballyalloly sand. The
Parliamentary Secretary spoke of the
extreme importance of being factual. Let
us be factual by all means. Let me refer
to Hansard, the Official Report of Parliamentary Debates for Tuesday, February
17th, 1942. In that report we find a
question was asked about this particular
sand for shelters.
Mr. Thomas Bailie asked the Minister
of Public Security whether he is aware
that sand is being delivered for use for
air-raid shelters from Ballyalloly, Comber, which has been condemned by at
least one local authority, and also by
officers of the Ministry; whether the use
of this sand is being forced upon the
officers of local authorities by the
Ministry; whether the sand in question
has been submitted for expert advice,
and if so, whether he will submit the
result of this analysis to the House; and
whether he is prepared, in view of the
vital necessity of providing shelters
which are sound, and in view of the
attendant risks of life and limb which
are involved, to assure the House that
only suitable and proper sand will be
used for this purpose.
Major Sinclair, Financial Secretary of
the Ministry of Finance, replied. I am
going to read part of the reply. He said:
Technical officers of the Ministry
visited the sand pit concerned and found
that while there were strata in the pit
which were unsuitable for use in shelter
construction, suitable material was also
present in large quantity.
I have been asked to reply. Arrangements have been made by the Ministry
for the supply of sand from the pit in
question, as it is conveniently situated
for certain areas in which shelters are
to be erected. Some of the deliveries
have been unsatisfactory, and the contractor was instructed to have them
removed. It is, of course, absurd to
suggest that the Ministry has forced or
will force any local authority to use
materials which do not comply with
specifications.
The point is that if some of this sand in
Ballyalloly is unsuitable and unsatisfactory, then in a case which involves
the lives of the people it should not be
taken from this pit. It should be
obtained from pits where there is no
possible doubt whatever as to the suitability of the sand. I could not put the
matter more strongly than that. There
may have been laughter in the House
when this matter was first raised, but it
is very sad that such things should be
allowed in a matter affecting the lives of
our people. I know that there is ample
sand to be obtained from other pits in
County Down
Down and elsewhere. Sand
should not be taken from a pit which has
been found partly unsuitable. If it is used
in the construction of shelters it may involve many of our people in needless
death. This is not a matter for laughter.
It is a matter to which the Ministry
should give most careful attention. If
other sand is available, as the Member
for North Down says, and as I can confirm, we should not be going to a pit
where some of the sand is unsuitable, and
which was admitted by the Ministry's
spokesman to be unsuitable on the 17th
February, 1942. The matter should have
the immediate consideration and concern
of the Ministry.
The protest made by the hon. Member
for North Down in this matter was very
convincing, and where the lives of the
people are at stake the Ministry should
take no risk. If wrong material gets
into the shelters the people will pay with
their lives. The Ministry should go to
pits where the sand is all suitable for the
purpose. Notwithstanding what occurred
on a previous occasion I am glad that I
still have the right to speak in a
democratic Parliament and institution.
One of the fundamental rights of
democracy is the right and liberty to
express one's views. I am delighted I
still have that right and will continue to
have it. I am not satisfied with what
the Parliamentary Secretary said. It
would have been far better if he had
got up courageously and said, "We will
end the wrongs." Then the public would

1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Sir Basil Brooke): The letter to which

of this House. The lady mentioned in
the question signed the letter while
deputising for my private secretary.
The arrangement under which certain.
officers of my Ministry had been acting
for and on behalf of the Ministry of Food
was terminated with my consent. In
deciding that it should be terminated I
was influenced by the fact that in the
matter of food rationing there could be
no question of differentiation as between
Great Britain and Northern Ireland, and
that all matters of policy and administration must, therefore, be settled by the
Minister of Food. In these circumstances
it appeared to me that there was no justification for the continuance of an arrangement which in the past had apparently
been taken to imply that my Ministry had
powers which, in fact, it did not possess.
by reference to the Section, the making
or termination of such arrangements is

made under the provisions of Section 63
of the Government of Ireland Act, 1920,
which authorises departments to make
them on such terms and conditions as may
be agreed. As the hon. Member may see

DRAINAGE AND RECLAMATION.
4. Mr. BROWN asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state when the
Government propose to place before the
House legislation to provide for largescale drainage and reclamation of land
to increase food and flax production;
whether he is aware that the United
States has sent over to Great Britain one

in the way of technical and machinery
assistance they can render; whether this
expert has been or will be invited to
Northern Ireland; and whether Northern
Ireland will share in such technical and
machinery assistance from America.
The
FINANCIAL SECRETARY
(Major Sinclair): I have been asked by
my right hon. Friend to reply. It is the
intention of the Government to introduce
legislation dealing with the question of
drainage after the Easter Recess. The
Ministry's officers have been in close touch
with the Departments concerned with
drainage both in England and Scotland,
from whom they have already received
advice and assistance. I have no doubt
that this co-operation will continue and
that whatever assistance the British
Ministries are able to obtain from the
United States of America will be shared
with the Government here, but naturally
with due regard to the drainage needs of
the United Kingdom as a whole.

Duty During Invasion

Duty During Invasion
HOUSE OF COMMONS
What to do During an Invasion.
DUTY OF POPULATION.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That this House do now adjourn."-
(Sir Norman Stronge.)
The PRIME MINISTER: With your
permission, and the leave of the House,
I should like to make a short statement
about the part which the civil population
of Northern Ireland should play in the
event of an invasion of this country.
Much interest has been aroused by a
statement made by Sir John Anderson
in the Imperial House of Commons last
week, and I feel, therefore, that the
House and the public generally would
wish to know something of the position
here. Hon. Members are aware that it
is on the Forces of the Crown, including
our own Ulster Home Guard, that we
would have to rely to meet and defeat
the enemy. But there is much that the
civil population can do to help the military authorities, and it is to this aspect
of the question that I particularly wish
to address myself to-day.
We are proud to be citizens of the
United Kingdom, sharing the common
risks and ready to play whatever part may
be allotted to us by the Imperial Government. In this connection, I should like
to emphasise that all advice given to
private citizens in Great Britain as to
their behaviour during air raids and in
invasion applies equally to the citizens of
Northern Ireland. All must, therefore,
"stand fast" under invasion conditions:
business must be carried on as long as
possible; in no circumstances should
people leave their homes to crowd the
roads. There is no safety in taking to
the roads, as thousands of unhappy
refugees found in France and Flanders.
It is not, however, a merely passive
attitude that we should wish to adopt.
We shall all want to hinder and frustrate
the enemy in every way that we can.
Before I describe the useful work which
private citizens can do in invasion, I
should like to diverge for a few minutes
to tell the House something of our
arrangements for co-operation between the
armed forces, the civil government, the
civil defence services, and the civil population. Naturally, I shall not give any
information which might be of value to
the enemy, but even with this limitation
in view, I hope to be able to show the
House that carefully thought out plans
have been made between all concerned to
ensure the maximum contribution in the
common task of driving the enemy from
our country.
Men who are fit will want to join the
Ulster Home Guard or the new National
Fire Service, and both men and women
can find useful work in the civil defence
services. If they have not already joined
up, now is the time to do it. All members of these services will have their own
work to do in invasion, and if the time
comes, I know that they will give a good
account of themselves.
The machinery of co-operation begins at
the top, with the Northern Ireland Home
Defence Executive, of which my colleague
the Minister of Commerce and Production is chairman. All the Departments
of our Government which will co-operate
with the military authorities are represented on the executive. So also is the
Ministry of Food. The Inspector-
General, Royal Ulster Constabulary,
attends the meetings to advise on police
and security matters, and the meetings
are, of course, attended by representatives
of the three fighting services. The executive has a joint civil and military secretariat to ensure that problems affecting
the interests either of the fighting services
or of the civil government are brought
promptly under review. Northern Ireland corresponds in size to a region in
Great Britain, and I think I am right in
saying that the machinery for co-operation between our civil departments and
the fighting services in Northern Ireland
is as complete and elaborate as in any
corresponding area in Great Britain.
Apart altogether from this central
machinery we have also arranged that in
invasion conditions representatives of the
civil government will be attached to the
headquarters of the various military areas
into which Northern Ireland is divided,
and this scheme, which we hope will
ensure an effective link between the
military commanders and the local services
in their areas, is supplemented by an
arrangement whereby, in the event of a
breakdown in communications, decisions
on behalf of the civil government can be
taken locally without loss of time.
We have also established a system of
co-operation in the various civil defence
areas between the Ulster Home Guard,
Duty During Invasion
Secret Session
1 APRIL 1942
the police-both regular and special-the
civil defence services, including the fire
service, and the local military commanders. Arrangements in this respect
are being made and improved steadily,
and in many areas they have already
reached a high degree of completeness.
All these services will have important
duties, either of active operations against
the enemy or of protecting the civil
population and property from enemy
attack.
The other local services which have
duties to perform in invasion deal more
specially with the needs and duties of the
civil population and, in referring to them,
I should like to explain how members of
the public can assist in strengthening the
country's will to resist and so ensure the
defeat of the enemy. As hon. Members
are aware, the Ministry of Home Affairs
is responsible for arranging the reception
and care of homeless people. Householders everywhere can obviously assist
greatly in this work by providing accommodation and food for those who have
been rendered homeless by enemy action,
or who are otherwise in need of help.
Householders may also be able to assist
by feeding or billeting members of the
fighting services.
concern to all, and the public can help by
co-operating in any arrangements or
directions which may be given by the
local officers appointed to look after this
important service.
Again, the national service officers of the
Ministry of Labour, situated in various
towns throughout the country, will be in
a position to direct able-bodied members
of the public to do such defence work as
may be
considered necessary by the
military commander. I am sure, however, that there will be a willing response
to requests for help of this kind, and that
the compulsory powers which the Government possess will have to be used only in
isolated cases. The local arrangements
for feeding the civil population made by
the Ministry of Food are also of vital
Reference has been made in the
Imperial Parliament to the establishment
of Invasion Committees in Great Britain.
Here in Northern Ireland the various
schemes which I have already mentioned
cover in large measure the duties to be
carried out by these committees. In the
smaller or remote areas, where the local
arrangements are not so elaborate, the
existing key personnel will co-operate with
the local military commander in whatever
measures he deems necessary to meet the
special needs of the district. The
Government are working in the closest
touch with the General Officer Commanding-who is always most helpful-in
perfecting and extending, where necesssary, our defence arrangements so that
they may be adequate to meet all the
requirements of the military authorities
in invasion conditions.
Of course, the success of these defence
plans will depend on the willing,
courageous, and unselfish co-operation of
all concerned. I ask for that, and I feel
certain I shall not ask in vain.

Oral Answers to Questions.
PRIVATE AND PUBLIC AIR-RAID
SHELTERS.
3. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Public Security whether he can state what
is the distinction between private air-raid
shelters and public air-raid shelters.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC
SECURITY (Mr. Grant): The description "private shelter" is usually
applied to one provided for the
exclusive use of an individual household, whether at the expense of
the owner or as part of a scheme
for the provision of free domestic shelter
by a local authority; the term is also
sometimes used in a more general sense to
include, for example, a shelter provided
for the workers in a factory or a commercial building. The domestic shelters which
are erected in streets for the use of the
occupants of the adjoining houses, being
normally shared by two or more households, are usually called "communal
shelters.' ""
"Public" shelters are in general those
erected in or near the main streets for the
accommodation of members of the general
public who may be out of doors and away
from their homes when a raid occurs.
Mr. SPEAKER: I must apologise to

MEDICAL INSPECTION OF
PERSONS COMING FROM BRITAIN.
Mr. McGURK asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether, in view of the
existence of venereal disease in Great
Britain, he will take steps to ensure that
every person coming to Northern Ireland
from Great Britain will be subject to
medical examination at the port of
embarkation.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The answer is in the
negative.
CONDITIONS OF EMPLOYMENT OF
IRISH WORKERS IN GREAT
BRITAIN.
Mr. McGURK asked the Minister of
Labour whether he is aware of the conditions under which Irish labourers who
are sent across the Chanel are employed;
whether it is a fact that no washing facilities are provided; blankets are seldom
changed; no hot water for baths is available, and sanitary conditions are bad in
very many cases; and if so, whether he
will make representations to the proper
authorities to have these workers provided
with the common decencies of life, in view
of their anxiety to help the national war
effort.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): The hon. Member will realise
that workers who have gone from Northern Ireland to Great Britain are engaged
in so many different occupations, ranging
from small private employment to large
Government undertakings, that it is quite
impossible for me to answer his question
in detail. No doubt, during the war,
conditions will not be perfect in all the
places all the time.
I may say, however, that welfare
officers, attached to the Ministry of
Labour and National Service, are
stationed all over Great Britain to look
after the well-being of workers, and when,
from time to time, complaints have been
brought to my notice and I have raised
the matter with the British authorities,
these officers have been very active in getting things put right. Of course if the
hon. Member has any particular case in
mind and will give me details, I shall be
happy to have it looked into.

contribution for the current and subsequent years.

It was faced on the one hand with pressure from the Belfast Corporation to
eliminate altogether the contribution by
local authorities in Northern Ireland
towards unemployment because of the
improved conditions in respect of employment since the passing of the 1937 Act.
Incidentally, though it is obvious that the
position in this respect has substantially
altered, the Exchequer still finds itself
called upon to make substantial payments
by way of unemployment assistance. The
representatives of the Belfast Corporation
further repeated a point of view which
they had expressed in 1937, namely, that
had Belfast been situated in Great Britain
in that year it is probable that a more
favourable result would have been
obtained under the block grant system
operating in Great Britain, because the
basis of distribution adopted in that area
pays special consideration to cities with
heavy unemployment.
The Belfast Corporation, for the reasons
which I have outlined, urged that there
was no justification for continuing to
impose upon local authorities responsibility for any contribution from their
rates towards unemployment relief so long,
at any rate, as the conditions of employment remained as they are at present.
The Government had no hesitation at all
in admitting that there was some force in
the contention put forward by the Corporation that account ought to be taken
of the change in employment conditions,
but when it came to consider the extent
to which it would be possible to effect a
reduction, it was faced with a difficulty
arising out of the practice followed in this
respect during war-time in Great Britain.
Hon. Members may ask why the
Government on this side should pay any
attention to the Great Britain position,
and in reply I would remind them that
during war time our Northern Ireland
finances have become closely interwoven
with British finances, and that this in
itself requires from us acceptance of the
principle of a parity of services, unless
we can establish that there are conditions
operating over here which warrant a
different standard of treatment. We
found that in Great Britain no reduction
was being made during the war in the
amount of the corresponding levy upon
local authorities.
grant, and the same deduction which was

The PRIME MINISTER I did not
make any charge, I only suggested that in
a matter of this kind we had to provide
against something being said which might
be detrimental to the national interest,
and therefore, as hon. Members opposite
have many opportunities of condemning
the Government in many directions in
accordance with their views, I do not see
that we were in any way unduly fettering
the Opposition in expressing their opinions.
on general matters in any way they desire
to do. In connection with the war, and
the position at the moment, I think that
on consideration, even hon. Members
opposite will feel that we ought to be

In the speech which the hon. Member
for Pottinger has just delivered he made
many charges against the Government,
but I give him credit for not having said
anything which I think would give information to the enemy which should not be
given under existing conditions. At the
same time, if we began to discuss the
Motion which the hon. Member has on the
Order Paper, no one could tell when,
perhaps incautiously, some Member might
say something that would be most
undesirable. I do not want the hon.
Member to feel that we are in the least
afraid of anything he may say against
us as a Government. We are prepared to
defend ourselves from any attack that he
or any other member of the Opposition
may level against us, for we feel we have
nothing to be ashamed of, We are here
to safeguard the position from the
national point of view, and that position
we are going to continue to safeguard.
them in that fashion notwithstanding the

spoken from this side of the House would

know the Government do not care for
the Members on this side, and that is
why 90 per cent. of the people are turning against the present Government.
They have been in control of this country
now for over twenty years, and because
of the huge majorities they received they
have treated the electors with the utmost
disrespect. They still continue to treat
Have the Government on one solitary
occasion ever asked any Member on this
side of the House who could help the war
production of the country to give
the Government any assistance? Unfortunately, the right hon. Gentleman
and his colleagues are running this war
the same as they would run a county
council or a rural district council. No
real war effort is being introduced by the
right hon. Gentleman. Why has no
Member on this side up to the present
been asked to come out into the open
with a right hon. Gentleman to try to
get the workers to bring about a better
production of the munitions of war?
Why do the right hon. Gentleman and
his colleagues run their war effort on
Glengall Street lines? Everyone admits
that Glengall Street methods are very
antiquated; in fact, they are So
antiquated that the electors when the
time comes will show their disapproval of
those methods by not returning the present Government to power. I feel a
great deal of the trouble has been brought
about through the Government not asking the Members on this side of the House
to pool their brains and assist the
nation in its time of trouble.
Do you realise that the Minister of
Commerce is also the Minister of Nonproduction? I will tell you the reason.
Who in Northern Ireland pays the
slightest attention to the Minister of
Production, or Non-production, because
there has been nothing done since he took
control? How can he go to any industrial concern and tell them what they
should do to speed up the production of
munitions when he does not know the
slightest thing about it. If you sent
him into a pork shop or a vegetable
garden he might know something about
it, but he knows absolutely nothing about
engineering, good, bad, or indifferent.
To send a man of that calibre into a shipyard or a textile concern is only a waste
of time.
I know one particular member who
went to deliver a speech in one of the
munition factories to get them to increase
their effort. He went to the microphone
and said, "Fellow-workers." To say that
and to be dressed like a lord put the whole
industrial concern into convulsions be-

cause they knew he was no fellow-worker
and could not hope to be. If you sent the

We on this side of the House have

done. I give way to no person on the

to address

You cannot send a garden expert to

the Minister of Production told the

Bills they know nothing about and other
Members do not know it. I feel that
the steps taken by the present Government are backward instead of forward.
Another 15 or 20 per cent. effort could
be made by the workers. If you give
them justice and appeal to them in the
right way and look after them the way
they should be looked after you will get
increased production.
You will have to take the workers into
your confidence. That is all they are
asking. I suggest that not alone should
the Members of this House pool their

munitions could not be placed on a better

side get many complaints about the
management. There are always two sides
to a story, but I think a good many of
the complaints of the workers are perfectly justified. I am satisfied there is
a great wastage of man power and woman
power which could be utilised, and I
would tell the Prime Minister that as
far as we who represent the intelligent
people of the country are concerned we
are prepared to give him all the assistance we can to increase war production
SO as to bring about the destruction
of Hitler and the establishment of peace.
If he does not use us he is entirely to
blame, and he will have to account for
his sins in the world to come. If the
present administration carry on as they
are doing the Prime Minister will destroy
his own party. I would not like to see
it destroyed, but the Government are
bringing about that destruction themselves.

Let us all try to increase the war effort
from now onwards. Let us all try to be
sensible and realise that the sons and
daughters of the fathers and mothers of
Ulster are fighting on foreign fields, and
we want to see the war won. If that is
done we will have performed a useful
service. As it is, the only people who
have the opportunity of speaking to those
engaged on war work are the right hon.
Gentlemen on the other side of the House.
I hope the invitation extended to the
Prime Minister and the Minister of Commerce and Production will be availed of,
and if it is we will give them some information which otherwise might have to be
divulged on the floor of this House. I
think the Member for Pottinger was
unfairly treated regarding his Motion by
the Chief Whip, and I hope some good
result will come from his efforts.
Question put, and agreed to.

(Lord Glentoran): The prices of potatoes
to be paid to producers and by
and by consumers in Northern Ireland are fixed in

RETIREMENT OF CIVIL
SERVANTS.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Finance whether he can state if all
civil servants who have attained the age
of sixty-three years are compelled to retire, and, if not, on what specific reasons
they are retained.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): The reply to the first part of
the hon. Member's question is in the
negative since an age limit of 63 years
has not been rigidly fixed for civil
servants in the employment of the
Government of Northern Ireland. The
retirement of established civil servants is
governed by the provisions of Article 15
of the Order in Council, dated 10th
January, 1910, which lays it down that-
It shall be competent for the head
of any department to call upon any
officer of such department to retire at
any time after reaching the age of
sixty on such pension as by the length
of his service he is qualified to receive.
"Retirement shall be compulsory for
every officer
on attaining sixty-five
years of age. But in special cases the
Treasury (in Northern Ireland the
Ministry of Finance) may, at the instance of the head of a department,
extend an officer's employment for a
further period, not exceeding five
years, on being satisfied that such
officer's retirement at sixty-five would
be detrimental to the interests of the
public service."
The existing practice in the Northern
Ireland Service is to regard sixty-three
as the normal retiring age of established
civil servants, subject to the power of
heads of departments—
(a) to require any officer to retire on
attaining the age of 60 years or at any
time thereafter;
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
28 APRIL 1942
(b) to retain an officer with his consent, up to 65 years of age as a
maximum, subject to the above qualification.
As to the second part of the question,
fully efficient officers who, upon attainment of age 63, have less than 35 years'
service, are usually allowed to continue
in post until they reach such an age
(not exceeding 65 years) as will enable
them to complete that number of years'
service; and, apart from this concession
to the individual, cases arise as abovementioned in which it is desirable, in the
interests of the Service, to retain
officer in a post up to or beyond the date
of his sixty-fifth birthday.

ENLISTMENT IN NORTHERN
IRELAND.
6. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Prime Minister whether he can state the
total number of men in Northern Ireland
who have joined His Majesty's Forces
since the outbreak of war, and how many
of these joining came from Eire.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers

HOUSE OF COMMONS
The PRIME MINISTER: Complete
information is not available of the number
of men from Northern Ireland who have
joined His Majesty's Forces since the
outbreak of war.
I am informed, however, that during
the period immediately preceding the
declaration of war and the 31st March
last, over 24,000 Northern Ireland
recruits enlisted in Northern Ireland.
The hon. and gallant Member is also
aware that, in addition, there were large
numbers of Northern Ireland men in the
fighting services and mercantile marine
before the war, while many have also
entered the services from Great Britain.
I have no particulars of the number of
Eire citizens who have joined His
Majesty's Forces.
Mr. BEATTIE: In view of the statement just made that 24,000 had joined up
prior to the declaration of war, is it not a
fact that at a public meeting the Prime
Minister said that 30,000 had joined up,
and are we, as Members of this House, to
take it that only 6,000 men have joined
the forces since the outbreak of war?
The PRIME MINISTER:
No, the
figures which I have given are perfectly
accurate.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is it not a fact that
the other night, during warship week, the
Prime Minister stated that 30,000 had
enlisted in His Majesty's Forces since the
outbreak of war?
The PRIME MINISTER: Yes, I
stated a week ago there were 30,000
because, as I have stated in the answer,
there were those who joined up in Great
Britain-Northern Ireland men-who
happened to be domiciled there, and in
addition to that, large numbers were in
the forces before the war broke out.
Mr. BEATTIE: If the Prime Minister
is in a position to get the numbers of
Northern Ireland men who joined in
Great Britain, surely he is able to get the
number of Irishmen who enlisted from
Eire? Why is he afraid to divulge the
numbers that enlisted in His Majesty's
Forces from Eire?
Mr. HENDERSON: Has the Prime
Minister anything to do with Ulster,
because a very large number of Eire
citizens joined the forces in Northern
Ireland, both male and female.
The PRIME MINISTER: I have
nothing to do with what happens in Eire.
The PRIME MINISTER: I do not see
why hon. Members opposite always seem
to desire to belittle Ulster's war effort.
Mr. NIXON: Is the Prime Minister
aware that the independent district of
Shankill is the best recruiting district in
the British Empire?
The PRIME MINISTER: I am glad
to hear that.
Mr. NIXON: Did you not know it
before now, you being Prime Minister?

11. Mr. NIXON (for Mr. Midgley)
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he is aware of the fact that road
workers employed by the Fermanagh
County Council are employed for nine
hours per day, six days per week, at a
wage of 6s per day and no allowance for
holidays; whether, in view of the fact
that the lowest agricultural wage in this
area is 46s 3d per week, he will take
immediate steps to compel the Fermanagh
County Council to bring their wages up
to a level more in keeping with modern
requirements, and at the same time insist
upon the men getting an adequate annual
holiday with pay.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am informed
that as from the 1st April the rates of
wages payable to road workers have been
increased and that the rates now
applicable are:-Gangers, 7s 6d per day;
surfacemen, 7s per day; casual labourers,
7s per day; quarrymen, 7s 6d per day;
and tar handlers, 7s 6d per day.
The payment of wages to employees of
a highway authority is a matter primarily
for the authority concerned.

FUEL RATIONING.
3. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he can
make any
statement on fuel rationing as it will
affect Northern Ireland; and whether it
is proposed to carry out the administration of same with the existing staff, or
whether in the event of any further increase in staff being contemplated, he
can state what such increase is likely to
be, both in number and in cost.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: With your permission I propose to avail myself of the
opportunity afforded by the hon.
Member's question to give a brief statement of the fuel position in Northern
Ireland.
The policy of the Government in regard
to fuel is to maintain equal conditions
with Great Britain, that is to say, firstly,
to ensure maximum production and,
secondly, to provide an equitable distribution of domestic supplies.
My Ministry has in the past week had
discussions with the Mines Department,
with the coal officers of the various areas
of supply, and in particular with the
Scottish suppliers. Hon. Members will
be aware that the question of fuel supply
in Great Britain has not yet been resolved
and, consequently, the programme of
supply to Northern Ireland could only be
fixed provisionally.
I am advised that the provisional programme which has been fixed is adequate
for the needs of the country. As to the
sources of supply, hon. Members will be
aware that there has been difficulty in
inducing the consumption of South Wales
coal in this country, particularly for
domestic consumption. Owing to other
demands on this type of coal, the programme of supply from South Wales to
Northern Ireland has been cut to less
than one quarter of the amount included
in last year's programme. The deficiency
is being made good from Scotland, which
now supplies nearly 60 per cent, of our
requirements, and from the north of
England.
current week to merchants whose share of
imports recently has been relatively small
and it is proposed to bring into operation
next week an ordered apportionment of
all supplies coming into the country.
Provision has already been made for
the supply of additional coal in the
On the question of rationing of supplies
of coal for domestic purposes, my
Ministry to-day made an Order limiting
the amount which may be supplied to any
one household within a given period.
Provision is made for eating into any
substantial stocks of coal which may
exist, but no person need be without an
adequate and equitable supply. On the
general question, it has been represented
to the Mines Department that if the bulk
allocation of domestic coal to Northern
Ireland as a whole does not exceed the
amount to which we would be entitled if
we were subject to the British rationing
scheme, we will not necessarily be expected to adopt that scheme or its equivalent. It will be for us, however, to
devise our own procedure for ensuring
fair distribution amongst consumers.
I believe that if importers, merchants
and consumers act in harmony and in a
spirit of fair play, having regard to the
exigencies of the national emergency, we
can achieve equity between domestic consumers, and I have grounds for confidence
that the districts in Great Britain which
are now to furnish our supplies will live
up to their undertakings and give us our
allocations regularly and in full.

rationing will
will be extended to coal

Sir BASIL BROOKE: Yes, sir.

Ireland in connection with the war effort
necessitated this further provision. Visits
of this nature will continue, and inevitably, therefore, a certain amount of
expenditure must continue to be incurred
in the réception of these welcome visitors.
I can assure the hon. Member that any
hospitality extended is on an extremely
modest seale and that costs are kept as
low as is reasonably possible.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask

and whether he can state if the hospitality referred to is liable to coupons
or rationing, and, if so, will he inform
the House why an illegality is being done

state what measures have been taken to

have been issued which it is hoped will
have the effect of preventing any danger
to public health through allowing mosquitoes to breed in static water reservoirs
installed for fire-fighting purposes.

give the hon. Member at the moment-

saying that it would not be in the

of the medical officers of health.

The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE

PURCHASE OF EGGS.
14. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state the
reason for reverting to the purchase of
eggs by number instead of by weight, and
whether the present method is to be
maintained.
Lord GLENTORAN: This action was
taken by the Ministry of Food in order to
simplify the method of payment for eggs
and the work of the packing stations. I
agreed to fall into line in Northern
Ireland, and I do not propose to modify
the position at present.
Lord GLENTORAN: We have no
intention of putting back the hands of
the clock, but this step is necessary owing
to war conditions. I am sure my hon.
Friend will agree that if eggs are sold in
this way in connection with the food
control in England, it is necessary that
we should follow that system here during
the war. We have no intention of
remaining on this basis after the war.
Mr. NIXON: How do you know?
Mr. GAMBLE: Does the noble Lord
not agree that it may be putting the
hands of the clock back when he has
gone back on what has been done for the
last number of years?
Mr. GAMBLE: Is the Minister aware
that by so doing we have lost the benefits
of all the good work put into this matter
by the Egg Marketing Board for the last
couple of years and that we are putting
back the hands of the clock ?
Is he aware
that it is very unfair to the producers of
eggs that they should be bought by number instead of by weight, as the people
who produce the heavier eggs will only
get the same price as those who produce
the smaller eggs? Will the noble Lord
give this matter his consideration?
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Minister's statement that the Ministry of
Food found it necessary to revert to the
old way of selling eggs, is that not
sufficient justification for sacking the Egg
Marketing Board along with some other
