Lord GLENTORAN: No. It is very
necessary to keep our machinery in being
so that when the war is over we can
continue our forward movement in agriculture.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Minister's statement of what will happen
when the war is over, how does the
Minister, or in fact anyone, know what
will happen when the war is over? If the
system invented by the Marketing Board
was found to be inadequate and impossible during an emergency why should the
Board be kept in existence for the
purpose of drawing money and reverting
back to it when there is no emergency?
REGISTRATION OF POULTRY-
KEEPERS AND SUPPLIES.
15. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state if
there are any differences between the
Northern Ireland scheme and the scheme
in operation in Great Britain, in connection with the registration of poultrykeepers and rationed feeding stuff
supplies; and if so, why such differences
exist, and whether it is intended that
such differences are to continue.
Lord GLENTORAN: I assume the
hon. Member refers to the Egg Control
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
5 MAY 1942
Scheme in operation here compared with
the scheme in Great Britain.
In Northern Ireland all eggs must be
sold to licensed collectors or packers who
buy on behalf of my Ministry, as agent
for the Ministry of Food, at prices of
3s 1d and 3s per dozen for first quality
eggs.
In Great Britain producers with less
than 50 hens are not required to sell to
licensed collectors or packers. If they
cannot get their eggs taken by a collector,
however, and sell their eggs by retail
they may not legally receive more than
the prescribed maximum retail price of
2s per dozen.
There has been no need for this exemption in Northern Ireland, where a complete organisation for the collection of
eggs has for long been in existence under
the provisions of the Marketing of Eggs
Acts.
I do not intend to make any change in
the position in Northern Ireland. Producers obviously suffer no disadvantage
in being debarred from selling eggs at 2s
per dozen when they can get 3s or 3s 1d
per dozen if they sell to a collector or
packer. Nor have consumers suffered
because the egg ration has been greater
in Northern Ireland than in Great
Britain to allow for the fact that some
non-rationed eggs are available there.
With regard to the issue of feeding
stuffs, all poultry producers with eight or
more birds in Northern Ireland receive
an issue of feeding stuffs. It has been
decided in future, however, not to issue
feeding stuffs to producers with more
than 20 hens unless they are registered
with an egg collector, as producers with
more than 20 birds should normally have
surplus eggs for sale.
Mr. NIXON: Is it not a fact that
owing to the operation of these boards
and inspectors there were practically no
eggs in Great Britain or Northern Ireland all the winter?
Mr. BROWN: Will the noble Lord
agree that he cannot have it both ways,
and in view of his reply to the previous
question that he changed the system of
purchasing eggs from that of weight to
that of number in order to keep step by
step with Great Britain, will he tell us
why he is not keeping step by step now
with Great Britain in regard to these
other matters contained in this question,
especially as there is in Great Britain
exemption for holders of 50 birds, whilst
here the exemption applies only to holders
of 20 birds?
Lord GLENTORAN: I am glad to
say that we sent across to England
360,000,000 eggs last year.
That was a
very fine effort on the part of a small
province like Ulster.
Mr. BROWN: Why has the noble
Lord departed from the step-by-step
policy when he told us he had to make

to keep step by step with Great Britain?
we

have not changed in this instance is because we are far in advance of the people

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Sir

The arrangement for the allocation of
cotton yarn and staple fibre to Northern
Ireland is intended to utilise Northern
Ireland's textile capacity and at the same
time to release labour for other forms of
work in the North-Western area of Great
Britain. Just as it may be necessary to

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Ways and Means,
Considered in Committee.
[Sir ROBERT LYNN in the Chair.]
Financial Statement, 1942-43.
of America, of the ruthless steps they
have had to take in order to provide the
necessary means of carrying on the war.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): During the last few weeks we
have heard both from the British
Chancellor of the Exchequer and
from the President of the United States
The figures now reached by these
national Budgets, I dare say, in years
gone by would have appeared far beyond
the means of the different countries, and
the response made by the taxpayers is, I
think convincing testimony of the general
determination to submit to whatever
sacrifice may be necessary in order to
ensure a successful issue to the present
struggle. The old sources of revenue
undoubtedly have been exploited, I should
think it would be almost impossible to
deny, to their utmost limit, and so the
necessity has become more than ever
inevitable to broaden the basis of taxation, and to secure as even a distribution
of the burden as possible.
The Chancellor of the British Exchequer
has adopted the policy of meeting almost
half of the annual expenditure from
revenue and the remainder by borrowing.
The imposition of the main revenueproducing taxes does not fall within the
powers of the Parliament of Northern
Ireland, but the subscribing to the
various Government issues is a matter
that rests upon our own local organisations in Northern Ireland and the
willingness of our people to invest their
savings in these Government issues.
War weapons weeks and warship weeks
have been held, in which the different
cities and towns and rural districts
throughout Northern Ireland each vied
with the other in subscribing according to
their means for various Government loans
and savings certificates, and deposits in
Savings Banks. In various ways Northern
Ireland has made a commendable effort,
and everyone who has contributed must
have a feeling of considerable satisfaction
in the proof thus afforded that in addition
to tax revenue, to which so many are
compulsory contributors, much has been
done voluntarily in the way of subscribing
to these issues.
In thus subscribing contributors can
entertain a feeling of a double gratification in that, while helping the country in
its need, they are at the same time making
a very sound investment of their savings.
So far as the attraction of investment
goes, I consider that that of the savings
certificates is the most satisfactory to the
greatest number. These certificates not
The Budget-
Minister's Statement
12 MAY 1942
only afford a means of saving to the
smaller contributor; they provide for the
automatic accumulation of the interest of
the sum originally invested, and further
than that they should serve as an inducement to the investor to save his money
now when it can only be spent to very
poor advantage, until some time in the
future when, as we all hope and expect,
peace and normal business conditions and
supplies of material will once again be
restored and money can be spent to so
very much better advantage.
To the now very numerous body of
income-tax payers it may be pointed out
that the income-tax concession as regards
interest earned on savings certificates gives
the equivalent of an investment at over
six per cent, if allowance is made for tax.
During the past financial year over
£3,000,000 has been invested in Ulster
Savings Certificates, an increase of over
£500,000 on the previous year, bringing
the total investments in the National
Defence Issue of Ulster Savings Certificates, the whole of which has been lent to
the Imperial Exchequer for war purposes,
to £6,300,000 at 31st March last.
The total amount invested in war
securities under all headings in Northern
Ireland since the savings campaign commenced in November, 1939, is approximately £43,000,000.
Apart from the references to special
efforts, I should like to refer to the sustained effort which is procuring such
results, which could not be achieved
without the continuous work of a vast
army of voluntary workers.
But let it be said that Ulster should do
much more in this direction even without
the stimulus and competitive element of
warships weeks, and there is no need for
me to re-emphasise the warnings of the
Chancellor of the Exchequer that savings
in even greater amounts must be forthcoming if the gap between revenue from
taxation and expenditure is to be successfully bridged. I do, therefore, appeal to
everyone who can to invest the maximum
amounts in the various forms of war
savings.
Income tax, which has always been one
of the main sourees of revenue and possibly
the means by which revenue is most easily
collected, has been inereased to such an
extent that in the United States Mr.
Roosevelt has announced as his intention
that not even the very wealthiest man
should be in the enjoyment of an income
of more than £6,000 per annum after
paying taxes and in the United Kingdom
income tax and super tax have been increased to such an extent that it would
require a taxpayer to have a gross income of somewhere about sixty-five
thousand pounds a year in order to have
a free income of about £5,000 a year,
taxation taking practically the entire
balance; and it has been stated that to
take from taxpayers all their income in
excess of £2,000 a year would only increase the amount of revenue by some
22 million sterling.
By these few illustrations Members will
understand the burden of financing the
war, and while it is the task of the
Minister of Finance to gather in every
penny of procurable revenue for this one
supreme purpose, namely, to prosecute
the war, it should be the duty of everyone in whatever capacity he acts, to
lighten the burden of public expenditure
in other directions. One hears the argument so often used, that when the British
nation is expending upwards of 18 million
pounds a day, why should exception be
taken to a modest expenditure of some
thousands or even tens or hundreds of
thousands on behalf of some desirable
social benefit or the relief of privation or
disability in some form or another.
Spending 18 millions a day is a very
different matter to producing 18 millions
a day, and the National Debt which has
to be met somehow some day is accumulating at a rate that is staggering. We
must all realise that the prosecution of
the war is our supreme task, and any
additional expenditure on our local
services will only be justified in cases of
urgent need and where no large amount
is involved.
In spite of the action of the British
Government in granting very substantial
subsidies to keep down the price of bread
and other essential commodities the cost
of living and price of commodities has
undoubtedly gone up considerably, but
we should remember that the main item
in the cost of living is the cost of labour
required to produce these articles with
which life is supported. Consequently,
increase in the cost of labour must undoubtedly result in increase in the cost
of living. Further, higher wages, unfortunately, do not always result in
The Budget-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Minister's Statement
[Mr. Barbour]
greater production, and so long as human
nature is what it is, it is the necessity
to support his existence that makes man
work, and there may be a disposition for
men only to work such time as may be
necessary for them to earn enough to
meet their requirements; but in the present war the necessity for labour is not
so much to provide for one's own requirements as in order to preserve what is,
after all, the most valuable privilege we
enjoy, namely, liberty and the right to
live in accordance with our own ideals.
And now to deal with those matters
which come under our own particular
control. The Government can take considerable pride in the fact that not only
is there no increase in its borrowings at
the end of the last financial year, as compared with the last previous year, other
than borrowings of which the entire proceeds are re-lent directly to the Imperial
Exchequer for war purposes-a principle
which we intend to maintain for the war
period but that steps have been taken
to effect substantial reductions in our
existing loans outstanding, and that our
statutory sinking funds have been fully
maintained.
Some facts which may be of interest to
the Committee in this connection are as
follows. I mentioned last year that we
had set aside £500,000 towards the
redemption of £2,000,000 Ulster 3 per
cent. stock, which matures for repayment
on 1st April, 1943, and that we hoped to
accumulate the full amount required by
the redemption date. I am happy to
say that the full amount has now already
been set aside.
Northern Ireland 33 per cent. stock,
1950-54, to an amount of £213,200 was
paid off during the year.
Holders of Ulster Savings Certificates
have drawn out during the year principal
sums of £345,000, together with interest
amounting to £85,000, and this money
has been found without reborrowing or
requiring the Imperial Exchequer to go
without any part of the National Defence
Issue of Ulster Savings Certificates which
we relend to the Treasury.
Treasury Bills, issued in the course of
the year solely for the purpose of financing the uneven flow of revenue, were entirely repaid before the close of the
financial year.
It is of interest that
these Bills were placed by tender with
London discount houses at rates closely
corresponding with those for Imperial
Treasury Bills, the average rate being a
small fraction over one per cent. per
annum-a remarkable result in the third
year of the war.
Exchequer borrowings from the Government Loans Fund for housing grants,
barracks reconstruction, Bann drainage
and voluntary schools, were reduced by
a total over £138,000 in the year, and
the Government Loans Fund was able to
effect a total reduction of £267,000 in
outstanding borrowings.
The Committee will recollect that we
took power in our recent Exchequer and
Financial Provisions Act to apply revenue
arising from the repayment of issues
made under the Loans Guarantee Acts in
past years, together with sums from our
reserves, towards the extinction of the
outstanding debt on the Suspense
Account of the Unemployment Fund. At
the close of the year in this manner no
less a sum than £1,342,000 was paid off,
reducing the amount of this debt from
£2,720,000 to £1,378,000, and of the
sum repaid £667,000 represents receipts
on Loans Guarantee Account. We hope
to be in a position to extinguish the
balance in the current year. It is unnecessary for me to emphasise once again
the success which has attended our Loans
Guarantee policy, whether from the
aspects of the provision of employment,
the maintenance during a time of depression of our industries-primarily, of
course, our shipbuilding industry-the
invaluable additions to the nation's
Merchant Fleet thereby provided, or
finally the eventual emergence of substantial accruals to our Exchequer. In
spite of the criticism that has at times
been directed at these guarantees, hon.
Members will agree that the results have
proved complete justification of the risks.
undertaken. Our contingent liabilities
under the Loans Guarantee Acts, as
Members will have seen from the return
circulated, are now under £2,000,000 out
of total commitments amounting in the
aggregate to over £22,000,000, and as
regards the sum of £2,766,000, which has
been issued from the Exchequer in the
process of nursing certain companies in
default, I am glad to be able to say that
the securities handed over to us against
these payments are regarded as adequate.

In addition to the steps taken to repay

Fund, in parity with the Great Britain

to keep our fund in parity.
That these results have been attained

I am budgeting for a decrease of
£216,000 on the actual receipts for last

RESERVED REVENUE.
Turning to reserved revenue, I do not
propose to recapitulate the very clear
exposition of the changes in taxation in
the directions both of increase and concession, which was given by the Chancellor
of the Exchequer in his Budget speech,
and the estimated effects on our share of
the revenue are set out in Table VI on
page 7.
I will therefore say no more than that
the figures speak for themselves as an
index of the buoyancy of the revenues of
our Province.
CUSTOMS AND EXCISE.
Customs and excise duties, exclusive of
the purchase tax, are estimated to yield
£12,509,000, an increase of no less than
£4,379,000 over last year's estimate.
The purchase tax is expected to produce
£1,360,000, an expected increase of
£170,000.
INLAND REVENUE.
The estimated revenue from income tax
and sur-tax in the year is £12,900,000,
an estimated net increase of £2,158,000
over last year, but a substantial proportion of this amount will fall to be refunded after the war in the form of
credits in the Post Office Savings Bank.
National defence contribution and
excess profits tax are estimated to yield
£5,000,000, representing an increase of
£3,000,000, but here again a substantial
proportion will represent deferred postwar credits.
figure. The total estimated receipts from
reserved revenue produce, therefore, the
unprecedented figure of £33,604,000.
RESERVED NON-TAX REVENUE.
The Post Office revenue is estimated at
£1,780,000, showing the very satisfactory
increase of £380,000 over last year's
MISCELLANEOUS RECEIPTS.
If hon. Members will now look at Table
VII they will see that there are certain
special receipts to be taken into account
and I need only refer to the item of
£200,000 from the Road Transport
Board which reflects the improved position
of the Board.
The total revenue from all sources is
estimated at £37,381,000.
RECOUPMENT OF WAR EXPENDITURE.
Finally, we have the estimated receipt.
from the Imperial Government in recoupment of excess expenditure on services
arising out of the war to which I shall
make later reference. This year it is
estimated that our expenditure on civil
defence and other services of an
emergency nature will result in the payment to our Exchequer of £4,416,000.
Our total receipts, including the last
item, are therefore estimated at
£41,797,000.
The estimated expenditure is
£20,413,000, leaving me with a provisional balance of £21,384,000 on the
credit side of the account.
I have already made reference to the
only increase in transferred taxation
which it is proposed to introduce, namely,
in relation to the existing Entertainments
Duty. In the direction of concession, I
propose to make provision for the preservation of licences for the sale of intoxicating liquor where a business for
the purpose of which such a licence was
granted has been temporarily discontinued by reason of circumstances attributable to the war, and I am also proposing to adopt the other concessions
embodied in the British Finance Bill in
so far as they are applicable in Northern
Ireland.
I have no further changes in taxation
to announce to-day, and provision has
been made for the effect of the various
increases and concessions as regards both
transferred and reserved taxation in the
figures which I have placed before the
Committee.
As to disposal of the estimated credit
balance, I am very gratified to be able to
announce that our provisional Imperial
contribution will amount to no less than

Minister's Statement
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
£21,300,000, leaving me with an estimated surplus of £84,000.
It may be argued by some that expenditure on Northern Ireland war-time.
services which is recouped directly to our
Exchequer by the Imperial Treasury,
might properly be shown as a deduction
from our Imperial contribution in order
to arrive at a true figure of what we are
actually contributing under that head,
but an examination of the basis on which
our war finances are arranged will make
a correct interpretation of the position
apparent. Our Imperial contribution is
based on the maximum amount available,
be it great or small, after provision for
expenditure on our transferred services
according to a peace-time level and on
parallel standards with the rest of the
United Kingdom. It has been decided in
agreement with His Majesty's Treasury
that expenditure on civil defence, and
expansions in our normal services arising
from war causes should-while being
controlled in Northern Ireland and subject to the authority of this House-be a
proper subject for recoupment from the
Imperial Vote of Credit introduced for
purposes. If then we disregard
technicalities and accept the postulate
that such types of service are essentially
Imperial, it follows that we must regard
the gross figure of £21,300,000 as being
a proper reflection of our Imperial contribution for 1942-43.
war
dividuals we are contributing in taxation.
pound for pound with our fellow-citizens
in Great Britain.
The essential basis of our agreement
with the Treasury is the indissolubility of
the finances of the United Kingdom as a
whole, which, of course, carries the
implications that standards of expenditure, including expenditure on social
services, whether in war-time or in times
of peace, and assuming that taxation.
basis are similar, will be maintained in
Northern Ireland generally on an equal
footing with Great Britain. It is possible that there may be a certain amount
of disappointment among our people that
the financial contribution of our Province
made up almost entirely of war taxation,
is not even greater towards the expenses
of what we all realise to be a war for
survival, having regard to the figure of
£2,400,000,000 which is being found
this year as revenue from the United
Kingdom as a whole. We have the satisfaction that this does not detract in any
way from the knowledge that as in-
It will be realised that our Imperial
contribution is a net contribution to the
war effort and to the cost of Imperial
Services after we have made full provision
for the cost of our peace-time transferred
services and of reserved services in
Northern Ireland. I have dealt at some
length with our war-time financial relationship with the Imperial Exchequer
following upon the promise I gave to the
hon. Member for Willowfield in reply
recently to a Parliamentary question he
had put to me, and I hope that my
remarks to-day will clear up the position
in this respect.
Our gratification at the substantial increase in the size of our Imperial contribution, and our anticipations of a small
surplus of revenue over expenditure on
our local Budget, should not blind us,
however, to the fact that such a contribution could only be achieved through
the direct and indirect taxation introduced by the Imperial Government for
war purposes, and that our status of
citizens of the United Kingdom involves
us in responsibility for the maximum
financial effort, through taxation and
savings, towards the successful prosecution of the war. We have now come
through two and a half years of war and
while we hear far more criticism and complaint of the Government's management,
I consider that having regard to the grave
disturbance which has resulted to our
predominant manufacturing industry, we
have much cause for thankfulness in the
great reduction in the numbers of our
unemployed, and for a small population
the revenue of the Province reveals that
production in the Province is on a much
more satisfactory level than is SO
frequently portrayed.
I have no doubt whatever as to what
the response of the men and women of
Ulster will be to the call for even greater
efforts whether financially, or in men,
material, and services, in order that
defence may be turned into attack and
that victory, peace, and security may be
attained for our beloved Province,
Kingdom and Empire. (Cheers.)

Northern Ireland which can contribute to
that war effort. I venture to say he has
not failed.

been as good as closed.

Mr. CAMPBELL: Does the Financial
Secretary believe in taxation without

Major SINCLAIR: I think that question has already been answered. We
have representation at Westminster.
There has been a lot of talk as regards
the question of taxable capacity. Of
course, taxation is based on that taxable
capacity. Let me take an example as
far as income-tax is concerned. If the
average income in Northern Ireland is
£100 and the income-tax is 10s the Northern Ireland man has to pay £50. If
the average income in England is £1,000
the Englishman has to pay £500. That
is how the question of taxation works
out. It is a very simple example, but
it shows that it is not a question of Northern Ireland being asked to pay more
out of income than in Great Britain.
It is exactly on the same basis.
The hon. and learned Member for
Central also suggested that the increase
in the rate of entertainments tax on
cinemas and other places was going to
hit the poorer people most. Actually the
rate of increase rises steadily with the

afford to pay for the higher seats. That
is only right and proper. The hon.
Member also referred to the public debt

complete provision for redeeming that
amount in 1943. Of the war savings

British Consolidated Fund stands as

it all over there is no reason to anticipate
that the public debt is anything but
adequately covered.

know whether we are going to get rid of
them or not.
The hon. Member went on to pay a
tribute to the Minister of Commerce in
connection with the importation of cotton
yarn. I think we can pay a tribute to
the Minister of Commerce for all he is
doing. He is just as determined as the
Secretary of State for Scotland to get the
maximum amount of war production work
for Northern Ireland. He is fighting
our battles day by day, in many instances
successfully. I am sure the right hon.
Gentleman would like to be able to say
he has been successful in every case. As
it is, he has been able to achieve very
satisfactory results for Northern Ireland.
Another point which the hon. Member
touched upon was the question of
hospitals. He seemed to think that these
should be all State owned and that the
voluntary system should be dropped. I
think the voluntary system has many
great advantages, both medical and moral,
and that it would be a pity from every
point of view if that system were changed
and the hospitals became State owned.
He referred to the fact that people were
begging in the streets for pennies. I can
only say he is lucky if he gets off with a
penny, and the hospitals would be very
unlucky if everyone was like him and got
off with a penny.
Major SINCLAIR: I shall be very glad
to send a little note to the hon. Member
for South Down asking for a subscription
to a hospital in which I am interested.
The same hon. Member raised a question
about farmers' income tax. The Ministry
of Finance at the present time is looking
into the effect of the new Act on the provisions contained in the 1918 Act, and I
will communicate the result of the investigations to the hon. Member. This
point which he raised is very interesting.
Mr. BROWN: On a point of correction. I did not say I got off with a
penny. I did not disclose what I gave;
I am sure I contributed as much as the
Financial Secretary. My conscience is
quite clear on the point. I did not
reflect on the estimable collectors, but on
the system which makes the street collection necessary.
The hon. Member for Woodvale referred first of all to the local contribution for education. This does, in fact,
go
into the Exchequer, but it goes out of
it again for what are purely educational
services. It is definitely related to those
services, and as hon. Members are well
aware, the Exchequer here bears a greater
share of the cost of the educational services than is the case in Great Britain.
The mere fact that the contribution goes
into the Exchequer on one side and goes
out at the other does not mean it is a
grant in favour of the Exchequer. It
might be if the services were less than
the grant, but as it is they are very much
in excess of it.
The hon. Member went on to talk about
the Imperial contribution being required
for defence. I was sorry to see such a
defeatist attitude adopted by the hon.
Member who is usually very bellicose. I
would prefer to have heard him say that
that money should be used not only for
defence, but for attack. We are not going
to win this war if we stand on the defensive all the time; we will have to attack
as well.
Mr. NIXON: The Financial Secretary
has done what is an unusual thing for
him, he has misrepresented me. I went
the length of saying I would give
£40,000,000, but I wanted it spent the
right way.
I would vote four-fifths of
every income in Northern Ireland, including my own, to win the war. What
I wanted to do with regard to this
£21,000,000 was to build whatever kind
of ships, destroyers or cruisers, that the
Imperial Government want and hand
them over, but by no means only for
defence. I am not defence; I am always
an attacker.
Major SINCLAIR: I am glad to have
that correction from the hon. Member

for Woodvale. As I said, I was rather
make the statesorry to hear him
ment-
Mr. NIXON: I did not say it.
Major SINCLAIR: I thought the hon.
Member said it. That point raises the
same question as was raised by the hon.
Member for South Down about brick for
brick. It is steel plate for steel plate.
It is a question for the Imperial Government to decide how they wish to make
use of the industrial capacity of Northern
Ireland. If they are prepared to place
orders here for battleships, cruisers,
destroyers, or whatever we are able to
make, we shall be only too glad to give
them what we can. Certainly, as far as
the £21,000,000 is concerned, there is no
reason why we should not regard it as
being part of our contribution to the war
effort as well as what we do in the way
of producing ships and munitions of war.
We have no control over how the
£21,000,000 is spent. If we give it over
to
the Imperial Government as an
Imperial contribution it is their affair
how it is disposed of, and we can only
hope they will spend it to the best
advantage.
Of course, as the hon. Member very
well knows, we have no control over
military lorries and the amount of petrol
they use. We have control over our own
civilian vehicles, but nothing whatever
to do with Army lorries. I agree it is
wasting money, but it is entirely outside
the jurisdiction of this Parliament.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Does the hon. and
gallant Gentleman consider it satisfactory to have no control
over the
raising and spending of £21,000,000?
re-
Major SINCLAIR: As I said before,
the £21,000,000 is raised by the Imperial Government, and we are
presented at Westminster by thirteen
Members or rather eleven. The hon.
Member for Woodvale further said that
the Government deserved no credit
for thinking of the loans guarantee. I
certainly agree with him. I do not think
the Government deserve any credit for
thinking of it, but they do deserve
credit for their pluck in carrying it out,
first of all, by guaranteeing such a large
amount of money, £22,000,000, and then
in spite of considerable reverses having
the pluck to nurse
of the lame
ducks and bring them through to the
final satisfactory result we were able to
show in the White Paper presented today. With the collapse of the Royal
Mail group in 1929-30 the Government
did not lose courage but went on with
the loans guarantee, and, as I say, the
result has been the very successful one
we have been able to present to-day.

The hon. and gallant Member for
Clifton raised the question of savings
certificates. I understand the question
of extending the limit has already been
under consideration and, in the meantime
at any rate, it has been decided against.
I am sure it is a matter that will exercise
the minds of the Chancellor of the
Exchequer and the Government, but at
the moment there is no intention of
making any increase in the limit.
The hon. Member for South Armagh
referred to the Loans Guarantee Acts.
These I should point out, apply only to
industry; loans to farmers have been
provided through other machinery, as the
Committee well knows. I do not think
there was very much else in the speech of
the hon. Member for South Armagh
which has not been replied to by the
Ministers concerned with the various
points which he raised.

Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.

Oral Answers to Questions.
BELFAST TOWN CLERKSHIP.
1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
number of years up to the retirement of
Mr. Archer, that the position of Belfast
Town Clerk was held with credit by
Ulstermen; whether the short list presented by the "Big Six" includes the
name of any Ulsterman; whether the
Minister has seen the list of applicants
for the position, and whether he directly
or indirectly banned all applicants from
Ulster or applications by Ulstermen.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I am not in a
position to state the exact number of
years up to Mr. Archer's retirement that
the position of town clerk has been held
with credit by Ulstermen. I believe,
however, that the position referred to
has been held by Ulstermen for at least
100 years.
With regard to the remainder of the
question, the short list presented to the
Ministry by the special committee did.
not, so far as my Ministry is aware, include the names of any Ulstermen, nor
did the list of suitable candidates
approved of by my Department. The
latter list was prepared after an examination of all the applications for the
position.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
latter part of the Minister's reply that
the Ministry will make sure that the
person appointed should be the best
qualified person, are there not highly
qualified people in Northern Ireland,
and is it a fact that the position of town
clerk in Belfast was held by Ulstermen
for the past 100 years, and does the
Minister know of any Department in the
Belfast Corporation the supreme head
being an Ulsterman where any scandals
arose up to date?
COST OF WATER COMMISSIONERS'
The hon. Member will, no doubt,
realise that the Ministry's only desire in
the matter is to ensure that the person
appointed to this important office is the
best person that can be obtained.
PREMISES.
2. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
total cost to the public of the newlyacquired Water Office premises.
Sir DAWSON BATES: My Department has no functions in connection with
the acquisition by the Belfast Water
Commissioners of the premises referred
to. Accordingly, I am unable to give
the information asked for.
Mr. NIXON: Is the Minister not the
supreme head of local government and
does not the Minister from time to time
interfere with all local government expenditure? That being so, why is it that
he has made no inquiries about the huge
expenditure of the Water Commissioners
on this unnecessary mansion?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The hon.
Member entirely misunderstands the position. The Belfast Water Commissioners
is a public utility body formed under an
Act of Parliament. That Act gives them
certain powers, and the only authority
we have from my point of view is to ensure that there is a proper audit of the
accounts. We have no control over the
Commissioners' functions.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Minister's statement that the Belfast
Water Commissioners are a public utility
body and therefore he has no jurisdiction,
is the electricity department not a public
utility body and does not the Government exercise jurisdiction, and does not
the Minister exercise jurisdiction over
all the public bodies in Northern Ireland when it suits him?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I can only
repeat again to the hon. Member, but
perhaps he will not listen to me, that this

RELIGIOUS INSTRUCTION IN
SCHOOLS.
3. Mr. BROWN asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of Education whether her attention has been drawn
to the statement made by Chancellor
Quinn at a recent meeting of the Synod
of the Church of Ireland that in 50 per
cent. of the secondary schools of Northern
Ireland no systematic religious instruction
is given, that in those schools in which it
is given the time devoted to it is unworthy
and inadequate, that not long ago five
teacher trainees when examined in religious knowledge were unable to answer
the simplest questions, and that they had
been from two to five years at secondary
schools, and that the Minister of Education had refused to meet the views of the
recent inter-denominational deputation on
the subject; whether she can state precisely the provision made by her Ministry
for religious instruction in public elementary schools and the precise position in
regard to secondary schools; and whether
her Ministry will reconsider the whole
matter with a view to making at least the
same provision for instruction in the facts
of Christianity in the case of the secondary schools as in the case of the public
elementary schools.
EDUCATION (Mrs. Parker): In reply
to the first part of the question, I have
seen a report in the Press containing the
statements to which the hon. Member
refers.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
With regard to the second part, a
complete statement of the position in
regard to religious instruction in the
public elementary and in the secondary
schools would be too long for me to give
in reply to a question. I may say briefly,
however, that in the elementary schools
which are under the management of local
education authorities the giving of religious instruction is governed by the
statutory provisions of the Education
Acts, while in the elementary schools
under voluntary management and in the
secondary schools it is a matter for the
managers or other controlling bodies of
the individual schools concerned.
In reply to the last part of the question
my right hon. and learned Friend the
Minister of Education is inviting the attention of the governing bodies of secondary schools to the importance of this
subject.
TRACTOR TAX.
4. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Finance whether in order to increase food
and flax production in Northern Ireland,
his Ministry will accede to the request
made by many chambers of commerce and
other bodies in Northern Ireland for a
reduction of the tractor tax in the case of
farmers who carry farm produce from one
farm to another, or between the farm and
the mill.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): The answer to the hon.
Member's question is in the negative.
Mr. BROWN: Is the Minister not
prepared to reconsider this matter in view
of its important bearing on agriculture?
Will he give an assurance that he will
look into the matter again?
COAL RATIONING.
5. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he is now in a position to make a further statement regarding fuel rationing as affecting Northern
Ireland, and whether in the matter of
coal rationing, some provision will be
made to meet exceptional circumstances,

CENSUS OF UNPROCESSED FLAX.
6. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he will have a census
prepared of the amount of flax in Northern Ireland still unprocessed and not
yet made available for the mills, and in
the light of this reconsider the question
of providing more flax decorticating
factories and more flax scutching mills in
Northern Ireland, or considerably extending existing facilities if shown to be
inadequate as a result of this census.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I am advised
that, working all the year round, the
existing scutch mills and the new flax
processing factories are capable of dealing with all the flax from the 1941 crop
as well as with all that will be produced
in 1942. As the hon. Member will
appreciate, scutching must now be regarded as a continuous operation throughout the year and not, as formerly, a
seasonal one. It would not be in the
national interest, nor, in fact, an
economic proposition, to increase plant
and machinery so as to reduce the period
of working to less than twelve months.
Mr. BROWN: In order to encourage
the growing of flax will the Minister see
that this processing is expedited so that
the farmers will be able to get their
money earlier than they do at present
owing to the delay in processing?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I think
economically it is sound that these
factories should work for the whole 12
months rather than for broken periods.
Mr. JOHNSTON: May I ask the right
hon. Gentleman why more of these
central factories have not been put up by
the Government in order to enable the

RATIONING OF COAL.
7. Mr. JOHN BAILEY asked the Minister of Commerce whether he is aware of
extreme dissatisfaction in rural districts
owing to the rationing of coal; whether the
farmers who used about 20 tons of coal
yearly to do necessary work will now be
confined to six tons, while the persons who
never bought more than six tons, and in
some cases much less, will be entitled to
six tons if they can use them; and
whether any allowance is made for coal to
be used in the boiling of swill and
potatoes for stock feeding.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The present
temporary restrictions are confined to coal
for domestic purposes only and do not
relate to fuel for industrial or agricultural
purposes. The latter part of the hon.
Member's question does not, therefore,
arise.

of His Majesty's subjects in Northern

COMPANIES.
8. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he can now give the
names of the members of the Antrim
Electricity Distribution Company, as
requested on 5th May, 1942, and, if so,
whether he can state the names and
addresses of, and the number of shares
held respectively by the members of the
Antrim Electricity Supply Company;
and whether he can state whether either
or both of these companies are registered
in London and are allowed by the
Ministry to default with impunity to the
detriment, loss and injury of a number
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The Antrim
Electricity
Distribution Company,
Limited, was registered in London and,
under the Companies Act, 1929, is under
obligation to furnish the Registrar of
Companies in England with a list of its
members each year.
The Antrim Electricity Supply Company was incorporated by an Act of this
Parliament in the year 1928 and is not
under any obligation to register a list
of its members at any Companies Registration Office. No lists of the names or
addresses of these companies are available
here.
As regards the concluding part of the
hon. Member's question, I cannot accept
his version of the situation. In framing
its draft Special Order the Distribution
Company voluntarily included in the
schedule the names of twenty-four towns
and villages in which the company was to
lay down suitable distributing mains
within two years, that is to say by the
year 1934. This programme has been
carried out in twenty-one of these towns,
leaving three towns still to be dealt with.
But the Distribution Company was forbidden by the terms of its Special Order
to supply electricity in these towns until
it had given the existing undertakers,
who were supplying electricity, an opportunity to sell their undertakings on terms
to be agreed, or, failing agreement, by
arbitration. The negotiations to that end
were protracted and had not reached
finality at the outbreak of war.
I may add that as against the default
in these three cases the company have
provided a supply of electricity in various
towns and villages which were not named
in the schedule.
Mr. NIXON: With regard to the
Minister's statement that one of these
companies is registered in London and
that the names and addresses are there
and not available in Northern Ireland,
does not the Minister know that the
names of the shareholders of these companies can be got on request for a nominal
sum, and is it a fact that the Minister
allows companies that he knows nothing
about to operate in Northern Ireland and
get public privileges and refuse to carry
out their obligations? He does not know
that.

HACKNEY MOTOR CAR PERMITS
TO DRIVE IN EIRE.
9. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he is aware that the
Department of Supplies in Dublin has
informed Northern Ireland hackney
motor owners that permits to drive in
Eire territory can no longer be given;
and whether, in view of the fact that this
step will take away more than half the
already restricted livelihood of many of
these men, and that hackney motor
owners from Eire can still drive in
Northern Ireland, he will make the necessary representations to have the withdrawal of the facility referred to modified
as far as possible.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend to reply.
I am aware from references in the Press
that under the Emergency Powers
(Mechanically-Propelled Vehicles) Order,
1942, the Government of Eire have restricted the use in Eire of Northern
Ireland Private cars and taxis.
I have, however, no information as to
how far the restrictions will impose hardship on owners and drivers of hackney
vehicles.
The hon. Member will appreciate that
the recent drastic cut in the basic petrol
ration for private cars, and the further
cut which will operate from the 1st July
in Northern Ireland, will, of necessity,
bring hackney vehicles more business than
at present and will possibly more than
compensate for any loss of traffic into
Eire.
At any rate, the action suggested by
the hon. Member would not improve
matters, because hackney vehicles from
Eire are not entitled to stand or ply for
hire in Northern Ireland, and the only
occasion on which such a vehicle can carry
passengers here is when it brings into and
out of Northern Ireland some person who
has hired it in Eire.
Mr. NIXON: Is it not a fact that
hackney omnibus vehicles from Eire cannot operate in Northern Ireland seeing
that they cannot run without petrol?

DEFECTIVE AIR-RAID SHELTERS.
13. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Public Security whether he
can state the exact number of air-raid
shelters inspected and found defective,
and the number of building contractors
who have not carried out the work
acording to the Government specification.
Mr. GRANT: The total number of
communal shelters which have been built
in Belfast is approximately 6,500. Nine
hundred and thirty-eight were built in
the months immediately following the
heavy raids, when adequate supervision
was admittedly not available. These 938
shelters have now been specially examined,
and it has been ascertained that 146 of
them were defective in greater or less
degree. Thirty-seven of these required
to be demolished and rebuilt. The remainder (a number of which were only
slightly defective) are being brought up
to specification.
The cost in all cases is being charged
against the contractors responsible, of
whom there are 18 in all concerned.
Special examinations have failed to
disclose a single defective shelter amongst
those built outside the period in question,
numbering about 5,500.

MORRISON SHELTERS.
16. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister
of Public Security whether he has given
orders that where Morrison shelters have
been issued to the occupiers of large
three-storied terrace houses, such shelters
should be erected in those houses instead
of in suitable out-offices, and, if so,
whether he has considered the danger of
a large house falling on the shelters and
occupants.
These shelters are, however, intended
for use within the protection normally
provided by the walls of an ordinary
house against blast and splinters; many
out-offices do not provide equivalent protection and are not therefore suitable.
Mr. GRANT: The answer to the first
part of the question is in the negative.
The shelters are specially designed to
withstand the debris load caused by the
collapse of a three-storey house, and are
not issued for use in houses containing
more than three storeys.
Mr. NIXON: Arising out of the reply,
does not the Minister with his own good
commonsense know that if a large threestoreyed house falls on a shelter full of
people they would be smothered long
before they could be dug out, and does

gone about these houses using his name
-not his christian name but his authority
-to say that where there was a suitable
garage and the shelter was put into that
and not into the three-storeyed house, it
would be taken away within fourteen
days?
Mr. GRANT: The hon. Member must
know from experience that to put a
Morrison shelter into a garage would be
an absurdity. There would be no sense
in it, because if there was blast within a
reasonable distance it would take the
whole garage away, but a three-storeyed
house, and I speak from personal
experience, is a fit and proper place in
which to put a Morrison shelter.
Mr. NIXON: I am surprised at the
Minister's opinion. That is all I can
say.

ought to refrain from talking as often as

in the Dominions in case you have any

that has been revised under the

rates which are applied to all industries

they lay down a distinct minimum for

Zealand does not exceed 40 hours, and it
is increasingly being applied from time

come to be revised.

In the first place, we have endeavoured

We want this legal minimum wage
based upon a decent standard of living
for all the producing elements in the community. In other words, we want a social
standard that will maintain in comfort
and decency every man, wife, and family
irrespective of profession or occupation.
That is what we mean by a legal minimum
wage. We do not intend that that legal
minimum wage should endanger what I
would call the higher-paid worker. Over
and above that, we want to consider the
value that the individual is giving to the
State, and, if we demand that, we are

THE COAL RATIONING SCHEME.
6. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Commerce whether he has
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Lieut.-Colonel Gordon]
received a resolution from the Council of
the Northern Ireland Coal Importers'
Association expressing the opinion that
the present rationing scheme of half a ton
of coal in five weeks, irrespective of the
size of the household or whether there is
any alternative method of heating and
cooking, is so manifestly unfair, that they
call upon the Ministry of Commerce to
abandon the scheme without delay, and
allow the trade to ration their customers

point out that there is neither transport
nor petrol to permit of the scheme being
worked, and what action the Ministry
propose to take in the circumstances.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Sir
Basil Brooke): I have received a copy of
the resolution to which the hon. and
gallant Member refers. As I explained
yesterday in answer to a question by the
hon. Member for South Down, this
scheme is merely a temporary one, is in
general similar to that in force in Great
Britain, and has been introduced here to
prevent the position from deteriorating
until a settlement is reached on the
question of coal supply in Great Britain.
As soon as circumstances warrant such a
step, the present system will be reviewed
by my Ministry in conjunction with the
Advisory Committee consisting of prominent members of the body to which the
hon. and gallant Member refers.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Would the
Minister inform the House how people
can obtain these half ton loads if the
Ministry of Transport has advised that
delivery of half ton loads is a waste of
transport?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I admit those
difficulties, but the position is that no
more half tons of coal can be made available without seriously jeopardising the
coal position. That is the real crux.
Mr. BROWN: Might I ask the Minister
to answer a question I put yesterday
arising out of this matter, namely, could
he tell us if before a definite rationing
scheme is embarked upon the House will
get the opportunity of discussing the
matter as has been done at Westminster?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: Yes, sir.
A VOLUNTARY LAND SERVICE.
Mr. BROWN asked the Prime Minister
whether he will cause the recent joint
appeal by himself, the Minister of Agriculture, and the Minister of Commerce
and Production for increased flax production to be followed by a similar joint
appeal for volunteers from every centre
in Northern Ireland for the Voluntary
Land Service so that all of the food and
flax crops may be successfully garnered;
whether in view of the recent suggestion
in the House that the civil servants employed by the Northern Government,
totalling almost seven thousand should be
encouraged to lend a hand in harvesting
operations this year, he will cause to be
circulated to all members of the civil service the Ministry of Information's account
of the excellent lead given in this matter
by the staff of the Ministry of Agriculture
at present stationed at Cookstown, who
have lost no time in forming themselves
into a land volunteer group to assist in
their spare time; and whether the Government will advise the fullest possible following of this admirable example and will
facilitate it in every possible way in all
departments of the civil service.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Lord Glentoran): I have been asked to
reply.
It is not proposed at this stage to take
the action suggested by the hon. Member.
Excellent progress is being made with the
Voluntary Land Service Scheme and, as
the hon. Member is doubtless aware, it is
being taken up with enthusiasm by local
authorities and the various branches of
the Ulster Farmers' Union. No useful
purpose would, therefore, be served at
this stage by flogging a willing horse.
With regard to the last part of the hon.
Member's question, offers of help have
already been received from branches of the
Civil Service and I am confident that the
Civil Service will, as in the past, play its
full part in the service of the country.

economy. Therefore, I object to that
salary of £939 altogether.
Then we come down to the doorkeeper. He gets an allowance of £10.
Two messengers get £434, and four other
messengers get £670, and so on. The
whole idea running through the Government Estimates and Government administration is to keep down the under-dog.
The messengers and porters have to be
here all the time and not merely when
Parliament is sitting, and they get this
magnificent allowance for their clothing.
I wonder how they will be able to get this
fancy dress at all in the future. They
certainly did not get it in the past on
their allowance. I would not object at
all if that was the rule of the House, and
if you had not some men over-paid and
some men under-paid, but a certain class
must be always overpaid. I would like to
see less of that, but the Government is
not going the right way about lessening
it.
There is a big change in the attitude
of the people towards these high salaries.
The Government know it and I know it,
because I tried it recently before 1,500
people. There is no propaganda that cuts
like salaries. I have tried it often, even
on the old Unionists. When I rub it in
I can see their countenance change. That
is the stuff. It is ridiculous to see the Prime
Minister running about through Northern
Ireland shouting "Save for Victory "
and having a Serjeant-at-Arms in this
House getting £939 a year.
I have heard
that discussed in many places, although
up to the moment it is not a subject that
I myself have introduced outside this
House. That is one thing I have not
introduced outside this House. I have

Mr. BROWN: The Financial Secretary

I wish to say that this lethargic spirit
continued throughout the proceedings. I
wish to make it clear that I make no

these important Estimates. We are
dealing with over sixteen million pounds.
A suggestion was made in reference to the
rules, regulations and orders that Members of this House had an opportunity of
seeing them and knowing about them
before they were published in the newspapers and conveyed to the public. That
is not so. Under delegated powers from
the Imperial Government those orders are
not brought to our notice in any shape
or form until they are published.
I suggest to the Prime Minister that in
future, in regard to these rules, regulations and orders something should be done
so that this House may consider them
before they actually become law. If that
were done it would be for the good of
the Prime Minister, the Government, the
House, and everybody concerned. In the
majority of cases under the present system, we have no knowledge until the
orders are published. I make no apology
for again asking the Prime Minister to
consider this matter. There is tremendous dissatisfaction in the country at the
present time, and I want him to know
about these things. The Coal Rationing
Order and the Eggs Control Order were
not brought to our notice in any shape or
form. It was only to-day that the
Minister of Commerce, in reply to a
question by me, told the House that we
would be given an opportunity of discussing the Coal Rationing Order before
it was made. The Prime Minister would
save himself much trouble and bother if
he devised ways and means whereby he
would make all the hon. Members responsible for everything that is done,
including these rules, regulations, and
orders.

Major SINCLAIR: With your permission, Sir Robert, I propose to include

they desire further information, or with
which they do not agree. I shall therefore speak in more general terms of the
activities of the Ministry, and I hope to
dispel some apprehensions and misapprehensions which appear to exist in
certain quarters.
I wish to refer in the first place to the
burning question of the increase in the
Civil Service which has arisen from war
causes. Recruitment and control of this
service is the primary responsibility of
my Ministry through its Establishment
Branch. Hon. Members will, no doubt,
have seen in the Press some time ago,
when discussions about fuel rationing in
Great Britain were taking place, a suggestion that in order to administer it some
15,000 clerks would be needed, and it is
a fact that the more our daily lives are
controlled, what we eat, what we drink,
what we wear, how we get from place to
place, and so on, restrictions which we
gladly accept in the knowledge that they
are necessary in these times, the more
we are thus controlled and rationed the
more people are required to ensure that
we get our fair share and no more of
what is going.
We here are under practically the
same restrictions as those in the rest of
the United Kingdom, and this Government, acting as agents for Imperial
departments, is operating many of the
controls. There are, of course, others
which are made effective direct from

I am not in a position to speak with

schools, potato and flax factories; the

Hon. Members are aware of the work that

Naturally this increase in responsibility

Remember that I have no objection to

these adventurers who have got the

Welcome to American Troops.
Mr. NIXON: I have pleasure in
moving this Motion which I am satisfied
will be passed unanimously. It reads:
"That this House welcomes the
arrival of the American Troops in Northern Ireland, and is pleased to note
that the Government and people are
doing, and will do, their best to make
all ranks as happy as possible; and that
Mr. Speaker convey this Motion to
all concerned in whatever manner he
considers most appropriate.'
As I said every man in Ulster worthy of
the name of Irishman will be in
favour of this Motion. There are a great
many reasons one might urge in favour
of it, but the first and foremost is that
the American Troops are here to defend
the cause of liberty, justice and right—
(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-as they
are well competent to do. We also welcome them because we have a lot in
common with them, and because we owe
a lot to America. As long as I remember
the surplus population of Ireland, north
and south, emigrated to the U.S.A.,
Canada, Australia, and New Zealand,
but principally to the U.S.A. from
Southern Ireland. As to the part of the
country that I come from it seemed looking back on it that everyone when he
came to a certain age went to the U.S.A.,
and the first message that the parents
received was that they had got work the
next day. The same applies, of course,
to Canada and Australia.
America is in the war. There was a
most treacherous attack made upon her
by Japan-no other treachery like it in
the world. In Australia the people are
in imminent danger of invasion and destruction, though I am satisfied they will
ward it off. But the danger is there.
Their leader is Mr. Curtin. I do not
know anything about that gentleman
except that he is a great leader and that
Curtin is a South of Ireland name. I
know that. Therefore, either he or his
ancestors went to Australia from Southern
Ireland. But the thing I wonder at
and cannot help wondering at is that
while Australia is fighting for its life the

First and foremost I had to find the
origin of the disturbance. To no one in
this House will I give a higher position
in advocating a National Fire Service
than myself. I am a nationaliser as far
as the Fire Service is concerned. I care
not about local or other authorities. The
Fire Service is now a national service.
It should always have been that, and I
hope it will continue to be one.
I now present it in the form of this
Motion urging that a Committee of this

and it is not a light disturbance, in our
National Fire Service. If allowed to

After a week or ten days of nationalisation it was found that Mr. White's

divisional officers, and Mr. White was

I think hon. Members will agree with

is divided up into divisions or battalions,
and the men in charge are responsible for
the training. The general is responsible

the brigades coming from all places and
at all times. He did it so often that the

Wednesday, 27th May, 1942.
The House met at Two of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answer to Question.
TRAVEL VOUCHERS FOR WAR
WORKERS.
Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Labour whether his attention has been
called to the announcement made by Mr.
Bevin, Minister of Labour in the Imperial
Parliament, with regard to the granting
of travel vouchers to transferred war
workers twice a year in the summer, and
whether he will make representations to
the Imperial authorities to secure some
alteration in the regulations which prevent Northern Ireland war workers in
Great Britain availing themselves of two
such vouchers in the summer months, as
they are allowed to travel home only once
every six months.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): The announcement about cheap.
travel vouchers for transferred war
workers to which the hon. Member refers
in his question was not overlooked by me,
and I may say that the matter has
already been under discussion with the
Ministry of Labour and National Service
in Great Britain. I will be glad to communicate with the hon. Member as soon
as a decision is reached on the matter.

The MINISTER OF PUBLIC
SECURITY (Mr. Grant): First of all,
I should like to say a few words in explanation to the House of the form in
which the Estimates for the services
under my control are presented to the
Committee. The precedent set last year
has been followed, and it will be
seen that in the case of Vote No. 1,
which provides the necessary money for
the staffing of the Department, the
Estimate is set out in full detail. When
we come, however, to Vote No. 2, which
provides the money for the Civil Defence
services themselves, the Vote merely provides for the total net sum required for
all the services combined.
I need not elaborate the reasons which
have led to the adoption of this course.
Far be it from me to withhold
inany
formation from the Committee which I
felt myself at liberty to give them. But,
if hon. Members will consider this
matter, they will realise that the publication in the volume of the Estimateswhich it is open to any person to buyof full details of the precise amount
which was being spent in Northern Ireland on every particular service would
be, to say the least of it, most unwise.
Having said so much I would, however, like to explain to hon. Members
that, in submitting the Estimates for the
approval of the Ministry of Finance, the
normal peace-time procedure has been
observed. The appropriate sum has been
allocated to each sub-head of the Vote as
set out at the bottom of page 169 of the
Estimates, and in due course my Ministry
will have to account to the Comptroller
and Auditor-General and to the Public
Accounts Committee for the expenditure
upon each sub-head in relation to the
amount which has been approved by the
Ministry of Finance as the appropriate provision for the individual service concerned.
Meanwhile, I can only apologise to the
House for the fact that I am unable to
give them the amount of detailed information of the proposed expenditure which
I should otherwise have liked to do, but

In the case of my own Department I
am happy to say that the spirit is good.
All are anxious to pull their weight, and
a great deal of willing and unselfish extra
effort is put into the job which is beyond
what is covered by the mere rules and
regulations. In turning to Civil Defence
matters generally, I should like at the
outset to pay a tribute to the local
authorities for the willing and helpful

-the Civil Defence Authorities in the
two cities, Belfast and Londonderry, and
the various borough, urban and rural
district councils that the immediate
burden of organising the Civil Defence
services in their respective areas lies.
With very few exceptions they have
nobly faced up to their tasks. It has
not been an easy job for them. Many
of them have had to endeavour, with
small staffs and few resources of their
own, to cope with an immense volume of
additional work which the
war has
thrown upon them, not only in connec-
Sometimes from debates in this House
one would be inclined to believe that the
Ministry and the local authorities spent
all their time having arguments with one
another. That is by no means a true
picture of the facts as they are.
Indeed,
I am happy to say that the relations
between my Department and the local
authorities taken as a whole are exceedingly happy, and I appreciate that credit
for this is in large measure due to the
local authorities themselves and their
officials. The system of payment of
grants has been improved, and as a result local authorities have been relieved
of what had previously constituted a
hardship, in that large sums in respect of
Civil Defence expenditure were charged
against local rates pending the payment
of the appropriate proportion of grant
from the Ministry. Payments on account
of grant are now made in advance on
estimated expenditure quarter by quarter,
a system which is much more equitable
to all concerned, and, I believe, has met
with general satisfaction.
some
There is no doubt, however, that the
burden of Civil Defence organisation
presses very hardly on
of the
smaller areas. It has, therefore, been
the policy of my Ministry to encourage
in suitable cases the grouping together of
adjoining local authorities for the purpose
of developing a common Civil Defence
scheme, or, at any rate, sharing the
services of Civil Defence staffs. Several
arrangements of this sort have been made
during the past year and are working
very successfully indeed.
There are obvious advantages to be
gained. Authorities by joining together
can, for instance, obtain the services of
qualified men who would not be available
at the salaries which one authority alone
would be justified in paying, and, by
bringing the Civil Defence services in the
several areas under one control for training and operational purposes, greater
efficiency is undoubtedly achieved than
would be obtained in a small area.
Generally speaking, grouping arrangements do tend to make the burden on
local rates-and indeed upon the Exchequer-less onerous than separate and
individual arrangements for every single
local authority.

The general financial basis of Civil
Defence is kept constantly under review,
and I think it is accepted that every en-
Ideavour has been made to achieve a fair
distribution of the cost as between the
ratepayer on the one hand and the taxpayer on the other. Many of the supply
difficulties which existed a year ago and
which were cramping the development
and operation of the services have been
resolved. Essential equipment is now
available in reasonable quantities to meet
the needs of all the services, and supplies
of the new battle dress uniform are in
process of being received and are being
issued to those local authorities who have
decided to equip the services in their
districts with it.
Good progress has been made with
what I might call the bricks and mortar
side of Civil Defence. It has been found
necessary to devote a considerable
amount of attention to the accommodation provided for the services generally
throughout the Province. In a great
many cases the accommodation, whilst
deemed sufficient in the preparatory
period before we had actually experienced
raiding on a heavy scale, was definitely
below the standards which were proved
to be necessary when the services were
projected into the operational stage.
Wardens' posts, first aid posts, gas
cleansing stations, report and control
centres have all received attention, and,
despite the prior demands of the fighting
services both for accommodation and for
materials, I am, on the whole, reasonably
satisfied with what has been achieved. A
certain amount still requires to be done,
however, before I shall be able to say
that the job has been completed to my
satisfaction, and, of course, experience
obtained in future raids may always lead
to changes in design and construction.
people well up to the standard of anything that has been provided elsewhere.

will permit me to say a word about airraid shelters. The subject has been very
much in the forefront in debates in this

rather hysterical statements have been

achieved, the vast majority of it excellent
construction providing shelters for our
It is true that in the few months
immediately following the heavy raids on
Belfast a number of shelters, representing
very small proportion of the total
number provided in the city, were not
built in strict accordance with the
specification. I do not want the Committee to regard me as excusing bad

being taken to have all cases of defects

On the operational side of the services
advantage has been taken of the lessons
learned from the raids here and elsewhere
to develop training and technique so as
to make the services fitted and capable to
the highest degree of performing their
tasks when the enemy renews his attacks.
Every month a conference of the A.R.P.
officers of the Province is held under the
chairmanship of an officer of my Department, at which all sorts of miscellaneous
problems arising out of Civil Defence
work are discussed. These conferences
have proved extremely valuable, in that
the experience of each is made available
to all, and fresh ideas are discussed and
developed for the common good.
I often wonder whether hon. Members
really appreciate what a large and
complex organisation the Civil Defence
services really are. Most people know a
certain amount about the wardens and
the casualty services. Then there are the
rescue and decontamination services, the
men who deal with demolition and clearance, the drivers and transport officers
attached to the various services, and last,
but certainly by no means least, there
the many schemes for providing
assistance to the population against the
effects of bombing which, for want of a
better name, are all grouped together
under the heading of welfare. There is
doubt that meeting the ordinary
human needs of people who have suffered
from the effects of bombing is one of the
largest and most difficult problems that
have to be faced.

To meet this problem Civil Defence
has worked out a number of sensible
schemes designed to help the man or
woman in distress. One of the first ideas
was the provision of rest centres to which
people who had been bombed out of their

money.

One of the biggest responsibilities of
my Ministry is, of course, the new
National Fire Service. Immediately the
Fire Services Bill became law I put in
motion the machinery to take over the
regular Fire Brigade and the Auxiliary
Fire Service in Belfast and a small
surrounding area. This step was taken
on the 1st April, and since then the new
service has been extended to the Lisburn
area, and more recently still to Londonderry, Limavady, and Strabane. I feel
that this new national service is facing
up to its difficulties in a manner which
reflects much credit on its commander
and officers. I hope that it will soon be
taking direct responsibility for all fires,
both air raid and ordinary, in every part
of the Province.

I am budgeting for some additional

Needless to say, every small town and

I shall also be spending money on the

I have not said a great deal about
money in presenting these Estimates,
because I feel that the money end of
Civil Defence is not the important thing.
The Government can provide the necessary equipment: it can provide the pay
of the full-time workers who take the first
brunt of aerial attack; it can provide air
raid shelters; it can pay grants to local
authorities to help them in organising
their areas, But all that is only the bare
skeleton of civil defence.
Civil defence does not come to life
until the people themselves, in their
houses, in their streets, in their villages,
in their towns, get together and use the
facilities which have been provided.
Civil defence is not bricks and mortar, or
equipment, or organisation. It is the
courage and resource and determination
of the people themselves.
I cannot buy these qualities-they are
part of our Ulster character; but if they
are not made available freely and willingly then there is nothing that we can
do about it. In every part of our cities,
towns and villages there is, I am glad to
say, an army of willing volunteers whose
devotion to their country and to the protection of their neighbours is without
money and without price. Those are the
poeple who carry the real burden of civil
defence; perhaps they carry it more
readily and more contentedly in the peak
of battle, as they did in April and May
of last year, than they do to-day when we
have had a long spell of freedom from
enemy attack.

I shall do what I can to remove any cause

Our people can do more for themselves

I believe that ordinary blast could not

know that nothing can stand up to a
direct hit. There is no dispute about
that, but building a shelter is not like
building an aeroplane.
There is nothing very much in the
whole thing; nothing that any architect
should not know all about-just bricks,
sand, cement, and wire reinforcement.
For years and years the Antrim and
Down County Councils have been making
posts for palings and for hanging gates
out of reinforced cement, and you can
hardly break them. They last for ever
and ever, and for the last 12 or 14 years
the piling of buildings in the city of
Belfast that used to be done with timber
have been done with reinforced concrete.
They are strong, and never rot.
I am

have had a certain amount of experience

Another point arose in yesterday's
debate that no one should be asked to
be responsible for administration without
authority. That is a fundamental
principle. I would say that no man worth
his salt, no man worth a damn, would
undertake responsibility without authority.
That is cardinal principle in any
administration. In the debate yesterday
on the Fire Services it was revealed that
the commanders of these services were
not responsible for the training of their
men. I made a note of that at the time.
So here you have got a man, who will
have to take the men into action against
fires and put them out. But the man
responsible for dealing with them, the
commander, apparently from what the
Minister said yesterday, is not responsible
for training the men to put these fires
out. In other words, you have got an
army commander who commands the
army in action without responsibility.
The commander should be responsible
for everything under his command.

no responsibility without

Taking the last point first, I thought I

these old shelters not because they were

war lasts so long, pull these new shelters
down and build even better ones. We
will, in other words, keep abreast of the
times. That is all we have been doing in
regard to public shelters.

The hon. and gallant Member for East

we have to be satisfied that each scheme

is the time I spoke in this House-a deputation of the residents came to me and told
me what was happening in the erection of
the shelters. I asked them to find the
inspector. I said they might get him at

Estimates

Civil Defence Services

they did find him. He came over to one

Those shelters never had accommodated
anyone.
There had been no blitz since
the shelters were erected. I do not want
to go too far in this matter as proceedings in court are pending. The people
never had recourse to them, but they had
watched the erection of the shelters from
their foundation and were dissatisfied.
They approached me about the matter so
that I could bring it to the notice of the
proper authority. I thought there was
going to be some reform and waited to
give every opportunity to the contractor
to do the work properly. When he had the
shelters finished the people said they would
not go into them if they were the last place
in the world to escape from bombs. That
is what brought the matter to a head.
Inspector McConnell was one of the men
who came over one day, but the people
could not find the other inspector. It
was the people found the shelters in my
division defective. It was not the
technical experts in the Ministry.

1. Mr. GAMBLE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state
the grounds on which he refused to recommend to the Petroleum Officer that
approval be given for the storage and
supply of petrol by Messrs. Faulkner
Bros., Railway Road, Castlederg, and
whether he will now reconsider his
decision.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): There has been no
change in the situation in regard to
petrol supplies at Castlederg since the
Petroleum Department decided on the
essential requirements of the area, and,
therefore, no grounds exist on which such
recommendation can be justified.
Mr. GAMBLE: Is the Minister aware

up to the Appeals Tribunal by the

out the need for it in Castlederg?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have no

if there are any other special circumstances I will do my best to make the
recommendation.

Prime Minister whether he can state
which Minister of the Government is

up the "Invasion Committees" in conjunction with the military authorities.
The PRIME MINISTER: This is an
Imperial service, as my hon. and gallant
Friend knows, and Invasion Committees
are being set up by the military authorities in Northern Ireland. The Northern
Ireland Home Defence Executive, whose
functions I described to the House in my
statement on 1st April last, is the body
through which the necessary co-ordination is secured in this as in other matters
affecting the interests either of the armed
forces or of the civil administration.

Minister give the names of this Northern
Ireland Executive Committee, which is

authorities.
