MILK SPILT OR LOST IN TRANSIT.
16. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state if
milk spilt or otherwise lost in transit by
collectors on behalf of the Ministry is
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
2 JUNE 1942
borne by the producers; and if so,
whether he can devise a scheme by which
the collector would satisfy himself at
time of taking over milk from the producer as to the quantity of milk in the
cans, and give a receipt accordingly, on
which payment to the producer would be
made.
Mr. MAGINESS: I have been asked
to reply.
Milk is not collected on behalf of the
Ministry. The price paid to the producer by the Ministry is on the basis that
delivery is made by him to the order of
the Ministry, and it is open to the producer to deliver the milk himself or to
arrange for the delivery. The question
of spillage or loss in the course of collection is accordingly a matter between the
producer and the person or firm who
carries the milk.
Mr. NIXON: Is it not a fact that this
milk to which the question applies must
be handed over to the Ministry, or someone appointed by the Ministry, and is it
not a further fact that in all commercial
transactions the person who takes
delivery is responsible at the place of
delivery, and would it not be very easy to
arrange that whoever takes delivery on
behalf of the Ministry from the producers
should check the milk in the cans and
give them a document at the time, instead of waiting until some of it gets
spilt and then giving them nothing?
Mr. MAGINESS: When the milk is
delivered to the Ministry at a certain
place, that milk alone is bought by the
Ministry, and if any milk has been spilt
before that it is a matter either for the
producer or the person who was carrying
the milk. That is not a matter for the
Ministry, who only buy when it arrives
at the place of delivery.
Mr. NIXON: Is not the place of
delivery the place where the producer
hands the milk over to the railway company or other carriers, who take it to the
depot or place appointed by the Ministry?
Mr. MAGINESS: Not necessarily.

made to suit yourselves and keep down
the producer?

May I claim that this result has been
secured by availing ourselves of every
possible opportunity to place our workpeople in employment? Even in Great
Britain, with its advantages, the live
register stands at about 130,000. Northern Ireland has been perhaps equally
affected by the restriction of purchasing
power through the application of the
rationing system, and also by the curtailment of production through restriction on raw materials; and naturally this
led to considerable unemployment. If I
had not sought openings for our people
in all quarters, the factors to which I
have referred would have raised our unemployment figures to a level that I
hesitate to think about.
Let us begin with a glance at the
general position. Leaving out those
under 16 years of age, at the outbreak
of war there were 18,041 women and
44,264 men on our register, a total of
62,305 to-day there are 18,678, made
up of 11,017 women and 7,661 men.
In Northern Ireland during the past
year we filled 77,266 vacancies-56,684
for men, 16,586 for women, 2,096 for
boys, and 1,900 for girls. This figure
represents almost a threefold turnover of
our register. I know that in the operation of placing our people on work of
national importance, they have had to
suffer inconveniences which, in peacetime, would hardly have been tolerated;
but this is a total war, and it cannot be
waged under peace-time conditions.
Not one of us is pursuing his normal
way of life. Those of us who are in the
civilian army are faced with restrictions
at every point, the men and women in
the fighting services are offering their
very lives in the war effort, and the men in
the workshops make very few complaints
as they carry out their important tasks.
I wish to stress this point: as far as is
humanly possible I have endeavoured to
mitigate the hardships caused to our
working population through having to
take up employment at a distance from
their homes. Our system of free travel
and of lodging allowances at least eases
the financial side of their burden.
I would take this opportunity of
soliciting from hon. Members in this
House their co-operation in my effort to
supply our war industries with the
requisite labour. I realise and regret the
effect on family life of asking our people
to take up work in other districts; but
so long as their services are not wanted in
the neighbourhood of their homes and are
required elsewhere, I feel that in this
life-and-death struggle I have no alternative but to ask them to accept that
employment. I agree with hon. Mem-

employment at any considerable distance
from their homes. Even the unmarried
women are apt to be needed in the family
circle to help with the housework, to
look after children, or aged or infirm
relatives.
It is not an easy task to carry on the
work of my Department in the face of
the almost insuperable difficulties.
have to encounter, but I think I am safe
in saying that we have filled our
demands for labour, if not completely,
then at least to a satisfactory extent,
although in very many instances the
employment has been in remote centres
where the problems of transport and
housing are intensified.
I would ask hon. Members to bear in
mind the factors I have mentioned: that
our registers contain, firstly, a number
of people not unemployed within the
true meaning of the word, and, secondly,
those whose efficiency is low on account
of age or disability, and, thirdly, those
who are precluded from taking employment away from their homes or whom I
am unable to place because of the lack
of lodging accommodation or transport
facilities. All these factors constitute a
very involved problem, for which there
is no easy solution.
to be made, to secure that the greatest
possible use is made of our man and
woman power in the present emergency.
I should very much like to be in a
position to tell the House of the extent
to which the problem has been met, and
of the many works for the Army, the
Navy, and the Air Ministry, for which
we have supplied labour despite our
many difficulties; but, as I have already
said, considerations of public security
prevent my doing so, and I can only ask
the Members of the House to accept my
assurance that constant effort has been
made, is being made, and will continue
We could not have attained even our
present measure of success without the
co-operation of the workers which, I am
glad to say, has been given freely by the
vast majority of our people. There were
some stoppages of work, but with one
exception they were of short duration.
In many cases, where differences of
opinion arose, we have been able to intervene successfully and arrange for a
peaceful settlement without any interruption of production.
In this connection I should like to pay
a tribute to the service rendered by the
National Arbitration Tribunal, of which
the hon. Member is a member, in deciding the issues presented to it. Its findings command universal respect, and I
feel that the community owes a debt of
gratitude to Mr. Justice Brown and his
colleagues for the painstaking and unselfish help they have given us. They
have played no small part in promoting
good-will and co-operation between
workers and employers. I am glad to
bear witness to the increasing growth of
this good spirit of mutual helpfulness,
for upon it depends our final triumph:
our triumph, not only over our immediate
enemies, but also over the evils that may
confront us when the war is won-as won
it shall be.

Ministry of Labour
Northern Ireland still have the problem
of unemployment. Why have we the
problem of unemployment? Because the
Northern Government was unprepared
for the situation as it surrounds us today. They refused to yield to the expressed will and desire of the Opposition
to provide sufficient workshop accommodation for the industrial population of
Northern Ireland. Hence they had to
revert to the most vicious system any
Government ever adopted, and that was
the breaking up of family life, the breaking up of the homes of the working-class.
people, and incurring huge expenditure
by having to charter ships, pay subsistence allowance, and rob the Unemployment Insurance Fund of the
contributions of the workers who were
shipped away. In my opinion the
Government has absolutely failed in its
duty, and the condemnation of the
people should be showered upon it at
every available opportunity. If we had
a general election the Government would
suffer defeat for its failure to recognise
its responsibilities on this question alone.
To my knowledge the Minister of
Labour has for the past eighteen years
had an uphill fight. He was prohibited
from placing the labour which he had at
his disposal into industry, and the reason
he was prohibited from doing that was
the failure of the Cabinet of Northern
Ireland to demand from the British
Exchequer the same conditions of citizenship as applied to those in Great Britain.
In looking over some notes of mine I
found that when the distribution of
£32,000,000 was being made by the
British Government to distressed areas I
advocated that a deputation should
proceed to London to claim our rightful
share of that money, and the excuse
made by the Northern Government for
refusing to do so was that Northern Ireland could not be classed as a distressed
area. In other words, there was the
taint of pauperism about this money,
although the people of England, Scotland, and Wales found nothing wrong
with the money they received.
To-day the former distressed areas in
those countries have more industries in
their midst than they can supply labour
for. Yet to-day we here have thousands
of our people unemployed, with thousands more working across the Channel.
We were entitled to receive our quota of
that £32,000,000, and we should have
demanded it and received it, and been
thought nothing the less of for it. After
this war we are going to be in the unfortunate position of not having sufficient
jobs for the number of unemployed there
will be in Northern Ireland. We are not
going to have sufficient employment in
which to place them. What is going to
happen? You cannot keep them in
England once the order is removed.
Thousands would be back to-day but for
the fact that they are compelled to remain
in England. The Minister has seen to it
that they cannot get back unless they can
give special reasons. The right hon.
Gentleman should pay tribute to his
colleague in the British House of Commons who has so ably assisted him in the
very difficult position in which he was
placed by the Government.

The hon. Member also referred to the
question of billeting allowances. There
seems to be some misapprehension
regard to these allowances. They are
paid by my Ministry to men brought
from home or from one part of the
country to another where they can show
to the Ministry that they have extra
expense by reason of the fact that they
have to keep their homes where they live
and also to pay lodging costs in their
new sphere of labour. If they can satisfy
the Ministry that they have extra
charges to meet and are under a great
deal of inconvenience by doing so the
Ministry pay this billeting allowance.
But if a man deliberately and of his own
accord leaves his own home in order to
make better provision for his wife and
family, and comes to Belfast or some
other centre to take up fresh work and
is not brought by the Ministry, he may
make a claim for billeting allowance, but
in no case is it paid. It is paid only
when a man is brought by the Ministry
to another sphere of labour and when
he can prove to the Ministry that in
consequence he has more liabilities and
requires more money to meet them.

LETTING OF COTTAGES AT
BESSBROOK.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): With regard to the
first part of the question, the rent of
labourers' cottages in the Bessbrook area
is 4s 6d per week. The answer to the
second part of the question is, I am informed, that a police constable has been
recommended for the tenancy of a vacant
cottage, but the actual letting of the
cottage will not take place until the
meeting of the Council on the 10th
instant. Accordingly, the remainder of
the question does not arise.
I might state, however, for the information of the hon. Member, that the
selection of tenants for labourers'
cottages is not subject to the approval of
my Department, and unless it can be
shown that the local authority has acted
in contravention of the statutes governing the matter I cannot intervene in
favour of a particular tenant.

4. Mr. HENDERSON asked the

aware of the conditions under which flour
has been stored in premises in Ardglass;
and whether it is a fact that a large

Sir BASIL BROOKE: As the hon.
Member will be aware this question is a
matter for the Ministry of Food.

have come to his notice.

PETROL SUPPLIES FOR AN
AMBULANCE.
9. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Public Security whether he can state the
circumstances under which the First Aid
Department of the A.R.P. refused petrol
supplies for an ambulance purchased by
a number of residents in Windsor for use
in the subscribers' district; whether the
purchase of this ambulance by private
subscription should be recognised in a
manner calculated to inspire imitation by
other districts instead of being hindered
by official red tape.
Mr. GRANT: The Civil Defence
Authority is, of course, precluded from
issuing petrol supplies for vehicles other
than those which are recognised units of
the Civil Defence Services.
I have already been in consultation
with those concerned, and am hopeful
that a satisfactory solution of the difficulty which has arisen in this case will be
achieved.
As regards the second part of the hon.
Member's question, I am in agreement
with his views. Everything which binds
a service together must not, however, be
regarded as red tape. Sometimes it is
better described as good organisation.

THE £10 PER ACRE POTATO

11. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he is
aware that a portion of the main potato
crop still remained to be planted on 1st
June, and that farmers who have not yet
finished putting in their potatoes on the
1st June are anxious that they will not
be excluded from the £10 per acre subsidy on that account.
Lord GLENTORAN: I am glad to be
able to assure the hon. and gallant
Member that in cases where potatoes are
planted after 1st June the owner will not
be excluded from receipt of acreage payment unless there is definite evidence of
bad husbandry. Growers who plant
potatoes after 1st June should, therefore,
write direct to my Ministry stating the
date of completion of planting.
Lord GLENTORAN: I have been
asked to reply.
I am not aware of the distressing scenes
described by the hon. Member. It is true
that owing to a seasonal falling-off in the
number of cattle coming forward for

reduce the allocation of meat to butchers

SHORTAGE OF MEAT SUPPLIES.
Mr. BEATTIE (by private notice)
asked the Prime Minister whether he is
aware of the distressing scenes which have
occurred in Belfast recently due to the
failure of the meat supply, and whether
he will now make immediate representations to the British Minister of Food to.
see that there is no repetition of the bungling and scandalous lack of foresight
which resulted in the people of Northern
Ireland, and especially Belfast, only getting in some cases between sevenpence and
fourpence worth of meat per week despite
the fact that they were guaranteed, along
with the people of the rest of the United
Kingdom, a weekly meat ration of 1s 2d.
I would point out that the fixing of the
meat ration at 1s 2d per person does not
carry any guarantee that that quantity
of meat will always be available. It simply
meant that no person could receive more
than 1s 2d worth of meat. I do know
that the people of Northern Ireland are
proud to share in any burden which the
successful prosecution of the war may
render necessary.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
the noble Lord is he aware of the indignation amongst workers that in an agricultural country like this we should suffer
a meat famine through the stupidity of a
group of officials? Why were the people
kept in the dark about this matter with
the result that a lot of dangerous rumours
got round the city? Is the noble Lord
aware that thousands of working-class
people only received one chop which was
so like tissue paper you could see through
it? Will he see that this does not occur
again in this part of the world?
Lord GLENTORAN: Although Northern Ireland is an agricultural country it
is part of the United Kingdom, and it
shares in all the hardships other parts of
the United Kingdom have to undergo.
There was no bungling whatever on the
part of any Ministry. The meat was not
there. The sevenpence worth we all got
and we shared it with our friends here
and in certain places across Channel at
the same time.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is not the noble Lord
aware that the only bungling that took
place was in Northern Ireland? Is he
not aware that in Britain the leeway was
made up by substitutes and that no shortage of meat rations took place in Great
Britain as in Northern Ireland?

aware of anything of the kind. I know

Question proposed: "That the House

this House is of opinion that the Government should reconsider their decision to
discontinue the grant to the Ulster

ܕ
This Motion speaks for itself. I want
to make it clear at the outset that I am
not seeking in this Motion to make a
general condemnation of the Minister of
Commerce who has carried out his duties
without fear, favour, or affection during
his term of office, but I do think the
matter is one for reconsideration by the
Government. In regard to this grant a
very definite promise was given by the
late Lord Craigavon, who said it would be
continued throughout the period of the
war. We had better have Lord
Craigavon's exact words. This is what he
said in a letter dated 7th November,
1939:
I discussed the whole situation with
my colleagues yesterday and we are in
agreement that provision should be
made to enable you to carry on, of
course on a reduced basis, during the
war. We therefore propose for next
year and in each succeeding year so
long as the war lasts to make a grant
towards the funds of your association up
to £1,000 a year based on every £1
collected by you, and you may expect
to receive a formal communication to
this effect from the Ministry of Com-

When I referred to the position of

When I suggested in this House that

after the interests of certain miscellaneous

The Minister of Commerce does not
contend that the work of the Ulster
Industries Development Association has
ceased. On the contrary, he contends
that its work is now being done by his
Ministry, and one of the reasons why I
object to the discontinuance of this grant
is that it means a still further increase
in the powers of bureaucracy. The staff
of the Ministry of Commerce has been
increased owing to the fact that the
Ministry now propose to do the work
formerly done by this association, but I
suggest that the work can be done far
better by the association than by any
body of civil servants in the Ministry of
Commerce. I am not for one moment
suggesting that the civil servants in that
Ministry are one bit inferior to those in
any other Ministry, nor do I make any
charge of any kind against civil servants
in any Ministry, but I do say that the
machine is getting too big, and that every
day more and more power is passing into
the hands of bureaucracy, and when the
war is won it will be difficult for this
House to recover the power and responsibility that it is allowing slowly to pass
from its hands.
I suggest that instead of increasing the
number of civil servants to carry out this
work it would be far better for the
Government to continue this grant to the
association. I therefore hope the Minister
of Commerce will see his way to reconsider this matter and continue the
grant, even if it is reduced to a sum of
£500. It would be an indication that
the Government is not entirely indifferent
to the future of all these small industries.
I am all in favour of building up our staple

of the present flax situation both as
regards the prosecution of the war and
employment in the linen trade. In the
flax season of 1942 we are faced with a
large reduction in the Ulster acreage compared with last year and the knowledge
that imports from abroad are likely to be
smaller still, if not reduced to vanishing
point.
Our Province is the main supply for
all the allied efforts and it is, therefore,
necessary that every effort shall be made
to increase next year's crop. This Parliament is not responsible for flax production
or supply that is the function of the
Ministry of Supply (Flax Control) and
this Government only acts as agents for
that Ministry.
Again, our Ministry of Agriculture
parts company with flax once it is grown
and sold by the farmer, and has little to
do with policy particularly as regards
processing and retting. This falls into the
hands of the Flax Control. It is in the
processing part of this policy that the
great mistake has been made, and from
this mistake most of our trouble arose.
There were before the war two ways of
treating flax before scutching-one, water
retting, and, two, dew retting. The
former was used exclusively in this
country, but it was at the expense of the
seed which could not be saved by dam
retting. Dew retting was too wasteful
of the fibre and was not much employed.
Recently a method which has been used
in Belgium to an enormous extent has
been introduced, namely, tank retting,
which produces the finest fibre and that
best suited for our mills in Ulster. This
method, if adequately supported by this
Government, would produce more and
better fibre, relieve the farmer from the
trouble of dam retting, and take the crop
off his hands in the straw state.
everything German was right it was gone
into on a large scale.
Very unfortunately a different method
has been largely made us of, that of
scutching the flax green and without
retting, with the most disastrous consequences. This experiment, while a very
old one, was adopted by Germany in 1933
when they could not purchase abroad,
but I understand was totally thrown
aside in 1940 when Belgium and Dutch
flax was available. This method, by
what means I know not, was sold to the
British Ministry of Supply, and as
Many processing factories have been
created in England at enormous costthe figures I got were over £2,000,000—
and for over two years this green flax has
been manufactured. The results have
been disastrous. The yield of fibre per
acre is not half what Ulster can give and
the cost is over five times the price given
our farmers. The fibre produced is not
suitable for the vast majority of
spindles and is more expensive to work
and the tow residue is almost unusable.
our
The position has become so bad that
British spinners of flax refuse to take any
more of this green scutched flax and are
demanding to be supplied with our waterretted material. The total breakdown
of the flax growing and processing in
England this year and last, and the reduction of our own acreage, have produced a crisis of no mean magnitude, and
the outlook for the linen trade next year
is very gloomy. This Government cannot refuse its responsibility and must
take such measures as will at least reduce
to some extent the results of this
disastrous policy which has been pursued
since the outbreak of war in spite of all
warnings from those in the trade who
feared what has happened.
This insane policy of blindly copying
a method because it is German has only
led to disaster, and it is high time this
House should know where the Government stands in respect of this policy, or
whether they have a policy at all, which
many people doubt. The flax situation
has been badly handled for the past ten
years, mainly by the present Government,
and it has finally got its death knell by
the policy of the Ministry of Supply.
The facts are well known to those in the
trade, but I do not think the ordinary
Member or even the Government has yet
realised the true facts of the situation.
It is too late to do anything for 1942,
but for next year's crop something must
be done; the acreage grown in Northern
Ireland must be increased and the crop
must be water retted to be of any service.
Now is the time to plan for next year, as
it will be too late if delayed. The requirements of the Imperial Government must
be gauged and an endeavour made to
meet them. How can this be done and
what is the remedy for all our flax
Flax Production

Flax Production
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Johnston]
troubles? I will try to set out what I
consider must be done and how.
First, if only 10 per cent. of the money
spent yearly and largely wasted in England were turned over here we could
grow and ret enough flax to satisfy all
the war requirements. Forty thousand
acres were grown in England last year
and 20,000 grown here would produce as
much fibre. The cost of the fibre in
England has been stated to be five times
per ton what the Irish farmer gets for
his flax, and it stands to reason and
common sense that it would be better to
encourage the Irish farmer to grow much
more.
The Ministry of Supply has haggled
over every 1s per stone for our flax, and
spent millions on flax they did not get.
If more encouragement were given, our
farmers could supply all the flax necessary
to maintain the war effort and to provide
enough for civil consumption. Our own
Government could give more encouragement to get more tank retteries going by
urging preference for the material to
build them, and again, it is quite feasible
to ret in open tanks with water kept
heated to a constant temperature and
produce a fibre much better than dam
retting, with the consequent saving of
the seed. I am quite certain that if these
policies are pursued we can get all the
flax we can reasonably require during the
war.
If only the Ministry of Supply would
divert their energies to get more flax
here and get it water retted, the greater
part of their trouble would cease. This
policy might entail a reduction of the
English acreage, but it would mean a
great saving in the end.
To wind up, the following things must
be insisted on:
No. 1. That all, or nearly all, flax
should be water retted.
No. 2.-That more encouragement
should be given to tank retting and
modern scutching methods. That at
least 50 of these plants should be ready
for 1943.
No. 3. That open tank retting can be
adopted when it is impossible to get the
closed reinforced tanks.
I do not think that the picture I have
endeavoured to paint is in the slightest
degree exaggerated. For over three years
we have been ruled by the Ministry of
Supply as regards our agricultural policy
in flax, our retting policy in flax, and our
scutching policy in flax, and I think it is
time that this House and this Government
should insist on
Our
some change.
Ministry of Agriculture has practically
nothing to do with the price of the crop,
and has nothing to do with the
grading after it leaves the farmers'
hands. Our Ministry of Commerce
has nothing to do with the crop
except to act as agents for the Ministry
of Supply. The Ministry of Supply has
been ruling the roost for the past three
years, and a nice mess it has made of it.
No. 4.—That the rest of the crop
should be dam retted, although by this
method the seed is sacrificed.
This policy was adopted because it was
German, and psychologically it went
through everything. You could only beat
the Germans by doing what the Germans
did. The Germans took the green sickness very badly, and therefore we had to
take it too in order to beat the Germans;
but it was a most disastrous policy,
because it ruined our flax fibre. If only
a tithe of the money that has been wasted
in England by building these retteries
had been spent over here there would have
been very little trouble about flax. I have
been doing my best for over five years
to get more tank retteries established in
Northern Ireland, and if the situation is
to be saved over 50 of these would have to
be set going in order that the 1943 crop
may be saved.
The situation need not have been so bad
if the people who knew something about
flax had been in charge of it, if our own
people over here who really know what
flax is and how to produce it and ret it,
had had the formation of policy; but they
had nothing to say to it. I think it is
time that the Government here should
have more to say in what is done with
our flax both in regard to retting and
the production of good fibre. You will
never produce fibre suitable for the mills
of Northern Ireland by the present
method. It has been demonstrated
beyond the shadow of a doubt to be the
most ghastly failure, and to-day in
England most of the straw is not being
used. I understand it is supposed to be
sold for making paper. I think this
Government cannot shirk responsibility to
our farmers and workers and to the people

SANATORIUM BRIBERY
ALLEGATIONS.
4. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
steps, if any, taken by his Department to
bring to justice all the persons implicated
in the alleged bribery charges in connection with the proposed purchases of the
Rathmore site for a Municipal Sanatorium
and the date on which the first bribery
allegations were made.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr.
MacDermott): I have been asked by my
right hon. Friend to reply.
The first allegation of bribery in connection with the proposed purchase of a
site for a Belfast municipal sanatorium,
of which I am aware, was made by
Councillor Wilton at a meeting of the
Belfast County Borough Council on the
3rd October, 1938. This was reported in
the Press on the following day and the
then Attorney-General directed the police
to make inquiry in order to ascertain if
evidence were available to sustain a prosecution. Councillor Wilton, however,
did not see fit to give any information to
the investigating officer and the necessary
evidence was not obtained.
the Ministry of Home Affairs on or about
the 14th June, 1941. A short time afterwards the report of the inspectors and a
transcript of the evidence and proceedings
at the inquiry were sent by the Ministry
to my immediate predecessor so that the
question of criminal proceedings might be
considered. This resulted in the papers
being transmitted to the police for further
investigation concerning the suggestion of
bribery in connection with the selection of
a site.
The question of bribery in connection
with the selection of a sanatorium site,
and with that at Rathmore, in particular,
was again raised during the inquiry
into the administraton of the Whiteabbey Sanatorium which commenced in
November, 1940, and it was referred to in
the comments and findings on the
Inspectors' Report which were issued by
These investigations commenced in
August, 1941, and are still current. That
they have not been concluded before this
is, I consider, most unfortunate; but it
is certainly not due to any desire to shelve
the subject, as I see the hon. Member
asserted last week. Nor is it the fault of
the police. I am satisfied their inquiries
have been made with ability and diligence; but progress has been slow because
it has been difficult; and information
recently obtained has extended the field of
inquiry so that further investigation is
necessary before it can be said that such
evidence as is material and forthcoming
has been collected. When this is accomplished and I hope it may be soon-I shall
give such directions in the matter as seem
to me proper.

Personal Explanation
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(at the close of questions): My attention has been drawn to Hansard of the
9th June, containing a supplemental
question put to me by the hon. Member
for Woodvale, affecting my honour.
I am not, and never have been, Mr.
McCrudden's solicitor in regard to the
proposed purchase by the Belfast Corporation of his property for the purpose
of a municipal sanatorium. In fact, on
more than one occasion when approval
for the proposed purchase was sought by
the Corporation, this was refused by
myself and my Ministry as being an entirely unsuitable site.
Consequently, I repudiate the vile
suggestions, first, that I was in any way
concerned in the suggested purchase, and,
secondly, that I have done anything to
impede the course of justice with regard
to suggested prosecutions for bribery.
Therefore, I demand that these vile
and cowardly suggestions made under
the cloak of privilege by the hon. Member for Woodvale should be withdrawn,
or that the hon. Member will repeat them
where he is not protected by the insurmountable fence of Parliamentary
privilege.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Sale of Ice-Cream (Temporary Provisions) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Lord GLENTORAN: This is a small
measure with a very simple object. Under
the Sale of Ice Cream Act, 1937, only
milk fats could be used in the manufacture of ice-cream in Northern Ireland.
In peace time this was a very desirable
This placed ice-cream manufacturers in
Northern Ireland in a difficulty inasmuch
as they are unable either to comply with
our own law as it stands or with the order
of the Minister of Food.
Accordingly it is proposed by this small
Bill to suspend for the period of the war
certain of the provisions of our Sale of
Ice Cream Act, 1937. When this is done
the use of vegetable fats in the manufacture of ice-cream will be permitted in
Northern Ireland in the same way as in
Great Britain and thus the legal disabilities under which ice-cream manufacturers in this area have suffered will be
removed. I beg to move.

Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to raise
a question in this House on the administration of the National Fire Service, a
matter that is going to have a very important bearing on the personnel of this
service. It has come to the notice of
firemen, section leaders and company
leaders that they are to be brought in
under a military rule or order issued by
Mr. Andrews, the chief of the fire service.
This order will compel them to adopt a
form of recognition of the officers of that
service similar to what is adopted by the
military, Air Force and Navy, and also by
the police. I cannot see why that order
can be rightfully introduced into the
National Fire Service. This service is
not a military or semi-military force. It
Adjournment-

National Fire Service

is not armed or semi-armed. It is purely
and actually a civilian force for the purpose of fighting fires and saving life in
areas that have been destroyed. I would
not be so sure of having this order
rescinded if it were not for the fact that
I have a friend in court. The Minister
of Public Security is himself one of the
advocates of the abolition of saluting.
He made a speech in this House some
time ago when he condemned all this arm
raising on the public road, giving black
eyes to civilians and knocking caps off
passers-by. He thought in his own mind
that his son should not continue on that
line as it was ridiculous and he received
substantial support through the Belfast
newspapers. Now we are going to introduce this system into a trade union. The
members of the National Fire Service are
trade unionists. They are not military
or semi-military. They are workers, and
if we allow this thing to go on we will

the unemployed when they visit the
labour exchanges to stand to attention and
salute the officers behind the counter.

discipline. The whole thing is ridiculous;
class distinction pure and simple.

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Sir Basil Brooke): In presenting to the
Committee the Estimates of my Ministry
for the current year, I am sure that hon.
Members will expect me to devote my
remarks, in the first instance, to the
Northern Ireland industrial contribution
towards the national effort.
From time to time I have acquainted
the House of developments in so far as it
was possible for me so to do without conveying information which might be
detrimental to the national interest. Let
me briefly recapitulate. When I first
tackled the task of war production I
found myself in the anomalous position
of being expected to undertake some
degree of responsibility for all production
in this area without having been entrusted with any direct supervision over
contracts placed here.
The position was unsatisfactory. We
had an unemployed reserve of labour of
some 70,000 workers, a substantial proportion of whom were being denied the
opportunity to play their part in the
national struggle. It was in these circumstances that I negotiated with the
three Supply Ministers and the Production Executive of the War Cabinet for
authority to concert, supervise and coordinate industrial war activities in this
area.
The Northern Ireland Regional Board
of the Production Executive, which was
at that time functioning, did a certain
amount of good work in bringing together contractors and contracting departments, but the machinery was
cumbersome and there was confusion
about the degree of responsibility which
the Board should undertake in relation
to the responsibility which should be
borne by the Northern Ireland Government in general, and my Ministry in
particular.
The Regional Board was abolished and
in its place I set up a Production
Advisory Committee on which employers,
trade unions, the Supply Departments
and the Ministry of Labour are represented. I am glad to take this opportunity of expressing my keen appreciation of the services so unstintingly given
by the members of that Committee.

one
The more one investigates this whole
question of production, the more
appreciates and sympathises with the
human problems involved. But there is
a distinct danger that all unwittingly
people may damage the war effort by
decrying the efforts of those engaged in
it. The maintenance of moral is an
important factor in this struggle and
constant criticism of the carping variety
is one method of playing the enemy's
game.
I have paid a tribute before to our
workers, and I do so readily again as I
know that the great majority are wholeheartedly out to defeat Germany and are
determined to do their best in the present
struggle. Once more I should like particularly to say how magnificently the
women have adapted themselves to new
conditions of work in furtherance of the
war effort.
I welcome the arrangements being made
for the establishment of joint works committees of employers and employees. This
is definitely a step in the right direction
and likely to remove minor grievances
which are always a cause of hindrance to
production. There never was a time in
the history of these islands when the
energies of every individual were more
urgently required in the national effort.
It is on that ground that I have appealed,
and do now appeal, to all workers to
maintain production and keep at their
posts even when an air raid alert is
sounded, especially where there is in the
factory a system of internal warnings of
the near approach of hostile aircraft.
On another point we have still to make
headway, and that is night-working. I
realise that the workers generally are putting in long hours and that long hours
mean inevitably some degree of staleness.
We have, however, this ever pressing
demand for increased production, and
Estimates-

Ministry of Commerce
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir B. Brooke]
there is also the necessity for utilising
every machine tool to the full. In these
circumstances I hope that more and more
workers will agree to extend the operation
of night shifts so as to make the most
adequate use of our productive capacity.
My right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Labour, has told the Committee something
of the progress being made with the labour
supply organisation which he and I
recently established. As hon. Members
will be aware, the object of this new
organisation is to ensure that the best use
is made of skilled labour within this area
by absorbing into industry semi-skilled
and unskilled labour. Only the initial
steps have yet been taken, but it is clear
from the first report received from the
labour supply inspectors that their
appointment is being amply justified.
A word about strikes. Our common
object is, with good will on either side, to
make the most efficient use possible of our
man-power resources, and I am sure we
all agree that strikes are deplorable in
these days. The machinery for adjusting
disputes is there. It should be utilised to
avoid the loss of precious time when every
man-hour counts.

much I am indebted to the Press for the
way in which they have handled this
subject. Their objective presentation of
Ulster's war effort has, I am confident,
contributed definitely towards the end we
all have in view.

what I said recently in answer to questions in this House. The Rationing Order
was made by my Ministry as a purely
Apart from matters immediately and
directly connected with war production, a
problem which has greatly occupied me
has been that of the linen industry for
which, in its peace-time activities, there
is, unfortunately, no place in war time.
The industry can be utilised only in so
far as it is required for the national effort.
The great textile industries of Great
Britain have also suffered severely from
restriction, but as alternative employment
of an essential character was available for
displaced workers, they did not have to
cope with the same unemployment
problem. In Northern Ireland no adequate
alternative employment exists, and my
problem has, therefore, been the dual one
of finding for our local industry the
largest possible amount of Government
work and of supplementing that work with
essential civil work on other textiles.
During 1941, the weaving section of our
linen industry succeeded in obtaining a
substantial amount of work on Government orders, both in cotton and linen.
Over and above this work, my Ministry
was able to arrange for a considerable
share of the flax supply to be allocated to
the industry in order to utilise the
currency-earning capacity of its export
trade. Unfortunately, however, Government orders began to decline in the
second half of the year, and the shortage
of flax and America's entry into the war
brought about a complete cessation of the
release of flax for export trade. The
year 1942, therefore, opened with gloomy
prospects for the industry, and the
weaving section, which, as I have said,
had hitherto been relatively busy, was
faced with a position almost as bad as
that which the spinning section, working
only on one raw material, had faced since
the loss of continental supplies of flax.
The House will appreciate that at the
present time it is absolutely impossible to

As I have said, the full flow of export

And now a few remarks regarding the
various controls. The word "control"
has to all of us an unpleasantly familiar
ring, but I believe we recognise its inevitability under the present conditions.
The whole system, of course, derives from
measures taken by the Imperial Government and is part of their planned wartime economy.
The first of these matters on which I
wish to speak is building and building
materials. Here, as Members will know,
Estimates-

Ministry of Commerce
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir B. Brooke]
a very stringent control is exercised
throughout the United Kingdom. In
Northern Ireland all private building
work costing more than £100 can be
undertaken only under a licence from my
Ministry. The use of building materials
is also strictly controlled. The aim of
these restrictions is to economise in the
use of shipping space for imported
materials and to conserve for vital war
uses the building material and labour
which we have available. The need for
economy in building work is most urgent,
and hon. Members will, I hope, accept my
assurance that if we have to adopt a
cheese-paring attitude in administering
the building regulations, these methods.
are justified by the assistance which our
economies indirectly contribute to the war
effort. In the control of material in short
supply we can best contribute to the
national interest if we vie with other
parts of the United Kingdom in enforcing
the maximum economies, rather than in
obtaining the lion's share.
In April of last year full powers in
respect of bricks, stone, cement, sand, tar
and bitumen were delegated to my
Ministry by the Imperial authorities.
We are thus responsible not only for distribution, but also for questions of
priority and for the allocation of labour
according to the needs and the importance.
of the particular job. In the discharge
of these functions my Ministry has found
it necessary to supplement the output

In addition, we have supplied a number
of portable crushers on hire to quarry

Hon. Members will see by reference to

A further control which I might mention in passing is that relating to profiteering in the sale of goods other than

The continuance of the war gives increasing prominence to the campaign for
the salvage of domestic waste. During
the past year my Ministry has continued
to co-operate with the Ministry of Supply
in its efforts to secure from Northern

to ensuring that our industrial and commercial position is re-established and improved as quickly as possible after the
cessation of hostilities.

should like to put it this way. The motive

I
In the most widespread and desperate
struggle the world has ever seen, the Allies
need everything their peoples can give.
All must be given if all is not to be lost.
As a temporary measure, the comforts and
pleasures, the likes and dislikes of the
individual citizen, traditional methods of
working must give way to the country's
need, so that eventually a society may be
preserved in which we can still live as free
people and not as the slaves of a dictator.
I repeat-total effort is needed in a total
war. That is what is demanded of us,
and that is what as Minister of Commerce
and Production I am resolved to achieve
in the sphere for which I am responsible.
I beg to move.

business transactions in the Whiteabbey
Oral Answers

Sanatorium prior to the appointment of
Commissioners had to be approved by
his Ministry; whether the purchase of the
black-out cloth from Porter's, High
Street, which was the subject of censure
by the Ministry's inspectors at the
Inquiry had been approved by the

Sir DAWSON BATES: Existing
statutes do not provide for the exercise
by my Ministry of supervision over the
administration of the Whiteabbey Sanatorium, as it is provided in the case of
most other local authorities, but any expenditure that attracts the 50 per cent.
Tuberculosis Grant requires the Ministry's approval.
Such sanctions are given, as they
necessarily must be, on the basis of the
information set out in the minute seeking approval, and, of course, cover no
more than the transaction as therein described. Consequently, in the event of
the minute being inaccurate, incomplete
and misleading, as it was in this instance,
the sanction is void and affords no protection or justification to the members of
the committee responsible for the payment.
Neither at the Inquiry nor at any time
have the committee been censured because
they purchased black-out material, which
was an obvious necessity for compliance
with the law. The Ministry's censure
was directed to the grossly irregular and
dishonest procedure in dealing with
quotations and to the disgraceful quality
of the material supplied.
I need hardly say that this procedure.
was not disclosed by the minutes, and it
seems almost unnecessary to remark that
the quality of the goods supplied-that
is to say the correct enforcement of the
contract is an entirely separate matter
from any sanction which is required to
be given before the contract is made.
The approval given to the purchase of
black-out cloth was a perfectly proper
one, and I accept full responsibility for

BILLETING ALLOWANCES.
6. Mr. THOMAS BAILIE asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he is
aware that billeting allowances to blitzed
families in billeted areas are, in many instances, being stopped owing to the wageearner insisting upon living with his
family; whether he can state the reason
for this apparently harsh treatment of
those who have already endured suffering
and loss, and whether it is a fact that,
where practicable, particularly in the case
of large families, the existence of family
life should be encouraged and
not
destroyed.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I should like
to explain in the first instance that no
billeting allowances are paid to any
families whose houses may have been
damaged by enemy action. Billeting
allowances are payable only to the householder in whose house persons have been
billeted. Homeless persons are normally
entitled to be billeted at Government
expense only for a period of a fortnight,
after which they are expected to be able
to make their own arrangements.
Members of the priority classes, that is
to say, women with children, unaccompanied children, aged and infirm persons
and blind persons normally resident in the
county boroughs of Belfast and Londonderry, the only two evacuation areas in
Northern Ireland, may be evacuated to a
reception area and there billeted. If the
wage earner joins his family in a reception.
area he has presumably given up his house
in the evacuation area, and the family
has, therefore, to all intents and purposes
become residents in the reception area.
The family is, therefore, in no worse position financially than if they had to pay
rent in Belfast or Londonderry, and the
Government would not, therefore, be
justified in relieving the family from payment of rent.
The Government agrees that in normal
times family life should be encouraged,
but in the present emergency family life
has to be sacrificed to the needs of the
Oral Answers

State. In Great Britain, conscription has
resulted in not only men but also women

I am sure the hon. Member would not

Britain.
It is the duty of able-bodied adults to
remain in evacuation areas and take their

wage-earners and their families in reception areas can in any way be termed
harsh treatment.

7. Mr. THOMAS BAILIE asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether the
minutes of the proceedings of the committee formerly responsible for the
administration of the Whiteabbey Sanatorium were regularly forwarded to the
Ministry of Home Affairs; whether the
recommendations contained in the
minutes as to appointments and to purchases were in all cases subject to the
Sir DAWSON BATES: My department has no statutory functions in
connection with the administration of
Whiteabbey Sanatorium, and it was for
this reason that it was necessary to obtain
authority from Parliament before the
Ministry was in a position to accede to
the. Corporation's request for an inquiry.
The Ministry's only concern with the
committee is to approve or disapprove such
part of its expenditure as ranks for the
50 per cent. grant, and the minutes only
come to the department for this purpose.
The committee is not required to submit
its minutes to the Ministry, nor is the
Ministry required or entitled to approve
of them generally.
The hon. Member will, therefore,
understand that the only functions of the
Ministry with regard to applications for
sanction to expenditure in connection with
purchases or appointments is to decide.
whether such expenditure is necessary,
and therefore expenditure on which grant
should be paid. Accordingly, neither the
Ministry nor its officials can be considered
in any way involved in the unsatisfactory
state of affairs found to have existed.
Mr. NIXON: Is it not a fact that
every payment by this committee appears
in the minutes with the sanction of the
Ministry of Home Affairs, and that at
the monthly meeting of the council an
attempt to raise or question anything
would be confronted in the minute with
the statement that it had been approved
by the Ministry? The very man who
approved of some of these transactions
went and held a sworn inquiry and
condemned them.
Mr. THOMAS BAILIE: Am I to
understand that the Ministry is only
interested in the
the proceedings to the
extent of the 50 per cent. grant?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The hon.
Gentleman is perfectly correct.

authorities as being a unit of food fit for

Paragraphs (a), (b) and (c) of subsection (1) of section one of the Sale
of Ice-Cream Act (Northern Ireland),
1937, which require that milk fat and
no other fat shall be a constituent of
ice-cream sold by any person.
I should like to know what other fat
is used in the manufacture of ice-cream
in addition to that prescribed. I was not
aware that it was made from anything but
the purest ingredients. I am not inclined
to agree to this Clause until the noble
Lord gives the Committee a clear interpretation of the legislation by reference which
is referred to in Clause 1 of the present
Bill.
Lord GLENTORAN: I quite appreciate the difficulty of my hon. Friend the
Member for Pottinger in understanding
what all these sub-sections mean. However, I think I will be able to explain
them to his satisfaction. Under the 1937
Act it was laid down, in order that icecream should be pure, that the only fat
used in its manufacture should be milk
fat. If a merchant was found selling icecream which did not contain the proper
complement of milk fat, he was prosecuted. Since the war broke out the
Minister of Food has had to conserve milk
for distribution amongst children and
other elements of the population. That
being so, an order was issued that milk
fats could not be used in the manufacture
of ice-cream. The registered ice-cream
merchant then found himself between two
stools. If he made his ice-cream with
milk fat he was prosecuted, and if, under
the 1937 Act, he did not make it from
milk fat he was also prosecuted. This is
a very simple Bill. Under it we are
allowing the ice-cream merchant to use
vegetable fat in place of milk fat, and by
doing so he will be enabled to carry on
his trade without breaking the law. That
is the explanation.
Mr. BEATTIE: The noble Lord has
given the members of the Committee an
insight into the historical background of
the manufacture of ice-cream. He has
stated that vegetable fat is now being
used as a substitute for milk fat, but he
has not told us what the vegetable fat
consists of, how it compares with milk
fat according to medical standards, or
whether ice-cream has deteriorated to
such an extent that it is injurious instead
of beneficial to those people who consume
it. I want the noble Lord-I know he
is quite competent to give the Committee
an assurance that there is no deterioration in the value of ice-cream made from
vegetable fat as compared to its value
when made from milk fat. If he gives
me that assurance I will be quite content.

Electricity (Emergency Supplies) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: In introducing this Bill to the House, I feel
that it is essential to draw particular
attention to the general purpose of the
Bill, that is to say, to provide for the
maintenance of an adequate supply of
electricity in war time, whatever may be
the emergency that arises. In other
words, I shall not be dealing with peacetime policy, either pre-war or post-war,
but purely with the emergency requirements of war time. Having made clear
the background, and indeed the whole
purpose of the Bill, by this statement,
perhaps I may proceed to outline its main
provisions.
Bill I am concerned solely to do what is
best in the national interest.
In the first place I should like to give
hon. Members a very short appreciation
of the position in regard to electricity
supply in Ulster at the beginning of the
war, but, at the same time, I hope I shall
be excused if, for security reasons, I cannot give chapter and verse for everything
I say. You will realise, sir, that any
detailed information about electrical
development and production during the
war is bound to be of theoretical and
practical use to the enemy. Furthermore,
I know the House will bear with me in the
difficulties involved by those restrictions
and realise that in bringing forward this
The past 10 years had seen a remarkable expansion in electricity development,
not only in the towns, but also in the
sparsely populated rural areas. Electricity
had ceased to be regarded merely in the
nature of a luxury, and had become a
normal amenity even in the artisans'
cottages in many parts of the country.
As hon. Members are aware, more than
one-third of the population of Northern
Ireland reside within the county borough
of Belfast, and outside this area, and
that of Derry, there is no urban population with population in excess of 20,000.
It is not surprising, therefore, to find that
the main public supplies of the Province
depend upon three generating stations,
one of which supplies not only the city of
Belfast, but also a substantial part of the
hinterland as well.
In present circumstances, I do not
propose to enter into any discussion of the
primary responsibility for the provision
of alternative or stand-by supplies of
electricity. Suffice it to say that a definite
obligation was laid on electrical undertakings to take steps to secure the due
functioning of their stations in the event
of hostile attack. The fulfilment of this
obligation by Belfast, which generates a
great proportion of electricity in the
Province, had been subject to such postponements and procrastinations that at
last the Government decided to permit of
no further delay in making sure of the
power supplies required for our war
effort. With the financial help of the
Imperial Government, three stand-by
sources of supply are either now operative
or are well advanced towards completion.
Consequently I am glad to be in a position.
to inform the House that in a short time
the provision against emergencies will be
reasonably assured. So much for the
general principles involved.
Coming now to the specific provisions of
the Bill, I shall naturally leave the details
to be dealt with on the Committee stage,
but I might outline the general framework so as to give a coherent idea of the
action which the Government proposes to
take, or which, in some cases, the Government has already taken in order to meet
the situation.
It follows naturally from what I have
just said, that it is essential that the
Electricity Bill—

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir B. Brooke]
Government should have power to set up
or acquire generating stations and main
transmission lines which are strategically
important from the point of view of maintaining war production in the Province. I
can assure the House that this power will
be used solely for that purpose, and if any
evidence is needed on this point, I would
indicate that there are provisions in the
Bill that prohibit the compulsory acquisition of the undertakings of the two
county boroughs. In my view if the
compulsory acquisition of these two undertakings had been provided for in the Bill,
it would have infringed upon peace-time
policy, and, moreover, any question of
merger would have taken a long time to
settle. Accordingly, no such provision
appears in the Bill. I trust, therefore,
that the Government ownership of the
stand-by system will be agreed to by the
House as a reasonable and indeed the only
practical policy.

But the Bill would be incomplete if
it did not pursue the matter to a finish
and provide for what is to be done in the
most serious emergency, should it ever
arise. I need not attempt to specify
what forms the emergency might take as
the imagination of hon. Members is
probably just as vivid as my own, but the
Government would be failing in its duty
if, on the occurrence
of such an
emergency, it did not at once take command of the situation. Provision is
accordingly made that in such circumstances the Government may direct the
operation of the whole or part of the
electrical system of the Province to the
end that it will be used to the best advantage in the national interest. At the
same time, the provision made for such
an emergency is capable of being used
for the purpose of ensuring that the
electricity supplies of the Province are
used to the best advantage at any time
in the national interest, and in the most
economical manner possible.

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
COMMERCE (Sir Wilson Hungerford):
All the speeches to-day have covered a
very wide field and at times have gone a
long way from the main features of the
Bill. I would really like the House to
come back to the main reasons why it was
necessary that the Bill should be introduced. Members will remember that
early in 1941 the Minister of Commerce
took over charge of increased war production. He was very disturbed with the
reports as to the supply of electricity and
asked for an investigation into the whole
position. He was very perturbed as to
whether there was a sufficient stand-by
to enable the necessary war machines to
be kept going, and the result of the
investigation proved that there was
absolutely no standby.
I would like the House to realise the
seriousness of the position in which he
found himself, because had the supply
from the Belfast Corporation, which
generated something like 90 per cent. of
the electricity used in Northern Ireland,
been subjected to a serious break-down not
alone would war production have almost
ceased, but our public utility services.
would also have ceased. As the Minister
has already stated there was nothing but
postponements and procrastinations, and,
therefore, after giving due consideration
to the investigations and the report, and
in order to allay the anxiety of the supply
services across the water, who were continually urging on him to take action, he
decided to erect the stations.
Having erected the stations, it was
necessary to get them under his control,
and it was also necessary that provision
should be made for the payment of the
stand-by plant. It has been accepted
that each industry must bear its own war
risk insurance, and, therefore, these
undertakings in Northern Ireland, who
should have arranged to provide a standby, having failed to do so the Government
had to do what they would not do, and it
was only right that the charge should be
levied upon these undertakings. That
is one of the reasons why this Bill has

The Member for Willowfield raised

reply now, although they are really
matters for the Committee stage. The
Ministry cannot transfer an undertaking
until it has been acquired, and therefore
it is not necessary to add the words,
"or acquire" to Clause 1, sub-clause 4.
With regard to Clause 4, the arrangement between the Board and the Corporation is specifically covered by the
Electricity (Supply) Act, 1931. The
Corporation Harbour Power Station is
a "selected station" and payment for
current is in accordance with the 1931
Act. As regards Clause 5, the financial
year is the financial year of the Ministry, namely, 31st March in each year.
With reference to the point about the
maintenance of a station, stations may
not be operated but must be maintained
ready to come into operation if required.
Estimated expenditure must include a
sufficient amount for acquisition of
undertakings, generating stations, or
main transmission lines.
The Member for Willowfield asked
how would the deficiency be distributed.
It will be distributed equitably amongst
other undertakings, not according to
sympathy or ability to pay, but according to the interest of the concern in the
stand-by system. The amount will be
only the net sum after allowing for the
Imperial grant, which is 50 per cent. of
the total cost. I may add that the

amendment to safeguard the pensions

The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Lord Glentoran): It may ease the situation if I reply to my hon. Friend, who
has very properly raised this question.
The answer is this. In order to get this
Bill negotiated it took a very considerable
time. We might have brought this in
in different ways. We might have
brought it in as an amendment to our
Minimum Wage Act, but I think, very
properly, the union officials rather look
upon that measure as a Magna Charta for
agricultural labour. They do not desire
that Act touched and therefore they want
us to bring in this Bill in this form. It
took a very considerable time, as no one
knows better than the hon. Member, to
arrive at this agreement. Once we pass
this short Bill the statutory Wages' Board
has to give fourteen days' notice to all
employees so that they may object. I
know my hon. Friend will understand
that by that time the flax pulling time
will have arrived, and it is for that reason
I have thrown myself on the indulgence
of the House and ask Members to be kind
enough to allow the Bill to go through.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Agricultural Wages (Flax Workers) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
Lord GLENTORAN: The object of the
Bill is to enable the Agricultural Wages
Board for Northern Ireland to fix standard rates of wages for workers engaged
on piece-work basis in the pulling and
scutching of flax. The procedure laid
down under the Agricultural Wages Act
(Northern Ireland), 1939, provides that
the Wages Board has to give notice of any
proposed Order fixing wages, and then
there is a fortnight after that during
which objections to the proposed Order
may be lodged. The board has then to
consider the objections and to confirm or
amend the proposed Order, as the case
may be.
It will be clear, therefore, that in
order to permit of the Board holding
the necessary meetings and having the
Order properly promulgated before the
commencement of the flax pulling season,
which, by the way, will be upon us very
soon, it is essential to have this measure
passed through both Houses at the earliest
possible moment. The Bill could not be
laid before the House earlier because
rather protracted negotiations had to be
carried out with both farmers' and
workers' representatives.
In this connection I am glad to be able to tell the House
that the Bill has the approval both of the
Ulster Farmers' Union and of organised
labour, so that it is really an agreed
measure.
The Bill is a very simple one. Clause 1
provides for the fixing by the Agricultural
Wages Board of standard rates of wages
for workers engaged for piece work in
pulling flax by hand and for workers
engaged in scutching flax or tow on a
piece-rate basis in scutch mills where the

Oral Answers to Questions.
EMPLOYMENT EXCHANGE
PROCEDURE.
1. Lieut.-Colonel HALL-THOMPSON
asked the Minister of Labour whether he
can state what procedure is adopted by
Labour Exchanges when selecting names
for nomination to unskilled employment.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): When vacancies are notified to
Employment Exchanges, unemployed
workers are submitted in three different
ways according to the nature of the demand.
Sometimes the prospective employer
asks for particular persons by name, and
if they are unemployed they are, of
course, sent to him.
The third way of filling vacancies is
that adopted for relief schemes where
preference is given to those with the
largest family responsibilities who have
been longest out of work. Again, other
things being equal, an ex-service man
would have priority over a civilian.
MENTALLY DEFECTIVE
a
In the great majority of cases, however, the employer merely asks for
certain number of workers. The Exchange officials ascertain the nature of
the job, the pay and conditions, etc.,
if these facts are not already known, and
then select the persons whom they think
best fitted to fill the vacancies. The
hon. and gallant Member will realise that
the officials in charge of this procedure
have had wide experience, and usually
the advantage of personal knowledge of
the people on the register, as well as the
Exchange records of their previous employment. The test is suitability for the
job; and the only slight modification is
that, other things being equal, an exservice man would be given the preference.
CHILDREN.
2. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state the number of mentally defective
children under 14 in Northern Ireland,
and the number over 14 and under 16;
how many boys and girls under 14 are
resident patients in Northern Ireland;
whether his Ministry considers it conducive to the mental and moral wellbeing of these most helpless children to
have them herded with irresponsible
adult mental patients whose language
and habits would be likely to have a
deleterious effect on the children:
whether he proposes at an early date
to set up a central home, preferably in
a rural area, for these children where
they could get fresh air, treatment,
games, and, if possible, some training;
and whether he can state the number
of mentally defective children under 14
in Antrim, Belfast, Armagh, Downpatrick, Derry, and Omagh Mental
Hospitals.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The number of
mentally defective children in Northern
Ireland Public Mental Hospitals is 46.
Details will be given in the printed
reply. I agree that it is undesirable
that mentally defective children should
have to be associated with adult mental
patients, but I regret that I see very
little hope of being able to set up a
separate home for such children or of
introducing legislation dealing with the
subject during the present emergency.

ALLEGED BLACK MARKET IN
BELFAST.
4. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state if
there is any foundation, in fact, for the
statements being made that in certain
working-class areas in Belfast a black
market is rampant, in which sellers of
eggs can extort 4s or 5s a dozen; and
whether he is satisfied that adequate steps
are being taken to detect such nefarious
traffic.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Lord Glentoran): I am not aware that
a black market in eggs exists in workingclass areas in Belfast, but if my hon. and
learned Friend or any other person will
furnish information pointing to any such
transactions I shall have the matter
investigated immediately.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Has the Minister
reason to believe that black markets are
in operation in Northern Ireland?
Lord GLENTORAN: No, sir; I have
not. The view of the Ministry is that
the inquiries my officers have made have
shown that very clearly. It is owing to
the differentiation in the way we manage
business and the way they manage it on
the other side. I am glad to say there
is a very small black market, if any, and
I am taking every step in my power to
see there is no black market.

ances paid to agricultural instructors in

Lord GLENTORAN: The salaries of
in
county agricultural staffs
Great
Britain vary considerably from county to

In Northern Ireland county agricultural organisers, known during the period

officers, are on a salary scale of £550 by

Ireland are paid at the same rates as are

is similar.

think this is very satisfactory, for the

When I introduced the Estimates for
my Ministry last year I referred to the
fact that there had been a considerable
evacuation of elementary school children
from the city of Belfast and that we were
busy dealing with the measures necessary
for their continued education in the

the provision of equipment. A good
many children were evacuated, and for a
our
Last year I told the Committee of the
excellent work the teachers had done in
the Rest Centres of Belfast; this year I
should like to pay a tribute to them, to
education committees, and to voluntary
managers all over Northern Ireland for
the way in which they have co-operated
in ensuring that the education of the
evacuated children should continue with
the minimum interruption. And here let
me say that a year ago there was a good
deal of loose talk about evacuated children
running wild in the country and refusing
to darken the doors of an elementary
school. There was very little in it;
parents, teachers and school attendance
officers were quick to put their minds to
the matter, and I assure you that, so far
the Ministry is aware, the general
standard of attendance by evacuated
children was good-indeed, I have been
told that in more than one district the
children from Belfast attended so regularly and so well that their average was
better than that of the local children.
This brings me to a matter which has
assumed great importance this year in
the realm of educational administrationthe use of school children on the farm.
Hon. Members will appreciate that here
the Ministry is pulled in two opposite
directions; by the people who say that
all considerations of education must give
place to the need for helpers on the land,
and by those who say that under no circumstances must there be any interruption, even for a day, in the education of
our children. Well, we have had consultations and discussions on this difficult matter with all concerned with the
Ministry of Agriculture, with the
teachers, and with members of education
committees.
We know that our chief and primary
duty is education, we know also the history of school attendance in the country
districts of Ireland, and we are all close
enough to the land to recognise the invaluable help that the farmer's boy or
girl can give in times of stress. We have
suggested a course of action to education
committees, who are sensible bodies well

There is one other matter I think I
should refer to. The Committee will see
under the heading F on page 127 that we
are asking for an Estimate of £28,000 to
recoup education authorities on their net
expenditure on the provision of milk and
meals for necessitous children. The
Estimate shows that we are prepared to

per cent. of their net expenditure on milk
and 90 per cent. of their net expenditure
on meals, and it is clear from these high
percentages that the Ministry is very
anxious that committees throughout the
country should set up schemes for the
purpose.
There has been a good deal of illinformed discussion on this matter, but
it is all very simple. It is definitely
established that an ill-nourished child
cannot benefit properly from the instruction given to it, and, on the other hand,
that the educational progress of a properly nourished child can be quite
remarkable. In England, the President
of the Board of Education stated clearly
when introducing his estimates that he
had consulted his own medical advisers
very carefully before making the statement that, thanks partly to the provision
of meals and partly to the fact that
some 3,250,000 children now got
milk in school, the health of the
children had positively improved, and that
the scheme had shown an "almost incredible" effect on the children "not only
in their physical well-being and zest for
life, but also in their alertness." I would
like to think that these words sank home,
not only in this committee, but outside it.
We must bear in mind that the present
scale of rations for the growing child is not
unduly generous and we cannot shut our
eyes to the fact that there are children in
the schools who by reason of their parents'
circumstances are ill-nourished.
We want education authorities to seek
out these children, to investigate the
means of the parents and if they find that
they are too poor to give their children a
good midday meal, to provide a free one
themselves, the cost of which the Ministry
will recoup to them to the extent of 90
per cent.
The education committee fixes
the standard of necessity on a scale which
it can determine itself and given goodwill
there is no reason why each education
authority in Northern Ireland should not
have a scheme in operation even if they
start on a small and experimental scale.
We also want education committees to pay
attention to those children who have no
time to go home for a midday meal and
to provide meals at the schools at a modest
charge-unless, of course, the child is
necessitous, when the meal will be free.
This is a sound proposal, well based on
educational principles and I hope that
hon. Members will agree with me that it
should be adopted, that we are earnest in
this matter, and that they will commend
it to the education committees in their
constituencies.
I am, perhaps, breaking my promise to

best ways in which youth can be helped
in the difficult years of adolescence-both
from a physical and mental standpoint.
I am sure the Committee's recommendations will be awaited with much interest
by all those who have the welfare of the

war and all the conditions inseparable

inseparable from and due to the times we
are passing through. The Ministry has
been actively assisting the development of
youth clubs during the past two years.
Grants are given to assist the promoters

activities and I am glad to say that
the number of clubs in existence
is now twice what it was in 1939.
What we need is a greater public
interest in this question, but there
are signs of a dawning recognition
of the public's responsibilities in this
matter.

is a fine thing to have our young people

About a month ago I was present at

in one of our schools. It was an occasion
when visitors were present. I saw the
children grouped together. I heard them
singing their hymns; I saw them taking

there will be just as valuable to them in

are likely to take away with them from

Leaders come from our primary elementary and technical schools, but if we

educational work.
I should like to endorse the ideals expressed by the Parliamentary Secretary
for the still further development of our
educational work after the war. In an
Act passed in England in 1918—it was
just after the last war-provision was
made for the education of young people
up to the age of 18. It proved too big
an enterprise for the country at that
time, but it may be that we will be able

give some sort of continuation education
to all our children after they leave the
elementary school until they are finally
launched on their career, or at least

part-time work would seem to me to have
two great advantages. First of all, it
would enable the young people to get an
insight into industry and into such things
as the methods of governing this democratic country, and in the second place
it would make them bigger men and
better men for the time when their work
is done. I wish to express my hearty
appreciation of the work that is being
done by the Ministry of Education.

It was created by the old vicious system
of the Board of Education, and was continued by the Ministry of Education.

Thirty-five per cent. of our teachers are
graded as "highly efficient," while 65
per cent. are only graded as "efficient."

The reply to the first part of the question is that the total number of pupils in
Northern Ireland on the 15th November,
1941, receiving education in secondary
schools was 14,447, representing 7.9 per
cent. approximately of the number of
pupils enrolled in public elementary
schools. I think that this is the percentage figure which the hon. Member is
seeking.
The total number of scholarships
awarded in the academic year, 1941-42,
by the various education authorities in
Northern Ireland, was 890. Of these
197 were junior scholarships in secondary
schools and 153 senior scholarships in
secondary schools; most of the latter
were made to pupils who formerly held
junior scholarships. Of the remaining
scholarships, 483 were scholarships in
technical schools, 27 in training colleges,
and 30 in universities.
Awards of other
other scholarships by
Queen's University do not come within

further University scholarships
