In 1923 the number of pupils receiving
instruction in secondary schools was 8,677
as against 14,447 to-day. The 8,677
represented 4.4 per cent. of the elementary
school population. In 1932 the number
had increased to 12,339, representing 6
per cent. of the elementary school population. There has been a steady increase,
but it has not been at as fast a rate as we
should have liked. In addition to the
pupils in secondary schools it must be
remembered that in connection with advanced education there are at present
3,360 pupils at day technical schools, compared with 2,501 in 1932.
In taking the figures I have given, I
think it is not quite right to condemn the
whole system because it does not appear
that a sufficient percentage of children
capable of receiving and able to receive
secondary school education are not receiving it. We should look at the progress we
have made. I indicated very clearly in
my speech that I hoped we would make
far greater progress in the future. I do
not think there can be any misunderstanding as to my views on the question of equal
opportunity, or whatever you like to call
it. There is very little difference between
the words "equality of opportunity" and
those I used in my opening remarks. We
should all recognise the enormous progress
which has been made during the past 20
years.
I should like to go into the question of
scholarships again. I think a comparison
should be made. I have no figures for
1923, but in 1925 96 scholarships were
awarded by local education authorities to
enable students to attend secondary
schools, and 22 went to students at universities. That compares with a total of 890
in 1941-42. There, again, we can see that
education authorities are realising their
responsibilities. Although we are all
agreed that it is desirable to realise these
responsibilities still further, I think it is
only fair to point out that a great amount
of progress has been made.
I need not go into the question of the
future because we recognise that a great
deal more progress must be made. I am
absolutely at one with hon. Members who
stated that every child who has the brains
or the intellect to profit by further education must in the future, in any selfrespecting State, receive such further
education by whatever means it is found
best to impart it. I think that deals with
the question of scholarships.
A great deal has been said by hon.
Members with regard to meals and milk.
The extraordinary thing is that many
hon. Members, the hon. Member for
Willowfield included, said they were
anxious for the continuation of public
and democratic control, yet in the same
breath they asked us to exercise compulsion. All I can say is that the progress
in this direction has not been as rapid as
I should have wished. I had hoped that
all the education authorities would have
brought in these provisions. It is quite
unnecessary for me to say that Belfast is
doing very well, and that County Down
is also giving free meals to something like
1,800 children. In Belfast 900 free meals
are being served daily.

Mr. NIXON: I would say that the

I know that owing to the way parliamentary procedure is organised if the
Government are defeated on a major.
measure they are expected to resign. I

Government should be expected to resign

I do not think it is generally realised
how greatly conditions have changed in
a city such as Belfast in the past 40 or so

governing body have now become. May
I, therefore, give a very few figures. In
the year 1898-the year of the passing of
the Local Government Act-the revenue
expenditure of the city was only £584,000
and the loan debt was £1,489,000. In
1922, the first complete year under the
Government of Northern Ireland, these
figures had increased respectively to
£1,603,866 and £5,347,225. In 1941
the revenue expenditure was £5,140,978,
and the loan debt was £10,647,874. Thus,
since 1898 the revenue expenditure has
increased nine-fold and the loan debt
seven-fold. I would ask hon. Members

The general structure of the Bill is

It is indeed one of the simplest Bills I

by Commissioners.
I should like to make it perfectly clear

the present proposal involves nothing

These are the essentials for democratic
Government. I think the essentials of
democratic Government surely are that
the wishes of the people, as interpreted by
their popularly elected representatives,
should be carried into effect so that the
services provided for the citizens will be
of a scope and character that will be
acceptable to the wishes of the citizens as
a whole.

the affairs of local authorities. Cases of

and, in any case, quickly come to light.
A much more mischievous influence is

Before reading these constructive proposals I should like to draw the attention
of the House to something that has been
forgotten. In the campaign that has
taken place in regard to local government
quite a number of people have assumed
that a body like the Belfast City Council

do by Act of Parliament. Beyond that
we cannot go. Some years ago I remember having a very concrete illustration
of this. When I moved a resolution in
the General Purposes Committee about
12 years ago the Council was then under
the jurisdiction of the late Sir Robert
Meyer-in regard to the establishment of
municipal coal depots for the relief of

show me any Parliamentary enactment
which denied us the right to do so. He
replied, "No, but I cannot show you one
which gives you that right, and until you
have the right you cannot do it." That
is the position in regard to local government.

These are the fundamental reasons why
I am moving the rejection of this Bill
to-day, which in Parliamentary phraseology involves moving that the Bill be
read a Second time this day six months.
We appeal to public opinion. We want
no misrepresentation. We do not want
to be placed in a white sheet of
pentance for something we have not done,
nor do we want to be clothed in sackcloth and ashes for allegations that do
not rest on fact. We know that mistakes
have been made. I know that things
have been done in municipal affairs that
ought not to have been done, and that
things have been left undone that ought
to have been done. That can be repeated
or quoted or asserted about every public
institution in the country.
Despite all their faults I appeal to the
Members of this House. Our system of
local government is our charter of local
liberty. Our charter dates back to the
seventeenth century. That charter has
been added to in modern times more
rapidly in accordance with the growth of
the community, as public intelligence
grew, as public amenities were expanded,
and as public services required. We have
had additions to it made in the form of
Acts passed by successive Parliaments,
and, as I have said, it is our charter of
local liberty, giving us the right to elect
our public representatives who will carry
on the services for the community.

I support the principle of the Bill for
two reasons. First of all and chiefly,
because the system of administering civic
affairs in operation in Belfast, and indeed
in most other cities throughout the
Kingdom, is antiquated and obsolete and
out of date and a nuisance and a waste
of time, and is an obstruction to decent,
busy, active, thoughtful, able men taking
that part in local government which they
ought to take. I have known men try the
Corporation-make an experiment and go
in and represent their constituency to the
best of their ability, and they were so
disgusted by the tediousness of the procedure that they felt they could not
manage their own business and look after
all the details which they were expected
to deal with in the Corporation business.
They simply retired. I support the principle of this Bill because the government
of our cities is a form of democracy which
is antiquated and out of date.
There are some things a committee can
do and some things a committee cannot

The PRIME MINISTER: As Prime
Minister and Leader of this honourable
House, I fully realise my responsibility
to make sure that this country is governed
impartially without fear and without
favour. We must have clean administration in local as well as in national affairs.
And I believe that the vast majority of
our people desire this. The desire of
the Government is, that no one shall be
able to point a finger of scorn at any of
our institutions, and that no one shall
again tarnish our city's record. I feel
it will be agreed that the Government

that Commissioners should be

Corporation that reforms were necessary,
and we appealed to them to reform themselves. The Corporation set up a Committee of themselves, as hon. Members
know, to make recommendations. Those

Committee, repented of their decision,
and rescinded their resolution and asked

the way they had been treated very

hon. Member for Willowfield is, in my
opinion, a very forgiving person, because notwithstanding-

It is, indeed, a regrettable record. I do

powerless in the hands of the others.

respect of such a certificate for a child

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): I have been asked by my right
hon. Friend to reply.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Can the Minister
state if a child attending a public elementary school desires to get a certificate to
be used later on, for instance, to get

the child to pay 3s 7d, or is 6d the
proper
fee?
The question of the fee payable for a
birth certificate is not governed by the
means of the applicant, but by the purpose for which the birth certificate is
required. As the law stands, a birth
certificate required for the purposes of
elementary education is issued at the
reduced fee of sixpence, but the statutory
fee of 3s 7d must be paid for a birth
certificate required for the purposes of
other branches of education; thus a person who is required to procure a certificate of birth before taking part in an
examination for a scholarship in a
secondary or technical school is required.
to pay 3s 7d for such a certificate.
Mr. BARBOUR: No. Not in order
to obtain employment. The only exception granted is in the case of elementary
schools, and for the purpose of the labour
exchange, in which case sixpence is the
charge for a birth certificate.

7. Mr. JOHN BAILEY asked the

wants 100,000 acres of flax grown in

can be accomplished.
Lord GLENTORAN: As the hon.
Member knows, I am at the moment in
negotiation with the Ministry of Supply
regarding the price of the 1943 flax crop,
which, my hon. Friend will appreciate, is
a very important factor in the position.
I am hopeful that the negotiations will
be completed in time to permit of an
early announcement of next year's price
and also to enable my Ministry to devote
its energies to the drive for increased
acreage. In that drive, of course, I shall
hope to avail myself of the hon. Member's
experience and advice.

Some members of the Government

It would appear to me that the Junior

Yes, it is going up the garden path; but
that is what he forgot to say. I will
leave that alone, and deal with what are
the principles which govern and underlie
and determine our system of democratic
government as we know it. What are
these principles? On a broad basis you
have the urban and rural councils, and
linked up with them you have the county
councils, city and borough councils, and
then at the top of the pyramid you have
Parliament to legislate and amend and
put into force laws. Always overriding
this you have the principle which has
been established throughout the centuries
and brought about by British wisdom and
genius for government. What is the
underlying principle? It is that the system
of government in this country is to maintain safeguards and buttresses against
central and bureaucratic control from the
executive outside and above and beyond the
power of the electorate. That is a principle

Whiteabbey Sanatorium. As a result of
that inquiry the Belfast Board of
Guardians was dissolved.
The Minister knows very well indeed
that I was bitterly opposed to the dissolution of the Belfast Board of
Guardians, and I fought it tooth and nail
while I was a member of the Government.
After the Board of Guardians had been
dissolved I went to the then Prime
Minister and said I wished to resign my
position in the Government. I was told
by the then Prime Minister that I must
accept what had been the collective
responsibility of the Government, and
that the matter was not of sufficient
importance to justify me in sending in
my resignation. I accepted that view of
the late Lord Craigavon, and remained a
member of the Government.
I was wrong, and I knew at the time
I was wrong, because I felt and said at
the time that the dissolution of the
Belfast Board of Guardians was the thin
end of the wedge by which the executive
was seeking to curtail the democratic
rights of the people. I made that complaint at the time, and I make it now.
I am confirmed in the view I then expressed. There is more danger to democratic institutions in this Bill than in any
measure which I have ever seen introduced in any Parliament in the British
Commonwealth of Nations. Here we
have an absolutely definite interference
1963 Belfast County Borough Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

by the executive with free institutions.
That is the point I make, and I speak in

dissolved. I did everything in my power
to prevent that being done, and I did
it on the principle that it was an interference with free institutions, and that it
was not the right way to deal with abuse.
I take up that position to-day. The
position taken up by the Government is
that in order to stop what is alleged to

there must be interference by the executive with the freedom of democracy. I
believe that is all wrong and cannot be
justified, and it will have very serious
influences in the country. What the
Government is attempting to do has
already split the Unionist Party—a split
it will take 15 years to repair. I do not
know but I say it with all seriousness
-how the Prime Minister, in those

The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Lord Glentoran): The gross increase of
£33,037 on Vote 1 is mainly in respect of
services carried out by my Ministry on
behalf of Imperial Departments, and is
offset by an increase of £29,139 in the
amount appropriated in aid of the vote,
The activities of my Ministry are SO
wide and varied that it would be difficult
in the form of a speech to deal adequately
with the numerous trading activities. Last
year I circulated to hon. Members a
memorandum which they were good
enough to indicate was very helpful. I
have followed the same procedure this
year, and I trust it has been helpful
again in giving hon. Members a picture
of the Ministry's activities and of the
developments which have taken place since
they last discussed my Ministry's estimates, and the reason for such developments.
Whilst the huge trading activities in
which my Ministry is involved, amounting
to a turnover of over £40,000,000 a year,
may loom large, and while they are undoubtedly necessary if we are to keep
down the cost of living and secure an
equitable distribution of the food available, it would be most unfortunate if we
allowed them to obscure the main purpose
of the Ministry, which is food production.
No useful object would be served by detailing the increases which have taken place
in the production of the various crops and
animal products. At the outbreak of the
war the Ministry set itself the task of
helping our farmers to make their farms
self-supporting, and I think it may be of
interest to the Committee to know what
progress has been made towards the
achievement of this object.
In the years before the war we imported
710,000 tons of cereals and other feeding
stuffs annually, and these were used by
our farmers in the production of milk,
bacon, eggs, beef, etc. Immediately on
the outbreak of war our farmers were set
the task of producing so much extra food
from our land that they could be independent of these imported feeding stuffs.
During the past year we have been able
to distribute to our farmers 250,000 tons
of feeding stuffs, mainly millers' offals,
leaving a deficiency of 460,000 tons. To
fill the gap our farmers produced in 1941
in extra grain and root crops the
equivalent of over 275,000 tons of im-
Estimates-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Ministry of Agriculture
[Lord Glentoran]
ported feeding stuffs. In addition, they
had available more than 200,000 extra
tons of straw and many thousands of
tons of grass silage, and we have thus
been able to weather the storm. In addition to their own very serious difficulties,
our farmers shouldered the principal part
of the linen trade's burden.
I am glad to be able to inform hon.
Members that despite the greatly increased acreage under food crops necessitated by the exigencies of the war and the
difficulties of price, the acreage under flax
this year promises to come up to our
estimate. In view of the pressing need
for flax arising out of world conditions,
I am at present in constant communication
with the Ministry of Supply with regard
to prices for the 1943 crop. These prices
I hope to be able to announce at a date
which will give farmers ample time to
make their preparations, and so avoid the
uncertainty which prevailed last year and
which undoubtedly had an effect on the
acreage sown. I need not stress how
valuable to our armed forces is this crop,
which for all practical purposes is purely
a Northern Ireland one.
All this has not been accomplished
without some change in the stocking of
our farms. It has, unfortunately, been
necessary to cut our pig stock by more
than one-half, as the requirements of the
pig population for the finer grain could
not be met. On the other hand, we have
actually-and this is quite extraordinary
-increased our population of cattle. Our
poultry population has been increased by
2 millions compared with 1939, and
Ulster is the only part of the United
Kingdom in which the milk sold off farms
has been increased since the outbreak of
the war.
These are achievements which
I think give ground for sober satisfaction
and which are in themselves an eloquent
tribute to the dogged and determined
manner in which our Ulster farmers have
responded to their country's call and by
so doing paved the way for victory.
quotas. Since the commencement of the
tillage campaign almost three years ago,
the number of cases which the Ministry
has had to take amounts to less than
than one in 500. So far it has been unnecessary for the Ministry to enter into
possession of a single farm, and that fact
alone is more eloquent than any words
of mine of the solidarity and loyalty of
our farmers to their country's cause.
There is one other aspect of this response by our farmers which is a solid
satisfaction to me, and which I am
certain will be equally so to every Member of the Committee. Hon. Members
will have seen from time to time reports
the Press of prosecutions against
farmers who have failed to fulfil tillage
I have already mentioned that during
the past year we have been able to distribute to our farmers through the
rationing scheme 240,000 tons of feedingstuffs, nearly all of it in the form of
millers' offals and oil cakes. We shall
not be in this fortunate position during
the coming year. The increase in the
milling percentage and events which have
happened elsewhere make it necessary for
us to tell our farmers that during 1943
-and, indeed, by the end of this yearthey will be able to purchase little, if
any, rationed feeding-stuffs.
The increased area under crop in 1942,
compared with 1941, will go a substantial
way to meet the loss, but not all the way.
I have, therefore, addressed to every
farmer in Northern Ireland a personal
letter explaining the situation to him and
calling upon him, with the help of the
Ministry's local officers, to do everything
possible during the next few months to
increase the growth of grass on their
pasture and to convert the surplus so
obtained into grass silage. I would ask
every Member for a rural constituency
in the Committee to exert his utmost
influence in this direction amongst the
farmers in his constituency.
I am fully conscious of the fact that
very serious difficulties lie ahead of us,
but, come what may, if the farmers of
this country continue to tear into their
task as they have in the past, and I receive the same generous and continuous
measure of support as I have done from
this House and from the Press, both town
and country, for which I am exceedingly
grateful, then I have no fear. We shall
solve our problems as they arise and continue to contribute our full quota to the
task of feeding both our men in the
Services and the civil population. I beg
to move.

This in my opinion is the most important estimate that comes before the
Committee because the life and well-being
of the people depend on it. If we are

from the land then our period on this

agriculture is the key to all other units
of life on this earth as far as mankind
is concerned. Our production from the

gone by. Our improvement in war-time

and some consideration must be given to

to-day would, I think, be an increase in

I feel that while there has been this

refer especially to the Minister of
Labour. While the Minister of Labour

was going to turn this debate on agriculture into a sort of comedy. He had a
great deal to say about the Parliamentary
Secretary, which I do not think he meant
-at least very little of it he actually
meant. He referred to himself as a
painter and said he might just as well
have been put into the job as a lawyer.
Put after what has happened in Germany
I would advise him to be careful.
I would also point out that the Opposition never tires of demanding that the
Government shall do certain things, and
that they shall take certain steps, and all
the blame or a great deal of it was attempted to be put on the Minister of
Agriculture for the failure in not saving
last year's harvest. They did not provide the necessary labour. They did not
do this or the other thing. But no
Government Department can do these
things which they are always being asked
to do from the other side of the House
without adding and continually adding to
the number of officials. That is just what
has happened and is happening, and is
bound to happen as long as this war lasts.
The very policy of government that is so
dear to hon. Members is through the
exigencies of the war to a large extent
being substituted for the pre-war form of
government under which we rejoiced to
live. Everything is being socialised for
the time being. It is being brought more
absolutely under Government supervision
and Government control with the inevitable result that in practically every
department of Government the number
of officials has increased and is bound to
go on increasing. In later days that may
serve as an argument if we want it.
Estimates-
Ministry of Agriculture
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Rev. Robert Moore]
In the meantime I simply wish to say I
have had a good deal of comings and
goings with this Ministry since the last
Estimates were presented, and I know
about a good deal of the work that has
been carried on by the Ministry. It has
involved a great deal of inspection by
officials. It has involved a tremendous
amount of control and restriction on the
individual activities of farmers, but I
think having said that we have to recognise that the duties that were laid upon
the staff of the Ministry of Agriculture
have been carried out with as little
friction and as little bad feeling as it
would have been humanly possible to
carry them out. I think that the Ministry
has probably one of the best indoor and
outdoor staffs employed by any Department.
Some points of real criticism were
made. The question about the new milk
factory in Co. Tyrone was mentioned. No
one regrets more than I do the amount
of feeling that seems to have been
generated about that matter, but I am
still satisfied that with the exercise of
good-will that difficulty could be overcome and the whole situation cleared up.
I hope all parties who are directly or indirectly involved in the matter will exercise that good-will, and that as a result
this feeling will be wiped out and swept
away, and that once again there will be
the same unity in regard to the question of
milk in Co. Tyrone as existed in the past.
I feel that this harvest is going to be
a very important matter for the whole
community. I think we all realise the
criticalness of the military situation
which involves shipping space and a
whole lot of matters I do not want to
specify in this debate to-day. As the
Ministry have been so successful up to
now, I only hope and wish them increasing success in their work and in supervising and encouraging the production of
still more and more food. The farmers
will play their part just as they have
done so extraordinarily well with few
exceptions up to the present. I was just
a little bit sorry that these Estimates
were treated rather more lightly than
they deserve. It is a question whether
any estimates brought before the Committee this Session or any that will be
brought before it in the course of the
Session are of more importance in the
national effort than the Estimates of the
Ministry of Agriculture. I would like
the whole community to realise the vital
part agriculture is playing and can continue to play if it is properly supported
and encouraged.
The question of voluntary labour was
also raised. I realise that the Ministry
of Agriculture decided that this was not
to be an official scheme. They gave it a
certain push at the beginning, and they
look to the different authorities in the
cities and towns to make the necessary
arrangements regarding organisations for
getting voluntary labour on the farms
during the harvest. There is one point I
would make. The Ministry undertook to
be responsible for publicity. We had a
good deal of publicity about the matter
when it was initiated, but things have
fallen a bit flat in the last three weeks
and publicity has slipped into the background. We are drawing near to the
period when these people will be actually
needed. I think the time has arrived
when the Ministry could do a great deal
more to bring this matter before the
public generally.

At that particular time many of the

America is very much more progressive
in regard to milk than we are. There
are cities like Toronto where pasteurisation is compulsory. Toronto has a population of three-quarters of a million.
Just before the last war, when I was
a boy, I was in the United States, and
at that time bottled milk was compulsory
in many of the large cities, including
New York, the second largest city in the
world. America was far in advance of
Great Britain and Ireland in regard to
the handling of milk. Since then they
have travelled very far, and it is quite
an ordinary thing throughout the United

governmental supervision, in the various

is any doubt in the minds of various

Tyrone I can give hon. Members a very
short account of the situation there. It
is this. There were a number of farmers
in Co. Tyrone giving their milk to the

since November, 1940, all milk has been

accordance witn une instructions of the

At the start the Ministry gave directions to the Department from whom they
had bought the milk to deliver it to the
creamery, but since then the increase in
the consumption of liquid milk, not only
Great Britain, but in Northern
Ireland, has been very considerable. In
addition, the amount of condensed or
evaporated milk which is necessary for
the armed forces of the Crown made it
essential that both here and in Great
Britain as much milk as possible should
be diverted from the manufacture of
butter into the liquid milk market. Consequently when Messrs. Nestlé's decided to
open a factory in Omagh for the very
purpose which we, as a Government, were
anxious to effect, namely, the diversion of
milk from the butter market into the
liquid milk market, we, of course, considering the offer we got from Messrs.
Nestlé's, had to say to the farmers from
whom we were getting the milk that we
wanted them to give that milk to Messrs.
Nestlé's.
It is an United Kingdom product at the
present time, and such we must
regard it.
as
We had to do that for three reasons.
We had to do it in the national interest,
and also because the prices paid by
Nestlé's to the Ministry of Food all the
year round is roughly between 1s 6d and
1s 7d, whereas the price paid by the
creamery to the Ministry of Food, taking
it all the year round, is 51d. In other
words, if we had continued to sell to the
creameries instead of to Messrs. Nestlé's
we would have been spending over 1s
per gallon of the nation's money. We
were saving 1s a gallon by diverting the
milk into Messrs. Nestlé's factory, and not
only were we doing that but we were
diverting it into a stream which was
absolutely essential to the progress of the
war and to the situation not only here
but in Great Britain. Last year we had
to divert a great quantity of liquid milk
from Northern Ireland to Great Britain.
We hope in the coming winter to be in
a position to divert even more. That
requires a considerable amount of
organisation. Milk can no longer simply
be produced and sold. We cannot look
at the product as merely a local product.
This establishment of Nestlé's in Tyrone
fits in with the United Kingdom plan.
We have got the financial benefit to
consider. When we see a factory that
can offer 1s 6d, whereas the creamery can
offer only 5d, surely the Ministry had
no option but to say to the farmers, "It
is our milk; we have bought it from you;
deliver it to Messrs. Nestlé's." We have
been told that the creameries will be deserted after the war. In point of fact,
in our general milk reorganisation if we
find milk has been diverted from any
creamery the offer is that the creamery
will get sufficient compensation to keep
its buildings and machinery in the same
state of repair as they are in at the
present time, so that when the end of
the war comes they will not find themselves in possession of ruined buildings;
they will be in possession of buildings
which from every point of view will be
in the same condition as they are in now,
and they will be able to compete, if they
can compete, with Messsr. Nestlé's after
the war.
I do not think anyone could cavil at
the method of compensation. It may be
that some persons will find themselves
out of work. We will endeavour, as far
as possible, to give those men employment; but we cannot guarantee to get
them employment. Indeed, that has
never been done when an industry,
owing to the effects of the war, has to
undergo certain changes. That, very
briefly, is the position in Tyrone at the
present time; we have got nothing to
hide.

Oral Answers to Questions.
GRADING OF FLAX.
1. Mr. JOHN BAILEY asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether it is a
fact that only nine per cent. get Grade I
and II for dam-retted flax and that these
grades are there only to deceive the
farmer and to enable the Ministry of
Supply to get flax 3s or 4s per stone less
than top price; whether, in view of this
small percentage, he will make representation to the Ministry of Supply to change
their method of grading, thereby enabling
the farmer to get a price which will at
least cover the cost of production.
•
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Lord Glentoran): The amount of flax
graded as I or II is in accord with the
figure mentioned by the hon. Member. I
cannot agree with and must deprecate the
statement that these grades were instituted and used by the Ministry of Supply
to deceive farmers. The hon. Member
may not know that six grades were insisted upon by our farmers although my
Ministry felt very strongly that classification into three grades was ample. The
hon. Member will appreciate that the
Ministry of Supply undertook to pay an
average price and that the amount falling
in the various grades does not, therefore,
affect the average return.

FINANCIAL FACILITIES FOR
FISHERMEN.
6. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he can state the details of the financial and other facilities
now available to fishermen to provide
new boats and equipment, etc.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: Under the
Fishery Loans Scheme, which has been
in force for a number of years, bona fide
fishermen may obtain loans for the purpose of acquiring a boat, engine, or fishing gear. These loans, which are secured
by a promissory note and sureties, are
repaid by fixed half-yearly instalments.
During the present emergency, with the
concurrence of my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Finance, I have introduced
a scheme which enables fishermen to
acquire new motor boats of an approved
type. The following are the main conditions governing the scheme:
The fisherman himself must deposit
one-tenth of the cost. The Ministry may
make an additional grant up to onequarter of the cost. The balance is provided by means of a loan from public
funds.
Mr. BROWN: While thanking the
Minister for his reply, might I ask will
he tell us the rate of interest to be charged
the fishermen in respect of these loans.
If the interest is not less than the bank
rate of interest there will not really be
any benefit received at all, in view of the
fact that fishermen can get loans from
banks.
So that the hon. Member may have an
opportunity of considering the details of
the scheme, I am sending him a copy of
a memorandum on the subject.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I cannot tell
the hon. Gentleman the rate of interest.
VOTE OF CENSURE.
Allegations against Minister of Home
Affairs.
Mr. NIXON: The House will recollect
that some time ago the Minister issued a
challenge to me to make certain statements outside about his association as
solicitor with Mr. McCrudden. That challenge I accepted, but the Minister did not
stand up to his challenge, with the result
that I have no option but to bring him
to bay in the precincts of this House. I
would have preferred a public meeting in
the centre of the city of Belfast, where
the citizens of Belfast could themselves
be the judge, and there the judgment
would not depend on the Party Whip or
on what has come to be known as vested
interests. In one of the debates on the
Corporation Bill I tried to get in this
evidence, but Mr. Speaker ruled that it
could not be put in in a debate of that kind
and said the only way it could be put in
was on a direct Motion. That is what
we are at this afternoon.
I may say by way of explanation that
some of the files are in my possession since
1939. I had intended to bring them up
in October, but after the war broke out
I had more than one interview with the
late Prime Minister about the war. The
one thing that the late Prime Minister
and I did agree about was the war, and
what should be done to win the war. The
late Prime Minister told me on two occasions that during the war he would allow
no legislation of a contentious or debatable nature. With that before me I put
these files in the safe and there they have
remained until the Government started
contentious legislation, which reflected on
a lot of people. Then I thought it time
to take the files out of the safe. I took
them out and here they are on this Table.
I
Vote of Censure
Vote of Censure
14 JULY 1942
The Motion that I move this afternoon
is:
That in the opinion of this House the
conduct of the Minister of Home Affairs
is deserving of censure for acting as
solicitor in the firm of E. & R. D. Bates,
2 Arthur Street, Belfast, in matters
which would come before him for his
decision in his capacity as Minister of
Home Affairs; and the House also
censures the Minister for his handling
of the charges of attempted bribery and
corruption in connection with the suggested purchase by the Belfast Corporation of the Rathmore site for a
sanatorium, and the charges of corruption and maladministration in connection with the contract for the extension
of the Armagh City Hall.
Now the Minister is the highest officer
in Northern Ireland. He has all power
in his hands. Magna Charta has not run
in Northern Ireland since 1921. People
of all religious denominations and all
political persuasions have been deprived.
of their liberty on the signature of the
Minister. Many have been deported, and
that being so the least we can expect from
the Minister-
Sir DAWSON BATES: On a point of
order. Has the hon. Member the right
to suggest that I or any member of the
Government have the right to deport
people from Northern Ireland? He ought
to know the law.
Mr. SPEAKER: On the point of order,
I think on a substantive Motion of this
kind the hon. Member really has a free
hand to bring anything he likes, Parliamentarily speaking, against the right hon.
Gentleman. Of course if it is a matter
that the right hon. Gentleman has not got
power over, well the hon. Member must
rely on his own judgment about that.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Surely the hon.
Member has no right to suggest a condition of law which does not exist?
Mr. NIXON: That is one thing I did
not do. What I said was that people of
all religious persuasions and all systems
of politics have been deprived of their
liberty on the signature of the Minister.
Mr. NIXON: I said deprived of their
liberty on the signature of the Minister
without judge or jury. I stand by that.
I can prove that anywhere in the world,
including the meeting that the Minister
avoided in the centre of the city. I base
anything I say this evening largely, that
is the vital part of it, on what should be
done in certain cases on a statement made
by the Attorney-General in this House.
Since I came into this House there is one
thing I have never done-I never had
occasion to do it that is criticise the
Attorney-General in his capacity as
Attorney-General. On the contrary I
have frequently paid tribute to the
various Attorneys-General in their capacity as Attorney-General. I may have
thought that a certain Attorney-General
was no great Minister of Public Security,
but as Attorney-General up to the present
he has been like his predecessors unimpeachable. I am going to quote the
Attorney-General now. I say that all the
Government's actions in regard to corruption should be based on what the learned
Attorney-General said. I am quoting
from Hansard of the 11th October, 1938,
page 1461, and the question is headed
"Alleged Attempted Bribery":—
Sir DAWSON BATES: You said
deported.
Mr. Beattie asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether his attention
has been drawn to a statement in the

Belfast Corporation, "That he had
been offered a sum of money to vote
for a certain site for the proposed new
sanatorium"; whether, in view of this
serious allegation, he is prepared to set
up a sworn inquiry to investigate the
charges made.
The Attorney-General: I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend to
reply.
On the 4th instant my attention was
drawn to the statement in the Press
referred to by the hon. Member. As
the particulars appeared to disclose a
serious offence against Section 1 (2)
of the Public Bodies Corrupt Practices
Act, 1889, I immediately caused inquiry to be made by the police in order
to ascertain if evidence were available
to sustain a prosecution, but Councillor Wilton, when interviewed by the
District Inspector, refused to give any
information.

The Attorney-General: The obvious
method of clearing any person who

is to obtain the necessary information

That is the soundest law that ever was

THE MINISTER OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Sir Dawson Bates) (who was
received with cheers): I cannot pretend
that the venomous attack that was made
on me yesterday and perhaps will be continued to-day by the hon. Member for
Woodvale comes to me with the least
surprise. It is the culmination of
twenty years implacable hostility towards
myself. I know he has disavowed any
intention or any degree of spite towards
In fact, he has stated here that the
person whom he blames for his dismissal
from the Royal Ulster Constabulary is
the late Prime Minister, Lord Craigavon,
me.
Before I proceed to discuss the charges.
made against me here yesterday, and before proceeding to disprove them in
detail, I should like to point out to the
House what I conceive my duty to be as
a Minister of the Crown in relation to
my private capacity as a solicitor. Private interests must never be allowed to
conflict with public duty.
Mr. NIXON: Hear, hear.
Sir DAWSON BATES: There is no
difficulty in keeping this principle ever
in mind. It is constantly in the mind
of any member of the solicitor profession.
It is elementary that he cannot act for
two clients at the same time where the
interests of those clients conflict.
Mr. NIXON: Hear, hear.
Sir DAWSON BATES: My own personal experience of 40 years, and a
family experience of over 100 years in
the same profession are enough to impress this upon my mind. Neither in
my public capacity nor in acting for
private clients have I ever transgressed
this rule which has been established ever
since the solicitor profession became an
organised one, that is, for a matter of
several hundred years. There is even
an older rule with still greater authority,
over 2,000 years old, which says: "No
man can serve two masters.'
Mr. NIXON: Hear, hear.
Sir DAWSON BATES: There is a
second consideration of which, although
it is a truism, I feel it is necessary to
remind the House once more, and that is
that the executive of the Government
under our Constitution cannot interfere
with the Attorney-General in the dis-
Vote of Censure
Vote of Censure

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
charge of his duties. He is free and
unfettered to institute any proceedings
for the vindication of the criminal law,
and he is in full and complete control
over those proceedings, and in obtaining
the necessary evidence to support any proceedings which he deems necessary to institute he has full, free and unfettered
control over the police force for that purpose. It will be within the recollection
of, I believe, all the Members of this
House that an Attorney-General in
England not so many years ago, a gentleman of the highest distinction in his
profession, was forced to resign because
he permitted himself to be influenced by
the Executive Government of the day in
regard to dropping a prosecution against
a certain individual. It is perfectly
obvious why this rule exists. Otherwise
the rule of law, which, after all, is the
outstanding characteristic of our Constitution, would disappear, and there would
be substituted therefor the political
fancies or wishes of the Executive Government of the day.
I can positively assure the House that
during the 21 years I have been a member
of the Cabinet there has never been any
attempt on my part or on the part of any
of my colleagues or on the part of the
Cabinet acting together to endeavour to
influence any one of the learned gentlemen who have filled or the learned gentleman who is filling the office of His
Majesty's Attorney-General.

Now let me come to the charges which

fashion. The first charge is that I, in

I understand it, the mishandling of the

purchase by the Belfast Corporation of

The first matter dealt with is the erection of the picture house owned by the
The hon.
Shankill Stadium Co., Ltd.
Member has described a journey to
Lisburn, and how he found after paying
1s fee-I hope this will lessen the income
tax-on examination of the memorandum
and articles of a company, Irish Theatres,
Ltd., that I had acted as solicitor for that
company. It is perfectly true that I
registered that company on the 28th day
of March, 1935. The memorandum and
articles were not prepared by me,
although that is but a small point. The
particular object of that company was to
book films; in other words, to carry on
the business of film renters. The company has never erected a picture house
throughout its existence.
Over a year later another company was
registered, the Shankill Stadium Co.,
Ltd. It was registered on the 19th
August, 1936. It is this company which
owns the picture house at the corner of
Tennent Street and Shankill Road. The
memorandum and articles of this company
were not prepared and the company was
not registered by me, and I have never
acted for this company. So much for the
truth of the hon. Member's statements. It
had an entirely different solicitor, but my
attention was drawn to this fact sometime
ago, that in a prosecution instituted by
the police for an alleged breach of the
Cinematograph Regulations, this company
was defended by quite another solicitor,
not even the one who registered it.
When this company, to which the hon.
Member attaches so much importance,
lodged plans for the erection of this
picture theatre, these plans were rejected
in the first instance by the Improvement
Committee of the City Council, the city
surveyor pointing out that the plans did
not conform with the regulations relating
to building frontage which had been laid
down by the committee. The plans were
duly modified and the city surveyor was
prepared to recommend that they be
passed, but on the 27th August, 1935, the
surveyor was forbidden to pass the plans
on the ground that the proposed theatre
was in too close proximity to a place of

I come now to the allegations with

Let me give the House a few facts.
My first professional connection with
Mr. McCrudden was acting for a company
in which he is interested, S. McCrudden &
Co., Ltd., in an action which was brought
against the firm by a dismissed employee.
This was in the year 1933. In the
following year I acted for him with regard
to the taking of a lease of premises in
London. In 1935 I acted for him in his
personal capacity, when he made a lease
of portion of the Rathmore estate for
building purposes to a man called
Armour. In the month of October, 1936,
I registered a company called The Chalet,
Ltd., which is a private company having
premises at Crawfordsburn, Co. Down.
When I acted first for Mr. McCrudden,
in the year 1933, it was quite impossible
for me, unless I had been a soothsayer,
to know or foresee that the Belfast City
Council would advertise for sites for a
municipal sanatorium in January, 1937,
and it was equally impossible for me to
foresee that Mr. McCrudden would offer
Rathmore as a possible site.
It was first clearly and distinctly
brought to my mind that Rathmore was
among the sites that had been offered to
the Corporation by a letter written to me
by the late Councillor Cochrane on the
9th August, 1937. In this letter he
urged strongly the supposed advantages
of Rathmore. This letter was formally
acknowledged by me on the 17th August,
1937, in which I pointed out that my

sites for a sanatorium could not be taken

With regard to his allegations that the
inspectors' recommendations were in conflict with the Ministry's findings, the
position of the inspectors with regard to
local government inquiries has been
explained on numerous occasions in this
House, notably on the 25th April, 1939,
when the matter was gone into most fully,
and when authorities were quoted by the
then Parliamentary Secretary.
Briefly, it was made clear that the
inspectors' functions are to obtain such
evidence as will enable the Ministry to
decide the matter at issue. They obtain
this evidence and make such comments on
it as they think will be of assistance to the
Ministry. It is within their province to
make recommendations if they consider
that it will be of assistance to the department to know how the matter appeared
to the inspectors, but the responsibility
for the decisions arrived at is not theirs,
but the Department's, and it has been

The Minister stated, in introducing the
Bill, that a definite obligation was laid
on electrical undertakings to take steps
to secure their due functioning. Is it
reasonable to suggest that the Belfast
undertaking alone should provide plant
to meet the national emergency, simply
because of the location of industries
in the Province, without receiving a grant
from the Treasury? What steps have
been taken by the other undertakings to
secure their due functioning? It would
appear that they had all hoped that
Belfast would see them through. Surely
the obligation of ensuring the due functioning is placed equally on all undertakers in the North of Ireland.
Prior to the Minister taking up his
present office, the Belfast Corporation had
in hand the dispersal of plant at a cost
to them of approximately £40,000, had
spent a considerable sum of money in protecting the equipment at their power
stations, and had actually acquired a
further site for a dispersal station, plant
for which could not be obtained from
Great Britain, either by the Corporation
or the Ministry. The costs incurred by
the Corporation in connection with the
Harbour power station extensions, which
works were cancelled by the Ministry,
were incurred with the full approval of
the Ministry by its consenting to the
raising of a loan by the Corporation for
the purpose of meeting the cost of the
works.
The transfer to the Belfast Corporation
of the new power station and transmission
line, in accordance with the above amendment, would be to the advantage, not
only of Belfast, but of all undertakers
taking supplies from it, and would be in
accordance with the desire of the
Ministry, as expressed by it in a letter on
the files of the Corporation.
This substantially embodies the point of
view pressed on the Ministry for some
time. We feel that this is just and
equitable, and, taking the long view, it is
calculated to serve the needs, from an
economic point of view, of all the consumers of electricity eventually throughout Northern Ireland.

Sir BASIL BROOKE: I may explain
that there is no sinister intention in this
sub-clause. The reason for its insertion
is that in the Electricity Acts it is necessary for authorised undertakings to ask
for the consent of the Ministry of Commerce when they are carrying out certain
operations. Obviously when the Ministry itself is an undertaker then it would
be foolish to go through the formality
of requiring its own consent. It is for
the purpose of eliminating this useless
procedure that the sub-clause has been
inserted, since it would have entailed a
great deal of unnecessary wording in the
Bill, if all the matters had been dealt
with in the Bill itself. It should be
noted, in addition, that there are ample
safeguards in the second paragraph of
the sub-clause, since any Order must first

Gazette, then laid before Parliament,

NEW CLAUSE (Tariff for electricity
supplied by the Ministry in bulk).
(1) Where the Ministry gives a
supply of electricity in bulk to any
authorised undertakers the price to be
charged by the Ministry for the supply
shall, in default of agreement and subject to the terms of any contract in force
at the passing of this Act, be in accordance with such tariff as the Ministry
may, by order, fix from time to time;
and the tariff shall be so framed as to
include as part of the charge and show
separately-
(a) a fixed kilowatt charges component; and
(b) a running charges component.
(2) Before an order fixing a tariff
-comes into force, it shall be laid before
each House of Parliament for the
statutory period, and, if either House
of Parliament before the expiration of
the statutory period resolves that the
order ought not to come into force, no
further proceedings shall be taken on
the order.
Brought up, and read a First time.
Sir WILSON HUNGERFORD: This
is a new Clause and introduces the main
safeguard asked for by the Belfast
Corporation. It ensures that a proper
price will be charged for any supply of
electricity given by the Ministry to any
other undertaking. This will ensure that
if there is any certified deficiency in
respect of the Ministry's operations it
will be a figure which can be properly
accounted for. It will draw a distinct
line between the non-productive cost of
the Ministry's operations in maintaining
stand-by stations and the commercial production cost of the electricity which is
sold to other undertakings.
This means that part of the cost of the
certified deficiency will not be passed on
to undertakings which take a supply from
the Ministry through the medium of an
increased charge for the supply. The
Ministry has no objection whatever to this
accounting procedure, but I should say
at this stage that in the event of an emergency arising I will at once take action to
ensure that the supply of electricity is
properly directed, and the accounting can
follow at the first available opportunity.
I think the House will agree with this
policy. I beg to move, "That the new
Clause be read a Second time."

Sir WILSON HUNGERFORD: I beg

*
The idea of this Amendment is to ensure that when an undertaking is taken
over by the Ministry the existing contracts of such an undertaking to supply
electricity in bulk to other undertakings
will also be taken over. This principle
is quite equitable, since it would throw
certain undertakings into a state of great
uncertainty if they were faced with the
breaking of a long term contract when
the Ministry takes over another undertaking which is under obligation to give
a bulk supply. This new provision will
stabilise the position.
Amendment agreed to.

Sir BASIL BROOKE: Members will
recollect that under the legislation passed
in 1937 to promote the establishment of
new, and the development of existing
industrial undertakings, a time limit of
five years was fixed for the receipt of
applications for assistance by way of
grant or loan. The Act was passed on
7th July, 1937, and the Bill now before
the House will make it possible for my
Ministry to entertain applications for
assistance up to 31st December, 1944.
In harmony with the policy adopted
in Great Britain on the outbreak of war
in regard to the legislation designed to

FLAG DAYS IN BELFAST.
1. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he will request
the Commissioner of Police to reconsider
his refusal to grant a flag day in Belfast
in aid of the Green Cross Fund, having
regard to the prevalent distress among the
families relieved by this fund; and
whether he can state the number of flag
days held or to be held in Belfast this
year.
Some time ago considerable public
opposition was aroused by reason of the
excessive number of flag days permitted,
and as a result the number was reduced
to cover only local hospitals and certain
charities of national interest. A few
organisations, which were outside these
limits, such as the St. Vincent de Paul
Society, were allowed to continue because
they had been granted permits for many
years.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The number of flag
days arranged for Belfast city during the
present year is 22, and no extension of
that number is desirable.
Many requests for additional flag days
have been refused, notwithstanding the
charitable cause for which they were proposed, and in these circumstances I cannot agree to the hon. Member's request.

right hon. Friend to reply. The rate of

4 per cent. Stock, 1945-1975, and Ulster

Oral Answers
Oral Answers
21 JULY 1942
IL
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): I have received the resolution
referred to in the hon. Member's question, but I must inform him that my
inquiries have not confirmed the allegations made in it.
It is not a fact that the majority of
the men carrying out joiners' work on the
contract mentioned have never previously
worked at the trade. We would never
think of sending an unskilled man to
carry out the work of a practical joiner.
Since this work began we have submitted 111 joiners, of whom 82 were local
men, and 29 came from further afield.
Further, I am informed that no joiners
have been sent out of Newry when there
were any local vacancies notified to the
exchange still open. The hon. Member
will realise that these undertakings make
large, urgent demands for skilled tradesmen, and that when the local supply
is exhausted the exchange cannot
leave vacancies unfilled if suitable
workers are available elsewhere. In
these circumstances, it must sometimes
happen that men are placed at work some
distance from their homes, and that
further local vacancies may be notified
shortly afterwards which have to be
filled by workers imported from other
places. In view of the urgent nature of
the undertakings, and in the interests of
the maximum war effort, this is at present unavoidable.
Mr. BROWN: Would the Minister tell
us that if the majority of the men
employed in this particular contract do
not come under the description of not

will agree that a number do come under

was refused admission to this contract

my authority to do that.

"That a sum not exceeding £44,100 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in course of payment during
the year ending 31st March, 1943, for the
salaries and expenses of the Ministry of
Home Affairs."-(Note £30,000 has been
voted on account.)
Sir DAWSON BATES rose.

you-

Sir DAWSON BATES: It will be

the general result, therefore, is a net

Ministry of £9,057.
The greatest increases, of course, Occur

It will, of course, be understood that
these services are all agency services, which
we are carrying out on behalf of the
Imperial authorities, and that all the expenses in connection with such services are
recouped to us. For example, it will be
seen that the total expenses for the
Evacuation Division amount to £46,809,
and in respect of this we receive from the
Ministry of Health a sum of £50,000.
Similarly, the total expenses of the
Petroleum Department amount to £24,102
and we receive in respect of this £26,655.
The recoupment in both these cases appears
to be greater than the actual expenditure,
but this is because there are certain expenses in connection with these particular
services which do not appear under their
particular sub-heads, but are merged in
other sub-heads, as, for example, travelling and subsistence and miscellaneous
expenses.
It may be taken, however, that the
general position is that so long as these
services are being administered on the
general lines of corresponding services in
England the British authorities are bearing the full cost of them, and I may say
that the attitude of the Imperial Departments with regard to the extent to which
we may depart from time to time from
what is being done in England in order
to suit our particular local needs has been
a most generous one.
It is also relevant to the matter that in
this year's Estimate we are able to show
a full year's recovery from the Imperial
Government in respect of staff employed
on these services, whereas last year it was
not possible to show it in full as some of
them had just been transferred from other
Departments.

With regard to the regular police, the

This small increase arises on making provision for a full year for the items which
I explained in detail when presenting the

I am happy to be able to say that, on
the whole, the public peace has been well
preserved during the past year, and this
state of affairs is due to the untiring work
of the Royal Ulster Constabulary, and to
the valuable assistance given to that force
by the Special Constabulary. As to

I only mentioned certain events that
have happened. I wish, before I pass
from this, to say that these men died in
the service of their country, and I would
like on behalf of the Committee to extend
to the relatives the sympathy of every
Member. These incidents exemplify the
need for unceasing vigilance and show
the necessity for maintaining the constabulary forces at the highest peak of
efficiency.
Hon. Members are, no doubt, fully
aware of the many additional duties
thrown on the constabulary by war conditions, and I am glad to say that these
burdens have been cheerfully accepted
by the force and are now attended to by
them as part of their normal work.
There is one item in the Estimates
which might convey a wrong impression
-I refer to the number of officers shown
as on war service. That this number is
small is not the fault of the police force,
as the small number is made up almost
entirely of men who had commitments
with the armed forces before the outbreak of the war and who were automatically recalled to the colours.
Very many men now serving in the
police were anxious to be permitted to
join the fighting services, but their
applications had to be refused. The
Government decided that the principle
governing service during the war should
be that every man must place his services
where they will be of the most value to
the State, regardless of any consideration
of inclination or of personal or other
prestige. It is inevitable that individual
heart-burnings should result from the
decision, but it is essential that the force
should be maintained at its maximum
strength to meet any developments which
may arise, and the Government could not
countenance the loss of trained men
which would have resulted if all members wishing to join the fighting services
had been permitted to do so.

The Estimate for the Special Constabulary, including the Home Guard,
shows a decrease of nearly £48,000, as
against last year's Estimate. This is
due mainly to the fact that an agreement
has been made with the Imperial Authorities whereby the supplies of clothing,
equipment and other stores for the Home
Guard will be supplied without financial
adjustment being made in this Vote.
Certain increases in other sub-heads,
however, offset the gross reduction in this
respect.
The work of the Special Constabulary
in these difficult times cannot be too
highly praised, and this force, by the
assistance and support it has given to the
regular constabulary, has more than
amply justified its existence. As hon.
Members have already been informed,
increase in pay has been granted to
mobilised members of the force.
No provision is made in this Estimate for the
sum involved, which will, if necessary, be
dealt with by a Supplementary Estimate.

The Home Guard has not yet completed its second year, and its training
on military lines is being continued. In
the event of actual or apprehended attack
by the enemy, the force will be placed
under military control and command so
long as the situation warrants that
course.
The local defence of our Province is
the primary object of the force, and the
zeal and enthusiasm displayed by its
members when training to fit themselves
for this task leave no room for doubt in
my mind that, if called upon, it will give
a very good account of itself.
I have referred before to subversive
activities, and these are responsible to a
large extent for the continued high rate
of expenditure on the prison service.
Over 300 persons have had to be interned
in order to safeguard the community,
and, much as this state of affairs is to
be deplored, the Government is determined to do everything in its power to
ensure that potential quislings and fifth
columnists shall not prosper here.
in their administration, I would say that
their work is greatly appreciated.
The prison service continues to be run
on the most humanitarian lines possible,
and to the staffs employed on the difficult
duty of looking after these institutions,
and to the voluntary workers who assist
In regard to Belfast Prison, I am glad
to be able to inform the Committee that
a small extra duty allowance has been
approved for the staff on account of the
difficult conditions under which they are
serving. Provision is not made in this
Estimate for the sum involved, but it
will be dealt with, if necessary, by the
Supplementary Estimate in due course.
Next comes the Estimate for the
Malone Training School and Reformatory
and Industrial Schools a relatively
small one.
The problem of juvenile deliquency
and the treatment of the young offender
is now receiving serious public attention,
and, while I sympathise with all those
people who would like to see these institutions abolished, I am afraid that this is
not feasible in present conditions. If the
maintenance of the institutions is essential, therefore, it is most important that
they should be 100 per cent. effective in
their efforts to train young persons who
may be sent to them to become good and
useful citizens. Only one of the institutions-the Malone Training School-is
fully under my control, and while I am
aware that many hon. Members take a
keen interest in the work of this school,
there are many others who do not appear
to do so, and to these I would extend an
invitation to visit the school to see for
themselves how the boys are looked after
and taught to become useful citizens. I
may say in passing that 95 per cent. of
the boys who leave this school never get
into trouble afterwards.
With regard to the other institutions,
the duties of my Ministry are mainly of
a supervisory nature, the schools being
run by voluntary organisations or under
the control of local authorities.
As regards the local government division, while the work on this side of my
Department has fallen off to an appreciable extent in some matters, as, for
example, housing, which it has been
necessary to postpone during the war so
far as any new housing schemes are concerned, certain very important emergency
services have devolved upon it, including
the emergency hospital services. Following the principle adopted in England and
approved by this House these are dealt
with by means of block estimates, and I

Coming now to the more normal work
of the division, it will be seen in Class III,
No. 7, that the Estimate for derating

1941-42. This increase is accounted for
by the payment of additional grants to
rural authorities. Under the Derating
Act of 1936, derating grants were fixed,
but, with the unavoidable increase that
has taken place in local expenditure, it
was found that the grants were insufficient
to cover the cost of essential services, with
the result that heavy burdens fell to be
borne by the ratepayers, and that a very
slight additional expenditure involved an
unduly increased rate. The Government,
therefore, decided that it should come to
the assistance of rural authorities this
year. Had it not done so a very substantial increase in rates would have been
unavoidable, but the increase in grants.
given has enabled local authorities in

As the Committee is aware, two Commissioners were appointed to take charge
of the tuberculosis service in Belfast, and

upon this
Department as a result of war conditions.
since their appointment; for example,

matters of this kind were discovered by
the Commissioners they did not hesitate

I am very glad, indeed, that this has
been the Commissioners' policy, for
there is always, I think, some temptation
to Commissioners to cut down expenditure at all costs in order to show a saving
over the administration which they have
replaced.

There has also been an additional
demand for accommodation at Whiteabbey since the Commissioners
appointed, and this is being met so far
as possible by the provision of some 50
additional beds which, of course, involves
further expenditure.
The Committee will be interested to
know further that since the appointment
of Doctor Clarke as Chief Tuberculosis
Officer it has been found possible to
administer the affairs of the Tuberculosis
Committee with part-time Commissioners
only, and this has, of course, effected a
saving in the salaries of these officers.
I am very glad to be able to say that,
generally speaking, the local authorities

since the war began, that is to say, 300

when men could be whisked off to the

warrant of a Minister without any
sanction or authorisation from any court.

The Member for Pottinger raised a
number of points, the first of which was
the increase in the numbers of our staff.
It is quite true that the numbers have
increased, but so has the work. To a
large extent the increase in the staff of
the Ministry is based upon the requirements of the Ministry of Food and the
Ministry of Supply. As hon. Members
know, the Ministry of Agriculture act as
agents in a great many cases for the
Ministry of Food. As the war goes on
regulations increase in number and become more stringent. All those regulations have to be supervised and put into
force by the staff. Consequently, the
more regulations that come out and I
can assure hon. Members that they come
out very frequently-the greater the
stringency, and the greater the necessity
for an increase in staff.
I will give merely one example. As
you know, part of the price for potatoes
is given by way of £10 per acre as a prepayment. That price, of course, is taken
into account in the subsequent price. I
do not suggest that it is in the nature of
a subsidy, it is in the nature of a prepayment.
That means every acre of
potatoes grown in Northern Ireland has
to be inspected by a member of the staff
of the Ministry. When one considers
there are about 100,000 farmers in
Northern Ireland, practically all of whom
grow potatoes, it means there are
probably more than 100,000 lands
or fields to be surveyed by the.
Ministry's officials in order to see that
the acreages tally with the claims put
forward by the farmers. Those are, as
a rule, temporary inspectors. The hon.
Member made reference to that, and I
can assure him that once the work is
finished, and this potato inspection is a
purely seasonal thing, those inspectors
are not carried on in their positions.
When the work is finished they are
simply turned off. That is the method
by which they are employed. They know
it is a purely seasonal occupation and they
accept it as such.
Then, in connection with land improvement, the number of claims during the
last year has increased beyond all
measure. We are glad to see that, because it means a tremendous amount to
agriculture in Northern Ireland, and we
are hoping that these applications will
continue to come in as they have been
doing up to the present time. The land
in Northern Ireland has been greatly improved during the last two or three years,
but that does not mean that it is perfect
at the moment. Improvement is going
on steadily, and indeed with an increasing tempo. We trust that it will continue.
The hon. Member also made reference
to the allegation that Great Britain is
not fulfilling its promise with regard to

misapprehension in that respect. Great
Britain is fulfilling its obligations with

course, the number we get depends not

The FINANCIAL SECRETARY
(Major Sinclair): In the first place I
can assure the hon. Member that while
requests from various Government Departments are sympathetically considered
by the Minister of Finance they are also
considered impartially. When money is
being allocated to a Department we see
to it that it is spent to the best advantage
of the people in Northern Ireland as a
whole. In the Ministry we consider that
to be our special function. With regard
to the other point raised by the hon.
Member, the contract system, I will have
one or two things to say on that when
the Public Works and Buildings Vote
comes forward. I realise that contract
procedure is one which has to be carefully watched. There are certain loopholes if the procedure is not a satisfactory one, but I submit that every precaution is taken by the Government to
ensure that the contract system is as foolproof as possible. Undoubtedly in the
past there may have been instances where
the mistakes to which the hon Member
has referred have occurred, but I have
no knowledge of them. If the hon.
Member would, in private, give me
particulars I will have the greatest
possible pleasure in going into the matter.
The abuses which can operate under
the contract system are very dangerous
so far as the public purse is concerned.
All contracts should be under the supervision of a small committee. Before
tenders are asked for or work given out
a committee should go into the matter

If that were done there would be a

Turning to details, hon. Members will
see that the Estimate for new works,
alterations and purchases, in sub-head A,

Apart from one minor work there are no
new items under this sub-head. The

This heading includes expenditure on
such miscellaneous matters as provision of
shelters, black-out arrangements, first-aid
equipment, beds and bedding for firewatchers, and the setting up of a central
emergency control centre, as well as
various other protective measures about
which I am sure the Committee will not
expect me to go into detail. The stocking
of dumps of emergency building materials,

largely re-votes, are included to provide
for final payments for works in connection
with the dispersal of staffs, provision of
additional accommodation, and the construction of the new police rifle range.
Major SINCLAIR: There is a net
decrease of £75,246 in this Estimate.
Briefly, it can be said that the reduction
arises because the 1941-42 provision was
swollen by the inclusion of substantial
amounts of non-recurring expenditure
rendered necessary by war conditions.
Hon. Members will recall that several
such items were provided for in the
Supplementary Estimate which it was
found necessary to take during the last
financial year.
Sub-head B (Maintenance, renewals
and repairs) shows a substantial increase.
The maintenance of the additional
accommodation required in connection
with the dispersal of some of the staff
formerly housed in Belfast offices, and
the increased activities of Government
Departments generally is responsible to
some extent for the larger figure. In
addition, after more than two and a half
years of war, during which maintenance
costs have been kept to a minimum, it
will soon be necessary to spend appreciably more on the upkeep of Government
buildings if they are to be preserved from
serious deterioration. Account must also
be taken of increased prices of materials
and heavier labour charges. Though
provision for expenditure of this nature
was included in the 1941-42 Estimates,
a good deal of the work had to be deferred
because of the more urgent calls of other
services.
I can assure the Committee
that maintenance expenditure will be
incurred only where it is absolutely
necessary and where it can be carried out
without interfering with the progress of
any more urgent work.
Hon. Members will note that under subhead F no provision is made this year for

out of the Government Loans Fund
towards the county councils' contributions to the expenses of the Bann Drainage
Scheme as the flood alleviation works
under the scheme have been completed.
It is expected that the total expenditure
on the scheme will not exceed the sum
of £891,000.
The Committee may be interested to
know that the scheme has proved even
more successful than was anticipated. Its
effectiveness is clearly shown by a comparison with the year 1876-77 when
Lough Neagh reached a record high level
with consequent widespread flooding. In
1938-39 the run-off from the catchment
area into the lough was of even greater
intensity for the first half of the winter
than in 1876-77, and no flooding took
place throughout the season. I propose
to have placed in the Library graphs
which have been prepared showing the
actual conditions existing for the last four
winters compared with calculated precontract conditions for the same period. I
think they will show the Members of the
Committee more clearly than I can express it the effect of the work on the
Bann Drainage Scheme.
No flooding has occurred on account of
the high-water lough levels during these
four winters, and if the drainage works
had not been executed flooding would
have occurred periodically to the extent
of 30,000 to 40,000 acres. Hon. Members
are aware that the main object of the
drainage scheme was to prevent as far as
possible within the limits of reasonable
expenditure the level of Lough Neagh
rising beyond 53ft. 6ins. O.D., but no
guarantee was or could be given that in
a very wet season that level would not be
exceeded and no flooding would take
place. There are certain small areas on
the shores of the lough which lie below
the level, which I have indicated, and
the fact that they are now dry during the
greater part of the year may induce their
owners to use them for tillage operations.
age scheme was prepared, and it was

Reference has been made on one or two
occasions in the House to the cost plus
profit system of placing contracts. I
have said before that the Government
dislikes this system and avoids it where
possible. It may interest the Committee
to have some further information on this
subject. In an emergency such as the
present the time factor, as the Committee
will readily understand, becomes the predominant consideration, and to it normal
contract procedure must be subordinated.
The cost plus system is only resorted to
in cases of extreme urgency, and the
majority of such contracts placed by the
Ministry for this Government were those
placed in two periods-immediately after
the outbreak of war or after the air raids
last year. They cover urgent protective
measures and the repair of vital buildings which suffered damage. During the
past twelve months no contracts for Northern Ireland services have been placed
on a time and material basis with the
exception of the demolition of a portion
of a large police barracks. The Ministry fully appreciates the advantages of
the competitive system even in war time
and during recent months has been able
to make a closer approach to normal procedure for urgent agency services, and
has succeeded in obtaining competitive
tenders for several important works where
speed of execution was an important
feature.

I know that the hon. Member for Pottinger has been a consistent advocate,
since I came into Parliament, for the
starting of a Police Federation in
Northern Ireland. The law does not
depend solely on the Act of 1922; there is
an Imperial statute of 1919, which was
adopted here in 1922, and which makes it
illegal for any person to join this Police
Federation. I appeal to the hon. Member
for Pottinger not to encourage in any way
any member of the police force to join
this body, because section 3 of the Act of
1919 provides that a police constable so
acting renders himself liable to instant
dismissal and forfeiture of all pension
rights.
I can readily see that young, inexperienced constables, knowing that there
is a Police Federation in operation in
Great Britain, might think inadvertently
it was lawful to join one here, and thereby
subject himself to these grave penalties.
Therefore, I would appeal to the hon.
Member to do all in his power to discourage these people from breaking the
law. I know he says he is a sort of father
and mother to this particular body, but
as a good father and a good mother I
would advise him to counsel his would-be
children to keep as far away from it as
ever they can.
With regard to the body that exists at
present for the advancement and consideration of the rights of all ranks, I
may say that resolutions from the representative body come to the Minister without being blue-pencilled. I asure you I
have seen them; I have perused them
myself, and I have seen no blue pencil
marks yet, except those I have made
myself in order to keep my attention on
some things. Another thing to remember
is that the men can meet separately from
the officers. There is a body for the
officers and a body for the men; but
usually they meet together. There is
such peace and harmony in the force, the
men trust their officers so much, and

With regard to what prevails in Great

in which there is such a high standard

many excellent men to be always certain
that merit has been recognised.
