LIFE OF THE PRESENT
PARLIAMENT.
1. Mr. JOHNSTON asked the Prime
Minister whether he has any statement
to make in regard to the prolongation of
the life of this House which will expire
on the 1st March, 1943.
The PRIME MINISTER: Yes, sir.
I am authorised by the United Kingdom
Government to state that it is proposed
to include in the legislation which will
be required for the purpose of continuing the duration of the United Kingdom
House of Commons, a provision enabling
the duration of this House to be prolonged for a year from next March
provided such prolongation is approved
by a resolution of this House.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
the Prime Minister whether this is the
result of the question put by the hon.
Member for Willowfield when the Prime
Minister replied that he would make a
statement on this question in this House
to-day.
The PRIME MINISTER: That is the
statement I proposed to make.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
whether the Prime Minister thinks this
is Parliamentary etiquette when the
Member for Willowfield put this question
in the House and the Prime Minister
assured him and his colleagues on this
side of the House that he would make
a statement in reply to the question put
by him.
The PRIME MINISTER: The proper
time to discuss the matter is when the
resolution is submitted to the House.
TEACHERS' PENSIONS.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Finance whether he can state the
number of retired teachers in Northern
Ireland and their average pension;
whether it is a fact that none of these
pensioners have received a bonus to enable
them to meet the increased cost of living,
but, on the contrary, that many of them
have had their pensions substantially reduced owing to the exactions of the
income-tax authorities; and whether, in
view of these circumstances he is prepared
to grant a bonus to all teacher pensioners
without waiting for a lead from the
Imperial Government.
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY
(Major Sinclair): I have been asked by
the right hon. Gentleman to reply.
In reply to the hon. Member, the
number of pensioned teachers of all
classes in Northern Ireland is 1,408, and
the average pension payable in the
financial year 1941-2 was £140 18s 6d
per annum.
With reference to the latter part of
the hon. Member's question, I have
nothing further to add to the reply given
by my right hon. Friend to a similar
question on the 23rd September, 1941.

Mr. NIXON: The sum is not big if it
is put to a proper use. Sometimes one
wonders what use this money is really put
to. An incident happened the last day
I was here that shows that secret information is being put to a very improper
use, a use contrary to all the orders in
connection with police administration
that I ever came across. It occurred in
this way. The Parliamentary Secretary
of the Ministry of Home Affairs thought
that he should read, for a joke, a letter
written by a person in custody. A letter
written behind prison bars was read for
a joke to make the House laugh. That
information must have been got in some
secret way, by the opening of that letter
and taking extracts from it.
I can tell the House what used to be
the Constabulary regulations on that
subject. The regulations were that all
possible facilities should be given to prisoners to communicate with their friends
or their solicitors, to write a letter or send
a telegram, which should be read by the
constabulary to see that nothing injurious
to the interests of justice was thereby
communicated. If there was anything
injurious to the interests of justice in that
letter appropriate action was taken
according to the circumstances, or according as the circumstances demanded, but
in no case was a prisoner's letter copied
so that an extract might be used to make
a joke at the expense of the man behind
the bars for the entertainment of any
political party. The man who would do
that would not be two hours in the police
force under the Imperial Government,
and two hours is not a long time.
Estimates-
Report

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Nixon]
This is an outrageous thing. It is contrary to orders, and, furthermore, I submit that it is a cowardly thing, a very
cowardly thing, because if that man had
his liberty and was at large I would like to
see the Parliamentary Secretary or any
other man making a joke of his private
letter. If there is nothing in a private
letter written by a prisoner that is injurious to the interests of justice, or of a
criminal character, it should be treated as
a man's private letter and sent on. It
should not be turned into a joke, and
more particularly so in this case, when
the liberty of the prisoner depends upon
the chairman and the treasurer of the
Strandtown Unionist Association. With
the chairman, they form the principal
appeal court for an internee in Northern
Ireland, that is, the chairman of the tribunal and the chairman and treasurer of
the Minister's Own association. The
right hon. Gentleman could not get a
nomination for candidature in Victoria
Division without their influence, and they
are compensated by being appointed to
paid jobs in a court of appeal against the
Minister's orders of internment.
Then letters are purloined and read for
a joke. I have often heard of prisoners'
letters being used against them when those
letters disclosed some crime or offence. I
have heard of letters being retained because if they were sent on they might give
away something prejudicial to the interests of justice, but never in the whole
course of the Imperial rule in Northern
Ireland or in England has a prisoner's
letter been read in Parliament for a joke
in order to entertain a political party.
That outrage on liberty is reserved for
Northern Ireland, and like everything
else, you can do what you like about it.

Oral Answers to Questions.
POST-WAR CONDITIONS.
1. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Labour whether he is aware of the
fact that the Imperial Minister of
Labour has declared his intention of
taking steps to prevent a return after the
war to the sweated conditions which prevailed in many industries, and has
determined to set up machinery to deal
with wages and conditions in the catering industry; and whether, in view of
this declaration by the Imperial Minister
and the oft-repeated assertion of this
Government to keep step by step with the
Imperial Government in social legislation, he will take immediate steps to
assure the workers that corresponding
plans and legislation will be speedily
initiated in Northern Ireland; and
whether, as a first step in this direction,
he will reconsider the advisability of
establishing Trade Boards for the wholesale grocery and drug trade, the hairdressing trade and the retail drapery and
grocery trades.
I can assure the hon. Member that any
decisions arrived at in Great Britain on
these subjects will be most carefully
examined here to determine what action
would be appropriate in relation to Northern Ireland. Meanwhile, I feel that
it would be premature for me to add
anything to what I said in this House on
the 25th June about the trades mentioned in the last part of the question.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): I am aware that the Imperial
Minister of Labour has under consideration the possibility of establishing for the
post-war period minimum wage regulation for all forms of employment, and
that discussions are proceeding about the
regulation of wages and conditions of
service in the catering trades.
Mr. MIDGLEY: Do I take it that on
a question like this we are never capable
of initiating a policy ourselves but must
wait on the other people doing it?
Mr. GORDON: The hon. Gentleman
will remember that I put a proposition
before him, and if he can conform to that
proposition I think he and I can discuss
the matter between ourselves.
ACCIDENT IN BELFAST PRISON.
7. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is aware that
a man imprisoned for a short period in
Crumlin Road Prison was seriously injured through falling from a ladder whilst
carrying out work allocated to him, and in

R.U.C. WIDOWS' PENSIONS.
8. Mr. THOMAS BAILIE asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he is
aware that the pension payable to the
widows of deceased members of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary is only £30 per
annum and to each child £10 per annum;
that in a recent instance in Holywood the
total sum of £60 per annum is proposed
to be paid to a widow and five children,
where the father has performed 20 years'
service; whether he will have the circumstances investigated from the standpoint
of need; and whether, in view of the
general increase in pensions of all kinds
he will take steps to have police pensions
raised to a figure commensurate with the
present cost of living.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Yes. I am
aware that the ordinary pension to the
widow of a deceased sergeant or constable
of the Royal Ulster Constabulary is £30
per annum and that the children's allowances are £10 per annum for each child
under 16 years of age with a maximum
of £30 per annum. These rates are
statutory, being laid down in the Royal
Ulster Constabulary Pensions Orders and
the maximum grants under these Orders
were authorised in the case referred to
by the hon. Member.
In March last year a Committee was
appointed by the Home Secretary, under
the chairmanship of Lord Snell, to review
the provision for the payment of pension
and allowances to widows and children of
members of the police forces in Great
Britain, and the recommendations made
by that Committee are still under consideration. I can, however, assure the
hon. Member that when a settlement has
been arrived at in Great Britain no time
will be lost in considering its application
to the Royal Ulster Constabulary.
One of the recommendations of the Snell
Committee was that the limit of £30 per
annum for children's allowances should be
removed and that allowances should be
paid in respect of all children under the
2331 Belfast County Borough Bill-

If anything was wanted to prove that

but I will deal with it when the time

I want to see things tightened up, and
I know they can be tightened up. If
the suggestions made by certain members
of the council had been accepted by the
Minister and included in an Amending
Local Government Bill all these matters
could still be left in the hands of the
elected representatives, and they could
have been made as watertight as it is
possible to make them, keeping in mind
the limitations of human nature. In the
final analysis nobody can guarantee that
any system is watertight. To make any
system watertight you have to assume
that the persons who manage it are
superlatively honest and beyond temptation. That has not been claimed for
administrators any more than for city
councillors and aldermen. By means of
education you can substitute national
effort for private gain. You want to
protect people who are out to serve the
community and leave, the world better
than they found it. You cannot
guarantee that if people go wrong on the
elected basis they will not go wrong on
the appointed basis. There is, however,
this difference. It is much easier to conceal things when the work is done by only
three or four than when it is done by
sixty. On the law of average the sixty
stand better chance of elucidating
points than when the work is confined to
three or four people.
For all these reasons I am opposed to
this Bill. I still believe it would be

NEW CLAUSE (Commencement and
duration of Act).
(1) This Act shall come into operation
on the first day of October, nineteen
hundred and forty-two.
(2) This Act shall continue in force
until the thirty-first day of March,
nineteen hundred and forty-six, and
for such further period as Parliament
may determine.
Brought up and read a First time.
The PRIME MINISTER: This new
Clause fixes the date upon which the Act
shall come into force, namely, the first
day of October next. It is intended that
it shall remain in force for three and a
half years, and for such further period as
Parliament may decide. It will be seen,
therefore, that the Amendment does not
necessarily limit the duration of the Act.
On the contrary, it ensures that, so far
as it is possible to do so, the Act will
remain in force for a sufficient time to
enable it to prove its worth to the satisfaction of Parliament. Surely this is
reasonable as well as democratic. After

AGRICULTURAL TRACTORS.
3. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state the
number of agricultural tractors delivered
to Northern Ireland since the Minister
took over control of supply, and the
number allotted to each constituency, excluding Belfast and Londonderry.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Lord Glentoran): My Ministry has not
at any time had control of the supply of
agricultural tractors to Northern Ireland, but has invariably taken all
practicable steps to assist in obtaining
as many tractors as possible for farm
work.
The Ministry had partial control of the
distribution of agricultural tractors in
Northern Ireland since the outbreak of
war, but did not assume complete control until the 16th June, 1942. Details
of the distribution of tractors by parliamentary constituencies are not available,
but the approximate number of tractors
in Northern Ireland at present is 4,000,
of which some 3,450 were supplied since
the outbreak of war. The existing
number is distributed
amongst the
counties as follows:-
--
Antrim, 820; Armagh, 465; Down,
1,400; Fermanagh, 245; Londonderry,
510; Tyrone, 560.

PLANS FOR POST-WAR ULSTER.
Mr. JOHNSTON (by private notice)
asked the Prime Minister whether he is
in a position to make a statement with
regard to the post-war policy of the
Government.
The PRIME MINISTER: I am sure
hon. Members will agree that the
efficient prosecution of the war effort and
the utilisation of all Northern Ireland
resources towards that end must continue
to be the primary consideration of the
Government at the present time. But it
appears to my colleagues and myself that
we must also think of the future and be
ready to play our part in translating into
practice in the post-war period the idea
of a full and free life for all, for which
the democracies are now struggling.
Hon. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.
Mr. NIXON: That will be a change.
The PRIME MINISTER: We must
all realise that the war has reached its
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
most crucial stage. The enemy is making
a supreme effort to achieve an early
victory. For him time presses, and he
is desperately anxious to avoid another
winter campaign. That is why he is
throwing his full weight into the
operations on the Russian and Egyptian
fronts and on our life-line in the Atlantic.
The Allies are determined, whatever the
sacrifice, that the cause for which they
are fighting shall triumph. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Only a complete and decisive victory over the Axis
Powers will enable us to carry out those
schemes of post-war reconstruction on
which our hearts are set.
Many of the problems which will face
Northern Ireland in the post-war period
will be linked up indissolubly with those
in Great Britain, but there will also be
many of our own, and it is to these
specifically that we must direct our
attention now. Whilst a complete and
detailed estimate cannot be given at
present of such problems or their solutions, I wish to outline to-day in general
terms the policy of the Government in
regard to them.
The Government are determined that
there shall be proper housing accommodation and reasonable living conditions for the people of Northern
Ireland, and that the remaining slums in
our towns, villages and country districts
shall be cleared. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) Proper housing accommodation
necessitatęs the provision of water,
sewerage, electricity and general hygienic
conditions, and the Government are also
determined to do their utmost to secure
that these objects will be attained as soon
as possible in the post-war years. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Considerable
progress has already been made by the
Committees which are investigating town
planning and water and sewage disposal schemes.
ployment. The Government are resolved
that these questions shall be tackled
thoroughly and energetically. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
The dispersal of many of our industries
has shown that transport and electricity
must play a large part in the development of new industries throughout the
Six Counties, and in the future of
agriculture and of those industries based
on agriculture which we wish to extend.
Cheap electricity and transport facilities
are undoubtedly a potent factor in the
encouragement of industry and agriculture, with its consequent effect on em-
Following the collapse of Denmark and
other European agricultural countries,
the farmers of Northern Ireland have
been called upon to put forth tremendous
efforts to fill the gap thus caused in our
food supplies, and they have nobly
responded. It is the policy of the Minister
of Agriculture to maintain and increase
both the quantity and quality of our
products, and to do everything to ensure
that the wider markets now available
shall continue in the post-war years to
be open for Ulster and that the position
already gained shall be permanent.
The question of the youth of the
country has been largely exercising the
minds of my colleagues and myself, for
upon the youth will depend the future.
of this Imperial province. The problems
of youth are, to a very large extent,
dependent on health and education. We
are anxious, as a Government, that no
child shall suffer from malnutrition, and
that all children of ability and intelligence will have equal opportunity in
education. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Many more scholarships must be given.
the school-leaving age must be raised,
and we must have a considerable
extension of technical and agricultural
education from which our future citizens
will get a training for those occupations
in which they afterwards intend to serve.
Schemes for the provision of good wholesome meals and milk to school-children
must be developed, and increased
facilities for physical training must be
afforded. Much has already been done
in this direction, but we, as a Government, are by no means satisfied and are
determined to give the youth of Northern
Ireland such a chance as they have never
had before. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) We must have in the future, as
far as humanly possible, an Al population, both as regards health and
education. The Government also feel
that an extension of maternity and child
welfare centres throughout the country
is absolutely necessary so that the death
rate shall be substantially reduced and
much suffering avoided.
Drainage has already been the subject
of legislative action by the Government,
and, while the amount which can and

will be done during the war period will
be of appreciable assistance in the war
effort, it is obvious that a great part of
this work must remain to be completed

Every effort will be made to assist our
industries to make their maximum contribution towards the expansion of the
export trade in post-war years, a development which will be essential to the future
welfare of the country. The future of
the linen trade and the home production
of flax will also continue to receive the
close attention of the Government, as
an effective solution of these problems
will greatly influence the employment
position after the war. Other matters,
such as local government administration
and cross-Channel traffic facilities, will
receive close attention.
The post-war programme I have outlined is an ambitious one. It is, however, largely our domestic concern, and
it will be for our own Government and
Parliament, together with our local
authorities, assisted by our people
generally, to carry it out. There are,
of course, many other major problems
which will also vitally concern us as a
part of the United Kingdom but which
must be dealt with in co-operation with
His Majesty's Imperial Government, such
as pensions, health and unemployment
insurance. These will be maintained at
British standards. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) Our financial arrangements
with the British Treasury ensure that.
At the same time, we intend to make
preparations at once in connection with
our own purely local problems. I have
entrusted my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Commerce, with the duty of
making the necessary arrangements for
the consideration of these urgent problems
which will arise at the end of the war
in the change over from war-time to
peace-time conditions, when so many of
our people will have to be reabsorbed
into peace-time industry-

The following questions appeared on
the Order Paper, on 28th July, in the
name of Mr. Brown:-
---
To ask the Minister of Labour whether
he can state if he has given or intends

of the unemployed available for helping
the farmers at
harvest time, and,
if so,
what steps have been taken
or are to be taken to avoid a
repetition of the disappointment and loss
caused during last year's harvest by his

To ask the Minister of Agriculture
whether he can state his Ministry's plans,
in addition to the Voluntary Land
Service Scheme, for providing adequate
labour for dealing with the increased.
acreage under crops.
Written Answers
Business of the House
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Lord GLENTORAN: I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend to reply,
and I propose to deal with this and
question No. 6 on the Order Paper together.
The hon. Member will recall that last
season, in effect, "flying squads" provided by the British Military Authorities were available throughout the
country and rendered invaluable help.
Arrangements have again been made with
the British Military Authorities for
assistance in the saving of crops this
season. An additional safeguard this
year lies in the Control of Employment
Orders which are now in operation.
Under these Orders agricultural workers
may be recalled from industry to agriculture, and agricultural workers who
become unemployed may be retained for
work on the land.
Throughout the year special attention
has been devoted to supplementing existing supplies of tractors and machinery.
There are now 1,250 more tractors and
550 more binders on farms than was the
case a year ago.
The Voluntary Land Service Movement
has been taken up enthusiastically in most
provincial towns, and special arrangements are being made in Belfast to obtain
Land Service Volunteers to help farmers
in the districts surrounding the city. My
Ministry has made contact with various
organised groups of young people, many
of whom are making their own arrangements to assist farmers. The Ministry of
Education, in addition to urging Education Authorities to make provision that
holidays in Public Elementary Schools
in country districts should be so arranged
that the pupils might be available to help
farmers, urged all Secondary School
Authorities to take similar action, as well
as to encourage their pupils to go out

It would have been possible, and is
possible, to have amended local government legislation in such a way as to leave
effective control of policy in the hands of
the elected representatives of the city.
The "Big Six" pointed out how that
I could be done. This Bill reverses that
method; it takes away from us the right
of being masters in our own house;
takes away effective financial control; it
takes away the right to decide what the
estimates should be for public health,
maternity and child welfare, education,
roads development, electricity, trams,
and everything else. It takes away our
effective control, and makes us subordinate to the will of three people who, no
matter how good they may be individu-
When I was serving my apprenticeship
in Northern Ireland I studied economics
in my spare time, and I was told it was a
sound basic principle that there should
be no taxation without representation.
That principle is being violated in this
Bill: this is taxation without representation. You cannot say we have adequate
representation when, in fact, you have
taken away the right to decide what our
policy should be, and how our money
should be devoted to each particular
service. When all those rights have been
taken away you have struck a fundamental blow at the principle of no
taxation without representation. These
are the fundamental reasons why I have
consistently opposed this Bill.
I want to see Belfast a proud and
honourable city. I say that, comparatively speaking-and I am not saying
this as a defence-it is much better than
many cities I could name; but I am not
excusing any wrong-doing in saying that.
I know many deficiencies have made
themselves manifest, but I think it is the
wrong way to remedy those deficiencies
by removing our constitutional rights.
As one who has served for eighteen years
in the local authority, and who has seen
the magnificent possibilities of local
government, I have seen a great deal of
public good achieved in the city of
Belfast. Having had those eighteen
years' experience, I have seen what could
be done for the public good in the wise
development of the social services, and
in the development of many things that
the Prime Minister outlined here to-day
in that long statement of his in reply to
the question addressed to him by the hon.
Member for North Armagh.
Many of the principles adumbrated by
the Prime Minister in regard to local
government affairs have already been put
into operation by Belfast Corporation.
For example, we are carrying outalthough they may not be perfect-school
medical services, the feeding of school
children, and the provision of milk, better
than any other authority in Northern
Ireland at the present time. Indeed, of
late we have been trying to make up the
leeway caused by the neglect of these

Death of the Duke of Kent.
The PRIME MINISTER: The melancholy news of the death of His Royal
Highness the Duke of Kent has come as
a profound shock to us all. In the prime
of his manhood a member of the Royal
House has died in the service of his
country. Throughout the Empire there
will be deep sorrow that one who possessed such splendid personal qualities
and who, in peace and in war, was ever
eager to devote his gifts to the public
service should have been cut off with such
tragic suddenness.
Here in Northern Ireland the Duke of
Kent was known and loved. Twice since
the outbreak of war he had visited us,
receiving on each occasion an enthusiastic
welcome from the members of the fighting forces, civil defence services and the
men and women in our war factories.
When His Royal
Royal Highness walked
through the bombed areas of Belfast,
making personal contact with the people
who had lost their dear ones and their
homes, he struck a chord that will never
cease to vibrate in their hearts.
In the name of the Members of this
House may I say how sincerely we sympathise in this sad hour with Their Majesties
the King and Queen, with Queen Mary
in the loss of a beloved son, and with
the other members of the Royal Family.
Above all our overflowing sympathy goes
out to Her Royal Highness the Duchess
of Kent and her children in their grief.
We humbly commend them to the care
of Him Who alone can keep bright the
flame of faith and hope.
Although the presence of the Duke of
Kent has been withdrawn from us we can
all find inspiration in his example of
service and self-sacrifice. He died at
the post of duty, but his memory will
remain in the hearts of those he loved
and in the annals of the country and
Empire to which his life was given. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. NIXON: It was with great regret
that I, and I may say all the people of
Northern Ireland, heard the sad news.
It is also with regret that I endorse, on
Point of Order

Point of Order
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Nixon]
my own behalf and on behalf of very
many people who think as I do, everything that the Prime Minister has said
about the Duke of Kent. I remember
through the courtesy of the Prime
Minister that on the Duke's last visit
here I had the honour to dine with him
in this House. I shall never forget it.
I did not think it would be the last time
we would have him. At all events such
is the course of war. Everyone from the
highest to the lowest suffers sooner or
later, and bears his sufferings with the
one determination to win through. The
Duke of Kent upheld the best traditions
of the Royal Family. I heard the traditions of the Royal Family well put
several years ago by a person in a comparatively humble position; and the tradition was this-that I never knew or heard
of any member of the Royal Family to
say a bitter word about any person or to
take sides, open or otherwise, with any
political party in the British Empire.
Everyone was the same to them, and we
will all remember the passing of the Duke
of Kent with sorrow and regret. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)

TRACTORS.
Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state the
number of tractors distributed through
his department to each Parliamentary
constituency in County Down.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Lord Glentoran): I regret that it is not
possible to give by Parliamentary constituencies details of the distribution of
tractors in County Down.
As stated in my reply to the hon.
Member's question of 30th July last, there
are at present approximately 1,400
tractors in that county.
POULTRY RATION.
Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state the procedure governing the distribution and
supply of poultry ration in Northern
Ireland, and whether the step-by-step
policy has been followed in respect of this
procedure.
Lord GLENTORAN: In Northern
Ireland rationed feeding stuffs are issued
to persons who own not less than 20 birds
and who deliver a reasonable proportion
of their eggs to registered packing stations
or collectors.
As I previously explained to the House
my Ministry does not follow a step-by-step
policy. We are an agricultural exporting
country and if we are to progress and
develop we must lead and not follow.
brought more into line with the Northern
Ireland scheme.
The hon. Member is no doubt aware
that conditions in Great Britain and
Northern Ireland are very different.
Northern Ireland as an egg exporting
country has always had a large number
of efficient packing stations capable of
handling all the eggs likely to be forthcoming. This was not the case in Great
Britain, but as the position there
improves the rationing of feeding stuffs
in that country is gradually being
"B" SPECIAL CONSTABULARY.
Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if he
received a complaint from the "B"
Special Constabulary, Aughnaleck, about
one of their officers, and, if so, what
action he took in the matter.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The complaint referred to from members of the "B"
Special Constabulary, Anahilt Sub-
District, was received by me and was
investigated. As a result I was satisfied
that the officer concerned was efficient
and that the arrangements in the subdistrict for the training of the force were
the most satisfactory that could be made.
The complainants were so informed.

Mr. Winston's appointment, to the

DEPUTY FIRE SERVICE
COMMANDER.


Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Public Security whether he can state the
salary and allowance fixed for the position of Deputy Fire Service Commander
in Northern Ireland; whether Mr. John
Allman has been appointed to the position, and whether there was any Ulsterman qualified for the position.
Mr. GRANT: The salary fixed for the
post of Deputy Fire Service Commander
is £700 per annum.
Mr. Allman has been appointed to the
position. As a former member of the
Belfast Fire Brigade he is entitled to a
rent allowance, but this is a personal
privilege which he shares with other exregular firemen, and is not related to the
post he holds.
There may be persons, Ulstermen and
others, who are qualified for the position;
but in making the appointment I picked
the man who, in my opinion, was best
fitted for the duties and responsibilities of
the job.

Death of
Mr. Byrne and Lieut.-Colonel Mitchell.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to report to
the House with the greatest regret the
death of two hon. Members, Mr. Byrne,
the Member for Falls, and Colonel
Mitchell, the Member for Queen's University. During Mr. Byrne's membership he earned the respect and affection.
of every Member in the House. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) He took a very
special interest in the social welfare of
the people whom he represented. He was
one of my Deputy Chairmen, and when
he took the Chair he acted with the
greatest possible dignity; such was the
affection that the House bore him that on
no occasion did any Member attempt to
take any advantage of him when he was
in the Chair. We shall miss him very
much indeed. His benevolence and kindnes of heart impressed us all very much,
and the moderation with which he put
forward his political views won the
admiration of the whole House. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
Colonel Mitchell, before he came to this
House seven years ago, had a most distinguished career. He spent the whole of
his life in the amelioration of human
suffering and human infirmities, and when

attention in all quarters of the House.
He spoke out his mind, and earned the
respect of the House for the way he did
So. He also was a most charming companion, and every Member, during his
period of seven years, conceived the
greatest affection for him. We shall miss
him in our councils. I am sure the whole
House will join with me in expressing

Members and our sympathy with their

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Finance Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY
(Major Sinclair): The Bill at present
before the House proposes to give legislative effect to changes in excise duties
which were foreshadowed in my Minister's
Budget speech and which have already
been the subject of a Financial Resolution
approved by the House. Clause 1 gives
effect to the Budget increases in entertainments duty which have operated since
31st May last by virtue of the Financial
Resolution of the House, to which I have
already referred. The rates now in
operation correspond with those in Great
Britain, the only divergence from the rest
of the United Kingdom being a concession, in that out-door sports continue for
the present to enjoy complete exemption
from duty in Northern Ireland.
The increased rates of duty on the
higher-priced seats have been adjusted to
obviate as far as possible the result of
awkward prices difficult to handle and,
while avoiding unnecessary increases in
prices to the public, to afford some scope
to entertainment proprietors for an increased yield to meet war-time increases
of expenses without attracting higher
rates of duty.
The remainder of the Bill deals with
liquor licences and fulfils an undertaking,
given by my Minister in his Budget
speech, to introduce any concessions given
in Great Britain in the amount of duty
payable by traders who have been affected
by war circumstances, and the Bill accordingly adopts, with the necessary minor
alterations to meet local circumstances,
the concessions already applicable in
Great Britain under the Finance Act,
Act, 1942. The phraseology of this part
of the Bill is necessarily technical, but the
general object is to take power to adjust
the amounts of retail liquor licence duty
payable by traders under war conditions,
and the related one of providing for the
suspension and subsequent revival of
licences for the sale of liquor where war
circumstances involve the temporary discontinuance of a licensed business.
The licence duties in question are those
of (a) on-licences, which cover the sale
of liquor for consumption on the premises
in public-houses, hotels, and restaurants,
etc., and (b) off-licences, which permit
sales only for consumption off the premises. It should perhaps be made clear
Finance Bill-
Second Reading

that the equity of the proposed concessions
arises from the present general and severe
shortage of supplies and the fact that, as
hon. Members are aware, the current
licence duties are based on an annual
value, fixed before the war, related to the
expectation of future trade in each
licensed premises, which expectation has
been falsified under war conditions which
were not visualised at the period of assessment. The remedy of a general revision
of the annual values of licensed premises
instead of concessions related to excise
duty has not been considered, because,
apart from its impracticability under wartime conditions, temporarily adverse trade
conditions are not peculiar to the licensed
trade.
Sub-clause (1) of Clause 2 deals with
the case where a licensed business is temporarily discontinued altogether owing to
war circumstances; for example, if a hotel
is requisitioned, or a hotel or public-house
is closed on account of war damage, the
licencee may be relieved of such proportion of his licence duty as corresponds to
the period during which he does not trade.
Sub-clauses (2) to (5) of Clause 2, with
the Second Schedule to the Bill, provide
for the administrative machinery necessary for the suspension and revival of
licences by the licensing courts and the
Ministry of Home Affairs, subject to the
satisfaction of and certification by the
Ministry of Finance or its agents that discontinuance is due to war circumstances.
Sub-clause (6) extends the scope of "war
circumstances" to cases where the execution of works necessary to enable
business to be carried on is prevented by
war conditions.

Clause 7 is in effect merely declaratory,
as it repeals a provision 117 years old
which has been treated as inoperative for
practically the whole period since its enactment. Section fourteen of the Excise
Licences Act, 1825, as originally enacted
appears to prohibit the issue of excise
licences for the sale of spirits, foreign
wine, or sweets (that is, British wines),
unless a licence was also held for the sale
of beer on the premises. Foreign wine
and sweets were expressly excluded from
this restriction by later legislation, which
also by implication entirely removed the
restriction, and the purpose of the proposed Clause is, by specific repeal of the
1825 provision, to remove all doubt as to
its non-validity and thus to bring the
legislative provision into line with the
recognised practice of over 100 years. The
repeal of the whole section will not affect
the position in regard to spirits onlicences, because, under present-day law,
a spirits on-licence can only be obtained.
as a full or composite publican's licence,
which covers the sale of every kind of
liquor. Hon. Members will appreciate
therefore that the matter is a legal
technicality, and that the proposed repeal
will create no facilities that have not in
fact existed since 1834. I beg to move.

owing to the blitzes, and then the peculiar

Nobody in drafting the different Licensing
Acts for Ireland ever contemplated such
incidents as took place in the city of
Belfast last year.

LIME FOR FARMING.
1. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he is
aware that many farmers were unable to
obtain lime during the period ending
31st August, and so take advantage of
the 75 per cent. Government subsidy,
and whether he will have the period extended to 31st December, 1942.
Lord GLENTORAN: I am aware of
the facts as stated by the hon. and
gallant Member. The increased subsidy
on lime was offered in order to stimulate
the demand for lime and to ensure the
full working of lime kilns during the
summer months. In this object it has
succeeded. As the hon. and gallant
Member is aware, the Land Fertility
Scheme is financed by the Imperial
authorities, and no provision has been
made for the payment of the lime subsidy
at the higher rate after the 31st August.
The normal subsidy of 50 per cent. has,
of course, been in operation since that
date.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Arising out
of that reply, can the Minister state
whether or not there is any chance of this
subsidy being continued at 75 per cent.
to those unable to obtain lime.
Lord GLENTORAN: No, sir. I do
not think there is any chance of their
continuing this, but they will continue.
the 50 per cent.

2. Mr. BROWN asked the Mnister of
Agriculture whether he can state if it is
a fact that some five or six milk sampling
and pasteurising depots are to be established by his Ministry in Counties
Armagh, Tyrone, Derry, Antrim and
Fermanagh at a cost of over £100,000,
and if so why no such depots are to be
established in County Down, famed for
the high quality and quantity of its milk.
production, and whether the Ministry will
reconsider the claims of County Down in
this matter, especially in view of the fact
that a flax spinning mill has just been
closed down in County Down throwing 400
workers out of employment, and that at
Newry and other centres flax spinning
mills have been closed down for some time
with no alternative employment, and that
the "industrial graveyard" conditions

Down particularly, entitle it to greater

establishing of new industries.
Lord GLENTORAN:
Arrangements
are being made by my Ministry for the
establishment of five or six whole-milk
depots. These depots are for the purpose
of receiving and pasteurising milk required
for liquid consumption in Belfast and
Great Britain, and they are being put up
in areas where it is impossible to divert
milk direct to the consumer. Farmers in
County Down have easy access to the
Belfast liquid milk market-their milk
can generally be collected and brought
direct to Belfast for treatment and sale
there. There is, consequently, no need
for the erection of a whole milk depot in
County Down.
In addition to whole-milk depots a
number of sampling centres are being
licensed by the Ministry for the purpose
of grading milk received from producers.
The milk will then be paid for at the
liquid or manufacturing price according to
quality. There will be five of these centres
in Belfast and one other in south County
Down, so that farmers in this area will

UNSCUTCHED FLAX OF THE 1941
CROP.
3. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state how
much of the 1941 flax crop still remains
unscutched, and what is the result of the
detailed survey of scutch mills which he
stated in the House on 7th July was
being made with a view to increasing
where necessary the scutching facilities for
dealing with the 1943 crop.
Lord GLENTORAN: The acreage of
the 1941 flax crop as yet unscutched is
472 acres, and in every case my Ministry's
local flax inspectors are doing everything
possible to assist in having these crops
processed as soon as possible.
The survey of scutch mills has now
been completed and it has shown that in
two areas facilities for handling the flax
crop are inadequate mainly owing to mills
having been destroyed by fire. I can
assure the hon. Member that steps are
being taken, where necessary, to give
assistance in the construction of new mills
and also in the renovation of burnt-out
or derelict mills. I am satisfied that there
will be adequate facilities for the 1942
crop, and the necessary steps are being
taken to ensure that for any increased
acreage in 1943 adequate facilities will
also be available.
Mr. BROWN: Will the noble Lord
please tell us precisely what steps have
been decided on in each area and when he
will put these into operation; and will he
bear in mind that nothing short of a 50
per cent. grant to put into through repair and modernisation of all scutch mills
will meet the situation which is a very
serious one as disclosed by the answer
to this question.

QUESTION OF BAIL PENDING
APPEAL.
7. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Attorney
General whether his attention has been
drawn to an appeal in the Belfast
Oral Answers

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Oral Answers
[Mr. Campbell]
Recorder's Court last week in which the
court reversed a petty sessions order convicting a man of knowingly receiving a
stolen bicycle, sentencing him to three
months' imprisonment and refusing to
allow him to stay out on bail pending the
hearing of the appeal; whether the law
affords any remedy against such refusal;
how long this man was detained in prison
before his innocence was established on
the appeal; and whether compensation
will be given by the Crown to him as
amends for
for his imprisonment; and
whether the Attorney-General considers
the law in this respect satisfactory.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr.
MacDermott): Yes, sir; my attention has
been drawn to the case to which the
learned and hon. Member refers.
The defendant concerned was convicted
on the 28th August last at Belfast Petty
Sessions for receiving a stolen bicycle and
was sentenced to three months' imprisonment. He appealed to quarter sessions
and applied for release from custody
pending the hearing of his appeal. The
learned resident magistrate did not think
fit to release the appellant, who remained
in custody until the 15th instant when
the conviction was reversed and the
appellant was discharged.
The decision of the resident magistrate
refusing the appellant's release was made
in the exercise of his statutory discretion
under section 24 of the Summary Jurisdiction and Criminal Justice Act (Northern Ireland), 1935, and is not reviewable
by way of appeal.
In this respect the law of Northern
Ireland follows what has been the law in
England since 1879 and the only criticism
regarding it of which I am aware lies in
the suggestion that the existing jurisdiction of the King's Bench to grant bail to
persons awaiting trial in custody should
be extended to cover cases of the kind
mentioned.
I would point out, however, that a
right of appeal respecting bail, with the
discretion of one court substituted for
that of another, would not render impossible instances such as that which has
been cited. As the learned and hon.
Member will appreciate, the question of
bail is sometimes a difficult one-particularly where a sentence of imprisonment
has already
already been imposed-and an
appellant's ultimate acquittal does not
necessarily mean that his earlier release
was unreasonably refused.
The answer to that part of the question
relating to compensation is in the
negative.
Mr. CAMPBELL: Would the right
hon. and learned Gentleman say whether
up to the year 1935 and for a period of
almost 100 years a man in similar circumstances who might enter notice of
appeal to the higher court would be released forthwith pending the hearing of
that appeal, and did the Government in
1935 suspend that right? In this particular case on the right hon. and learned
Gentleman's own statement has not a
very obvious injustice been done to an
innocent man who was detained in
prison, though innocent, for a period of
about three weeks? In view of these
circumstances will he consider whether or
not there ought to be some higher court
to review decisions of resident magistrates
who refuse to allow a presumably innocent
man out on bail until his appeal is heard
by the higher court?
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: The
hon. and learned Member is correct in
saying that previous to 1935 appeal was
followed by an automatic release, but the
change in 1935 bringing the law here into
conformity with the law in Great Britain
after nearly 60 years was effected by an
Act of this Parliament. So far as any
change in the future is concerned, I quite
appreciate that logically there seems to
be no reason why the jurisdiction of the
King's Bench should not go further than
it does. I understand that the Minister
of Home Affairs has already noted this
matter for consideration at some suitable
opportunity.
Mr. CAMPBELL: May I ask if we are
to take that very satisfactory answer as
an assurance that this matter is under
review, and that steps will be taken to
give the King's Bench jurisdiction in
similar cases by legislation?
Mr. NIXON: Is it not a fact that this
was a respectable man working on war
work, that he was an innocent man and
was deliberately deprived of his liberty
by the resident magistrate on a Bill introduced and passed in this House some
years ago changing the law as it stood
so long as I remember?

Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Minister

underground shelters before winter, and

SECURITY (Mr. Grant): No extensive
programme for the provision of deep,
underground shelters such as is implied
by the hon. Member's question has been
undertaken nor is, so far as I am aware,

Member's question is in the negative.

Lord GLENTORAN: The matter of
the new milk scheme was raised by the
Member for South Down and the Member
for Woodvale. This scheme did not arise
out of any Act emanating from this
House. It has arisen from the fact that
under the 1920 Act we act as agents for
the Ministry of Food. On 26th October,
1940, an Order was made by the Ministry of Food whereby every person who
produces milk in Northern Ireland is required to place all milk produced by
him at the disposal of my Ministry and
deliver the milk to my Ministry or to its
Order.
I would like to tell my hon. Friends
on both sides of the House that the whole
milk position in Ulster has completely.
altered within the last few years. Actually
there is 50 per cent. more liquid milk
drunk than previously. I believe that if
the social schemes which are now in progress in the city of Belfast and Ulster
generally are carried to fruition, which
we hope they will be, this consumption
of milk will increase. A great deal of
the increase arises from the fact that we
give children and expectant mothers free
milk. That means that an immense
amount of liquid milk which was not
used before is being brought on to the
market. Previous to the war the milk
market consisted of areas round Belfast
and other cities. We find now that round
the city of Belfast the milkmen are not
able to produce enough milk to meet requirements, for many reasons which hon.
Members on both sides know. One is the
difficulty of wages and employment near
Belfast. Another thing is that ground
has been taken over for aerodromes.
Therefore, for one reason and another
the milkmen cannot produce the milk
required by the citizens of the different
cities, and so we are drawing on a wider
area throughout the country.
I want to be clear on one point which
the hon. Member for Woodvale raised
and I want to make him quite clear at
the same time. Arising out of some remarks which I made at the opening of
Nestlé's Creamery to the effect that our
milk was not good enough for the
Americans, I would like the House and
everyone to be quite clear that it is not
a question of our milk not being good
enough for the Americans, but the fact
that the Americans wanted a class of milk
we were not able to produce in quantity.
They insisted on having pasteurised milk,
and up to the time we got this great
factory we were not in a position throughout the country to give them this pasteurised milk. I am not going to argue
whether pasteurised milk is the final
answer to all the ills which people say
arise from milk. My hon. Friend from
the University can argue that point much
better than I can. I am just going to
talk to my hon. Friend in a business way
which he understands.
It is my job as Minister of Agriculture
to give the people who buy our milk the
sort of milk they want. If the American
army want pasteurised milk I ought to
be able to give it to them and I am now
in a position to give it to them. This
scheme will put me in a position to give
If the people want pasteurised milk
I will give it to them.
it.
Mr. NIXON: And if we do not want
it you will give it to us.
Lord GLENTORAN: No, we will not
force you to drink any kind of milk you
do not want to drink. Hon. Members
will see that quite a new problem is

for liquid milk. To meet this wide demand we have provided under the
scheme five large depots which will be
able to deal with milk by brine and other
methods, so that it may be cooled and
pasteurised and so on. We will also have 27

In that way we are going to leave it open
to every farmer in Ulster to become a

going to raise the status of those men,

milk, as both my hon. Friends know,
than there is for manufactured milk.

you
a financial difference it would make to

Therefore, I think, we were justified in
carrying out this scheme. It is not
difficult for me to defend it, and I am
glad to defend it in this House. I hope
the explanation I have given will convince
Members on both sides that we have done
this in the interests of the war effort
primarily, and in the interests of our
own people in the cities, and, in addition,
it gives us a chance to put the farmers
in a position to make a decent living
after the war if we can hold this market
after we have got it, which I think we
can. I think the scheme will prove of
benefit to the people of Northern Ireland, and will assist the war effort.

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Lowry): I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend to reply.
As far as I am aware no instructions

INFANTILE MORTALITY.
5. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state how
infantile mortality in Northern Ireland
compares with that in England, Scotland
and Wales, and how the maternity and
ante-natal clinics in Northern Ireland
compare, numerically and otherwise, with
those across the Channel, and what steps
the Government have taken to have these
put on the same basis as elsewhere and
established in all centres here.
According to the latest records available, the number of deaths of infants
under one year of age per 1,000 of live
births was:-Northern Ireland, 77 (year
1941); Scotland, 83 (year 1941); England
and Wales, 56 (year 1940. The figure for
1941 is not yet available).
In regard to the latter portion of the
hon. Member's question, I should point
out that the formulation and operation of
schemes in connection with maternity and
child welfare are matters for the local
authorities. I have no reliable information as to the nature and extent of the
schemes in operation across the Channel,
and, accordingly, a comparison on the
lines indicated is not possible. I should
like to point out, however, that so far as
Northern Ireland is concerned, the
Government encourages the setting up of
such schemes by the payment of grants
not exceeding 50 per cent. of the approved
net expenditure.
Mr. BROWN: May I ask the Parliamentary Secretary, in view of the facts.
given in his answer, will the Ministry
agree that this matter should not be
allowed to wait over until after the war,
as has been suggested by the Prime
Minister in his post-war policy statement?

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Sir Basil Brooke): The present position
of the spinning section of the linen industry is far from satisfactory. While
limited supplies of
of alternative raw
material have been made available, flax
spinning machinery cannot be so readily
adapted as weaving machinery to the use
of other raw materials, and with the present scarcity of flax I can hold out no

section.

however, arrangements have been made to
augment our flax yarn supplies with supplies of other material suitable for the
production of utility cloths and Government requirements. Arrangements have
also been made for our making-up trade
to devote the bulk of its capacity to the
production of Government and utility
goods, and the prospects of these two
sections appear to be much more satisfactory than was formerly anticipated.

MILK COLLECTION SCHEME.
Mr. BAILEY (by private notice)
asked the Minister of Agriculture whether
it is a fact that under the new milk collection scheme farmers will be required to
deliver their milk at collecting points and
that milk will not be collected at the farm
or lane end.
Lord GLENTORAN: I am aware that
certain misunderstanding exists on this
question. As from October 1st all milk,
with a few exceptions, will be collected
by or on behalf of my Ministry. Collection routes have been rearranged so as
to avoid overlapping and to see that only
one lorry or other vehicle collects milk on
each route. This means that many
carriers will be collecting from farmers
for whom they have not carried before
and whom they do not know. Consequently each farmer has been given a
convenient collecting point at which he
should have his milk on Thursday morning. If, however, the lorry is passing his
lane end and he notifies the lorry driver
that he will leave his milk at the lane
end, the milk will be collected there.
Subject to the economical use of petrol,
the Ministry is anxious to facilitate
farmers in ever possible manner. Except
in exceptional circumstances, however,
milk will not be collected in the farmyard.

us what can be done to overcome the difficulty created in the case of people living
a considerable way from the collecting
point and having no means of transporting
their milk to that collecting point?
given. We are going to facilitate farmers

There was a question raised about the
repair of blitzed houses.
I have something to say about that. The Corporation, if they wish, can come in and do
first-aid repairs or complete repairs, on
serving notice on the landlord or agent
for the neglect of his duty. In a great
many cases the Corporation did first-aid
repairs to houses, and, generally speaking,
did them very badly and unnecessarily
spent a lot of money. Then it was quite
open to the landlord or agent to employ a
contractor to complete the repairs.
Although I heard complaints about the
payment for the repairs, I would say that
the complaints were largely unfounded.
When the repairs are completed, if the
accounts are proper and are brought to
the War Damage Commission they send
out an architect to see that the repairs
have been done. They are entitled to do
that. And if everything is in order they
pay the amount, or make a deduction, at
a reasonable time.
It is necessary to say that, because I
had a complaint about houses in Malvern
Street, and I saw myself a lot of houses
that had no glass put in them. I am
speaking now about a week or ten days
ago. The people are being famished. I
know there is no excuse. I know that of
my own knowledge, because glass is available, labour is available, and the contractors are available. What I was wondering was whether something could be
done in cases where there has been neglect
by either the landlords or the agents to
compel them to put in glass now that
winter is coming on. I think there is
power in the Bill. If the landlord or
agent defaults, the Corporation can do it.
Then we know that quite a lot of largely
imported men on these jobs were not
working at all. I make no bones about
that. In one particular case I complained to the Financial Secretary about
men going off the job at two o'clock or

DUBLIN SOLICITOR'S NORTHERN
VISIT.
1. Mr. MIDGLEY asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether it is a fact that
Mr. M. Beattie, Solicitor, Dublin, who
was in Enniskillen on 6/9/42 was interrogated by the R.U.C. and told he had no
right to be there; whether it is a fact
that Mr. Beattie had a passport giving
his identity, and whether in view of this
he can state who was responsible for the
action taken.
The
PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Lowry): I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend to reply.
Mr. Beattie was asked by the constabulary at Enniskillen on the 6th
September last to produce an approved
document of identity, and after some
hesitation he produced an Eire travel
permit card.
The action was properly taken under
the authority of Regulation 1 (a) of the
Civil Authorities (Special Powers) Acts
(Northern Ireland), 1922 and 1933.
Mr. Beattie was treated with courtesy
by the policeman and was not told that
he had no right to be in Enniskillen.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
BILL PRESENTED.
Expiring Laws Continuance Bill,
"to continue certain expiring laws as
respects Northern Ireland," presented by
the Minister of Finance, supported by

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
The County Court Jurisdiction Bill
was postponed until Thursday.
Children (Juvenile Courts) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. LOWRY: This very short Bill is
based on one of the recommendations of
the Lynn Committee which sat in 1935
and made a comprehensive report in
1938. I presume by reason of the situation at that time, and undoubtedly by
what occurred in the following year, no
steps were taken, but last year, in the
autumn, the Government set up a small
departmental committee to consider each
of the recommendations of that committee. The departmental committee recommended that the personnel of the
juvenile courts should be rather different
than it was when those courts were first
set up.
The duties of the guardians will be to
assist the resident magistrates in arriving
at a conclusion in the individual cases.
They will be entitled to interrogate any
person produced as a witness, including, of
course, the child if it is such a case that
the child has to attend the court, and
they may advise the resident magistrate
as to what is a suitable step or steps to
be taken in the particular case. Beyond
that they will not have any other functions or duties. The provision to which
I allude is sub-clause (4) of Clause 1:
As hon. Members are doubtless aware,
the constitution of the juvenile court is
settled by Section 3 of the Children
Act, 1908; that is to say, in those days.
it was constituted by justices of the peace.
A change has occurred in the interval in
the personnel through the passing of the
Summary Jurisdiction Act of 1935, and
it has been thought desirable both by the
members of the departmental committee
and those who have spoken on the subject
from time to time and who are interested
in this matter, that what I might call a
lay element should be introduced into
these courts, and, consequently, it is
proposed that when a court of summary
jurisdiction is sitting for the purpose of
hearing a charge or an application relating to a child or young person there
should be associated with the resident
magistrate two persons to be called
children's guardians, appointed in accordance with the provisions of this Bill. It
is considered that one at least of these
lay persons should be a woman.
A children's guardian when sitting
with a court of summary jurisdiction
may interrogate any person giving
evidence on the hearing of the charge
or application before the court, but
shall not otherwise exercise any judicial
functions.
The appointment of these guardians is
provided for in sub-clause (2):
The Governor of Northern Ireland
shall appoint as children's guardians for
each petty sessions district such number
of persons qualified to deal with
juvenile cases as the said Governor may
think necessary.
com-
In the recommendations of the Lynn
Committee it was provided that a Central
Advisory Council should be set up for
the purpose of endeavouring to select suitable persons.
That Central Advisory
Council has never been set up, and so in
the meantime the departmental committee recommend that the local county
borough and regional education
mittees be asked to nominate suitable
persons. They also suggest that these
committees should have regard to the
youth welfare organisations that have
been active in the past. Without
endeavouring to give an exhaustive list it
is contemplated that such bodies as the
Boy Scouts, Girl Guides, Boys' Brigade,
Young Men's Christian Association,
Young Women's Christian Association,
St. Vincent de Paul Society, the Down
and Connor Diocesan Youth Council, and
such other similar bodies as may be functioning in the different parts of the
country will be consulted by the education
committees and asked to give their assistance in nominating suitable persons for
ultimate appointment as children's guardians. It is hoped that when the matter
is set about in this way suitable panels
will be arranged for every petty sessions
district and that in the future the resident
Children Bill-

magistrates will get assistance that will
be helpful to them.
This Bill has now been brought
forward. There has been a good deal of
correspondence, agitation and so forth for
some time past, but I would like to assure
the House that juvenile delinquency in
Northern Ireland is not anything like as
bad as some people contemplate. When
the statistics were brought up to date it

THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Sir Basil Brooke): There are one or two
points that have been raised that I would
like to deal with before I come to the
main issue raised by this Motion. The
Member for Shankill, I think, was completely devoid of any knowledge of the
subject. He did not produce one relevant argument. His statements were
entirely wrong and misleading, and I do
not propose to answer them because they
did not deal with the point at issue.
The Member for South Down has raised
one or two points of importance. He has
rightly stated that the Lancashire cotton
mills are working to full capacity, but
that is because they have concentrated. But it is no argument to say
that because the Lancashire cotton mills
have been concentrated and are thus
working to full capacity our mills, which
have not been concentrated, should also
be working to full capacity.
The hon. Member made. a certain
amount of play about the 472 acres of
flax which have not been scutched. It
sounds a lot, but in fact it represents
exactly half of one per cent. of the total
flax acreage of Northern Ireland, so that
it is really of no great consequence and
would not help in solving our problem.
I would like to point out to the hon.
Member that from the committee presided over by the Parliamentary Secretary of my Ministry some very useful
work has resulted. My own Ministry is
responsible for some eleven new factories
to deal with the processing of flax. The
Flax Development Committee have also
done a considerable amount of work and
have placed the country in a position to
deal with all the available flax in normal
times.
the prosecution of the war or not. I
think it was decided that Northern Ireland would place everything at the disposal of the Empire in order to win the
war.
Coming to the main point embodied in
the Motion, I would like to assure the
hon. and gallant Member for East Down
that I have a great deal of sympathy with

and very fairly, but there is this overriding principle by which I must be
guided, because, it is a principle laid down
by this House at the beginning of the
Is Northern Ireland going to play
its full part in the war effort by making
all its machinery and people available for
war.
Mr. BEATTIE: There was one. dissentient voice.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I have forgotten
that dissentient voice. Are we to argue
that as a result of the war we should try
to solve our unemployment problem.
When I have seen various Ministers on
the other side I have never argued from
the point of view that this is an opportunity for us to solve our industrial unemployment problem. I have argued
that here are men and women anxious to
play their part in winning the war and
they should be given every opportunity
to do so. The principle that all our
resources are available in the Allied cause
applies in this case. I want to point out
that the Minister of Aircraft Production
has had to bring in those who are best
competent to advise him, and it can
perfectly well be argued that the advice
which he receives is wrong.
The point is that the spinning trade
itself agreed in the appointment of the
Deputy Flax Controller and, as far as I
know, they have complete confidence in
him. If an expert has advised the
Minister of Aircraft Production that in
his opinion, having gone into the various
aspects of the case, certain spinners were
most competent to deal with the limited
raw material available, and could spin
the best yarn, and spin it at a lower cost
and with less waste than if it were spread
over the whole spinning industry, he is
bound to act accordingly. As a result of
that advice this particular firm was, unfortunately, not considered.
I may tell the hon. and gallant
Gentleman that, in spite of what the
Member for Shankill has said, I have
made personal representations to the
Minister himself, and I have told him of
the very great hardship that has been
caused, so I hope he will not think I just
sit back when these things happen and
say, "That is too bad." I look into the
matter and see if there is an alternative.
As far as an alternative is concerned I am
prepared in this case to consider the possibility of allocating other material which
might be suitable for that particular mill,

Motion made and Question proposed,

Mr. MIDGLEY: I rise to raise a
matter of which I gave notice earlier in
the afternoon. It will be recalled that at
question time to-day I read out a question
of which I had given private notice, which
was along the following lines:
To ask the Minister of Home Affairs
whether his attention has been directed
to the investigation conducted by the
Executive of the Belfast Trades Council
which revealed that 600 vacant houses
in Belfast are being held for sale at
greatly inflated prices, and whether,
having regard to the number of people.
in the city who find it impossible to
rent houses, he will take immediate
steps to control all houses in Belfast
and surrounding area with a view to
housing the people who have no homes.
I want hon. Members to throw their
minds back to events of last year when
we were subjected to grave enemy action.
It is a fact that at that time the slogan
was "Stay put." Many people in the
city of Belfast despite the fact that their
homes were destroyed did stay put in the
sense of staying in any home they could
get placed into at that particular time.
There are two classes of people who may
be said to be affected. The Parliamentary
Secretary of the Ministry of Home Affairs
dealt with one section this afternoon. He
dealt with that section of people who had
their homes destroyed and who were
removed to other areas outside the area
of Belfast, and other people whose homes
were badly damaged and who were
removed to an outside area pending the
reconstruction of their homes. He pointed
out, I suppose legally quite correctly, that
in such cases those people were entitled
to the first option of their homes, but I
should like on that point, and it is not
a cardinal point, to emphasise that that
aspect of the law has not been given effect
to in the city of Belfast, because I was
able to bring to the attention of the civic
authority in Belfast and the Estates
Committee of the Corporation cases in
which the people were actually refused by
the landlord or agent homes which had
been reconstructed and of which they had
been tenants before the enemy action took
place.
I want the attention and sympathy of
the House for a few minutes on this question, and I want, above all things, the
intelligent interest and co-operation of
the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of Home Affairs. I do not want him
to try, in his legal way, any wisecracks on
this question or to indulge in any
frivolity. This is far too serious a question
to indulge in frivolity, because, as I was
able to demonstrate this afternoon and
can demonstrate now, it is a fact that
large numbers of people in the city at
present are actually dispossessed of their
homes. They have been evicted. They
have had their homes destroyed. They
had been placed in temporary homes, and
now they are being ejected from these
homes. I want to ask the Parliamentary
Secretary to face up to this question from
the point of view of the seriousness of it.
I have already exhausted all my constitutional possibilities inside the Belfast City
Council. I have had repeated deputations of people affected by this set of circumstances, and I have explored every
possibility through the estate department
and every possibility through the development sections in Belfast Corporation, but
without avail.
Therefore, on those grounds the law
does not safeguard that particular
category of people. I know it is all right
for the Parliamentary Secretary to shrug
his shoulders, as he characteristically
does, to dispose of this question on legal
ground. For the lawyer everything that
is legal is all right. There is nothing
like leather to the cobbler, and I suppose
the lawyer thinks it all right to shrug his
shoulders and say this is a matter for the
law. These people have redress at law.
In those cases the law has not been given
effect to, but it is the other cases that do
not come within that category that I wish

It is not right in the nation's hour of

persons who

Unless there are security objections

The most recent information the Ministry has concerning the crops on their
lands is to the effect that 6 acres of oats
have been cut and that 2 acres remain

cultivation and harvesting of crops are

Member will appreciate the urgency of

The FINANCIAL SECRETARY
(Major Sinclair): This Bill is a repetition.
of the Expiring Laws Continuance Bill,
1941, and proposes to continue for a
further year, that is until the 31st
December, 1943, the three enactments
mentioned in the Schedule to the Bill.
Hon. Members may like to be reminded
that the Act also provides that in regard
to a public harbour undertaking charges
may only be increased so as to meet extra
cost and not to permit of a profit being
made. Similarly in any other
charges may only be modified so as to
allow of a reasonable return for the
undertaking.
case
The Harbours, Docks and Piers (Temporary Increase of Charges) Act, 1920,
empowers the Ministry of Commerce to
make modifications in the statutory provisions regulating harbour charges to
meet increased costs, and obviates the
need for an undertaking to seek the
authority of this House on each occasion
that such a modification is required.
The Local Government (Emergency
Powers) Act, 1921, as hon. Members are
aware, empowers the Minister of Home
Affairs to appoint an administrator to
carry on the duties of a local authority
which, in the opinion of his Ministry, has
failed in the performance of its statutory
duties. The Government desires that
such power should be retained for
another year.
The Local Authorities and Jurors
Books (Temporary Provisions) Act, 1940,
provided for the discontinuance of local
elections and for the postponement of the
preparation of jurors books for one year,
these provisions being continued until the
end of this year by the Expiring Laws
Continuance Act, 1941. The reasons
underlying the passing of the Act in
1940, namely, the unsettled state of
affairs on account of war conditions,
apply, unfortunately, with equal force
to-day, and the Government feels, therefore, that the Act should not yet be
allowed to lapse. I beg to move.

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): In reply to the hon. Member,
I would like to explain that during the
week commencing the 14th September the
Belfast Employment Exchange was requested by the firm in question to submit
for interview any electricians either trade
union or non-trade union who were signing the unemployed register. The man
to whom exception has been taken was
sent for interview at the firm's request
and started work with them on the 24th
September. The strike commenced that
evening.
The worker whose employment resulted
in a stoppage of work was not brought
to Northern Ireland by the Ministry of
Labour, but at the time of engagement
was residing in Northern Ireland. In
these circumstances his submission by
the Employment Exchange was not a
breach of the arrangement by which unemployed tradesmen resident in Eire may
be brought to Northern Ireland with the
approval of the trade union concerned.
I have been informed that this man is
not a member of a trade union.
I am sure the House will appreciate
that my Department cannot discriminate
between union
or non-union workers
except where an order specifically states
that trade union members only are
required.
With regard to the last part of the
hon. Member's question, it should be
understood that each individual has the
right to decide for himself whether or
not he will seek admission to a trade
union.

DISPUTE AT AIRCRAFT FACTORY.
Mr. NIXON (by private Notice) asked
the Minister of Commerce whether, in his
capacity as agent to the Minister of
Production, he will state if the management of a local aircraft factory summarily dismissed two shop stewards,
thereby precipitating a strike; whether
this dismissal amounts to a violation of
the Defence Acts; whether the manager
of the firm in question stated to the
employees that he wanted to reduce production; whether the Minister gave
orders to the effect that production
should be reduced; whether the Minister,
officially or otherwise, interviewed the
management of the factory about the
matter; whether a similar interview was
given to
to the representatives of the
workers, and whether the Minister will
order all concerned, including the two
dismissed stewards, to resume work
immediately, pending a legal investigation into the whole matter.
The working times arranged at the
factory in question are based on a six-day
working week of 57 hours. Unfortunately there has been considerable
absenteeism, with the result that an
average of only 52 hours a week has been
worked. The management has found
itself obliged to ask a certain number of
workpeople to come to duty on Sunday
in order to balance production, even
though the Select Committee on National
Expediture advised that work be confined to six days a week. A list giving
the names of those required on Sunday
is posted at the works on the previous
Friday.
On Sunday, October 4th, a number of
men and women workers, including the
two shop stewards, came for duty
although their names were not on this
list. The management requested the
workers to leave, the two shop stewards
intervened, and incidents occurred which
led to the shop stewards' dismissal. I
am not aware of any legislation which
deprives management of this function.
There has been no question of reducing
production. It is solely a case of first
balancing production, and second, shop
discipline.
Along with my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Labour, I have discussed
with the management the difficulties
which have arisen.
The Minister of Labour has also had
conferences with representatives of the
workers on three occasions. It has been
emphasised to them, firstly, that the
strike is illegal, and, secondly, that there
has been a breach of agreements entered
into between the Federation of Employers
and the Trades Unions, whereby negotiating machinery has been set up for the
handling of all disputes, including the
particular class of dispute with which we
are here concerned. We have, therefore,
urged the workers to return to work, with
the promise that immediately after resumption the negotiating machinery will
be set in motion.

Minister's statement implying that the

not only will it do good, but that it will
do something, even if it is only something small, to restore public confidence
and public esteem in our parliamentary
institutions. By the way we comport
ourselves in this House, by the way we

are sneered at and rejected, at least

to create in the public mind a better
feeling of respect in regard to Parliamentary institutions and democratic
government, and I do not believe we will
ever get it to the utmost extent unless

It is not good enough that the House
of Commons of Northern Ireland should
be hamstrung by tradition, which can
have no other effect at the present time
than to retard democratic development
and the true realisation of democracy in
Parliamentary government. I remember

Lord GLENTORAN: I rise to oppose
this Motion, and I do so on behalf of
every individual and of every party in
this House who love liberty. This is the
most reactionary Motion that has ever
been brought before this House of
Commons. In all the years I have served
