reactionary Motion as this: it cuts at
the liberty of the Labour Party; it cuts
at the liberty of the Independents; it
cuts at the liberty of the Progressive
Unionists; it cuts at the liberty of every
minority in this House.
Our Parliament here is modelled on
the Mother of Parliaments. It is quite
true to say that the hon. Member for
Willowfield did look up rules and regulations on several matters with reference
to this Motion, but this great structure of
freedom which has been built up at Westminster has not been built up by rules
and regulations, but on custom, which
protects the privileges of minorities. It
is perfectly clear to anyone who has
studied the traditions of the British Parliament that this custom, which has gone
on for centuries, was established so that
the great, strong, well-organised party
machines could not capture the seats of
the small minorities, but that the small
minorities should be given a chance to
put their house in order and then to come
and ask the House to be given those privileges which it would be lunacy to give
up.
All that is required is that a Member
of this House who belongs to the Party
concerned should come forward, and then
he would get the entire support of the
House for his Motion. That is the rule
which stands for the freedom of action,
for the privileges of the minorities which
I am standing up for in this House, and
which I always stood for when I was
Chief Whip, that minorities should get
fair play in these matters.

to any kind of productive work in any
part of Great Britain provided I have
got legitimate business concerning my
members, and in which their interests
are affected. It is quite obvious to me
there is a desire on the part of this firm
to torpedo or sabotage any effort for the
maintenance of a good organisation inside the firm, and for that reason I ask
the Minister to face up to it.
We have here one non-union man being
maintained although an industrial dispute
has taken place in which the labour of
100 people has been dispensed with. From
the national point of view I ask the
Minister to face up to this question, which
is most serious and most important. Is
it better to have working 100 people who
are organised workers, and with whom an
agreement exists between the Ministry and
the trade union, is it better to have those
hundred people producing for the national
cause in a spirit of goodwill and conciliaton, with a spirit of determination, with
a spirit of maintaining, as the Minister
has assured me, a high level of production or to have those hundred people
outside deprived of the opportunity of
producing for the national cause, because
of one non-union man brought in from
Eire?
I say here, and I say it with a great
deal of seriousness-and mark my words
-if the Ministry persist in allowing a
situation like this to develop you may
take it from me-I am sorry to have to
say this that you are sowing the seeds
of future trouble in this community.
Make no mistake about that. History
has a habit not of repeating itself in its
entirety, but of repeating its ugly phases
2751 Industrial Disputes in Belfast HOUSE OF COMMONS
Industrial Disputes in Belfast 2752
[Mr. Midgley]
now and again and one of the ugly phases.
of the past years arose through misconceptions or misunderstandings in the minds
of the people with regard to the way
labour power had been exploited in certain
places. Any person who to-day consciously or unconsciously creates an incentive towards a repetition is, in my
opinion, guilty of a breach of citizenship.
The whole situation is fraught with
danger for the future. I ask the Minister,
therefore, to face up to this firm with all
the constitutional power he has at his disposal under the regulations, a copy of
which can be bought in His Majesty's
Stationery Office in Belfast. I have read
the regulations myself. Power is given
to the Government to see that the work
of any institution or any industry is
carried on under conditions that conform
to the national requirements. If at any
time it is clear that the heads of a firm,.
even though it is a privately owned or a
privately controlled firm, are not conducting their business and administering their
affairs in conformity with the best interests
of the national cause, the Government has
power to transfer the management of that
firm into other hands in the national
interest.
One of the workers' grievances in
Northern Ireland is that all the power
vested in the Government in war time so
far has substantially been used as far as
duress is concerned on the workers, and
very little authority has been brought to
bear on the employer. In this firm, who
boast of their traditional open shop and of
the right to employ workers who have
never been organised, who have indicated
on occasions innumerable that they prefer
non-union labour if they can get it-in
this firm there is a disposition at the
present moment to exploit this situation
to the dislocation or to the unhappiness
of the union with the end in view of
driving a wedge into the electrical end of
the organisation.
I speak with deliberation and earnestness
when I say that, according to the
philosophy I held for over twenty years,
I opposed Nazi-ism and totalitarianism,
and the implications of those movements,
when it was not popular to do so, when
few people of an orthodox way of thinking
in Northern Ireland were prepared to
align themselves against the totalitarian
powers. In those days I opposed Hitler
and Hitlerism, and I opposed Mussolini.
In scores of places all over Great Britain
I have taken part in campaigns to oppose
the false pretensions of Fascism and a
surrender to them.
I ask the Minister to stand up to this.
Do not let any tradition of Cabinet rank
or Cabinet prestige, or Cabinet anything
else, stand in the way of a humane
approach to this question. I personally
speak with all sincerity. I do not wish
to parade any aspirations of mine as
being peculiar to me, because I know
there are many people in this House who
feel as strongly as I do on this matter.
I know what would be involved in the
triumph of Nazi-ism. I know what the
result would be to human and democratic
institutions. I know that all that is
sweet and best and lovely in life would
be submerged if Nazi-ism triumphed.
Therefore, I want the best effort of every
section of the community put forward in
order that we may triumph in this war,
not just for the sake of winning the war,
but in order to retain our right to a
better way of life, and that we may
enlarge our democratic horizon when we
have cleared this obstacle of aggression
out of the way. I want my fellow
workers throughout Northern Ireland,
where I can influence them, to hold to
that point of view. I will try to stimulate
them in doing so in the most unselfish
spirit. They are entitled to justice; they
are entitled to the things they have built
up throughout the years, and they are
entitled to their democratic rights in
regard to settling questions. They are
not getting that right from this firm.
One man brought from Eire is being
used to keep people out. No constitutional or constructive attempt on a large
scale has yet been made to bridge the
gulf dividing the people up there. The
men are holding a meeting to-morrow
night at which this point of view will be
put forward. Owing to the fact that I
will be out of town it will be impossible
for me to accept the invitation to attend,
but if I could be in town to-morrow night
I would take my place on the platform
and put forward the point of view I am
putting forward because of the fundamental principles involved.
I appeal to the Minister, and to his
assistants on the Civil Service side who
can radiate influence with the firm, to
take steps to bring this deplorable dispute

The Member for Willowfield is aware,

two types of shops, the closed shop and
the open shop. The closed shop is a shop
that employs members of the union only,

opinion might be, I have no power to

never

and conditions, but the firm also take up
the attitude that they, as employers,

they have the right to employ whoever

where the clash comes.

IRON GATES AS SCRAP.
2. Mr. BROWN (for Lieut.-Colonel
Gordon) asked the Minister of Finance
whether he is aware that in County
Down iron gates to farm yards, stack
yards, cattle pens, sheep pens, and to
fields giving on to the county roads, have
been listed for removal as scrap iron;
and whether he will inform the House
how farmers are to keep their stocks in
their farm yards and in their fields when
these gates are removed.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): The scheme for the collection
of iron and steel railings, recently begun
in Northern Ireland, is only an extension
of the scheme which has been in operation for some time past in Great Britain.
The scheme is, of course, compulsory, the
Department responsible being the Ministry of Supply, and it is on behalf of that
Department that the Ministry of Finance
is carrying out this work in Northern
Ireland.
tion of a comprehensive list is necessary
if an inventory of our resources of this
valuable form of metal is to be obtained.
On lines generally similar to those
adopted in Great Britain my Department
has arranged for the listing of iron and
steel railings and gates throughout Northern Ireland as a preliminary step to
the removal of available metal comprised
therein. It does not, however, follow
that all the fixtures listed by the local
officials will be removed, but the prepara-
So far as farm and field gates are concerned it is not proposed, for the present,
to requisition isolated farm gates and
field gates on lands which have an agricultural valuation. Moreover, railings
and gates enclosing livestock will not be
removed, and exception will also be made
in favour of railings (including gates)
necessary to protect growing crops and
orchards bordering on public highways
where there is a risk of damage or theft
of the crops.
Mr. BROWN: May I ask the Minister
when the Government intends to implement their promise to hand over the railings around the Stormont Estate in connection with this scheme?

laid on the table of the House disclosing
Sir DAWSON BATES: As the name
of the road indicates this is a private road
and the responsibility for maintaining it
rests with the respective owners or

to be put into proper condition rests with

Mr. BROWN (by private notice)
asked the Minister of Labour whether
the attention of his Ministry has been
drawn to the shocking accident
Donaghmore on Tuesday last when
lorry conveying thirteen men from work

purpose; whether he will advise the

Sir DAWSON BATES: I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend to reply.
My attention has been drawn to the
unfortunate accident, the consequences of
which I very much regret.
Vehicles of the type which was used
are not designed for the carriage of
passengers, but, when carefully driven,
are not dangerous, and here and elsewhere they are frequently used to carry
workers to and from work even where
suitable public services are available.
Some time ago the Great Northern
Railway Company, with the collaboration
of the Northern Ireland Road Transport
Board, established a service to carry
workers from various points in County
Armagh to the site on which the men
from Newry are employed, the workers
being brought to and from the trains
by omnibus.
That service could easily have been
extended so as to cover the Newry area,
but before it had been operated for more
than a week or so it was deserted by the
workers who preferred the more
dangerous, but quicker method of travelling by lorry. I am, however, having
inquiries made as to whether a railway
and omnibus service such as I have mentioned cannot again be provided.
As regards the
suggestion that
omnibuses should be provided, I can
assure the hon. Member that the only
obstacle to the adoption of that course is
the fact that omnibuses are not available,
and could be obtained only by withdrawing them from equally important work,
and, as the distance involved is considerable, any attempt to divert omnibuses would entail loss to the war effort.
I am not in a position to express an
opinion as to whether the lorry in ques-
'ion was driven too fast, but the hon.
Member is possibly aware that the

The
FINANCIAL SECRETARY
(Major Sinclair): The Resolution is in
several parts and deals with separate and
miscellaneous financial matters. The first
part relates to the Civil Contingencies
Fund, which as hon. Members are aware
is used for meeting urgent expenditure in
anticipation of covering approval by Parliament in Votes of Supply. The Exchequer and Financial Provisions Act, 1941,
permitted a temporary increase in the
capital of the fund by an amount not
exceeding £250,000 and this, together
with the fixed capital of the fund of
£100,000, made available a maximum
amount of £350,000. The powers given
by the 1941 Act expired on the 30th
September, by which date the advances
made to the fund were repaid to the
Exchequer. In view of the continued
uncertainty and the probability of unforeseen commitments arising out of war
circumstances, it is desired to extend for
a further period the legislative powers
permitting an increase of £350,000, and
the resolution proposes that the increased
provision shall be available until 31st
March, 1944.
Part (b) of the Resolution deals with
the Ministry's borrowing powers and is
concerned more with the administrative
machinery than with conferring upon the
Ministry any fresh borrowing powers. In
the past the Acts have restricted the
application of the proceeds of borrowings
to particular purposes, and the Ministry
was precluded, save in the case of moneys
raised by means of Ulster Savings Certificates, from making other issues which
might be authorised by Parliament. The
Bill which will follow the Resolution will
contain a clause to enable the Ministry
to pool the proceeds of all borrowings by
2773 Financial Provisions [Money]-

20 OCTOBER 1942
Committee
the Exchequer other than Treasury bills,
a power, as I have indicated, which
which already exists as regards the use
of moneys derived from the sale of Ulster
Savings Certificates.
Paragraph (c) relates to the Claims Fund
set up under the Intoxicating Liquor Act
(Northern Ireland), 1923. An anomalous
position exists as regards the levy payable annually under the Act of 1923 by
the holders of retail liquor licences, who
were required under the Act to provide
the wherewithal to meet the compensation payable on the extinction of what
were commonly known as the spirit
groceries. Provision already exists for
the remission or refund of a proportion
of the liquor licence duty itself when a
licensed business is discontinued during
the currency of an annual licence and
the same concession has been made in
relation to the licence duty to meet the
case of suspension of business arising out
of war circumstances. There is, however,
no statutory authority for a similar remission or refund of the compensation
levy and this part of the resolution, and
the Bill which will follow it, empower
the Ministry of Finance to remit a proportion of the levy where a proportion of
the licence duty itself is being remitted.
In actual practice this will mean that the
amount of the levy so remitted will be
made, good by the remainder of the licence
trade so that no loss to public funds is
involved in this arrangement.
Hon.
Members will, I feel sure, agree that this
proposal is only logical and equitable.

General. It is proposed in this connection to provide for the retention in office
of the present holder of the post until he
has attained the age of sixty-eight years,
that is, an extension of one year.
I feel
sure the Committee will agree that the
services of this valuable officer should be
retained. The members of the Public
Accounts Committee will appreciate how
valuable those services
are. I beg to
move.

Then I gather from the speech of the
Financial Secretary that the Auditor-
General's term is going to be extended
for another year. I think he is 67 and it
is going to be extended until he is 68.
So far as the Auditor-General is concerned, he is a very competent man, and
I have nothing to say of him except what
is to his advantage. I do not want anyone to get up later and pretend that I
have done otherwise.
The Comptroller and Auditor-General is
in rather a different position to any other
civil servant in Northern Ireland, because he is in a supreme position so far
as accounts are concerned, and his decision can be exercised against the
Government. In short, when a man is
appointed Comptroller and Auditor-
General, so long as he does his work he is
above Government interference, and that
is the way to keep him. The minute you
put him in a position when he only
retains his position by virtue of a vote in
this House from year to year on the
recommendation of the Government then
he is in a different position, and I say
that without any disrespect to him. When
a man is in a position that depends upon
a vote in this House once a year he is not
in an independent position. I am not
saying the man's disposition is such that
it would yield to that, but I say that
when it becomes necessary to move a
Motion in this House to retain his services, then in practice and on moral and
all other grounds the independence that
the Comptroller and Auditor-General
should command has gone.
Sixty-five is the retiring age, and
evidently year after year this Motion has
been brought forward to carry him to 66,
67 and now 68. That means that although
he would not yield to the temptation, it
is open to him to say, "If I do not please
the Government this year they will not
bring in a Motion next year extending
my retiring age to 69." That is possible
if a man was weak enough to look at it
in that way, and on those grounds the
thing is wrong. It might not be so
wrong in regard to civil servants in any
other position, because no civil servant
except the Comptroller and Auditor-
General has the power possessed by him.
All other civil servants are for carrying
2777 Financial Provisions [Money]-

20 OCTOBER 1912
Committee
out the policy of the Government. That
is their function, not to make policy, but
to carry it out. That is why I always
argue that a civil servant does not always
do what he would like to, but what his
employers order him to do.
The Comptroller and Auditor-General
has, very wisely and very properly, been
placed above all that. His duty is not to
carry out the policy of the Government
at all, but to exercise a check on expenditure. When I say a check on expenditure I mean a check on anything legally
authorised by this House. I might think
it extravagant and another man might
not, but if it is authorised by this House
it is the duty of the Comptroller and
Auditor-General to see that what the
House authorises is carried out. That
authority of the Comptroller and
Auditor-General is more likely to be
exercised against the Government than
against any other person. Consequently
he is put in a position above the Government so far as his official duties are concerned, but when he is over age and only
retains his position from one year to
another by virtue of a Motion brought
into this House annually by the Government, then I say that that independence
and supremacy he possesses is gone, and
that should not be.
In saying all that I allege nothing
against the present occupant of the office.
So far as I have heard and know he does
his duty faithfully and well, but that is
no reason whatever why the Government
should alter the position. Some very
good civil servants have been allowed to
go at 65 years of age, and I think the
Government should weigh a rule like this
well and keep to it as far as possible. Of

Mr. FERGUSON: I beg to move to
leave out, in sub-clause 1'(a), the words
"slander, libel and". The purpose of
this Amendment is to enable the county
court to deal with libel and slander cases
where the damages do not exceed £100.
As the law stands at present a litigant
who wishes to institute a case for libel
and slander has to take the matter to the
High Court, where an application can be
made to have it remitted to the county
court. This Amendment will enable the
matter to go to the county court provided
the suitor does not go for more than £100
damages. It will thus enable small cases
to be dealt with more expeditiously than
at the present time. I cannot see why
the county court, which has power to
deal with other cases involving up to
£100, should not have control of cases
of libel and slander where the amount
involved is similar.

than once illustrated by questions by

Statement of Post-War Policy.
Mr. THOMPSON: I beg to move,
That this House approves the statement made by the Prime Minister on
the 30th July last with regard to postwar policy, and assures the Government
of its support in the furtherance of
such policy.
The Prime Minister put housing and
town-planning in the forefront of his
post-war programme, and I am sure the
House would welcome any further statement he may desire to make to-day,
especially in regard to progress made by
Mr. Davidge and his colleagues. I hope
that gentleman has secured the services of
our leading architects, builders, and the
city surveyor, in the important task he
has undertaken so that we may have a
programme of post-war housing and
planning that will be a real credit to our
Province. I also hope that the whole
plans, including the financial details, will
be so far matured that there will be no
unnecessary delays when hostilities are
over and materials again become available.
Some of us remember the long delays
which took place after the last war, owing
to differences of opinion between the
Government and Belfast Corporation over
the financing of various building schemes.
And here might I suggest that the time
has arrived when the whole question of
local government finance should be reviewed so as to avoid these periodic disputes. The tendency is to throw more
and more responsibility upon the Government. Our present system is based upon
the conditions existing in 1898, the time
of the introduction of the present Local
Government Act, and since then the procedure has been more or less haphazard.
I would be hard to convince that an Act
so old is suitable to-day for a Province
which has developed and made the progress which Northern Ireland has. I
would be glad if the Government would
give this important question of finance.
their early consideration.
Transport and electricity should also
be taken vigorously in hand at once, so
that when housing and town-planning do
take a definite step forward we may have
the light, the power and the transport to

We must put forward every effort not
only to win this war, but to make the
very best of our opportunities when the
war is over. I sometimes think we are
not half grateful enough for the many
privileges we still enjoy in this Province
to which we are proud to belong. It is
the duty of the Government to keep
before our people the actualities of this
great struggle in which we are engaged,
the real issues at stake, so that they may
realise not only what victory will mean,
but the horrors which defeat would bring.
We are fighting for our great Christian
heritage, those things without which life.
would not be worth living. Let us, then,
give to our people that real Christian
leadership in which we all profess so
fervently to believe. When I was thinking this matter over in my own home
this morning a thought came to me and
I pass it on to the House for what it is
worth. It is simply this. We come into
the House each day and utter these
phrases: "Thy Kingdom come. Thy will
be done in earth as it is done in heaven.”
And I am satisfied, at all events in my
own mind, that when we place that idea
in the forefront of post-war policy then
we will commence to make real headway.
I am sure when the Prime Minister on
the 30th July last introduced this matter
he had no less a motive than that high
standard in bringing forward the postwar programme.
Lieut.-Colonel HALL-THOMPSON: I
am very pleased to second this Motion,
because I feel we are in agreement with
everything that the Prime Minister said
in his post-war statement. None the
less I feel we must keep our feet on the
ground, and take first things first and
concentrate on the winning of the war,
and, mindful of what we failed to do
last time, the winning of the peace. Because unless we can win both the war and
the peace it is useless to concentrate on
post-war conditions. One of the first
things that will be required after the
winning of the war will be the rehabilitation of a starving Europe, and we must
contribute our quota to the feeding and
clothing of Europe. Unfortunately the
last war taught us that war does not
necessarily make a land a place fit for
heroes to live in, so that looking forward
to the future we must realise that one of
the first things we will have to do will
be to find employment for the demobilised
soldiers and also employment for those
at present engaged on war work.
Now if we are to carry out the Prime
Minister's scheme of town-planning and
building which we all hope will be done
and done successfully I believe we shall
have to have the price of building
materials controlled and the purchase tax
will have to be removed from those
materials.
Mr. HENDERSON: And vested
interests.
Lieut.-Colonel HALL-THOMPSON :
Again, looking back, we remember the
houses which were built, particularly by
the Belfast Corporation, immediately
after the last war. Owing to the cost of
material and building they were such
that they could not be let at an economic
rent. They were let in the first instance
at 22s 6d a week, which the average
working man was not able to pay.
In due course the rents had to be
reduced with the result that the taxpayer was at a loss. So that I believe if
we want good houses well situated, as
has been suggested by the mover of this
Motion, we must try to take such steps
as will enable these types of houses to be
built and let at an economic rent. I am

In Northern Ireland we must remember that our largest industry is

[Mr. Midgley]
My Amendment, therefore, would read,
if accepted by this House, "That this
House regrets the Prime Minister's
failure . . ." and so on.
I decided to move that Amendment
because I thought it was the most constructive thing to do. To say that I was
surprised to see an expression of confidence on the Order Paper is to put it
mildly, especially as it was in the names
of the Members for Ballynafeigh and
North Derry. The Derry and Antrim
constituencies are so familiar in their
complexity in relation to the Imperial
and Northern Ireland Parliaments that
one wonders what constituency a man is
actually Member for. I hope I have
named the constituencies of the hon.
Members correctly. I was surprised to
see two such names on the Vote of Confidence, because one is that of a clergyman, who is supposed in his daily life,
not on Sundays only, to try to inculcate into his own life and the lives of
others the lesson given expression to this
afternoon by the mover of the Motion.
I was surprised in his case because he is
a gentleman who has made no secret of
his profession-that all political, economic
and industrial life must be run along
God-lines-that is his expression-must
be God guided, God inspired, God endowed and everything else. Now, you
have a combination of two people holding
ideas like those and find them coming
along here and moving a Vote of Confidence in the Prime Minister who by
his own words in July last condemned his
and his colleagues' work for the past 20
years. It proves conclusively that the
Prime Minister and his Cabinet colleagues
have been pursuing a policy diametrically
opposed to the extension of those views
which were given expression to by the
mover. It is cause for surprise on the
part of ordinary living people.
Before I get on to deal with the
Amendment from a constructive point of
view, I would first like to deal with some
of the sentiments expressed by the mover
and seconder in relation particularly to
myself. I do not know why the Member
for Clifton promoted me intellectually to
the eminence which he has done, but I
accept it in the kindliest and best spirit.
I believe he meant it sincerely. He referred me to the question of world conditions, especially in regard to wages in
depressed countries that took part in
competition in the export world with our
products. I think the implication of his
statement was plain, and I am very glad
of the opportunity of referring to the
matter, because for the last 23 years,
since I left France, my life has been a
record of constant national and international effort for the alleviation of
depressed races. I refer to the International Labour Office side of the work
of the League of Nations, about which
many people are singularly ignorant, and
which is pushed in the background at
every opportunity by people who never
made a study of the magnificent work
carried on by that organisation.
I am glad to say I was not only an
affiliated member of all organisations in
Britain that supported the International
Labour Office, but was a direct contributor to the research department and everything I could possibly do from the time
of my emergence. from the Army at the
end of the last war right up to the present moment has been done in an endeavour to raise the standard of depressed
nations. One of the things I deeply
deplore is that respect for international
law has been so completely destroyed in
regard to economic conditions throughout
the world that we have got to start
all over again and attempt to repair
not only the ravages of the rapacious
gentlemen who have. flooded the earth,
but to rebuild so that the world will
avoid the mistakes made in bygone days
and prevent the curse of Hitler or the
counterpart of that ignoble person again
asserting itself. I should like at this
juncture to say for these reasons that I
am all for international action. I am
not going to allow the Prime Minister to
palm me off to-day as he has often tried
to palm us off with any assurance.
Reference was made to the smallness of
Northern Ireland, and the Member for
Clifton said it lent itself to bold schemes
of reconstruction.
I accept that as a test. New Zealand
is a comparable country to Northern
Ireland not only in regard to agriculture
and population, but in regard to its
whole aspirations. That community has
accepted the dictum that it does lend
itself to bold experiments with the result
that it leads the world in relation to social
services. It has done that by accepting
the principle outlined by the Member for

as sweated industries. The result was
that the Imperial Government, including
the Imperial Minister of Labour, had to
set up legislation known as trade board
legislation in order to defend the workers
from the rapacity of those who were
feathering their nests at that particular
time in what were designated sweated
industries. Therefore we come back to
this point. The working classes were not
able to live in the houses because they
were not getting a fair wage and so could
not afford the rent. In other words, the
workers who produced the houses by
their skill and brains were not able to go
in as tenants because they did not receive sufficient back for the building of
the houses to enable them to pay the rent.
Those are the economics of the whole
position.

SAFEGUARDING SMALL
RETAILERS.
2. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he can state if the
plans for ensuring that small retailers
get their fair share of supplies as announced recently at Westminster will
apply to Northern Ireland, and, if not,
whether he will take steps to have the
scheme extended to Northern Ireland.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Sir Basil Brooke): I am informed that
it was not the intention of the President
of the Board of Trade to include Northern Ireland in this scheme. It will be
appreciated that the position of small retailers in Northern Ireland is not
necessarily analagous to that prevailing
in Great Britain where conditions may
differ materially. I can, however, readily
assure the hon. Member that if it
appears that Northern Ireland traders
would benefit from inclusion in the scheme,
I will pursue immediately the question of
its application to Northern Ireland.

six months.

The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Lord Glentoran): From a crop point of
view the harvest has been one of the best
ever grown in Ulster. The saving of it
has been a herculean task, the rainfall
being greater than for the past sixtyfive years.
Thanks to the energy of our
farmers, aided by the powerful assistance
rendered by the volunteers and military,
a great part of this harvest is already
saved. It is too early to give any kind
of accurate report, but from the amount
already in I am satisfied that, in spite
of the weather, it will be a fine harvest.

ploughing old pasture land for 1942 crop

number of applications received for the
1942 ploughing grant in County Tyrone
11,134, involving a sum of £82,548, have
already been paid, 255 have been cancelled as ineligible, and only 55 claims

43,509, involving some £344,852, have

the prices for which we are negotiating.
I think we will get better prices and better
arrangements.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
The
FINANCIAL SECRETARY
(Major Sinclair): The terms of this
Resolution are not, I am afraid, entirely
self explanatory, and the fact that hon.
Members have not got copies of the Bill
before them places them rather at a disadvantage. I will endeavour, however,
to make the position as clear as I can.
With regard to the first part of the
Resolution, it is not proposed to make
any alteration in the stamp duties. What
is intended is to place beyond doubt what
has hitherto been the assumption as to
the meaning of part of the Finance
(1909-10) Act, 1910. Sub-section (1) of
section 74 of this Act places a certain
ad valorem duty on any conveyance or
transfer operating as a voluntary disposition inter vivos, that is, where the
parties concerned are both alive. Subsection (2) of this section provides that
all such conveyances or transfers shall not
be deemed to have been duly stamped
until the Ministry of Finance has expressed its opinion thereon or, to use a
phrase that is perhaps more familiar,
until they have been adjudicated. Subsection (6) of this same section enumerates
certain types of these conveyances or
transfers (for example, a transfer of
stock from one trustee to another) and
declares that these shall not be chargeable with the ad valorem duty. It was
assumed as a matter of course from the
time that the Act became law that these
documents, which were not chargeable
under sub-section (1), also did not come
within the terms of sub-section (2), and
accordingly it has not been the practice
for the past 30 odd years to have them
submitted for adjudication. A recent
decision of the English Court of Appeal
has disproved this assumption however,
and in order to legalise past practice and
to give effect to what it is felt was the
intention of the Act, it is now proposed
to state specifically that the documents in
question shall not be required to be submitted for adjudication. Similar legislative action has already been taken in
Great Britain.
ments of the Imperial Government, and
as the Commissioners of Inland Revenue
are already empowered by statute to
furnish information to our Estate Duty
Branch, it has become increasingly desirable that we should be in a position to
reciprocate this facility. It is proposed,
therefore, to legislate accordingly. Bearing in mind the observation of St. Paul
that "rulers are not a terror to good works
but to the evil," I feel sure that hon.
Members will agree that this strictly
limited amount of liberty should be
accorded.
The latter part of the Resolution deals
with the obligations as to secrecy which
are binding upon the officials of the
Ministry of Finance with regard to the
information that they obtain in the collection of taxes. As the law stands at
present, such information may not be
divulged even to the Revenue Depart-

29 OCTOBER 1942
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 29th October, 1942.
The House met at Two of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Paper Presented.
Ministry of Labour:
Report of Court of Inquiry appointed
by the Minister of Labour to inquire into
the causes and circumstances of a trade
dispute in an aircraft dispersal factory.
(By Act.)
Written Answers.
DEPREDATIONS BY FOXES.
Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state the
result of the recent conference between
his Ministry and representatives of the
county council regarding measures to
prevent depredations by foxes, and
whether it is proposed to introduce
legislation on the matter.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Lord Glentoran): At the conference, to
which the hon. Member refers the representatives of county councils unanimously
requested the Government to defray from
the Exchequer one half of the cost of a
scheme for the destruction of vermin,
chiefly foxes, the other half to be a charge
on the rates. It was agreed that the
contribution from the rates should be
obtained by empowering each county
council to levy at its discretion a rate
for the purpose up to a maximum
poundage of a halfpenny upon the
occupiers in the rural areas in
the county, agricultural land being
exempted. The Government has decided
to adopt the proposal, and it is hoped to
introduce the necessary legislation at an
early date.
BELFAST DOCKERS' STRIKE.
Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state if there was
a strike of dockers at Belfast some time
ago; whether he can state the cause of
the strike in question, and the date, etc.;
whether it was settled in a few hours on
the principle of the status quo; whether
it is a fact that there has been no labour
trouble there since, and whether he can
explain why he did not adopt a similar
procedure in connection with the strike
at the aircraft factories?
The. MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): I assume that the hon.
Member refers to a dispute which occurred
at the Belfast Docks on 19th September
last. The cause. of this dispute was the
question of continuing the discharge of a
vessel over Sunday. A joint conference
of the parties under the. auspices of my
Department was held on the 22nd
September to consider the matter. As a
result of this conference it was arranged
that the discharge of the vessel would be
resumed on the following morning, the.
workers' representatives indicating that
the matter in dispute would be referred
to the National Executive of the Union
for consideration and advice. No stoppage
of work on the question of discharging
vessels on Sunday has since been reported
to my Department.
As regards the latter part of the
question, I feel that the hon. Member
will agree that no useful purpose would
be served at the present juncture by
comparing modes of procedure in dealing with disputes in cases where circumstances are different.

show, as far as possible, neither profit nor

Clause 2. Sub-section (4) and subsection (6) of section 6 of the Government Loans Act, 1939, are complementary. One provides that where the

As regards subsection (6), though a

Fund to meet temporarily any such

income. Parliament will, however, be

Clause 4. This clause proposes to write

been outstanding for a number of years.
The loan was issued in 1924 and the borrowers early got into difficulty in the

collected being that due in 1930. In
addition to defaulting on the loan repayments, the borrowers were also in arrears
with their land purchase annuity payments. Much leniency was shown, and

As the House is aware, two bodies have
been set up to deal with the preparation
of the post-war plan for physical reconstruction. One of these is the Planning
Advisory Board, and the other the
Planning Commission.
The Planning Advisory Board is, as its
name implies, an advisory board. It is
composed of persons nominated by local
authorities and certain important outside
bodies such as commercial and professional
institutions, the National Trust, the Ulster
Tourist Development Association, the
building industries, etcetera, and its
function is to make suggestions and advise
on matters of principle arising during the
preparation of the plan. The Member
for Central complained that he took a
census of the religions of the members of
the Board and found none belonging to a
certain denomination. I do not think the
question of religion should arise, provided
a man is qualified to sit on the Board.
The Planning Commission, on the other
hand, is an entirely technical body consisting of the planning consultant, the
technical officers of those local authorities
who are planning authorities, and technical officers of Government departments,
and it is their business to assist and
advise in the preparation of local plans,
and to secure the co-ordination of these so
that ultimately one consistent and
coherent plan for the whole Province may
be produced.
It is not without interest in connection
with this Motion that at their first meeting the Planning Advisory Board adopted
a resolution setting out what they considered to be the essentials for securing
improved living conditions both in urban
and rural areas, and that from the terms
of this resolution it is evident that so
far as their functions come into the
matter and I would point out that the
Board is concerned with all such matters
as public health, housing and social
services-the Board is in full agreement
with the Government's ideas.
The Planning Commission also has
made good progress with the more technical side of the work which, as I have
explained, is its particular concern.
In the meantime, however, a great
deal of work has to be done in connection
with skeleton plans-prepared in the first
instance on a regional basis—to cover the
Province as a whole and serve as a basis
for the co-ordination of all local plans.
These skeleton plans, of course, concern
no one local authority more than another,
and it was the impossibility of producing
such plans without some such combination
of local planning officers as the Planning
Commission affords that has been the
great stumbling block to any consistent
and coherent planning being carried out.
Such skeleton plans, of course, do not go
into details, but they are of the very
greatest importance. as a foundation for
future local plans, and cover in a
general way such matters as roads,
essential by-passes, traffic considerations,
and open spaces. Two general meetings
of the Planning Commission have been.
held, and a great many meetings of the
Area Committees for Belfast, Londonderry and the Inland Regions. A start
has also been made by a number of local
authorities in the preliminaries of the
local plans, and I would emphasise the
extreme importance of these planning
operations being continued and maintained in the most efficient possible
manner.
Whether the funds available immediately after the war are copious or
restricted, it is of the utmost importance
that they should be expended in the most
useful and economic manner possible, and
this can only be secured if our plan is

A very real effort has been made since

Very little, to my astonishment, has

must be subordinated to that main
object, but that does not mean that the
proposals which the Prime Minister has
outlined will for one moment interfere
with the successful prosecution of our
war effort. They should not only not
interfere, but they should actively encourage and increase the war effort.
Therefore, to judge whether those proposals be good or not one has got to
visualise, or try to visualise, what postwar conditions will be like. I do not
profess to be able to prophesy, but there
were several movements or trends in the
last 10 or 20 years which were clear to
all thinking individuals.
It does seem to me that the trend
of the movements we have seen in the last
two decades will continue.
I may be
entirely wrong. There may something
come in which will turn things in a
completely opposite direction. But it
does seem as if the war has quickened
the movements which were visible before,
and therefore one can see, perhaps not
very definitely, some of the conditions as
they will be after the war. And one
must see what those conditions will be
before one judges the effects of the
Government's proposals upon them. I
think—and again I am only expressing a
personal opinion-that there will be the
following tendencies in the post-war
period:-
(1) There was very noticeable in prewar days a gap between extreme wealth
and extreme poverty. The tendency even
in pre-war days was to narrow the gap,
and that tendency has been quickened
since. the war began. Apart from the
payment of the war debt, the necessities
of post-war reconstruction will, in my
2953 Government Post-War Policy
Government Post-War Policy 2954
29 OCTOBER 1942
opinion, force the continuance of the
heavy taxation of the. wealthy class. I
may be wrong; I am only expressing a
personal opinion.
(2) I think the tendency is for social.
services to increase to a very considerable
extent. That increase will necessitate a
considerable expenditure in the immediate.
post-war years. If that expenditure is
made carefully it should ultimately result
in a decrease in expenditure due, in my
opinion, to the fact that there will be a
reduction in the post-war drain on the
Unemployment Fund.
(3) There is a tendency to see that
opportunity is not the prerogative of any
section of the community. In pre-war
days we saw the door of opportunity
beginning slowly to open. That movement
has become. quickened, and I think there
will be a tendency after the war to force
the door wide open, and not only to force
it wide open, but to keep it wide open.
When I talk about opportunity, I mean
in particular education, not only technical
and agricultural, but secondary and
university education. That has been the
tendency for the past twenty years, and
I think the movement will be greatly
quickened in the post-war years.
(4) Civic consciousness will become
more apparent. I should personally hope
that there will not be the elimination of
individualism, but there will be an acceptance of the fact that one can no longer
use one's property or business or occupation to the detriment of the community
as a whole. It may be that the principle
of civic responsibility will be accepted. I
cannot say. But, at any rate, there is
the beginning in the minds of people a
realisation that it is, when all is said
and done, not more than the principle
enunciated two thousand years ago of
one's duty to one's neighbour.
(5) That, I think, implies as a proposition that the State will assume a more
direct concern over the individual. That
was the tendency in pre-war days. There
was a great deal of encouragement given
by the State to individuals. The reason
for that was, I think, because there was
a demand becoming bigger and bigger for
State assistance, and you cannot have
State assistance without a certain amount
of State supervision.
post-war years a greater amount of work
from everybody than there was in the
pre-war days. If one postulates, as some
people do, that it is the duty of the State
to provide work, the natural corollary is
that it is the duty of the citizen to accept
that work when it is offered. There will
be no room for the idle person in the new
State. This new world can only come
after hard work and sacrifice on the part
of every one. One can take the language
of Mr. Churchill and say that peace will
not bring an end to toil and sweat. If
anyone imagines for a moment that all
we have got to do is to sit back in an
armchair and watch the opening of the
new world he will get a rude awakening
sometime.
(6) I would say that if there is to be
a new world there will have to be in the
Any money which the Government may
expend after the war must come from
somewhere, and money expended by the
State can only come from one source, and
that is the earnings of the individual.
There are no golden coffers into which the
State can dip, and unless there is going
to be a taxable capacity of the individual,
that is to say unless there is going to be
plenty of work for the individual the
income of the State will fall, and if the
income of the State falls then the schemes
which the State may initiate will have to
be cut down proportionately.
(7) I think there will be a tendency
to attack social evils from a different
viewpoint. To a large extent in pre-war
days, not only on the part of this Government, but on the part of every Government, there were grants made for unemployment relief, grants made for sickness
benefit, grants made for old-age pensions.
Undoubtedly that relief, that benefit, and
those pensions did a very considerable
amount of good in alleviating to a very
considerable extent the hardships that
existed. But if by unemployment relief
we can create sufficient work so that there
would be no unemployment, if by more
consideration given to the health of our
people we could, at any rate, partially
eliminate sickness benefit, and if we could
encourage savings on the part of the individual, we might to a large extent
eliminate the necessity for old-age pensions. We could not do that altogether,
but it would be far better to encourage
savings, and to discourage the attitude,
"Do not save; you will always be sure of
10s at the end of your life." I think
there will be a tendency on the part of
the Government to encourage savings.
2955 Government Post-War Policy HOUSE OF COMMONS
Government Post-War Policy 2956
[Mr. Maginess]
That movement has started in the war
period, and it will be encouraged when
the peace comes.
(8) There will be a tendency to pay
more attention to the physical and
mental well-being of the young. I think
the House has generally welcomed the
Prime Minister's proposal in that respect.
I have heard many favourable comments
upon the Prime Minister's speech, and
in nearly every case reference was made
to that part of the speech which dealt
with the young people. We can have, as
the Prime Minister has said, an A.1.
nation, but we can only have it if we
pay attention to the mental and physical
well-being of the population in youth.
(9) Again, in my opinion there will be
in the future an elimination, or partial
elimination, of the sectional interests
which played a very large part in public
life before the war. I do not say that
those sectional interests were all wrong.
I merely say that each section must take
an interest in the well-being of the whole.
Before the war, business, trade unions,
agriculture, commerce, the small man and
the great man, were more or less pulling
against one another. I think there will
be a tendency to foster that comradeship
which the war has established, to discourage the different interests from
pulling against one another, and to
encourage them to pull with one another
for the common benefit of all.
One would not like to see State rights enforced merely to prove a theory. The
State can only exercise its supreme right
to remedy a wrong that exists, but there
has been this tendency to recognise, as
well as the individual right of the owner,
the communal right of the people as a
whole. And finally, I think there will be
a tendency as between individuals to come
closer together, one for the benefit of the
other. So this Province of ours will come
closer to others. The war has shortened
space. The war has brought different
nations and communities into closer touch
with each other.
(10) Again, I think there will be a
tendency, which was very noticeable in
pre-war days, and still more noticeable
since the war began, to show that the
ownership of property carries with it
responsibilities as well as rights. In the
old days there was mainly one responsibility on the property owner, and that
was to pay taxation. One looks now
rather to the owner of property as something in the nature of a trustee. The
community has certain rights over property as well as individuals. I do not
contend that those rights will in every
case be used, or should be used. I do
not think the State rights, if they are
acknowledged, need to be used so long as
the owner of property realises that he has
a responsibility to the community as well
to himself. I think-again, this is only
my opinion that that tendency will
spread in the years that are to come.
I think the tendency will be in future
for Ulster to play a more prominent part
in the economic and cultural development of the post-war world. As I mentioned before, anything the Government
can do, any proposals which the Prime
Minister may promulgate at the present
time to be undertaken in the post-war
years must be paid for, and must be
paid for by the money which this community produces. You either have to
get it in taxation or by borrowing, but
either directly or indirectly the money
must come from this community. And
there is no good in this community or
any other community starting and trying
to build a new world unless it has the
means to do it. You cannot call for a
new world-and I am one of those who
believe that a new world is possibleyou cannot call for a new world to be
built among the stars unless you are
determined to start to build on solid
earth. Anything that is done for the
community must be done by the community. No government either on this
bench or on any other bench can take a
pencil and a piece of paper and create a
brave new world. That must only come
if the people are willing for it.
There has been much blame cast upon
the Government for its alleged sins of
omission in the past 20 years.
If one
studies the world's history in the past 20
years can one not see that every government in the world made mistakes, and
every government seemed to have no
direction at all. We are more or less
marching through the desert. I do not
call countries like Germany, Italy and
Japan countries for the purpose. I am
talking about civilised communities, communities which were anxious to improve
themselves, communities which knew

detain the House very long, but I desire
to raise a very important matter arising
out of the recent industrial disputes.
There has been circulated in the House
this afternoon the report of the court set

Industrial Courts Act, 1919. I take
it this is more or less a public document,
and I now want to avail myself of the
opportunity of saying one or two things

will be the Minister of Labour-to make
a statement this afternoon which may go
a long way towards clarifying public
opinion in regard to the issues at stake.
I wish to say that I have absolutely no
apology to make, either in this House or
outside, for the statement I made at the
beginning of the dispute. I held then,

during the war. In my humble opinion
it would be well to leave that committee
in existence. I told these men that I
knew the chairman of the committee, that
I was in opposition to him for a number
of years, and that he was always a fairminded man. I have no occasion to withdraw that opinion which I expressed to
thousands of these men. I am sorry the
strike occurred. I am glad they are going
As I said the men are as anxious as the
Government for the defeat of Hitler.
When the dispute is a small thing there
should be no bully work. The parties
should come to an agreement as soon as
possible. I know there is certain machinery
by which the trade union movement and
the heads of industry can settle disputes.
Recollect that this thing came to a head
at once, as in a moment because two men
were thrown out. I am not going into the
merits of the case. Then the others said
they would go out. They were out before
anything could be done. That is really
how it occurred.
It is not on parallel grounds with the
other dispute which I now come to if I
am permitted. The facts are not in dispute. I will reiterate them briefly and
if I make a mistake I want to be corrected. A man came here from Eire and
took up residence somewhere round
Belfast. He registered at the labour
exchange as an electrician. Mackie's
sent to the labour exchange for electricians
and the labour exchange sent up a few
men, including this man. We are safe in
presuming that the other men were trade
unionists, and that they were men who
lived here, and probably went through
the lean period when there was no employment at all.
This man, who was a
stranger and in no trade union, was
accepted and appointed. The other men
were left out.
That would not be tolerated in any
country in the world. Supposing I was
out of a job, and one of the Cabinet
Ministers was out of a job, and we were
getting employment in Dublin subject to
joining a trade union, we would be very
peculiar men if we did not join it. I
have some little experience of things like
that, and so has the Member for Ballynafeigh. When we were on the Electricity
Committee many a time it was reported
by the trade union officials that a man
who was not in the union had got a job.

We had no law to make him join the
union, but we had a discussion, and we
invariably came to the conclusion that
we were not going to allow the undertaking to be upset by reason of one man
refusing to join the union. We conveyed.
that to the manager, and we said that if
the man would not join the union the
manager knew how to get rid of him.
We never had any trouble, because the
manager acted accordingly.
With the exception of the lawyers, the
doctors have the strongest trade union
in the world. The teachers have a union.
Everyone has a union in these days, and
I am surprised that the Government of
Northern Ireland, with all their talk
about getting work in Northern Ireland
for Northern Ireland people and about
keeping work for ex-service men when
they come back, allowed this man to cut
right across their professions. Ι am
amazed at it. But the Minister will get
up after a little while and say that they
have no power. He might not tell that
to me.
I know a little smatter of law.
I know there was an Act of Parliament
passed since the war commenced placing
all property in the hands of the Government if they want it for anything in
connection with the war effort. That
being so, they can tell any employer to
stop doing something calculated to impede
the war effort. They can even order a
man to leave one employer and go to
another, and prosecute him if he does.
not go. If they can do that, they can
compel an employer to put one man right
so far as the union is concerned. One of
the strikes is practically over, and it is
up to the Government to put an end to
the other.
Mr. GORDON: If it were any other
time, and if it were another occasion,
I would take upon myself to discuss the
whole question of the strikes that have
taken place in the city. The speeches of
the hon. Members for Woodvale and
Willowfield have been fair and reasonable,
and I do not think the hon. Member for
Woodvale would expect me to compare
the attitude of the employer with that of
the worker, or the attitude of the worker
with that of the employer. I am sure
he would not want me to enter into a
discussion of that kind. He knows that
the strike in one large concern has been
settled most satisfactorily. As soon as
No person regards strikes with greater
disfavour than I regard them. I am at
one with both hon. Members when they
say that our first anxiety is to win the
war, and I say from this House to every
representative of every union in
in the
whole country that before he proceeds to
strike, let him use the appropriate
negotiating machinery of the union.
There would not be any strikes if the
negotiating machinery of the union was
used first. I agree with the Report of
the Court of Inquiry which says that
shop stewards perform good work provided they do not go beyond the duties
that devolve upon them as shop stewards.
They have no right to order a strike.
They must first of all report to their
District Committee, and the District
Committee must report to the Executive
Committee before any strike can take
place. Any strike that has taken place
in the city of Belfast should not have
occurred until the appropriate machinery
of the union was brought into being.
I do not want to say one word that
would be calculated to injure the progress
that is taking place at the present time.
The Minister of Commerce and I spent
from early yesterday morning until nine
o'clock last night trying to solve an
exceedingly difficult position, and I am
glad to say that we got an agreement
between the Executive Committee and
the firm concerned. Although the discussions to-day have been protracted I
am hopeful that the Executive Committee will be able to lead the members
of their union to see that the offer was a
fair one and at once bring the machinery
of negotiation into being in order to
eliminate the difficulties and obstacles
that have been placed in the way. I feel
sure that if the trades unions all over
the country would adhere to the laws
and rules that govern their organisations
we would not in the future be troubled

Adjournment
with any strikes. I align myself with
the two hon. Members on the Opposition
side in asking the strikers to resume
work, and in the future, before any
steps are taken to create trouble, to retard production, and to play the part of
Hitler and Mussolini, to use the
machinery of negotiation.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: As Minister of
Production I would like to back everything my right hon. Friend as said, and
also the sentiments expressed by both
hon. Members opposite. I think the
House will recognise, without my
emphasising it, that ever since the war
began I have been jealous about Ulster's
position. As Minister of Agriculture I
suggested that our farmers should do
their part, and more than their part in
the war.
Since I have had the honour
of being Minister of Commerce I have
visited Ministers on the other side, not on
the plea that they should solve our unemployment problem, but that our people here
should be given an opportunity of playing
their part in the war, as I knew they
would. I am still convinced, in spite of
the troubles that have existed, that 90 per
cent. and perhaps more of the men in
in this country feel as we do. They are
out to win the war. They will do everything they can to win it. Unfortunately
tempers got high, and misunderstandings
arose. I will not say anything more than
that.
The thing which stands out is that for
some considerable time past there have
been sporadic outbreaks of strikes here.
and there, partly, as the hon. Member for
Willowfield stated, because some workers
feel, perhaps, that the machinery is too
slow, and that by striking-it may not
seem a terrible offence to them at the
time-their difficulties can be overcome,
and they will get what they want. If
they realised that their action might prevent one aeroplane from going over
Germany on a bombing expedition, or
might prevent one tank going to Lybia
and giving the knock-out blow they might
take a different view. It is difficult to
get men to realise the urgency of the
position as it exists to-day.
Second to that-I think it is an important point-if men take unofficial action
they are undermining the trade union
movement, and that movement means and
will mean their safety. By undermining
it they will lose something that is, indeed,
very valuable and something which they
and their forefathers have spent a long
time in obtaining. That point takes
second place. The war must come first.
But if the trade union movement is undermined by men who are not disciplined
and who do not realise the danger and
the disaster they may bring to the
country, the sooner they are made to
realise the position the better. We cannot carry on a war of this kind without
disciplined men and women. Individuals
cannot stand alone.
I would appeal to the thousands of
good and true men in this country not to
allow themselves to be led by agitators,
and to think before they take an action
which not only brings disaster to their
own interests, but which may help Hitler
to continue the war for even one month
longer than can be helped. As Minister
of Production I am not, despite the remarks we have heard, an employers' man.
I am a man out to win the war, and so
long as I can help in this direction I
will use every means in my power to do
so. I appeal to all to forget the past,
get down to work, and if they have a
grievance to put it forward in the proper
manner and use the machinery at their
disposal.
Mr. NIXON: With the permission of
the House I just want to say one word.
The Minister gave me the lead before he
sat down by stating that we should forget the past and get on with the work.
I want to emphasise that appeal. The
only way to allow them to forget the past
is by having no prosecutions.
Question put, and agreed to.

The Drainage Act, which was passed
by the House last June, envisaged the
undertaking of certain emergency drainage schemes by county councils with
Government financial assistance, and in
order to facilitate the councils still
further in the carrying out of such
schemes it was decided to adopt the recommendation of the Drainage Commission that the Government should
acquire a general pool of major dredging
equipment that could be hired out where
Hon. Members will, no doubt, be
interested to know the extent to which
county councils have availed themselves
of the generous assistance afforded by the
Drainage Act I have just referred to, and
I am authorised to say that four schemes
are at present under way. These are the
rivers Cusher and Creggan in County
Armagh, and the rivers Whitewater and
Loughries in County Down. The Whitewater scheme is virtually complete. The
Cusher is nearly 70 per cent. complete,
the Creggan over 50 per cent. complete,
and the Loughries under 40 per cent.
complete. Of the four schemes it is
thus anticipated that, in addition to the
Whitewater, the Cusher and Creggan will
be completed by the end of this month.
But this, of course, subject to no unforeseen circumstances arising or to
weather conditions. Of the Loughries
scheme only the essential parts will, however, have been completed by the end of
the season. The Government contribution to these schemes is not, of course,
borne on this Vote, but the grant of the
necessary sums will be moved by my
right hon. Friend, the Minister of Home
Affairs on the next Estimate.
The next item in the Estimate is in
connection with the Lough and River
Erne Drainage. As hon. Members may
be aware, the members of the Lough
Erne Drainage Board resigned in the
year 1940. The primary function of the
Board was to maintain the waters of
Lough Erne at certain statutory levels,
and it was essential for the prevention
of flooding that this function of the
Board should be continued. The drainage
district comprises lands both in Northern
Ireland and in Eire, and my Ministry
entered into an arrangement with the
Office of Public Works in Dublin, under
which the cost of the operation of the
sluice gates at Belleek should be borne
by the two departments. The total
annual maintenance costs are expected to

With regard to the quarrying of limestone, we have a big plant near Cookstown for dealing with limestone. This
plant is turning out one hundred tons of
ground lime a day, which is magnificent. In addition, there is a plant now
working in Benburb, and all over the
country we are rejuvenating and assisting
these lime plants, because they are of
quite exceptional value at the present
time. Most of the farmers appreciate
their value, but in spite of these new
mills we cannot supply the demand. I
think I can say that by next spring we
shall be just about in a position to meet
the demand from the farmers.
It is very
gratifying to know that our farmers have
recognised the value of this lime and are
willing to pay for it in order to improve
their land not only now, but for the
future.

£20,000 of that sum represents increases

Sir BASIL BROOKE: In regard to
Item B, Carrickfergus Harbour, I may
say that that harbour is being used as a
supplementary harbour. It had become
silted up, and a certain amount of brick
work had broken down. That expenditure was required to allow ships of bigger
draught to get into the harbour, and
also for some underpinning. This represents 25s for each 20s to be contributed
by the local council.
Item C-grants under the Civil Defence
Act, £174,000-represents a grant of 85
per cent. for further works and improvements in Belfast Harbour. That has
been agreed upon by the various Ministries concerned in order to enable more
ships to enter the harbour and to have a
quicker discharge. That is war expenditure; it would not have been necessary
but for the war.
With regard to the stone crushing
plant mentioned by the hon. Gentleman,
I may say that before the war the only
stone crushing plant in this country was
that required by the county councils. In
view of great activities which I need not
mention here, not only in connection with
air-raid shelters but in relation to other
matters, it was found impossible to deal
with the quantities of stone required by
the use of local machinery. Therefore,
my Ministry purchased a certain number
of mobile crushers and put in a very
large plant which, in fact, has solved the
Supplementary Estimates-

Harbours
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Basil Brooke]
difficulty and has benefited civil defence
to a very great extent.
As to reserve of coal, the House will
recognise the extremely difficult position
which users of coal are in. I felt it was
most important that the poorer people
of this country, who have not storage
room for coal in their houses, should
have the benefit of a reserve stock which
has been purchased by the Government
and will be put in a certain reserved
place. The coal trade of this country
usually kept their supply on the other
side of the water and shipped it from
the mines, with very little reserve here,
and hon. Members will realise, in view of
the precarious position created by the
war, how necessary it was to take action
of the kind I have indicated. I think it
was a wise thing for the Government to
purchase this coal, and the £100 shown
is the estimated loss that the Government
may suffer as a result of the coal losing
weight through double handling. I
think that is a sufficient explanation.
The grant to the Tourist Development
Association is slightly more than a token
payment. The Services approached me.
some time ago with a view to setting up
an Information Bureau for the troopsour American Allies and our own. I

certain financial support to the extent of
the additional expense which the association will be put to by the transfer of
their activities to more extensive
premises in a more central part of the
city.

Oral Answers to Questions.
EXPORT OF BARLEY.
1. Mr. THOMPSON asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state if it
is a fact that barley sold in Northern
Ireland for malting purposes is subsequently exported to Eire for brewing
purposes, and, if so, why does the Ministry refuse to permit export to England
and Scotland for purposes of human
consumption; and whether it is a fact
that pearl barley is sold to the householder in Northern Ireland at round
about £100 per ton when it is purchased
from the farmer at prices ranging from
£14 10s Od to £21 per ton.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTER OF
AGRICULTURE (Mr. Maginess): I
have been asked to reply.
With regard to the first part of the
question, I have no information but am
having inquiries made. The Order prohibiting the export of barley from Northern Ireland is one made by the
Minister of Food. The retail price of
pearl barley is also a matter entirely for
the Ministry of Food, and as it does not
concern my Department I have no official
information, but if the hon. Member desires me to do so I shall endeavour to
obtain official prices for him. The prices
of barley sold by a farmer for feedingstuff purposes may not exceed £14 10s a
ton. The maximum price of barley bought
from the farmer for malting is £35 per
ton. These two prices have been fixed
by the Minister of Food.
Mr. MAGINESS: I do not think the
figures quoted by the hon. Member are
correct.
Mr. THOMPSON: Is
the Parliamentary Secretary aware that the price
paid per ton in Ulster to the farmer is
£21 or thereabouts, but the price paid to
the farmer in England is somewhere
about £60 to £80 ton.
per
I would like
to know if we can have any further information on this point. I shall also be
grateful for the information the Parliamentary Secretary has promised to give.
Mr. THOMPSON: I have no doubt
about them.
REPAIR OF DAMAGED HOUSES.
5. Mr. THOMPSON asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is aware
that a large number of houses still remain unrepaired in Belfast; that a
number of owners have been refused permission by the Local Authority and the
Ministry of Home Affairs to have repairs
carried out, because it is stated the repairs would cost more than the value of
the houses pre-war; also that many of
these houses could be repaired at a cost
of a little over £100, and the pre-war
price is calculated at about £80;
whether he will consider reviewing his
Ministry's present attitude owing to the
fact that houses are so urgently needed
and this price would be considerably
under to-day's price for building new
houses.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The reply to the
first two parts of the question is in the
affirmative.
With regard to the third part, while
it may be correct that repairs costing
rather more than £100 can be carried
out to make habitable certain houses
referred to by the hon. Member and the
pre-war value of which was approximately £80, it should be remembered
that the carrying out of these repairs at
this cost would not restore the said houses
to their pre-war condition, and consequently the War Damage Commission is
not authorised to make a "cost of works"
payment.
With regard to the last part of the
question, I am to remind the hon. Member that the extent to which repairs may
be permitted is a matter primarily for
the War Damage Commission who have
to meet the cost of the repairs and who
must act within the provision of the War
Damage. Act, 1941, and no question of
policy on the part of my Ministry arises.
I would also point out that my Ministry is only concerned if the repairs are
carried out by local authorities, and that
there is nothing to prevent a private
Oral Answers
Fisheries Bill
5 NOVEMBER 1942
owner approaching the War Damage
Commission, before he
he undertakes repairs, to ascertain if the Commission
would make a "cost of works" payment
in respect of the proposed repairs. If
they cannot do so, it is still open to the
owner to repair his property, and in this
case he will receive compensation after
the war.
HOUSING SITUATION.
6. Mr. THOMPSON asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he will consider
the advisability of arranging for the
building of a limited number of new houses
each month, so that the housing situation
may be eased to some little extent; and
whether it would be possible to lay
foundations for 20 to 30 houses per
month.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I would
assure the hon. Member that I am very
conscious of the desirability of providing
as many new houses as possible and at the
earliest possible date, but he will, I am
sure, understand that the position in
Belfast is no different in this respect from
that of many cities in Great Britain
which have suffered similar damage, and
that both here and in Great Britain there
are very serious difficulties in the way of
providing new houses at the present time
which have so far prevented any active
measures being taken.
The hon. Member may, however, rest
assured that we are, and for some time
past have been, in close touch with the
Imperial authorities in regard to the
matter, and that the moment it becomes
possible to provide houses, either in large.
or small numbers, immediate steps will
be taken to that end.
I cannot at the moment give any
promise or undertaking beyond saying
that in the matter of providing new
housing accommodation we are not behind England at present, and that the
hon. Member may rest assured that the
position is being closely watched.
Mr. THOMPSON: Would the Minister
of Home Affairs investigate and find out
if houses are at present being built in
certain parts of England and Scotland,
and, if so, would he undertake to follow
the same procedure in Northern Ireland?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I had the
privilege of having a deputation from the
Belfast Corporation to-day, and I explained that we are in exactly the same
position as England with regard to the
question of new houses. Certain statements appeared in the Press which are
entirely erroneous. I can assure the
hon. Member no new houses have been
built in England.

Oral Answers to Questions.
CLOGHER VALLEY RAILS.
1. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Finance whether he can state
to whom the steel rails of the Clogher
Valley Railway were sold, and at what
price.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have been asked
to reply.
The permanent way, consisting of
approximately 37 miles of main line and
3 miles of sidings; sleepers and fixings;
point crossings, rail switches, signals and
fittings; turn table, metal bridge; weighbridges; spare rails and fixings, lamp
standards and telephone system, were sold
by public tender, advertisments for which
appeared in newspapers circulating both
in Northern Ireland and in Great Britain.
The highest tender, submitted by the
firm of Messrs. G. Cohen, Sons & Co.,
Ltd., was accepted, the price being
£33,555. The purchaser was charged
with the expense of lifting, collecting and
removal of all materials in a safe and
reasonable manner. I am unable, therefore, to state separately the actual price
received for the steel rails.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Arising out
of that reply, will the Minister state
whether or not these rails are being sent
out of the country?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, sir. I
have no knowledge beyond the fact that
the firm that gave the highest bid got
the material I referred to.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Will the
Minister find out whether or not these
rails were sent to the Free State, instead
of being sent to Great Britain as scrap?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I beg your
pardon. I did not hear the hon. Member's question.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Will the
Minister find out whether these rails were
sent to the Free State, instead of Great
Britain to make steel tanks?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Certainly: I
will inquire, but I do not know.
PRICE OF POTATOES.
2. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether he is
aware that considerable dissatisfaction
exists owing to the difference in price paid.
to farmers in Northern Ireland for
potatoes as compared with the controlled
prices in Great Britain.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Lord Glentoran): I think there is some
lack of understanding with regard to
potato prices, and I am glad to have this
opportunity to explain the position.
For the purpose of controlling the
price of potatoes the United Kingdom
has been divided into nine zones. The
maximum price in each zone is different
and is fixed so as to allow for the variation in the cost of transporting potatoes
to the normal markets. In consequence
of this arrangement, the present maximum price in each zone in Great Britain
shows approximately the same comparative increase over the pre-war price. The
Fisheries Bill-

Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Lord Glentoran]
same principle has been applied in fixing
the price in Northern Ireland, which constitutes one of the nine zones, and, if
anything, the increase over the pre-war
price is comparatively greater than in
other parts of the United Kingdom.
The House will be glad to know that
this year there was a very substantial
