Order for Second Reading read.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: The Bill before
the House is designed to enable boards
of conservators to raise additional revenue
in order to meet any increase in the cost
of providing adequate protection for the
fisheries in their respective districts. As
the existing licence duties are the maximum fixed by statute, the only way in
which such an increase in expenditure
could be met under the present conditions
would be by Exchequer grants. The
Government has been obliged to have
recourse to this method in the case
Hon. Members will have observed that
the Bill is permissive and that it does not
compel a board to increase the present
rates of duty. The power conferred by
the Bill is purely discretionary and can
be applied, within the limit of an additional 50 per cent., in whatever degree
the Board considers necessary. It will
also have been observed that salmon rods
are excluded from the instruments in respect of which a Board is empowered to
increase the existing rate of licence duty.
Under existing law an annual salmon rod
licence taken out in any one of the four conservancy districts is valid without further
payment in the other three. It will be
obvious that, if all the Boards did not
increase the duty on salmon rods, or did
not increase it to the same extent, there
would be an inducement to salmon anglers
to take out their licences in the district
in which the rate of duty was lowest, and
thus deprive the other boards of their
fair share of revenue from this class of
instrument. Obviously, therefore, the
discretionary power which the Bill proposes to confer cannot be applied to
salmon rods.
There is, of course, the alternative of
excluding salmon rods from the list of
instruments in respect of which boards
would be given discretionary power, and
of fixing a specific higher rate for salmon
rods in the Bill itself. I have rejected
this alternative on two grounds. The first
is that some of the boards have expressed
their objection to any increase in the present rate of duty on salmon rods. The
second reason is the opposition which the
House expressed to an increase in the duty
when the matter was raised on a former
occasion. In the Bill which ultimately
became the Northern Ireland Fisheries
Act of 1928, it was originally proposed to
increase the duty on salmon rods in all
districts from £1 to £2 per annum.
Religious Instruction 3046

Strong opposition to this proposal was
expressed as the Bill proceeded through
its several stages, and my predecessor
finally agreed to compromise by fixing
the rate at 30s per annum.
The opposition to the larger increase was based on
the fact that in certain districts salmon
angling is the recreation of the working
man, and also that it was in the interests
of the fisheries to encourage salmon
angling, as anglers are the strongest
enemies to poaching and illegal methods
of fishing. The same arguments would
still apply, and for this reason, apart
from the other which I have mentioned,
the Government has decided to leave the
present rate of 30s per annum unaltered.

As a corollary to the power to increase
the rates of licence duty, boards are also
empowered by the Bill to increase, within
a similar maximum of 50 per cent., the
annual rate payable by the owners
users of productive commercial fisheries.
Under existing law a person using such
a fishery pays an annual rate which, when
added to the total amount of licence duty
paid by him during the year, represents
10 per cent. on the poor law valuation of
the fishery. It will be obvious that cases
might arise in which an increase in the
rates of licence duty, even to the maximum extent of 50 per cent. allowed by
the Bill, would not in itself result in an
increase of revenue to the Board, and
that, in order to procure such an increase,
the Board would need to increase the
present annual rate. Power to do so to
the same maximum limit of 50 per cent.
is, therefore, conferred by the Bill.
I hope that, with the discretion which.
it is now proposed to vest in them, Boards
will be in a position, if not to dispense
entirely with financial assistance from the
Government, at least to avoid having to
look to the Government to make good by
way of Exchequer grants any additional
expense to which they may be put owing
to the increased cost of providing the
necessary protection services. I beg to
move.

The PRIME MINISTER: I beg to
move, "That in pursuance of section two
of the Prolongation of Parliament Act,
1942, this House resolves that sub-section
(4) of section fourteen of the Government
of Ireland Act, 1920 (which relates to the
duration of the House of Commons of
Northern Ireland) shall, in its application
to this House in this present Parliament,
have effect as if six years were therein
substituted for five years."
""
As hon. Members know, our Parliament owes its existence to the Government of Ireland Act, 1920, and only the
Imperial Parliament can alter or
authorise a departure from its terms.
One of its clauses provides that the House
of Commons of Northern Ireland when
summoned shall, unless sooner dissolved,
have continuance for five years from the
day on which the summons directs the
House to meet, and no longer. The five
years authorised, as far as this House of
Commons is concerned, will expire on the
first of March next, and the Government
here have discussed the matter very fully
with His Majesty's Ministers on the other
side of the Channel.
increased by one year, and the third
course was for the British Government to
put in their Bill a provision giving power
to this House to act in the matter as it
thinks right, at its sole discretion. That
is the course which we have decided upon,
because we think it is the fairest, most
in keeping with the dignity of this
Chamber, and also more democratic, if I
may say so.
There were three courses open to us.
One was to allow things to go without
alteration. That would have meant that
we would have been placed in the turmoil
of a general election before the first of
March. The second course was for the
British Government, in their Prolongation Bill, to insert a clause to the effect
that the life of this Parliament would be
Having come to that decision, I think
I ought to tell the House just what the
position is. The Prolongation of Parliament Act, which was passed at Westminster and received the Royal Assent on
the 2nd October, lengthened the life of
the Imperial Parliament by one year for
the third time. It is now entering its
eighth year. It also gave power to us to
lengthen the life of this House of Commons by one year. We are now, of
course, in our fifth term. I wish to
acknowledge at this stage the helpful and
the interested and able way in which my
right hon. Friend the Secretary of State
for Home Affairs dealt with this matter
in the British House of Commons, and
in fact deals with all matters affecting the
interests of this Parliament of ours. I
also wish to acknowledge the support
which was given to this view by our
Imperial Members.

Socialist Members. I do not attach much

little importance. Again, my hon. and

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 26th November, 1942.
The House met at Two of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
DISCRIMINATION AGAINST
DISPENSARY DOCTORS.
6. Dr. LYLE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he is aware that
the Ballymena Board of Guardians in
granting a war bonus to all their other
officials with salaries up to £500 per
annum, excluded their dispensary doctors
although the expenses incurred by them
in performing their duties have been
greatly increased under the conditions
caused by the war, and what action, if
any, he proposes to take.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I am aware of the
facts as stated by the hon. Member. I
would point out that the Ballymena
Board of Guardians in awarding war
bonuses to their staff have adopted a
similar policy to that in operation in all
departments of the Civil Service, in that
full-time officers in receipt of a salary
exceeding £500 per annum and officers on
a part-time basis, except in a few isolated
cases, receive no war bonus. Accordingly
I am not prepared to recommend the
Board to amend their proposals to cover
dispensary doctors who are part-time
officers.
Dr. LYLE: Would the Minister of
Home Affairs inform me what day of the
week, what hour of the day, or what
month of the year dispensary doctors are
not on duty, and therefore how they can
be considered part-time officers only?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The hon.
Member will understand that a dispensary doctor engages in his own private
practice and in some cases the dispensary
duties come after the private practice.
Dr. LYLE: Further arising out of the
answer would I be permitted to correct
the Minister of Home Affairs?
The hon. Member must take some other
occasion to keep the Minister informed.
Mr. SPEAKER: No. Supplementary
questions must be short questions of fact.
Dr. LYLE: Is it not a fact that the
duties of the dispensary doctor must come
first in every instance, and that his
private practice must be done only in his
spare time after he has performed the
duties of the dispensary doctor?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The hon.
Member will admit that he has a certain
amount of spare time, but I do not wish
to cast any reflection on dispensary
doctors. After all I do believe dispensary doctors place their poor patients
before their private patients.
Mr. MIDGLEY: I should like to ask
the right hon. Gentleman to consider the
advisability of removing such an
anachronism as a dispensary doctor altogether and also poor-law guardians and
fall into line with Great Britain in these
things?
Sir DAWSON BATES: That is a very
big question, and I am sure the hon.
Member would not expect me to discuss
it by question and answer.

many occasions informed the House that

possible to establish an institution for

subject has been received from the

report is at present being considered.
The fact that Northern Ireland is a
long way behind Great Britain in regard
to legislation on this subject has not been
overlooked by the Government.

pronouncement at an early date on this
matter?

selecting a medical officer against the

give an assurance to the House that,

section of the community shall in future
be the inalienable right of the R.U.C.
As to the remaining parts of this question, I propose to say only that while the
doctor appointed was not the choice of
the men, I am satisfied that the appointment is in the best interests of the Force
as a whole. The same remarks apply to
the previous appointment to which the
hon. Member has referred. That the
choice on that occasion was a right one

appointed gave entirely satisfactory
service in the period of over six years
during which he held the post.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The regulations governing the appointment of
medical attendants to the Royal Ulster
Constabulary do not preclude the appointment of a doctor who resides within
reasonable distance from the area allotted
to him, and I am satisfied that in this
case the doctor appointed resides sufficiently close to his area to allow of the
satisfactory performance of his duties.

Oral Answers

Oral Answers
15 DECEMBER 1912
The accounts designed to show the details
of the figures have, with the approval of
my Ministry, been omitted for reasons of
security.
For these reasons this course has been
adopted, both here and in Great Britain,
in the case of many public utility undertakings, including the railways and the
London Passenger Transport Board, and
my Ministry, by order under the Defence
(General) Regulations, has relaxed the
obligation placed upon the two main
railway companies operating in this area
to prepare accounts giving details of
receipts and expenditure. It was considered that the principles underlying this
course applied, with at least equal force,
in the case of the Transport Board.
With regard to the second part of the
question, I find it difficult to understand
the hon. Member's point.
The operating or trading profit for the
year is not carried to the balance sheet,
but in accordance with universal practice
it is carried to the Appropriation Account
(No. 6), and it is the net balance on this
account which is brought into the balance
sheet.
This procedure is fully detailed in
paragraphs 12 to 17 of the report, which
I think must have escaped the notice of
the hon. Member.
The balance sheet of the Transport
Board for the year ended 30th September,
1942, has been drawn up so as to exhibit
a true and correct view of the Board's
affairs at that date, and of their operations for the year in question, and has
been so certified by the auditors.

Unemployment Assistance (Determinaof Need and Assessment of Needs)
(Amendment) Regulations, 1942.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): I beg to move, "That the Regu
lations made by the Ministry of Labour on
Unemployment Assistance-
Regulations
15 DECEMBER 1942
the 4th day of August, 1942, under Section
33 of the Unemployment Assistance Act
(Northern Ireland), 1934, as amended by
the Determination of Needs Act (Northern Ireland), 1941, be hereby
approved."
The two Regulations, with which the
Motions now before the House are concerned, were made to increase the rates
of unemployment assistance and supplementary pensions respectively. They
form part of a plan to help the condition
of people who have to look principally to
State funds for their means of support,
and they are similar-I might almost say
identical-in character. It would, therefore, give a clearer picture of the whole
situation if I dealt with them together;
and with the permission of the House I
propose to take that course.
In June last His Majesty's Government in Great Britain undertook to see
if anything could be done to alleviate the
difficulties created by war-time conditions
for persons in receipt of unemployment
assistance or supplementary pensions.
After inquiry the Government found
that, without anticipating the work of
the Beveridge Committee in framing a
long-term comprehensive scheme for
social improvement (which is now in
hand), the immediate position could be
improved by taking action in three
different ways:-(1) by an all-round increase in the scale rates for assistance
and supplementary pensions which we
now have before us; (2) by improvements
in the special winter allowances; and
(3) by the supply of clothing and
blankets to those who particularly needed
them.
The existing powers of the Assistance
Board were wide enough to put the
second and third of these into operation
without any new regulations; but I
should like to say a word or two about
them to make the picture complete. In
previous years the winter allowances
were given from the 1st November to the
end of March. This winter they started
as usual on the 1st November, but will
be continued to the end of April; and
they will be increased from about 2s a
week to 2s 6d a week in the average run

disclosed that in 4,334 cases there was a
shortage of blankets, some wanting one

ordered 6,000 blankets, many of which
have been distributed to the very poor
applicants.

Shortly after the report was received
the Government of Ireland Act
passed and separate legislatures set up
for Northern and Southern Ireland, and,
whilst the Government of Southern Ireland had a sufficient sense of its duty to
the community to cause it to adopt some
of the recommendations of the Council,
most surprisingly our legislature completely ignored this report and proceeded
to perpetuate all the defects so clearly and
specifically set forth in it, by entrusting
to the Ministry of Labour the management and supervision of National Health
Insurance and by combining in the
Ministry of Home Affairs such diverse
functions as maintenance of law and
order, local government administration,
and public health and medical services
generally.
The inevitable result has been that the
Ministry of Home Affairs, finding itself
fully occupied with its other duties,
especially the maintenance of law and
order, has been obliged to neglect its
health functions, and, whilst making a
success of its legitimate functions throughout a very trying period extending from
its inception to the present date, has permitted a deplorable state of affairs to
continue in the sphere of public health
and medical services generally.
Since this Government was set up two
major Acts dealing with public health
have been passed in Great Britain which
have no counterpart in our legislation.
Our legislators had gone to sleep, but
prodded by the growing discontent of
a portion of the electorate with existing
conditions, they set up the Departmental
Commission on local government administration in Northern Ireland which
reported in 1927.
After a further period of repose lasting
for four years and then, again prodded
by further manifestations of irritation, in
1931 the Ministry of Home Affairs issued
a circular stating that a Bill was being
prepared to deal with poor law and public
health reform, and promising (1) to
broaden the basis of administration and
divorce medical services from poor law
relief; (2) the abolition of Boards of
Guardians, and (3) the appointment of
county medical officers of health, and
other reforms.
That is 11 years ago and this Bill,
this conception by the Ministry of Home
Affairs is still enfolded in the womb of
futurity, and, as its period of gestation
has been so abnormally prolonged without as yet any sign of approaching labour,
I fear that if it ever arrives at parturition
—which I very much doubt-the ultimate
product of conception will be, not a sturdy
infant, but either a still-birth or a monstrosity, or both.
The Ministry again went to sleep for
six years, and in 1937 it was partially
aroused from its somnolent condition by
a renewal of discontent at the very high
maternal and infant death rates in Northern Ireland as compared with those in
England and Wales. Here are the comparative figures:-Maternal death rate
for England and Wales, 3.65 per 1,000;
Northern Ireland, 6.06-an increase over
England and Wales of no less than 66
per cent; infant death rate, England and
Wales, 59; Northern Ireland, 77; Belfast,
101, since increased to 122 per 1,000an increase for Northern Ireland over
England and Wales of 30.5 per cent. and
for Belfast of 71.18 per cent. In the same
year Belfast Corporation voted the sum of
£12,000 for maternity and child welfare.
and £39,000 for the maintenance of
public free libraries.
In the year 1940 in Leeds, a city fairly
comparable with Belfast as regards population and industrial conditions, the
infant mortality rate was somewhat high
at 61 per 1,000; but in Belfast it was
exactly 100 per cent, higher at 122 per
1,000. These figures require no comment;
they speak for themselves and with no
uncertain voice.
In 1937 the Ministry wakened up for a
sufficiently long time to appoint a committee to inquire into the maternity services of Northern Ireland. This committee reported, but after five years that
report still reposes unpublished in the
dusty archives of the Ministry. Why?
Is the Ministry afraid to publish it, afraid
to reveal to an indignant public the defects
that exist, and its own failure to deal
with those defects? I challenge the
Ministry to publish this report.
Many are of opinion that these commissions, held at considerable cost to the
taxpayer and with much loss of valuable
time by both the witnesses and the personnel of the commissions, were mere
camouflage, intended only to soothe and

I am living in the Larne rural

I thereupon reported the full circumstances of the case to the Department
of Health under the Ministry of Home
Affairs. One of their officials (a
medical officer) came to investigate the

Instead, two of their councillors were

No further action was taken, and the
nuisance was not abated. I had two

him if there was any difference in Public

rural districts. The answer was in the
negative. I then asked him if it was
the duty of the Larne Rural Council to
have this nuisance abated. He said it

Finally, the tenants threatened to leave

forced to open legal proceedings in the

Here we have the case of a sanitary

One hundred years ago a certain brand
of stout was thought to have valuable
medicinal properties because it was made
from Thames water, which, of course,
contained a modicum of sewage. Is
medical science, as interpreted by the
Ministry of Home Affairs, a century
behind the times?
Worse still, we find, if we believe my
friend's story-and I see no reason to
disbelieve it-that the principal medical
officer of the Ministry is hindered in his
attempt to do his duty by some sinister
influence within the Ministry, and this
confirms a suspicion which has for a long
time been present in my mind, that the
medical officers in this Ministry, who have
always been capable and conscientious
men, are cribbed, cabined and confined
by those set in authority over them.
Are these not sufficient proofs that
health functions are completely alien to
the legitimate work of this Ministry, and
that in respect of these it has shown itself
to be apathetic, inept and inefficient, and
that the time has long passed when a
properly constituted Ministry of Health
should be formed?
I have heard two arguments, and two
only, against the formation of a Ministry
of Health. One of these is that there
are too many Ministries already, which
may well be the case, and may well be a
valid argument against the continuance
of one or more of the existing Ministries,
but which is not a valid argument against
the formation of a Ministry which is
regarded as a necessity in every other
part of the United Kingdom, and, indeed,
in any civilised community. And this
leads one to inquire if the duties performed by our latest creation could not
be adequately performed by the Ministry
of Home Affairs if the latter were
relieved of its work in connection with
medical and health services. To most
people the duties of the Ministry of
Public Security-and they are not very
onerous-would seem to be much more
nearly akin to the legitimate functions of
the Ministry of Home Affairs than are
those now performed by the latter in connection with medical services and public
health.
In England, with its population of over
40 million, four-fifths of whom are domiciled in crowded danger areas, there is no
separate Ministry of Public Security.
This is looked after by the Home Secretary as an addition to his normal duties,
so one would imagine that in Northern
Ireland, with a population of about one
and a quarter million, three-fourths of
whom live in safe areas, a separate
Ministry can hardly be considered
essential.
The other argument raises the question
of cost. We are told that we cannot
afford it; whilst on the contrary the fact
is, as I shall prove, that we cannot afford
to do without it. Our present health
services are regarded solely from the uneconomic view of the expenditure on them
instead of from the really economic view
of value for money expended. They are
cheap, I grant you; yes, cheap and
nasty, but far too dear if regarded from
either an economic or humanitarian viewpoint; and I ask you to take a comprehensive survey of the relative cost of a
properly organised and administered
system as contrasted with our present
wasteful and inefficient absence of system.
On one side of the scale place the esti
mated cost of the system I advocate, and
let your estimate err on the side of
liberality, for parsimony here is criminal.
On the other side place the following
items-the cost of all medical and health
services as at present administered, much
of this simply wasted; the economic

Which side of the scale now weighs
heaviest? If I were given to extravagant language I might be tempted to say
that our Ulster Government has out-
Heroded Herod in this matter of the
slaughter of the innocents. But whilst
Herod slew his victims deliberately and
presumably in a speedy and merciful
manner, confined the energies of his
executioners to a limited class, and did
not, so far as history relates, leave any
of his victims to survive to drag out a
maimed and miserable existence, our
Government, acting the part of the
Pharisee of old, passed by on the other
side, and with apparently indifferent
eyes, for more than 20 years, watched
the thousands of deaths and disablements
caused by preventable disease, ignoring
the recommendations of the Irish Public
Health Council and those of its own
Commissioners, which, had they been put
into effect, would have preserved for the
State a very large proportion of these
victims of apathy, inefficiency and ineptitude, victims who should to-day be
healthy and valuable citizens.
If you
calculate the mere money value to the
State of these, I confidently assert that
the total sum would far exceed the cost
of establishing a Ministry of Health and
co-ordinating and re-organising the
medical and health services.
This is a purely utilitarian point of
view, but there is another which should
be taken into account, the Christian point
of view, and if we refuse to do so, then I
say that our vaunted Christianity is no
better than a hollow sham and an
organised hypocrisy, and I would urge
each Member of this House to examine
his conscience and ask himself the
question, "Am I my brother's keeper?"
If the answer is in the affirmative he must

In justice to my constituents and myself, I must make my position clear. I
am a supporter of the Government
because, although it has made mistakes.
-and what Government or what man is

Britain. I cannot see any alternative
Government which would not weaken and

consider to be of paramount importance
to Ulster and to the Empire. But I reserve my right to criticise when criticism
seems necessary, to play in fact the thankless part of candid friend, and I will
continue in season and out of season, in

Mr. BROWN: I rise with great pleasure to second the Motion, and I consider
it a very great honour indeed to be

The position has been that for 21 years

and startling facts advanced by the Member for the University to-day, and in the
speech he made in this House in October
last, are such that no Government could
possibly ignore them, or they would do

the ground covered by the eminent doctor
who has moved this Motion, but I want
to emphasise the fact that at present this
question of public health is not the concern of any one Ministry, but of several
Ministries.
The position is that there is a department of the Ministry of Home Affairs
which controls the public health services,
the Ministry of Labour is charged with
the administration of the medical benefit
Acts, and the Ministry of Education
looks after the health of the school
children. Unlike England, we have no
Ministry of Health, or Board of Health.
as they have in Scotland and Wales.
This matter of public health actually
extends more or less into all the Ministries. Therefore, it is absolutely essential
that we should have a Ministry of Health
set up in Northern Ireland, and set up
at once. If I wanted a text for my speech
I could not find a better one than the
speech of the Prime Minister in Belfast
last night. He told a meeting that infantile mortality in Northern Ireland was
far higher than it should be, and that it
was a disgrace. Are we going to continue with this disgrace, or are we not?
That is the question we have got to
decide to-day.

Take, again, the position of midwives.
Midwives are paid at a very low rate,
and, like dispensary doctors, it has now
become impossible to get them. One of
our greatest exports is medical men. It
is a pity that the best medical brains have

When a nurse or a midwife is particularly

there has been no midwife for the last two

the board of guardians will not pay a

course they cannot get anyone to accept
the position. The position of a midwife
in a country town, like Portadown, is

makes essential the formation of some
authority. The death rate among confined women is too high. They will not
leave their own homes, and we cannot

could go to, but they should and must

I will mention one other very important
matter with which I come in contact in
the course of my own work. It concerns
the Ministry of Labour. A working man
goes sick. Very often he cannot afford
to get a certificate and go on to the sick
list, and what is happening is this. He
gets unemployment benefit, and by doing
so he has about £2 10s 0d coming into
his house, and he is able to exist on that
quite well. On the other hand if he is
honest, goes sick, and gets a medical
certificate he receives from 15s to 18s a
week, and it is impossible for a working
man to keep himself and his family and
pay his rent on 15s or 18s a week.
My contention is that if a working
man goes sick it is the duty of the community to get that man back to his work
as soon as possible, because he is needed.
There should be some supplementary
grant, or some nourishment or other
necessities, given to that unfortunate.

Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Lord Glentoran): This Bill of which I
am moving the Second Reading is called
the Scutch Mills and Flax Bill, and I
think perhaps I ought to say a word or
two to the House about it before going
into details. It is a Bill arising out of
the war.
It is one of those Bills which
we have had to bring in to increase the
efficiency of our flax production and linen
for aeroplane cloth and those other valuable assets which come from flax, and
which are so much used in our military
effort at the present time. The necessity
for this Bill arises from the following
circumstances. Previous to the war I
regret to say the acreage of flax in this
country had fallen to somewhere about
20,000 acres. The result of that was
that the scutch mills all over the country
had fallen into disuse. Then as the
House is aware we made a great effort
and we raised our production of flax to
90,000 acres and then, after a very bad
year, last year we got it up to somewhere
about 73,000 or 74,000 acres. The result
of this great increase in acreage is that
farmers who had grown and retted this
flax found that they had in their haggards
and stackyards a lot they simply could
not get scutched.
of Supply and the Treasury in conjunction with my Ministry and the Farmers'
Union that something would have to be
done to assist these men to put their mills
into order. The result is this Measure,
which I hope, will have a satisfactory
effect. But apart altogether from the
actual expense of building these mills
there is another very grave risk which
you know and most of the House know,
because we are very much connected with
our national industry, the linen industry.
Flax is very inflammable, probably one
of the most inflammable products we
have. There have been throughout the
country constant fires, and the situation
got so bad that eventually it became
impossible to get flax insured.
Then the very vital question arose as to
how these scutch mills could be got into
order and made efficient for scutching. I
need not explain at any length to the
House that the cost-the war cost-to
scutch mill owners, who are not big men,
would have been almost impossible. And,
therefore, it was decided by the Ministry
This Bill is to help to insure these
stacks. I think that will be a tremendous encouragement to the flax growers,
and will give great confidence to these
gentlemen who own scutch mills. That
is the real essence of the Bill and the
reason for it. Briefly, the Bill contemplates the setting up of two funds. (1)
The Scutch Mills Fund; and every person
operating a scutch mill, unless he is
already fully insured, shall pay to the
Ministry by way of contribution to this
fund certain sums calculated on output.
These sums will be calculated on the
amount which may reasonably be expected
to meet all claims. When such scutch
mill is destroyed or damaged by fire, the
owner shall be entitled to be paid out of
the fund, by way of compensation, such
amount not exceeding 50 per cent. of the
cost of reinstatement of the mill as the
Ministry may determine.
The second fund is the Flax Fund, and
similarly every person on whose behalf
flax straw is scutched on commission at
a scutch mill or flax factory shall pay to
the Ministry such sums as may be prescribed and which will be based on the
amount which the Ministry may expect
to have to meet, by reason of such
flax being destroyed by fire, in which case
the owner of such flax will be paid out of
the fund, such amount calculated by
reference to the acreage from which the
flax was produced as may be determined.

as may from time to time be required.
It will be noted that the contributions
by the owners of the scutch mills or the
flax are compulsory, and consequently
provision is made in the Bill for the recovery of any sums which a person has
failed to pay.
The Bill also makes provision as to the
storage of flax and precautions against
fire, and this part of the Bill applies both
to scutch mills and flax factories. The
regulations which the Ministry may make
under the Bill shall be laid before each
House of Parliament, which can resolve
that such regulations shall be annulled.
It also makes provision for those cases
where the damage is caused by malicious
injury, and the owner recovers compensation under the Malicious Injury Code.
In such a case, as the owner will have
recovered from the rates the amount of
his loss, the Bill makes provision for him
to repay to the Ministry any sum which
has been paid to him under the Bill.
All these conditions have been settled
as between the Ministry of Supply, the
Ministry of Finance and my Ministry,

The hon. Member for Antrim said that

would have to pay by way of insurance
levy, and how much they would get in

flax fund is intended to be self-supporting, that is to say, the levies in any one
year will be assessed at a rate which is
found to cover the estimated or guessed
damage which will occur in that year, so
that it is not possible to say definitely
what the levies will be. It will depend
to a very large extent on the number of
fires in the previous year. We do not
wish to have in any one year either a big
balance or a big deficit in the fund, and
consequently the rates will be struck at
such an amount as will cover the damage
which may reasonably be expected. I

who have not contributed to the fund.
The fund is meant to be self-supporting
and, therefore, we cannot ask for premiums now to pay for damage which is
already done.

Order for Second Reading read.
Lord GLENTORAN: The Bill, of
which I am moving the Second Reading,
arises from the great destruction caused
throughout the country by foxes. The
sudden influx of foxes into our country is
phenomenal. Up to eight, nine or 10
years ago such a thing as a fox was never
seen in the counties of Down or Antrim,
or in fact in any of the other counties of
Northern Ireland. I have been looking
up the files of the Down Hunt and of a
very ancient hunt, which had its centre
at Doagh in County Antrim, and I could
not find a single instance of a fox ever
having been seen or hunted; yet, for some
extraordinary reason, within the past few
years there has been an influx of foxes,
and they have increased to an alarming
extent.
Another very interesting feature about
this matter is that in England, Scotland
and Wales, where foxes have always been
prevalent, game, ducks and other fowl
have been able to avoid them. England
is swarming with foxes, yet they do not
do much damage, but in this country
where in the past they were unknown they
are most destructive. They clear all the
game off mountains, and they do great
destruction amongst turkeys. I was
speaking to a man who had lost all his
turkeys in this way. These vermin do
endless destruction. They are getting
worse because in the hilly country last
year I am afraid it will be worse this
That
season-they began to eat lambs.
is a very serious matter from the point
of food production.
During the past two or three years
steps have been taken privately to deal
with this menace. We had a professional
fox catcher in North Antrim and each
year he killed anything from 100 to 150
Agriculture Bill—

Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Lord Glentoran]
during the early part of the season. This
man was called up and is now with his
unit. In Tyrone and Derry so much per
head was offered for foxes, and a great
number were destroyed in this way. The
funds have now dried up and we have
been approached by the Farmers' Union
and other bodies to see if something can
not be done to deal with the menace. This
matter was dealt with in the ordinary
way through county funds. A small
agricultural educational grant was given
to the counties and this money was used
for the purpose, but that money is now
required for educational purposes.
After much negotiation with representatives of the various counties and
my right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Finance, we came to the conclusion that
the destruction of foxes was really a
national affair and that it was up to us
to assist the county councils. That being
so we brought in this Bill, the chief
features of which are as follows:
Discretionary power is granted to each
county council to levy an annual rate not
exceeding d in the £ upon occupiers in
the rural areas of the county, the produce
of which would be devoted entirely to
meeting one half the expenses of operating the scheme in the county for the
destruction of vermin. The scheme at
the outset will be confined to foxes. The
remaining one half of the expenses will
be a charge on Government funds. Thus
to every £ raised locally another £ will
be added from the Exchequer. Agricultural land will continue to be derated in accordance with the provisions
of the Local Government (Rating and
Finance) Act (Northern Ireland), 1929.
The schemes will be operated by the
County Committees of Agriculture and
will be subject to the approval of the
Ministry of Agriculture.
regarded as equitable. Any sum raised
from the rates for the purposes of a destruction scheme would, of course, not
rank for a derating grant.
Representatives of county councils have
agreed to the expenditure on schemes
being met on a 50-50 principle as between
local authorities and the central Government. It is felt that the ordinary taxpayer is interested in the preservation of
food from the ravages of foxes, even
though the destruction of these pests is
primarily the concern of the food producer. For this reason a grant from the
Exchequer of a sum equal to one half
the expenditure on destruction schemes is
That is really what this Bill amounts
to. Again, I must apologise to my hon.
Friends on both sides of the House for
this Bill being brought in so late. The
reason it has been brought in so late is
that it was the subject of prolonged
negotiations. Everyone who is interested
in this matter is aware that all the
counties, with the exception of one,
agreed to come into the regional scheme,
and owing to this difficulty we could not
bring the Bill in any sooner. That being
so, I leave myself in the hands of the
House in this matter.
It is well known that December,
January, February and March are the
four months of the year in which foxes
breed, and they are the only months
when these vermin are really vulnerable.
At that period you can trace them to the
holes or crevices where their young are,
and they can then be destroyed. Once
the month of March is out, looking for
a fox is like looking for a needle in a
bundle of straw. As we are now in the
month of December, I am very anxious
to get this Bill through the House.
Even now, with the guarantee that this
House will give, it is hoped that the
scheme for the killing of foxes will be
put into operation immediately, thus
putting an end to the great loss and
destruction of food. I beg to move.

I read a medical work by a Dr. Moore,

Nothing spreads plague so much as rats;

THE MINISTER OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Sir Dawson Bates): I can
safely say that in this House we are all
actuated with one desire, that is to make
the health services better than they are,
but there are different methods of carrying that out. The mover of the Resolution has approached the matter, if I may
say so, from the wrong end. The main
basis of his argument is that setting up a
new ministry automatically accomplishes
a vast improvement in the public health
services, and that attitude seems to have
been adopted without any examination
and led to the conclusion that the central
administration is defective.
Having listened to the arguments put
forward by the mover of the amendment,
I am prepared to accept it because I believe it indicates the proper course to take
and the one which will have the best
results. When I say that, I would like
to thank the hon. Member for the
remarks he made regarding the efforts of
the Government to improve the health
services. One has only to look back over
the time since this Government was
formed to realise the enormous difficulties
they have had to contend with. First of
all, he mentioned the question of law and
order. That in itself involved the Government in an enormous amount of
money which might have been spent on
much better objects. Apart altogether
from that, on every conceivable opportunity I have had friendly fights with
the Ministry of Finance. I received any
amount of sympathy, but the whole difficulty was finance.
Then, again, it is suggested that the
local authorities have not pulled their full
weight. All I know is that during the
twenty years I have been in office I have
seen an enormous improvement in the

share of responsibility. The old saying

ago
set up a technical committee to deal with

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Scutch Mills and Flax (Fire Insurance)
[Money].
Considered in Committee under Standing Order No. 65.
[Sir ROBERT LYNN in the Chair].
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That, for the purposes of any Act of
the present Session 'to provide for the
establishment and maintenance of funds
for the payment of compensation in
certain cases to the owners of scutch mills
and to the owners of flax, where the mills
or flax are destroyed or damaged by fire;
for the proper storage of flax and the
taking of precautions against fire at scutch
mills and flax factories; and for purposes
connected with the said matters,' it is
expedient to authorise the Ministry of
Finance at any time to advance out of the
Consolidated Fund to the Scutch Mills
Fund or the Flax Fund, established under
such Act, such sums as may from time to
time be required to meet any temporary
3209 Scutch Mills and Flax Bill-

17 DECEMBER 1942
Third Reading
deficiency in either of the said funds, and
to provide for the repayment to the
Exchequer out of moneys subsequently
standing to the credit of the Scutch Mills
Fund or the Flax Fund, as the case may
be, any sums so advanced, together with
such interest thereon, if any, as may be
determined by the Ministry of Finance."
-(Governor's Recommendation signified
-Sir Basil Brooke.)
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY
(Major Sinclair): This resolution is
largely self-explanatory, but I think it
well to emphasise that ultimately this
insurance scheme will impose no burden
on the Exchequer. As has already been
explained on the Second Reading of the
Bill, the funds to be established will be
fed from levies raised from the benefiting
parties, but, as it is probable that claims
will be made before these funds
adequate to meet them, it is necessary to
make interim provision from some source,
and the Consolidated Fund is regarded as
the appropriate medium for this purpose.
are
My attention has been drawn to the
fact that a statement by my hon. Friend,
the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of Agriculture, in his reply on the
Second Reading yesterday, is open to the
interpretation that in the event of there
being continuing deficits in these funds
the Ministry of Finance would come to
the rescue. I wish to make it quite clear
that this resolution gives my Ministry
no other power than to make temporary
advances from the Consolidated Fund.
Such advances are to be repaid at the
earliest possible date from moneys subsequently standing to the credit of the
funds, and I can assure hon. Members
that it is not the intention that these
funds should be anything other than selfsupporting. In the long run payments
from the funds will not exceed the
amounts paid into the funds by way of
the levies. I beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.
Resolution reported, and agreed to.

Rev. ROBERT MOORE: I raised the
point on the Second Reading that an
amendment should be moved to permit
of certain matters being referred for the
advice and counsel of the Ulster Farmers'
Union. I brought the matter before the
representatives of the flax growers this
morning and those representatives are
prepared to accept the undertaking given
yesterday by the Parliamentary Secretary, and therefore I do not move the
amendment. I do not know whether I
am strictly in order, but some Members
seemed in some little doubt or under
some misapprehension as to the working
of the Bill as it stands as to the scheme
that will be brought in for the insurance
of the flax destroyed or that may be destroyed at scutch mills.
Hon. Members will notice that there is
not any provision in the Bill to cover
administrative costs, and what I want to
point out if I am in order is that the
Ministry of Agriculture and the
growers hope that there will not be any
administrative costs and that the scheme
will be pretty well automatic. Of course,
we are hoping that the cases of fire in
scutch mills will be few and that cases of
compensation which have to be paid will
be very few.
When I raised the point yesterday
about the Farmers' Union being taken
into consultation on certain matters
under the scheme I was not doing so just
for the sake of getting the Farmers'
Union into the limelight or anything of
that kind; but as I pointed out yesterday
the fund is to be subscribed entirely by
the flax growers and there was a case put
up that the growers, therefore, should
have something to say in the disbursing

of the fund. If we had insisted on that

inspectors, certain officials, and all the

The Ministry of Agriculture as things
stand has got all the information necessary for the administration of the scheme
and while the war lasts that information
is secret. It could not be disclosed to
any staff that the growers might have set
up to administer the scheme on their own
behalf. It would have meant duplication
and overlapping and various difficulties of
that kind. By agreement with the
farmers and the flax growers' representatives this arrangement has been come to
as the most economic and most expeditous. At the same time we are
giving way on the democratic principle
that those who pay the piper have some
right to call the tune and we hope the
Ministry will consult the representatives
of the growers both as to the amount of
the levy that may be required from time
to time and the amount of compensation
that will be available.
not
There is one other point to which I
might draw the attention of the House.
As the Bill stands there is not any limit
to the time of its application or any limit
to its duration, but in practice, it seems
to me that the arrangements envisaged in
this Bill will automatically end when the
Ministry of Supply ceases to take in any
more flax. Automatic arrangements
under the scheme can only operate so
long as the Ministry of Supply is taking
over all flax on a graded basis, and this
deduction can be made when the grower
is paid for his flax. When we lapse into
pre-war conditions again other arrangements for administration of the scheme
will require to be made. I merely point
out that to all intents and purposes this
is purely an emergency measure.; it is a
wartime scheme. I beg to support the
Third Reading.

Motion made, and Question proposed,

(Sir Norman Stronge.)
Mr. BROWN: I wish to raise a matter
relating to public health arising out of
the administration of the Ministry of
Home Affairs. We have heard much about
Adjournment
Chief Medical Officer

17 DECEMBER 1942
public health during the last week and
again to-day in connection with Bills not
directly concerned with the Ministry of
Home Affairs. I read with considerable
alarm in the paper some time ago that when
Dr. McCloy, chief medical officer of health
of the Ministry of Home Affairs, resigned,
it had been decided not to fill that vital
position, and that a doctor in the Ministry
of Labour was to be asked to carry on. I
would like a statement from the Minister
on that very important matter, because
in my humble opinion, for what it is
worth it is not worth very much
perhaps it is a mistake to leave a position of that importance vacant at the
present time.
We have heard much this week of the
great qualifications in public health of
Dr. Thomas Carnwath. Did the Ministry
consider whether it would be possible to
secure the services of Dr. Carnwath in
even a temporary capacity? If they could
do so I think it would be a good move
from the point of view of the public.
health and welfare generally. I would
like some statement as to the intentions
of the Ministry in this matter. It may
be that they wish to have first the report
of a Committee to be appointed by this
House. That Committee is to be given
six months in which to report, but, in
the meantime, I think it is wrong that
we should leave that important office
vacant for at least six months. In the
conditions under which we are living it is
more important than ever before that the
utmost possible attention and the greatest
possible amount of time should be given
to the question of the public health.
I do not want to create a job. Dr.
Carnwath is no friend or relative of mine.
I never met the man in my life. I have
read the highest testimonials to him, and
when I read the wonderful report he presented on public health in the city of
Belfast I said, "There is a man whose
services should be availed of in the public
life of Northern Ireland in some capacity
in connection with public health." I was
profoundly impressed. I am not reflecting on the Minister or his Department. I
merely want to know what is the attitude
of the right hon. Gentleman in this
matter. I do not agree with the proposal
to leave this tremendously important
office of chief medical officer of the
Ministry of Home Affairs vacant. I
suggest that a doctor from another
Ministry cannot possibly, even for six
months, satisfactorily discharge the duties
connected with both Ministries. Therefore I ask the Minister of Home Affairs
to make a statement as to his intentions.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Lowry): It would appear
that this is not the burning question that
the hon. Member for South Down would
have one believe. However, in order that
he at least may be reassured, I would say
that the gentleman who has been Chief
Medical Officer for the Ministry of
Labour has been asked to carry on in a
temporary capacity, and by reason of the
happy decline in his duties, his Ministry
are satisfied that he can do the work properly and efficiently. He is a gentleman
of the highest distinction in his own
profession. He has had many years'
administrative experience. If the hon.
Member for South Down will only reflect
on one or two matters, he will see that,
first of all, to fill this important position
is not practicable and, second, it is quite
obvious there will have to be reorganisation. It would most improper for this
Ministry to anticipate any advice they
may get on a subsequent occasion. The
hon. Member may set his mind at rest.
The health services will not be neglected.
We are satisfied they can be carried on
efficiently. The other suggestion which
he made is quite unnecessary. We are
quite satisfied that the present doctor is
proficient, both professionally and
administratively.

SALES OF GRASS-SEED.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: In asking
this question, I may point out that the
date in the body of the question is wrong.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Lord Glentoran): I am aware that
grass-seed has not been moving as freely
as is desirable at this season of the year,
but I have no reason to believe that
merchants have ceased buying. The
delay in clearing farmers' stocks partly
arises through the difficulties incidental to
bringing into operation the new scheme.
relating to fixed prices, but owing to the
much larger crop this year, storage is presenting a greater problem than usual.
My Ministry has been able to assist
merchants in obtaining supplies of bags.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Lord Glentoran]
While I am not in a position to give the
undertaking suggested by the hon. and
gallant Member, I am confident that,
with the exercise of good-will and
patience by all concerned, the present
difficulties will be overcome, and that a
market will be provided for all seed still
remaining in the hands of growers and
which is not below the standard of the
lowest quality for which a price has been
fixed.

of that reply if any cases are brought to

certainly do what I can to help. The

there is a large surplus of seed this year

is brought to my notice I will do what I
can to facilitate the farmers.

that the surplus is due to the request of

[Mr. John Bailey]
any statement regarding the potato acreage payment for 1943.
I know it is not necessary to urge the
House to pass this Motion, because I
believe that every Irishman worthy of
the name must agree with it. We like
the United States soldiers and personnel
amongst us first, because they are our
Allies, and second, because to a certain

They have made a wonderful impression

know what they are doing now for our
children both here and in Great Britain.
Lord GLENTORAN: Yes, Sir. My
Ministry has just completed negotiations
with the Ministry of Food, and I am
now in a position to state that a payment
at the rate of £10 per acre will be made
in respect of lands under potatoes in
1943. The terms and conditions have
not yet been finally settled, but I do not
think there will be any appreciable departure from the 1942 Scheme under
which the owner of the potatoes at 1st
June is entitled to the payment, provided he farms, or is in possession of,
one statute acre or more of agricultural
land, and has not less than one rood
under potatoes. As was the case last
year, the acreage payment will be regarded as a part of the grower's return
for his crop, and accordingly the tonnage
prices for the 1943 crop will take account
of this payment. Full details of the
Scheme will be issued by my Ministry at
a later date.
Mr. MINFORD: Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware that the £10 per acre
going as bonus to the potato growers is
not sufficient according to the price they
are receiving in the market, and would
the Minister ask the Ministry of Food
to raise the price or raise the bonus in
order to give the farmers an economic
return for their labour?
Lord GLENTORAN: These and other
matters will all be raised by the Prices
Committee in London.

The point is that the Government are

The people are engaged in all kinds

Mr. NIXON: I have pleasure in
moving the Motion standing in my name.
It is in my opinion the most important
Motion that ever came before the House.
It reads:
That in the opinion of this House
the Government have failed to take all
possible and adequate measures to provide accommodation for people whose
houses were destroyed or damaged by
enemy action, and that immediate
action in this respect should now be
taken.
The persons responsible for the supreme
superintendence of repairs are certainly
neglecting their duty, because there are
numbers of houses, even at the present
time, in which glass has not been put. I
was looking at them in Malvern Street the
other day, and also in other streets. I know
definitely from my own personal knowledge
and experience that there is no excuse for
that, good, bad, or indifferent.
I got
glass in thirty-nine houses myself, so I
know what I am talking about. It was a
bit difficult at first in some cases, but there
is nothing to prevent glass being put into
every house in the city of Belfast that
suffered from enemy action.
The House will observe that the Motion
is comparatively narrow and is confined
entirely to householders who have suffered
through enemy action. I can conceive
nothing worse than a person having his
house brought down over his head by a
bomb and then being left without a house
through the winter. Recollect that this
is the second winter those people have to
face without houses. They might be
divided into two classes. There are the
people whose houses could have been made
habitable, but were not made habitable.
This is not to be taken as an attack on
what is known as the War Damage Commission. So far as I know, the function
of the War Damage Commission consists
of inspecting repairs through their architects which is quite proper-examining
accounts for repairs, and, if the accounts
are in order, paying them. Up to the
moment I have discovered no justifiable
complaint against
against the War Damage
Commission.
Furthermore, again in fairness to the
War Damage Commission, there is
nothing to prevent the owners, agents,
contractors, the Corporation, or whoever
undertook the work from being paid for
it. When accounts are properly submitted there is no delay in payment. I
saw the War Damage Commission cutting
down an account, and they were right.
There are numbers of people suffering in
the way I have indicated and in other
ways, and it does not seem to be anyone's
particular business to see they are looked
after. There are other repairs that could
have been carried out which are not
carried out.
In regard to the repair of these houses
there was a ramp, and a bad one. There
have been a few prosecutions of contractors for putting in wages they were not
paying, and I brought evidence of the fact
to this House and it resulted in a prosecution. There has been no general detection.
I saw men on a house going off the job
at 2 p.m., and I brought the matter to
the notice of the Financial Secretary of
the Ministry of Finance. The Financial
Secretary made inquiries and admitted to
me that the men did go off at 2 p.m., and
the excuse was that they were going to get
their
I wonder how many men in
pay.
this House would let men away from their
work at 2 p.m. to get their pay. On the
other hand, I have had complaints from
householders who thought they would
never get them out.
I represent a working-class constituency,
and where I see idleness I am not afraid
or ashamed to get up in this House and
expose it. Attempts were made at one
time to intimidate me from doing that,
but I did it. I found that it pleased the
people immensely to expose what was going

Question proposed.
Mr. THOMPSON: I desire to move
an amendment to the motion that has
been proposed. The amendment I propose is:-
Leave out all the words after "Government" and insert "should continue to
take all practical measures to provide
accommodation for people whose houses
were destroyed or damaged by enemy
action."
My reason for proposing this amendment is that I do not agree with
the words of the resolution, which
states that the "Government have
failed to take all possible and adequate
measures. I entirely disagree with that
and I am going in a few brief words to
prove to the House that that is absolutely
contrary to fact. What are the facts?

How has this matter been dealt with?
It is dealt with in this way. A representative of the Belfast Corporation, a
representative of the War Damage Committee, and a representative of the Government investigate the whole subject of
blitzed houses in Belfast. I want to
congratulate the Belfast Corporation on
the steps they have already taken to deal
with this matter in conjunction with the
other parties I have already mentioned.
I am going to give the House some
figures of a startling nature, and they
are these. In Belfast 3,200 houses were
completely demolished as a result of air
raids. In addition, over 53,000 dwelling
houses were damaged and of this number
3,962 were badly damaged. What has
happened up to the present time? The
Belfast Corporation carried out repairs
to approximately 41,000 houses, including 2,438 badly damaged. If that is not
a satisfactory record I do not know what
is. I do not believe there is a single, city
in England or any other part could boast
of a better record than the Government
and Belfast Corporation are able to show.
It has been argued, and I quite agree,
that there is still something to be done,
but the Government are perfectly alive
to the situation.
There is one suggestion, however, I
would make to the Minister of Home
Affairs. There are quite a number of
houses in Belfast at the present time that
are being put for sale and I suggest that
the matter might be, investigated. Perhaps some of these houses might be
utilised in order to accommodate many
people who are in need of houses at the
present time. I understand that Birmingham and some other cities across the
water are now taking steps to try to
find ways and means whereby they may
be able during wartime to ease the housing accommodation. Any person who
thinks about the matter at all is perfectly well aware that one of the greatest
difficulties is the question of timber. I
cannot see. how we can face up to the
question of building houses if we have not
the timber to build them. It is folly for
any person to talk about building houses
if there is no timber available. We all
remember what happened after the last
war when a number of houses were
erected with uuseasoned timber. The
result was lamentable. I hope, we will
never be forced to build houses in Nor-

Oral Answer to Question.
SALES OF GRASS SEED.
Mr. JOHN BAILEY (by Private
Notice) asked the Minister of Agriculture whether, in view of the increasing
difficulties farmers in Northern Ireland
are experiencing selling their grass-seed,
and the fact that the seed, if it continues
to be stemmed back on the farm, may
become valueless for sowing purposes, he
is yet in a position to add anything to
the reply he gave to the hon. and gallant
Member for East Down on this subject.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Lord Glentoran): As the hon. Member
is aware, in order to protect farmers
producing grass-seed an Order has been
issued fixing statutory prices for grass
seed purchased from farmers. These
prices, I am happy to think, met with
general satisfaction.
At the same time, statutory prices
have been fixed for the sale by the
machiners of the cleaned grass-seed,
giving them a generous margin of 20s a
cwt. The crop is a heavy one, and it is
probable that there will be at the end of
the season a surplus beyond the normal.
The farmers have answered well and truly
the call of the Government for an increased production of grass seed, and I
am most anxious that the crop should be
purchased by the trade and not left on
the farmers' hands. After negotiation.
with the Ministry of Agriculture and
Fisheries and the British Treasury, I
have offered the grass-seed machiners the
following terms:-
periods last year. Such advances cover
the purchase price paid to the farmer
and the trade margin of 20s per cwt.
The advances will be free of all interest
and will only be repaid to the Government when the surplus seed is sold.
a
To finance at their full value on
monthly basis all surpluses carried by
the trade above the amount of stocks
they carried in the corresponding monthly
Secondly, on July 1st, 1943, when the
grass-seed season closes, for the surplus
above normal which is then carried
forward, and on which the full advance
will have been made by the Government,
further Government assistance will be
given in the form of an allowance of 10s
per ton per month to cover storage, wastage, etc., as well as a rebate of 3s per
cwt. on the original advance by the
Government to cover any loss of germination by the time the seed is sold by the
trade.
I have further been authorised to give
an undertaking that the wholesale prices
when fixed next year will not be less than
those now prevailing and thus the trade
cannot be carrying forward stocks on a
falling market. I realise that if a substantial surplus has to be carried forward from July, 1943, with the 1943 crop
shortly thereafter coming into the market,
further steps may have to be taken to
ensure the sale of the 1942 crop surplus.
But as the finance for this abnormal 1942
surplus will have been found by the
Government, I had hoped it would have
been clear to our grass-seed machiners
that they were taking no undue risk. It
is, as the hon. Member will readily
realise, impossible to formulate definite
proposals for dealing with this aspect of
the problem until later when its magnitude or otherwise can be measured and
not guessed at as at present.
As the hon. Member will see, the proposals have been devised with the object
of permitting the trade in increasing
volume to flow through its normal
channels.
I am sorry to have to add that our
grass-seed machiners have intimated that
they are not prepared to accept these
proposals which are the joint effort of the
three Agricultural Departments put forward with Treasury approval unless, and
I am quoting their own words, "they are
guaranteed against loss of profit, that is
20s per cwt. on surplus carry over after
1st July, 1943."
In effect, this is asking the Government
to assume financial responsibility for the

operation of the trade. I regret that this
position should have arisen because I
consider the terms offered to the trade
most equitable, and I am exploring as
rapidly as possible and in consultation
with the English and Scottish Agricultural Departments what other means
are available for dealing with the matter.

Mr. MINFORD: Is the Minister of
Agriculture aware that farmers to-day are
holding very large stocks of grass-seed
and that those farmers are requiring cash?
What steps does he propose to take to
help the farmers out of this difficulty? Is
the Minister also aware that the farmers
have not suitable storage to ensure that
the seed will not lose its power of germination? This is a complicated situation,
and presents a very serious outlook to the
farmers and to the trade. It would be
wise for the Minister to call a conference
of the farmers, the cleaners and all others
concerned. The right hon. Gentleman
mentioned a figure of 10s a ton for storage. In my opinion that sum is insufficient because the grass-seed will lose
its power of germination no matter how
well it may be stored. I am not surprised
that the cleaners have refused the offer
made to them by the Minister.

The Greetings to British and American

REPLIES FROM COMMANDING
OFFICERS.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to report to
the House that I have received replies to
the message which the House instructed
me to send to the British Forces and
American Forces in Northern Ireland just
before the Recess.
The first reply is from General
Franklyn:
In reply to your letter of the 12th
January.
All branches of the Service in
Northern Ireland are very grateful for
the kind message of good wishes sent to
them by the House of Commons, which
has been communicated to all ranks and
which has been much appreciated by
them.
Yours sincerely,
(Sgd.) H. E. FRANKLYN.
The second one is from Major Frederick
J. Kraschel, A.D.C. to General Hartle:
General Hartle has asked that the
enclosed message from the American
Forces in his command be conveyed to
the Members of the North Ireland
House of Commons, together with his
personal thanks for their thoughfulness
in remembering the United States
Army in the United Kingdom at
Christmas time.
The General hopes very much to visit
Northern Ireland before too long a time
has passed, and at that time will surely
call on you.
In the meantime, he
wishes you a very happy New Year.
This is the message:
Then there was another letter from
Brigadier-General Leroy P. Collins, U.S.
Army, who was in temporary command of
the American Forces in Northern Ireland :
The Officers and Men of the United
States Army stationed in the United
Kingdom thank the House of Commons
of Northern Ireland for the gracious.
and heartening message conveyed to
them at Christmas time, and extend to
the Members and their constituents best
wishes for 1943, together with the hope
that it may see the fulfilment of our
common determination for a victorious
peace.
Your thoughtful letter of 23 December enclosing the message of Christmas
Greetings from the House of Commons.
has just reached me. A copy of this
message was delivered to my Public
Relations Officer, Major McInerney, on
Christmas Eve and was in turn published to all units of the United States
Army stationed in Northern Ireland.
On behalf of the officers and men of
the United States Army I desire to
express my appreciation to the House of
Commons for this message.
I shall look forward with pleasure to
the opportunity to have dinner at the
Speaker's House with you on my next
visit to Belfast. May I reciprocate
your kind message of good wishes for
the New Year.

Oral Answer to Question.
EIRE DOCTORS IN NORTHERN
IRELAND.
1. Dr. LYLE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether it is a fact that in
the case of many middle-aged doctors
who have joined H.M. Forces, younger
recently-qualified men, many of them
from Eire, are acquiring the practices of
these men; whether the doctors who have
come into Northern Ireland from the Free
Written Answers

Written Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Dr. Lyle]
State since 1st January, 1940, will along
with other workers be sent back there
immediately after the war, as promised
by the Prime Minister at a recent demonstration; and whether there are now
more doctors in County Tyrone than in
peace time.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
HOME AFFAIRS (Mr. Lowry): On
behalf of my right hon. Friend, I would
inform the hon. Member that I have no
official information as to the arrangements made by doctors who have joined
the Forces, as they do not come within the
purview of the Ministry, but are made
privately by the doctors concerned.
With regard to the second part of the
question, the Residence in Northern Ireland (Restriction) Order, 1942, made by
the Home Secretary under the Defence
Regulations, applies to all persons over
the age of 14 who were not resident in
Northern Ireland immediately before the
first day of January, 1940, and doctors
who come within the category of persons
to whom the Order applies will not receive
any preferential treatment at the termination of hostilities.
I have no information as to the number
of doctors now in County Tyrone.
Written Answers.
BLIND PENSIONS SCHEME.
Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he is satisfied with
the new Blind Pension Scheme adopted
by Armagh County Council; whether the
system of investigation is in keeping with
the terms of the 1938 Act; and whether
he can state the total number of blind
persons in County Armagh and the
amounts of supplementary allowances.
granted to them.
In reply to the second part of the
question, preliminary investigations are
carried out in County Armagh, as in most
other areas, by officials of the Blind
Welfare Association (an approved Society
for the Welfare of the Blind) who make
recommendations to the County Council.
The system in operation in no sense conflicts with the provisions of the Blind.
Persons Acts.
Mr. LOWRY: On behalf of my right
hon. Friend I would inform the hon.
Member that an improved scheme of
assistance for blind persons has recently
been adopted by the Armagh County
Council on the representations of my
Department. I am satisfied with the
scheme, which is similar to that which
has been operating satisfactorily in
County Down for some time past.
With regard to the last part of the
question, the total number of blind persons in County Armagh is not known,
but the number of claims received by the
County Council for supplementary allowances is 209. It is anticipated that the
amount to be paid in respect thereof for
the financial year ending March, 1943,
will be approximately £3,000.
STATE OF MILL ROW, ARMAGH
Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state what
action, if any, was taken by Armagh
Rural District Council as to the insanitary
state of Mill Row, Armagh; whether
his inspector's report was considered by
the Council, and, if so, what action has
been taken.
Mr. LOWRY: On behalf of my right
hon. Friend I would refer the hon.
Member to the reply given by the
Minister to a similar question on the 15th
October, 1940.
The conditions and circumstances outlined in that reply still obtain.
ARMAGH APPEALS TRIBUNAL.
Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Labour whether he will consider the
advisability of having the
the Appeals
Tribunal reinstated in Armagh in view of
the serious delay in having cases dealt with
by the Assistance Board in Portadown;
and whether he can state if Armagh Area
Office receives intimation from the Board
the
to sittings of
tribunal in
Portadown.
as
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): In view of the reduced numbers
of appeals arising in the Portadown,
Armagh and Lurgan areas, it was decided
for reasons of economy that all cases
should be heard at one centre in Porta-
Written Answers
Prorogation
16 FEBRUARY 1943
down, and it is not considered advisable
to make any alteration in the direction
indicated by the Hon. Member.
Under arrangements made recently the
tribunal sits normally in two out of every
three weeks, usually at intervals of about
ten days, and this, in view of the numbers
involved, seems the most practicable
arrangement.
If there were separate hearings at
Armagh, the result would be either that
greater delays would occur until sufficient
cases had arisen to justify holding a
tribunal, or that tribunals would be
sitting at excessive and indefensible cost
to hear a trifling number of appeals.
The Board's office at Armagh is informed of the arrangements for dealing
with its cases.
ALLEGED VICTIMISATION OF
WORKERS.
Mr. AGNEW asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state if certain
workers employed by Messrs. Henderson
& Eadie, Lisbellaw, were
ere victimised
because of their trade union activities;
whether five employees were dismissed by
the firm; and whether he will consider the
setting up of a Trade Board for workers
in the woollen industry in Northern
Ireland.
Mr. GORDON: In reply to the first
part of the hon. Member's question, I am
informed that four of the five men concerned left the employment of this firm
of their own accord and that the services
of the fifth man were dispensed with
because he refused to do work which he
had performed for a number of years.
With regard to the last part of the
question, I have already informed the
hon. Member that I have no evidence to
show that the conditions in the woollen
trade are such as to warrant the establishment of a Trade Board.
I need not assure the hon. Member,
however, that I am always open to receive
representations from any industry with a
view to the improvement, where necessary,
of arrangements for the settlement of
wages and conditions of employment.
The sitting was suspended until 2-30
p.m., and on resuming,
PROROGATION.
.-
A Message was delivered by the acting
Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod, as
follows:
be
I am commanded by the Senate to
inform this honourable House that the
Proclamation of His Grace the Governor
of Northern Ireland proroguing this present Session of Parliament is to
communicated in the Senate forthwith,
and, further, I am commanded to invite
this honourable House to attend in the
Senate in order to hear the said Proclamation read.
The House went, and, having returned,
Mr. SPEAKER (standing in the Clerk's
place at the Table): I have to report that
the House has this day attended in the
Senate, when the Proclamation proroguing this present Session of Parliament
was read by the Speaker of the Senate
as follows:-
:-
BY HIS GRACE THE GOVERNOR OF
NORTHERN IRELAND.
A PROCLAMATION.
For Proroguing the present Parliament
of Northern Ireland.
WHEREAS it is provided by section
eleven of the Government of Ireland Act,
1920, as modified by and in pursuance of
certain enactments amending the said
Act, that the Governor of Northern
Ireland shall, in His Majesty's name,
summon, prorogue and dissolve the
Parliament of Northern Ireland:
AND WHEREAS it is desirable that
this present Parliament of Northern
Ireland should be prorogued to the
twenty-third day of February, one
thousand nine hundred and forty-three:
NOW I, JAMES ALBERT EDWARD,
DUKE OF ABERCORN, KNIGHT OF
THE MOST NOBLE ORDER OF THE
GARTER, KNIGHT OF THE MOST
ILLUSTRIOUS ORDER OF SAINT
PATRICK, Governor of Northern Ireland, by this Proclamation do publish
and declare His Majesty's Pleasure that
the said Parliament be, as from the
reading of this Proclamation in the
Parliament of Northern Ireland, prorogued to Tuesday, the twenty-third day
of February, one thousand nine hundred
and forty-three.
Prorogation
Prorogation
HOUSE OF COMMONS
one
And I do hereby further declare His
Majesty's Royal Will and Pleasure to be
that the said Parliament shall on the said
twenty-third day
day of February,
thousand nine hundred and forty-three,
assemble and be holden at Stormont for
the despatch of divers urgent and important affairs, and the Senators and
Members of the House of Commons of
Northern Ireland are hereby required to
give their attendance accordingly.
Given this sixteenth day of February,
one thousand nine hundred and forty-three.
(Signed by his own hand),
ABERCORN:
GOD SAVE THE KING.
End of the Fifth Session (opened

Tuesday, 3rd February, 1942) of the
Fifth Parliament of Northern Ireland in
the Seventh year of the Reign of His
Majesty King George the Sixth.
