HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 20th January, 1942.
The House-which stood adjourned
from Tuesday, 30th December-met at
Two of the Clock, Mr. SPEAKER in the
Chair.
Message to the United States.
SECRETARY OF STATE'S REPLY.
Mr. SPEEAKER: I have to inform
the House that I have received two communications from Mr. Anthony Eden,
Foreign Secretary. The first one acknowledges the receipt of the message
which the House asked me to send for
transmission to the Government of the.
United States of America, and the second
one reads as follows:-
You will recall that in my letter of
the 4th January I told you that I had
forwarded to the United States
Ambassador the message from the
House of Commons of Northern Ireland to the Government of the United
States of America, which was enclosed
in your letter of 30th December, 1941.
The United States Ambassador has
now requested me to transmit to you
the following message from the Secretary of State :-
"My Government deeply appreciates
the message of solidarity which you
have kindly forwarded. The American
people will be encouraged in the effort
which they have now whole-heartedly
undertaken by the example of those
who have fought so valiantly as the
people. of Northern Ireland for twentyeight months against
enemy-Cordell Hull."
our common
Oral Answers to Questions.
GRIEVANCES OF THE BLIND.
1. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether, in view of his
recent statement in the House that the
remedying of some of the grievances of
the blind and the removal of certain
hardships they are suffering, would
require legislation, he can state if the
other grievances capable of being
remedied under existing legislation to
which the attention of his Ministry has
been called, have yet been remedied.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): With regard to the
first part of the question, it is expected
that, in view of the substantial financial
assistance to be given to local authorities
by the Government as recently announced,
county councils will adopt a more.
generous attitude towards the blind and
that the present grievances of blind persons will be alleviated to a very great
extent without the necessity of the introduction of legislation.
My department has always been willing to investigate specific instances of
hardship, and if further cases are
brought to my notice I shall be pleased
to take them up with the county councils
concerned.
With regard to the latter part of the
question, the county councils have, in response to my representations, agreed to
reinvestigate the cases of those applicants
whose circumstances were brought to my
attention by the deputation from the
North of Ireland League of the Blind.
Mr. BROWN: Is it the intention of
the Minister to place legislation before
the House dealing with the position of
the blind in cases where they cannot be.
helped under existing legislation?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have already
explained to the hon. Member that I
hope. the result of these grants being
given by the Government to county
councils will be a more generous spirit
on their part.
Mr. BROWN: If the county councils
do not act in the generous spirit indicated by the Minister will he see that
they carry out the necessary action in
the matter.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I cannot
imagine that the county councils are so
bad as the hon. Member indicates.
BANGOR BUS ACCOMMODATION.
2. Mr. THOMAS BAILIE asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he is
aware that there is a serious lack of bus
accommodation for those travelling from
Bangor on war work on routes not
covered by the railway; that this lack of
transport is likely seriously to affect the
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
20 JANUARY 1942
war effort, and whether he will take the
to ensure that the
necessary steps
Northern Ireland Road Transport Board
provide adequate travelling facilities for
these workers.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am aware
that certain difficulties exist regarding
the provision of transport facilities at
certain hours on routes from Bangor not
served by the railway. Those concerned
are in close contact with the Transport
Board and fully appreciate the difficulties.
which exist. Every effort will be made
to provide transport facilities, but the
hon. Member will appreciate that only a
limited amount of transport is available,
and I can assure him that it is being
utilised to the best advantage in the
interests of the war effort.
Mr. THOMAS BAILIE: Does the
right hon. Gentleman not consider that
priority in such cases should be given to
those engaged in war work.
Sir DAWSON BATES: That is what
we are doing, and if the hon. Member
would care to go into the matter with me
I will give him greater details than I can
across the floor of the House.
PROVISION OF TRAINING
CENTRES.
4. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can now state if any
progress has been achieved towards securing one or more war-work training centres
for the unemployed for Northern Ireland
similar to the forty or fifty such centres
in Great Britain, and whether any warwork factories have been secured for
Northern Ireland to absorb the bulk of
Northern Ireland's 27,000 unemployed.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): For reasons which I have explained from time to time in this House,
I have decided that, in the circumstances
with which we are faced, training can
best be provided in Technical Institutes
and in employers' premises, and my
Ministry is granting every possible
facility in these directions. I would add
that training for war work is proceeding
at a number of Technical Schools in
Northern Ireland, and up to the present
the number of persons trained at these
schools is considerably in excess of the
number of suitable local vacancies notified
to my department.
As regards the second part of the question, which relates more particularly to
the jurisdiction of my right hon. Friend,
the Minister of Commerce, I would point
out that there has been a steady expansion
of war work in this area; a fact which is
borne out by the reduction in the number
of persons registering for employment of
41,478 during the year ended December
last.
Mr. BROWN: Does the Minister share
the hope recently expressed by the Minister of Commerce that all these 27,000
unemployed will be absorbed by the
spring?
Mr. GORDON: The hon. Gentleman
can rest assured that we will make every
effort to get as many absorbed as possible.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
can the right hon. Gentleman state to the
House the percentage number of finished
trainees that found employment at home,
and whether it is a fact that the large
reduction in the live register of unemployed is due to the new trade or calling
which the right hon. Gentleman has taken
upon himself, known as the exploiting of
human beings.
Mr. GORDON: The hon. Gentleman
is labouring under a great misapprehension. There is a great deal of work going
on all over the country which has absorbed
thousands of men. But I admit that I
have sent a number of skilled and unskilled men over to the other side of the
water to work on munitions of war. I
propose to continue to do that.
Mr. BEATTIE: Does the right hon.
Gentleman say it is the policy of the
Government to pursue a course whereby
45,000 women, girls and men are driven
from their homes? Is that the policy of
the present Government?
Mr. GORDON: I do not know that
45,000 have been driven from their homes.
Work has been offered on the other side of
the water to a number of men and women
who were unemployed. I have taken the
precaution to visit certain centres on the
other side to see whether the conditions
were good, whether the environment was
good, and whether the wages paid to those
I have sent across were such as would
maintain them decently and comfortably.
I was so perfectly satisfied that I came
back a few weeks ago with the full determination that we in Northern Ireland
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Gordon]
would play our part in providing manpower to maintain the output of production necessary to maintain our war effort.
Mr. WARNOCK: May I ask the
Minister whether he considers it is playing our part in providing manpower to
send our people, who are not liable to
military service, to take the jobs in
England of men who have been called up
under the Military Service Act?
Mr. SPEAKER: May I point out that
questions are not to elucidate opinions,
but are put with the object of getting facts
from the Minister. We are proceeding
too far in the direction of debate on this
whole question.
FLAX GROWING AND PRICES.
5. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state if that
part of the Resolution regarding flax prices.
and grading adopted by the House on 21st
October, 1941, which called for the continuance of the strongest possible representations by the Government to the Ministry
of Supply to secure a more satisfactory
method of grading flax, has been implemented; and if so, whether he can state
the precise details of how a more satisfactory method of grading flax has been
or will be brought about.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Lord Glentoran): I cannot at this stage
add anything to my replies to previous
questions. The matter of flax grading is
still under discussion between the Ministry
of Supply, this Ministry and the Ulster
Farmers' Union. If and when any agreement to change the present system is
reached, an announcement will be made.
GRADING OF CATTLE.
6. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he will take steps to
have the grading of cattle in Northern
Ireland carried out by a panel of three as
in Great Britain, one of these three being
a referee, instead of by the present method
in existence in Northern Ireland of having
the grading done by one person without
any appeal by the producer from his decision; whether he can give the House details
of the respective systems, and can state
why Northern Irleand has not hitherto
kept step by step with Great Britain in
this matter.
Lord GLENTORAN: The hon. Member
is not correct in defining the duties of the
panel of three which carries out the purchase of fat cattle in Great Britain. There,
the cattle are graded by certifying authorities consisting of three persons, normally
a farmer, a butcher and an auctioneer.
The three members of the certifying
authority are equally responsible for the
grading, and in any case where a unanimous decision is not reached, the majority
view prevails. There is no appeal from the
decision of the panel. The Ministry of
Food's own live stock inspectors endeavour
to ensure that a uniform standard of grading is maintained in Great Britain at the
different collecting centres throughout the
country.
As the hon. Member knows, in Northern
Ireland purchasing is carried out by
veterinary officers on the permanent staff
of my Ministry. These men are specially
selected and they have had very considerable experience in the grading of cattle
as they have been grading cattle in Northern Ireland since the coming into operation, some seven years ago, of the live stock
subsidy scheme. In Northern Ireland
uniform grading on the part of the
various purchasing officers is secured by
the supervision of the Ministry's headquarters veterinary staff.
While in its main lines the meat and
live stock scheme is identical for the whole
of the United Kingdom, details of the
administration of the scheme vary in some
respects as between England, Scotland and
Northern Ireland owing to the fact that
all relevant conditions are not identical
in the three countries.
I may add that nowhere is the grading
of fatstock carried out with greater
accuracy and fairness than in Northern
Ireland, and, further, I would make it
clear that it is just as great a fault on the
part of the grading officer to give too little
for a beast as to give too much. His duty
is to give the exact price according to the
estimated killing out weight.
With regard to the last part of the hon.
Member's question, whilst the step-by-step
policy has been most beneficial from the
point of view of our social services, my
Ministry's policy is to lead the way and
not to follow in agricultural matters since
agriculture is our principal industry and
we are large exporters. The hon. Member
must know that our farmers do not desire
to go back to the old system under which
Reconstruction of Government 2562
Oral Answers
20 JANUARY 1942
they had to offer their fat cattle in the fairs
and take their chance as to the best prices
they could get.
Having regard to all these facts I am
not prepared to alter the present system.
Mr. BROWN: May I ask the noble
Lord if his Ministry has received from
the Ulster Farmers' Union or from a
number of branches of that union requests
for the same grading system as exists
across the Channel, and if so, can he tell
us what his attitude is towards those
requests?
Lord GLENTORAN: No; on the contrary, I have never had any unanimous
desire from the farmers to do away with
the present system. I have had many
complaints from farmers who thought
they did not get enough, but I have
never heard from any union, or at any
meeting, that they want to do away with.
the present system and go back to the
fairs, where they would have to take what
the dealers want to give them.
Mr. BROWN: Is it a fact that a
number of branches of the Ulster
Farmers' Union have in fact asked to have
the same system as exists across Channel
instead of the system that exists here?
Lord GLENTORAN: No. I find on
the contrary that the Farmers' Union and
the farmers I see are quite satisfied with
their own system in Ulster, and think it
is just as good a system as anywhere else.
and better than in England.
Mr. BROWN: May I ask the noble
Lord has he not seen in the Press reports
from numerous branches of the Farmers'
Union containing resolutions passed by
them calling for the same system as exists
across the Channel?
1941 GREEN FLAX CROP.
7. Mr. BROWN asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can now state
what increase in prices to meet the heavy
increases in production costs is to be given
to growers in respect of the 1941 crop of
green flax straw, and whether
increase
is to be made in prices for the 1942 crop?
any
Lord GLENTORAN: The hon. Member, no doubt, has seen the announcement
which I issued on Friday last, the 16th
instant, to the effect that to compensate
for increased costs of harvesting in 1941,
processors will pay an extra £2 per acre
to farmers from whom they purchased
unretted flax straw. This payment will
not be made by those processors who have
included in their contracts a war clause
providing for additional payments to the
farmer in the event of an increase in the
price of the fibre. This means that every
farmer who sold his crop as green straw
to a processor will be entitled to a payment of £2 per acre, except in cases where
the harvesting was undertaken by the
processor. Farmers who, having no contract, have green straw in stacks, and sell
such straw after the 16th of the present
month will not be entitled to the £2 per
acre.
Mr. BROWN: May I ask the noble
Lord does he not think it very unfair
that those who sell their straw after this
date in January should not receive the
increase, in view of the fact that it is
due to no fault of the producers that
they have not been able to sell their flax
up to the present?
PRIME MINISTER'S RECENT VISIT

The PRIME MINISTER: I feel it is

add anything at present to the official
statement I issued on my return from
London.
The Orders of the day were read and
postponed.
Reconstruction of the Government.

the policy of the Government has become ineffective, resulting in widespread dissatisfaction as to its efforts in
relation to the social, economic and industrial problems of Northern Ireland
and its supervision and prosecution of
the war effort, and in order to secure
that measure of agreement necessary
to the successful furtherance of the

How well Mr. Churchill succeeded the
results now demonstrate. They demonstrated something else I think this cannot be challenged-that events from the

because we had potential fifth columnists

time. I should like the House,
therefore, to compare with that the lack of

time to time. When you get up to talk

of the issues which come before the House
the reply which is invariably given when

from here to the other side to delay to as

In spite of the hostility and opposition

Then they say, "Behold, look at our

2565 Reconstruction of Government
Reconstruction of Government 2566
20 JANUARY 1942
Now, since the inception of the Government of this small State of Northern
Ireland it has been announced from time
to time that a step-by-step policy would
be followed. By the way, in using the
words "small State" I do not want anyone
to misunderstand me, because I do not use
them in any derogatory sense, but because
there is within a small State not only
ample opportunity to do something but
every reason why something should be
done because of its smallness. Some
people can only work in a small environment. If they have any creative genius
they ought to be able to exploit it in a
small community. For over twenty years
the only policy adumbrated in this House
and also outside this House is the alleged
step-by-step policy. If that policy were
pursued all the time consistently there
might be something to be said from a
Ministerial point of view, but there was
the confession of a Minister a few minutes
ago when he declared that he had departed from that policy and that it was
his intention to remain separated from it.
What is true of that Minister is also true
of other Ministers from time to time.
They have departed from the step-by-step
policy in the strict interpretation of
certain phases of social development, as I
mean to indicate here this afternoon.
At the moment it is true to say that
fundamentally, so far as this State is
concerned, there is no similarity between
the policy followed here and the policy
laid down by the Rt. Hon. Winston
Churchill. There may be a variety of
reasons in the Prime Minister's mind,
which he has not yet disclosed to the community but which he may disclose in this
debate, as to why he follows his present
policy and adheres to his determination
that there should be only monopolistic
powers in the administration of affairs in
Northern Ireland. But I would like to
say this, and I make no apology again for
saying it, that all those people in the community who are prepared in the day of
war to unite for the safeguarding and
wellbeing of the community in defence of
democratic institutions have a right to
participation in every phase of life so far
as the masses of the people are concerned.
Therefore. I challenge the Government
to face up to this issue, which was laid
down in the Imperia! Parliament in the
middle of 1940, and which was then
accepted as the philosophy to save the
nation, and which did result in the saving
of the nation, which united the Labour and
the trade union movements as nothing
could have united them. Nothing had
been done before, and nothing has been
done since, to unite them as they then
united, and I claim-and I think it is not
too big a claim to make that as a result
of that unity brought about by the policy
of the Rt. Hon. Winston Churchill,
Britain was saved. Britain could not
otherwise have been saved. Britain has
been saved in so far as it has been possible for her to be saved to the present
day, but we are not yet out of the wood,
and it is because I realise we have a long
way to go I want to see the best that is
yet to be being achieved by better effort
on our part, better determination, and
better co-ordination of the energies and
activities of every section of the
community.
In trying to think late last night of
what the policy, or lack of policy, of the
Government could be likened to-and I
do not claim any degree of originality in
what I am about to express-I thought
that having regard to the messages which
I have been able to get from Cabinet
quarters in London during the past twelve
months, messages which I know have come
to members of the Northern Government,
journeys which have been made by members of the Government, journeys which I
have made myself, sometimes having
ascribed to me journeys which I did not
carry out at all-as a matter of actual
fact, last week I was alleged to have been
in London with members of this Government when I was actually in Manchester
meeting my own Executive-but taking
into account all those journeys, and I
know that momentous issues have been
discussed on many of them, as was hinted
here by one Member this afternoon, I
have tried to puzzle out what fundamentally is the policy of the Government
here.
I can only liken it unto this, that
Northern Ireland in relation to the
Imperial powers at the present time is, in
a sense, like one vast telephone exchange
with the Prime Minister sitting at the
switchboard and the rest of the Cabinet
Ministers acting as communication plugs.
That is what it seems to me to be like at
the present time. Substantially there has
been no initiation of policy. For example,
in reply to a question this afternoon the

There is no agreement upon policy whatsoever. I think that all the facts bear out
the contention that substantially there has

have been content for the past 20 years to
shelter behind the pioneering and educational work carried out by the publicspirited people of Great Britain who want
to see a better order of society. They
have followed that pioneering work and
social legislation, and invariably, or in

Government ought to know that there is

Ireland with regard to this lack of policy.
The Prime Minister may, metaphorically
speaking, close his eyes and his ears,
although he would need to do it very
effectively in order to drown the reverberations which have resounded through
Northern Ireland in consequence of this
deplorable policy of the Government.
There is deep dissatisfaction on the part
of the people. They are particularly dissatisfied with the unemployment problem
which was referred to here this afternoon.
Sometimes when you take up a paper if
you were innocent enough you gather the
impression that abnormal development had
taken place as the result of some magnificent piece of work on the part of the
Government of Northern Ireland, that as
a result of a magnificent co-ordinated
effort they had reduced the unemployment
problem from a figure in the vicinity of
60,000 to approximately 27,000 or 28,000.
That is the number registered as unemployed at the present time. But when
you take into account that not less than
70 per cent. of those people have been sent
to industrial centres in Great Britain and
that at the present time we have 27,000 or
28,000 unemployed, and add those two
numbers together there is not a very distinct achievement to be placed to the
credit of the Northern Government from
the point of view of an improvement in
the unemployment problem.
In saying that, I am speaking as one
who served his apprenticeship in a trade
whose members were used to going across
the water. I know what it means to go
across the water to work. I know that
took place in the industry that I followed
when I did follow a useful industry, because like the majority of politicians in
this House I have long since ceased to
follow anything creative. In those days,
however, I was used to the principle of
going across the water with my colleagues.
We regarded it as part of the industrial

pays the highest possible tribute to the
integrity of the Civil Service, and, so far
as the Civil Service of Northern Ireland is
concerned, I entirely agree with him. We
certainly have a Civil Service of the highest
integrity. I do not make the slightest
suggestion against them in that respect.
Lord Perry states:
It may be assumed that many such
men will have spent all their lives
sequestered from the hurly-burly in
which less apparently fortunate citizens
have toiled and sweated.
The point he makes, and that I make here
to-day, is the growing tendency on the
part of Parliament to delegate its governing functions to the Civil Service. We
authorise bureaucracy to bring in certain
rules, regulations and orders, and we
never see them. We pass legislation
in this form time after time, and
we have not the faintest idea of what is
happening. It is often very difficult to
reconcile them with the original intention
of Parliament. All these matters should
come before the House for approval.
This is a matter in which something will
have to be done. Lord Perry says:-
Legislation is no longer content to
register the will of the Parliamentary
majority and leave the fulfilment of
that will to the supervision of the
Civil Service. It now registered the
readiness of Parliament to delegate its

When he met me he told me what his
inspectors found and the steps his inspectors took under his direction. When
I talk about that I talk about something
I know of. On no occasion did he let
anything go by default that it was possible for him to control.
The House will realise that an M.P.,
who has his eyes open, will see many
things in that respect that it is not in
the public interest to divulge at this
Table. For instance, if I see something
bordering on fraud, and if I divulged
that publicly then that is a warning to
those people who are not likely to be
caught. Instead of that I can communicate with the Financial Secretary
who takes action and has taken very
effective action. There is a general
improvement. I think it was about one.
of the biggest problems that any Government could be confronted with the
problem of putting these houses into
proper repair or at least sufficient repair
to enable the people to return to their
homes and live in them.
Now we come to the Ministry of
Labour. I have often criticised the
policy of the Ministry, but I have never
criticised its administration, and I could
not. The Minister is well served
by his staff. Any case brought
before him or his private secretary, who
is one of the best, is investigated, and if
the law allows him to do anything he
does it and will let you know about it.
He would sooner send a letter that you
had been successful than that he could do
nothing. It would be only right to say
that the Prime Minister was just as
courteous when he was Minister of
Labour. Any fair-minded man will have
to admit that. But the Minister is
responsible for the under policy and we
cannot congratulate him or his predecessor on the state of unemployment that has been going on for years and
years.
Mr. HENDERSON: Shame.
Mr. NIXON: It was not the fault of
the Minister, but was largely the fault

going on? Thousands of men who are
idle are signing on, looking for a day's
work.
Mr. HENDERSON: Shame.

metal in Northern Ireland was going to
Germany to be made into bombs to drop

and bone. We all know the sorry story

Mr. Allen was brought over

After Mr. Allen was duly inspected it

Arrival of American Troops.
PRIME MINISTER'S STATEMENT.
The PRIME MINISTER: With the
permission of the House, I desire to say a
few words. Twenty-four hours ago
the Union Jack and the Stars and
Stripes flew side by side at a Northern
Ireland port when a military contingent
from the United States of America landed
on our shores. An event so historic and
so significant is worthy of a permanent
record in the annals of this House.
Those who witnessed, as I did, the
arrival of the troops felt a thrill of emotion
when His Grace the Governor, representing His Majesty the King, greeted the
officer in command, and the Secretary of
State for Air spoke eloquent and stirring
words of welcome to the officers and men
at the quayside. It was my pleasure to
join in the greeting in the name of the
Government and people of Northern
Ireland, and representatives of the Navy,
Army and Air Force were there to extend
a welcome on behalf of the British fighting
services.
I deemed it fitting to express through the
Press the satisfaction we all feel at the
presence of the American troops in our
midst, and I take the earliest opportunity
in this House of assuring the General
Officer commanding the American Troops
in the United Kingdom, and all the officers
and men serving under him, that Northern
Ireland bids them a heartfelt welcome.
President Roosevelt, whose statesmanship, vision and courage have won the
admiration of us all, told the world a few
weeks ago that American forces would be
sent across the ocean to take their place in
the fighting line. He has kept that promise. The troops now in Northern Ireland are a splendid body of men-young,
alert, well disciplined and equipped.
Between the United States and Ulster
there are many bonds that can never be
broken-bonds created by kinship and
language, identity of outlook, and a common faith in democracy. Many men and
women of Ulster birth have gone to the
United States and are playing their part
in the life of that great Republic. I am
confident that the officers and men of the
American Army now in Northern Ireland
will soon feel at home among us and
experience the warm-hearted hospitality
that is so characteristic of our people.
All the resources of the British Empire
and the United States are now combined
to defeat the common enemy. I feel sure
that this House will join with me in saying
to our American allies, as we do to our
own forces and those of all nations ranged
against the Axis Powers-"God speed
your victory."
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like, on behalf
of all the working-class people in Northern
Ireland to join with the Prime Minister
in the statement he has just made. (Hon.
Member: Hear, hear.) The only thing I
do feel regretful about is that we all had
not the opportunity of meeting the boys
from over the Atlantic, but I hope that
the people of Ulster will give them that
homely comfort which is so well known of
the Ulster people, and try to make them
feel that they are still in their own land.
I think they will find in the working-class
people of Northern Ireland that homely
feeling and kindness, and that Irish hospitality for which Ulster people are well
noted. I feel that we cannot appreciate
too highly the great services that the
U.S.A. are going to render to the cause
of the Allies. They have already shown
it in materials, and now they are showing
it in man-power. I must say here, on
behalf of the working-class people, and I
may say the Ulster people as a whole, that
we give them a hearty greeting to our
shores, and we hope they will make themselves at home while here. We call on
the Ulster people to extend that homely
feeling to the troops now in our midst.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. MIDGLEY: I should like, with the
permission of the House, for a couple of
minutes to join in expressing my concurrence with the sentiments so well
expressed by the Prime Minister. I rejoice to know that representatives of the
fighting forces of the great democracy of the
United States are present on our soil, and
I hope I will be pardoned for taking this
opportunity of saying that I trust that the
great historic event that took place yesterday will mark the beginning of a new
Prorogation
Prorogation
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Midgley]
policy throughout the whole of Ireland
and not in Northern Ireland alone. I trust
before long there will be a recognition on
the part of those concerned in the destiny
of this country as to the community of
interests which ought to prevail amongst
all the democratic countries of the world,
and that very soon the people of Eire will
cease from following the policy they have.
followed before and recognise the necessity
of taking their rightful place in the
Commonwealth of Nations who are in the
vanguard in the common fight, not only
for the defence of democracy but for the
liberation of the subjugated peoples
throughout the world. I should like to
express my deep satisfaction that many
of the people, who must be kinsmen of
those who left this part of the country,
are now returning to the land of their
fathers. I trust that the magnificent
welcome expressed on behalf of the
Government, and which will be re-echoed
in the hearts and minds of the people of
Northern Ireland, will kindle a flame and
blaze of love and admiration for the traditions of our part of this land which will
enable those who return to the United
States to carry back the happiest memories
of the days they spent amongst our people.
PROROGATION.
A Message was delivered by the acting
Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod, as
follows:-
I am commanded by the Senate to
inform this honourable House that the
Proclamation of His Grace the Governor
of Northern Ireland proroguing this present Session of Parliament is to be
communicated in the Senate forthwith,
and, further, I am commanded to invite
this honourable House to attend in the
Senate in order to hear the said Proclamation read.
The House went, and, having returned,
Mr. SPEAKER (standing in the Clerk's
place at the Table): I have to report that
the House has this day attended in the
Senate, when the Proclamation proroguing
this present Session of Parliament was
read by the Speaker of the Senate as
follows:
BY HIS GRACE THE GOVERNOR OF
NORTHERN IRELAND.
A PROCLAMATION.
For Proroguing the present Parliament
of Northern Ireland.
WHEREAS it is provided by section
eleven of the Government of Ireland Act,
1920, as modified by and in pursuance of
certain enactments amending the said Act,
that the Governor of Northern Ireland
shall, in His Majesty's name, summon,
prorogue and dissolve the Parliament of
Northern Ireland:
AND WHEREAS it is desirable that
this present Parliament of Northern
Ireland should be prorogued to the
third day of February, one thousand
nine hundred and forty-two:
NOW I, JAMES ALBERT EDWARD,
DUKE OF ABERCORN, KNIGHT OF
THE MOST NOBLE ORDER OF THE
GARTER, KNIGHT OF THE MOST
ILLUSTRIOUS ORDER OF SAINT
PATRICK, Governor of Northern Ireland, by this Proclamation do publish
and declare His Majesty's Pleasure that
the said Parliament be, as from the
reading of this Proclamation in the
Parliament of Northern Ireland, prorogued to Tuesday, the third day of
February, one thousand nine hunderd and
forty-two.
And I do hereby further declare His
Majesty's Royal Will and Pleasure to be
that the said Parliament shall on the said
third day of February, one thousand nine
hundred and forty-two, assemble and be
holden at Stormont for the despatch of
divers urgent and important affairs, and
the Senators and Members of the House
of Commons of Northern Ireland are
hereby required to give their attendance
accordingly.
Given this twenty-seventh day of
January, one thousand nine hundred and
forty-two.
(Signed by his own hand),
ABERCORN.
GOD SAVE THE KING.
